q: A binary relation \(R\) on a set \(X\) is reflexive if:
explain: Reflexivity (Def. 1-1) requires \(xRx\) for every member of \(X\). The first option is completeness, the third is symmetry, and the last is far too weak (one self-related element is not enough).

q: A binary relation \(R\) on \(X\) is complete if:
options: for all \(x,y\in X\) with \(x\neq y\): exactly one of \(xRy\), \(yRx\) holds
explain: Def. 1-2: any two members can be compared, possibly both ways (indifference is allowed). 'Exactly one' would forbid ties, 'and' would force everything indifferent, and the last option is transitivity.

q: Which of the following correctly states antisymmetry of a binary relation \(R\) on \(X\)?
options: For all \(x\neq y\): if \(xRy\) then not \(yRx\)
explain: Def. 1-5: two different elements never relate both ways. The first option (without \(x\neq y\)) is asymmetry, which also forbids \(xRx\); so e.g. \(\geq\) is antisymmetric but not asymmetric. The third option is symmetry.

q: To show that a relation \(R\) is not transitive you must exhibit:
explain: Transitivity says \(xRy\wedge yRz\Rightarrow xRz\); its negation is one triple where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. A cycle \(xRy,yRz,zRx\) is not by itself a violation (indifference among three items is a cycle and is transitive). The third option breaks completeness.

q: True or false: every complete binary relation is reflexive.
explain: True. Completeness holds for all \(x,y\), including \(y=x\): then '\(xRx\) or \(xRx\)' must hold, i.e. \(xRx\). This is why Def. 1-4 of a preference relation does not list reflexivity separately.

q: True or false: every reflexive binary relation is complete.
explain: False. Equality on \(\R\) is reflexive (\(x=x\)) but not complete: neither \(1=2\) nor \(2=1\). Reflexivity only concerns pairs \((x,x)\) and says nothing about distinct elements.

q: True or false (PS1 a(i)): there is no binary relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric.
explain: False. Equality \(xRy\iff x=y\) is symmetric, and antisymmetric because the hypothesis '\(x\neq y\) and \(xRy\)' never occurs (vacuously true). Any relation that relates elements only to themselves (including the empty relation) is both.

q: On \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) let \(R=\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\}\) (PS1 a(ii)). Which statement is correct?
explain: Not symmetric: \((1,3)\in R\) but \((3,1)\notin R\). Not antisymmetric: \((1,2),(2,1)\in R\) with \(1\neq2\). The recipe: one one-way pair kills symmetry, one two-way pair between distinct elements kills antisymmetry.

q: PS1 a(iii). 'Proof' that symmetric + transitive implies reflexive: fix \(x\), take \(y\) with \(xRy\); then \(yRx\) by symmetry, so \(xRx\) by transitivity. Why is this proof spurious?
options: Symmetry cannot be applied to the pair \((x,y)\)
Transitivity requires three distinct elements, but here \(z=x\)
It assumes that some \(y\) with \(xRy\) exists, which need not be true
It only proves \(xRx\) for one \(x\), not for all \(x\)
explain: The step 'take \(y\) with \(xRy\)' presumes existence. The empty relation on a nonempty \(X\) is symmetric and transitive (vacuously) yet not reflexive. Transitivity has no distinctness requirement, and \(x\) was arbitrary, so the other options are not the flaw.

q: True or false: if \(R\) on \(X\) is symmetric and transitive, and for every \(x\in X\) there is some \(y\in X\) with \(xRy\), then \(R\) is reflexive.
explain: True. Under the extra hypothesis the 'easy proof' becomes valid: from \(xRy\) symmetry gives \(yRx\), and transitivity applied to \(xRy,yRx\) gives \(xRx\). The PS1 a(iii) proof only fails because such a \(y\) may not exist.

q: Let \(R=\emptyset\) (the empty relation) on a nonempty set \(X\). Which properties does \(R\) have?
options: Symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive, but neither reflexive nor complete
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive (an equivalence relation)
explain: Symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity are 'if ... then' statements whose hypothesis (\(xRy\)) never holds, so they are vacuously true. Reflexivity and completeness demand that some pairs be in \(R\), so they fail on a nonempty \(X\).

q: Which properties does the relation \(<\) ('strictly smaller than') on \(\R\) have?
options: Transitive and antisymmetric only (not reflexive, not complete, not symmetric)
explain: \(1<1\) fails, so \(<\) is not reflexive, and hence not complete (completeness implies reflexivity; the pair (1,1) fails). It is transitive, and antisymmetric since \(x<y\) and \(y<x\) never both hold. It is clearly not symmetric.

q: Which properties does \(\geq\) on \(\R\) have?
options: Reflexive, complete, transitive, antisymmetric; not symmetric
Complete and transitive only; not antisymmetric
explain: Any two reals are comparable, \(x\geq x\), and \(\geq\) chains. If \(x\geq y\) and \(y\geq x\) then \(x=y\), so it is antisymmetric. It is not symmetric (\(2\geq1\) but not \(1\geq2\)), so it is a preference relation but not an equivalence relation.

q: Consider 'is a sibling of' on a set of people (nobody is their own sibling). Why is it not transitive?
options: Because two people may have no siblings at all
Ann sib Bob and Bob sib Ann, but Ann is not her own sibling (take \(z=x\))
explain: Transitivity must hold for all \(x,y,z\), including \(z=x\). With \(x=z=\) Ann, \(y=\) Bob: \(xRy\) and \(yRz\) hold, but \(xRz\) (Ann sibling of Ann) fails. The relation is symmetric, and people with no siblings do not violate transitivity.

q: Consider 'is the parent of' on the set of all people. Which statement is correct?
options: It is symmetric but not transitive
It is antisymmetric but not transitive
explain: If \(x\) is parent of \(y\), \(y\) cannot be parent of \(x\), so it is antisymmetric. It is not transitive: a parent of a parent is a grandparent, not a parent. It is not complete (two strangers are unrelated) and not symmetric.

q: On \(\R\) define \(xRy \iff |x-y|\leq 1\). Which statement is correct?
options: \(R\) is reflexive and symmetric but neither complete nor transitive
\(R\) is complete and symmetric but not reflexive
explain: \(|x-x|=0\leq1\) and \(|x-y|=|y-x|\), so reflexive and symmetric. Not complete: \(0\) and \(5\) are unrelated either way. Not transitive: \(0R1\), \(1R2\) but not \(0R2\). So it is neither an equivalence nor a preference relation.

q: Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(R=\{(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(a,b),(b,c)\}\). Which statement is correct?
explain: Not complete: neither \((a,c)\) nor \((c,a)\) is in \(R\). Not transitive: \((a,b),(b,c)\in R\) but \((a,c)\notin R\). Adding \((a,c)\) would fix both problems at once and give the ranking \(a\succ b\succ c\).

q: Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(\pr=\{(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(a,b),(b,a),(a,c),(b,c)\}\). Which utility function represents \(\pr\)?
explain: The relation is complete and transitive, with \(a\sim b\) (both pairs present) and \(a\succ c\), \(b\succ c\). A representation needs \(u(a)=u(b)>u(c)\); the values 5, 5, -1 work. The first option wrongly makes \(a\succ b\), the third makes everything indifferent, and the last reverses the order.

q: Is the relation \(a\pr b,\ b\pr c,\ c\pr a\) with none of the reverse comparisons (i.e. \(a\succ b\succ c\succ a\)) on \(X=\{a,b,c\}\), together with \(x\pr x\) for all \(x\), a preference relation?
options: Yes, it is complete and transitive
No: it is transitive but not complete
No: it is complete but not transitive
explain: Every pair is ranked one way, so it is complete. Transitivity would give \(a\pr c\) from \(a\pr b\), \(b\pr c\), but only \(c\pr a\) holds. A strict cycle can never be a preference relation; it also cannot be represented by any utility since that would need \(u(a)>u(b)>u(c)>u(a)\).

q: On \(\R\) define \(x\pr y\iff x\geq y-1\) ('\(x\) is at least as good as \(y\) unless it is more than 1 unit worse'). Is \(\pr\) a preference relation?
options: Yes, it is complete and transitive
No, it is complete but not transitive
explain: Complete: if \(x<y-1\) then \(y>x+1\geq x-1\), so \(y\pr x\). Not transitive: \(0\pr0.8\) (\(0\geq-0.2\)) and \(0.8\pr1.6\) (\(0.8\geq0.6\)), but not \(0\pr1.6\) (\(0\geq0.6\) is false). Small differences pile up: indifference that is 'just noticeable' is intransitive.

q: In the course (Def. 1-4), a preference relation on \(X\) is a binary relation that is:
explain: A preference relation is complete and transitive; reflexivity follows from completeness. Antisymmetry is not required because it would rule out indifference between distinct alternatives. Reflexive+symmetric+transitive is an equivalence relation.

q: Given a preference relation \(\pr\), the strict preference \(x\succ y\) is defined as:
explain: 'I prefer x to y' means \(x\) is at least as good and \(y\) is not at least as good. '\(x\pr y\) and \(x\neq y\)' wrongly makes distinct indifferent items strictly ranked. 'Not \(y\pr x\)' is equivalent only because \(\pr\) is complete; the definition itself is the last option.

q: Given a preference relation \(\pr\), indifference \(x\sim y\) is defined as:
explain: Indifference means each is at least as good as the other. 'Neither' is impossible under completeness. Indifference does not require \(x=y\); distinct alternatives can be equally desirable. The last option is just completeness and is always true.

q: The model of preferences \(\pr\) is designed to capture which kind of statement?
explain: The slides stress that the model records only the individual's ranking of alternatives, not the intensity of feelings. Statements about 'much better', 'slightly' or 'love/hate' carry intensity information that \(\pr\) cannot encode.

q: In economics (Topic 1), a decision maker's choices are called rational when:
options: they maximise the hedonic pleasure of the decision maker
they agree with what a reasonable outside observer would choose
they are best according to the decision maker's own preferences, whatever those preferences are
explain: Rationality is consistency: choosing what is best according to one's own (complete, transitive) preferences. What those preferences are is left to the decision maker; 'economics is not judgmental'. Money maximisation and hedonic pleasure are particular, not required, preferences.

q: Let \(\pr\) be a preference relation. Which property is needed to prove that \(x\succ y\) and \(y\pr z\) imply \(x\succ z\)?
explain: First, \(x\pr y\pr z\) gives \(x\pr z\) by transitivity. Second, if \(z\pr x\) held, then \(y\pr z\pr x\) would give \(y\pr x\) by transitivity, contradicting \(x\succ y\). So not \(z\pr x\) and \(x\succ z\). Antisymmetry is not assumed for preferences.

q: In proving '\(x\succ y\) and \(y\pr z\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(x\succ z\)', after getting \(x\pr z\) one argues by contradiction: suppose \(z\pr x\). Which conclusion yields the contradiction?
explain: From \(y\pr z\) and the supposed \(z\pr x\), transitivity gives \(y\pr x\), which contradicts '\(x\succ y\)' (that includes 'not \(y\pr x\)'). \(z\pr y\) together with \(y\pr z\) is no contradiction (it would be indifference), and preferences need not be antisymmetric.

q: True or false: if \(\pr\) is a preference relation, \(x\sim y\) and \(y\succ z\), then \(x\succ z\).
explain: True. \(x\pr y\pr z\) gives \(x\pr z\). If \(z\pr x\), then with \(x\pr y\) transitivity gives \(z\pr y\), contradicting \(y\succ z\). This is one of the standard consequences of transitivity.

q: For a preference relation \(\pr\) and the derived \(\succ\), which statement is true?
options: \(\succ\) may fail to be transitive even though \(\pr\) is
\(\succ\) is transitive and never holds in both directions (asymmetric)
explain: \(x\succ y\) and \(y\succ x\) would require both 'not \(y\pr x\)' and \(y\pr x\), impossible: asymmetry. Transitivity of \(\succ\) follows from the result \(x\succ y,\ y\pr z\Rightarrow x\succ z\). \(\succ\) is irreflexive, not reflexive.

q: For a preference relation \(\pr\), indifference \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation. Which properties of \(\pr\) deliver, respectively, reflexivity and transitivity of \(\sim\)?
options: Reflexivity from completeness (\(x\pr x\)); transitivity from transitivity of \(\pr\) applied in both directions
Reflexivity from transitivity; transitivity from completeness
Reflexivity is assumed separately; transitivity from antisymmetry
explain: Completeness with \(y=x\) gives \(x\pr x\), hence \(x\sim x\). Symmetry of \(\sim\) is built into its definition. If \(x\sim y\sim z\), then \(x\pr y\pr z\) and \(z\pr y\pr x\), so transitivity of \(\pr\) gives \(x\pr z\) and \(z\pr x\), i.e. \(x\sim z\).

q: An equivalence relation is a binary relation that is:
explain: Def. 1-6: reflexive, symmetric, transitive. Symmetric+transitive alone is not enough (the empty relation, PS1 a(iii)). Reflexive+antisymmetric+transitive is a partial order such as \(\geq\); complete+transitive is a preference relation.

q: An equivalence relation \(R\) on \(X\) partitions \(X\) into equivalence classes. For the indifference relation \(\sim\), these classes are:
options: sets that may overlap, each containing a best element
the upper contour sets \(\{y: y\pr x\}\)
disjoint indifference sets: \(x,y\) are in the same set iff \(x\sim y\)
explain: Equivalence classes are disjoint and cover \(X\); two alternatives share a class iff they are related. For \(\sim\) these are the indifference sets (later, indifference curves). They are singletons only if there is no indifference between distinct items; upper contour sets overlap.

q: True or false: if \(\pr\) is a preference relation on \(X\) that is also antisymmetric, then \(x\sim y\) implies \(x=y\).
explain: True. If \(x\sim y\) with \(x\neq y\), then \(x\pr y\) and \(y\pr x\) for distinct elements, which antisymmetry forbids. So antisymmetric preferences are exactly the 'strict' ones with no ties between different alternatives, and every indifference set is a singleton.

q: On \(\R^2_+\) let \((x_1,x_2)\pr(y_1,y_2)\iff x_1+x_2\geq y_1+y_2\). Which statement is correct?
options: \(\pr\) is a preference relation and its indifference sets are the lines \(x_1+x_2=c\)
\(\pr\) is not complete because \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) cannot be compared
explain: \(\pr\) is induced by \(u(x)=x_1+x_2\), so it is complete and transitive. \((1,0)\sim(0,1)\) (both sums equal 1), so they are comparable (indifferent), and since they are distinct \(\pr\) is not antisymmetric. Indifference sets are the downward-sloping lines of constant sum.

q: A function \(u:X\to\R\) represents the preference relation \(\pr\) if:
options: \(u(x)-u(y)\) measures how much \(x\) is preferred to \(y\)
explain: Def. 1-7 requires the equivalence in both directions. The one-way conditions are too weak: e.g. a constant \(u\) satisfies the first for any \(\pr\). Utility differences carry no meaning (ordinal utility).

q: True or false: if \(u:X\to\R\) satisfies '\(x\succ y\Rightarrow u(x)>u(y)\)' for all \(x,y\), then \(u\) represents \(\pr\).
explain: False. Indifferent items may receive different values. Example: \(X=\{a,b\}\), \(a\sim b\), \(u(a)=1\), \(u(b)=0\): the condition holds vacuously (no strict pairs), yet \(u(a)\geq u(b)\) while \(b\pr a\) requires \(u(b)\geq u(a)\), which fails. Representation needs the full 'iff'.

q: True or false: for any function \(u:X\to\R\), the relation defined by \(x\pr y\iff u(x)\geq u(y)\) is a preference relation.
explain: True. It inherits completeness and transitivity from \(\geq\) on \(\R\): \(u(x)\geq u(y)\) or \(u(y)\geq u(x)\) always, and \(\geq\) chains. Consequently, a relation that is not complete or not transitive can never be represented by a utility function.

q: If \(u\) represents \(\pr\), which of the following holds for all \(x,y\)?
explain: From \(x\pr y\iff u(x)\geq u(y)\): \(x\succ y\) means \(u(x)\geq u(y)\) and not \(u(y)\geq u(x)\), i.e. \(u(x)>u(y)\); \(x\sim y\) means both inequalities, i.e. equality. The other options mix weak and strict or give meaning to magnitudes.

q: Marco's preferences over \(X=\{\text{Old Fashioned},\text{Margarita},\text{Mojito}\}\) are Old Fashioned \(\succ\) Margarita \(\succ\) Mojito. Which function does NOT represent them? (values listed in that order)
explain: Any strictly decreasing assignment along the ranking works, whatever the magnitudes or signs: (3,2,1), (100,0,-7) and (1,1/2,1/3) all do. (3,2,2) gives Margarita and Mojito the same value, which would mean indifference, contradicting Margarita \(\succ\) Mojito.

q: With \(|X|=100\) alternatives, how many unordered pairs of distinct alternatives must be compared to write down a preference relation as a list?
explain: \(\binom{100}{2}=\frac{100\cdot99}{2}=4950\). (9900 counts ordered pairs of distinct elements, 10000 all ordered pairs.) The point of the slide: a utility function compresses this long list into 100 numbers.

q: Cinema (slide 20): seats \((r,c)\), rows \(r=1,\dots,10\) (row 1 at the screen), columns \(c=1,\dots,10\) (exit on the left). Priority 1: sit as far back as possible; priority 2 (same row): as far left as possible. Which function represents this lexicographic preference?
explain: \(11-c\in\{1,\dots,10\}\) rewards left seats within a row, and the weight 10 on \(r\) makes the worst seat of row \(r+1\) (\(10r+11\)) beat the best seat of row \(r\) (\(10r+10\)). \(r+(11-c)\) lets column override row (e.g. (1,1) gives 11 > (2,10) gives 3); \(10r+c\) prefers right seats; the third swaps the priorities.

q: Cinema example with \(u(r,c)=10r+(11-c)\). What is the utility of seat (row 3, column 4), and which seat is the best?
explain: \(u(3,4)=30+11-4=37\). The best seat is in the last row (furthest back) and the leftmost column: \(u(10,1)=100+10=110\), the maximum value. (1,1) is at the screen, which the individual likes least as a first priority.

q: Cinema example again (rows and columns \(1,\dots,10\); back rows better, then left columns better). For which real numbers \(k\) does \(u(r,c)=kr-c\) represent the preference?
explain: Within a row, \(-c\) correctly favours the left. Across rows we need the worst seat of row \(r+1\) to beat the best of row \(r\): \(k(r+1)-10>kr-1\iff k>9\). At \(k=9\) seats \((r+1,10)\) and \((r,1)\) tie, wrongly creating indifference. Non-integer \(k\) like 9.5 also works, so '\(k\geq10\) only' is wrong.

q: Given a preference relation \(\pr\) on \(X\), \(x\in X\) is maximal with respect to \(\pr\) in \(X\) if:
options: there is no \(y\neq x\) with \(y\sim x\)
explain: Def. 1-8: \(x\) is at least as good as every member of \(X\). '\(x\succ y\) for all \(y\)' is impossible (take \(y=x\)) and would exclude ties at the top. '\(y\pr x\) for all \(y\)' is the definition of minimal.

q: Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(a\sim b\) and \(a\succ c\) (and \(\pr\) a preference relation). The set of maximal elements is:
options: \(\emptyset\), since no element is strictly better than all others
explain: \(a\pr a,b,c\) and \(b\pr a,b,c\) (since \(b\sim a\succ c\) gives \(b\succ c\)). Maximality requires only weak preference, so ties at the top give several maximal elements. \(c\) is not maximal because not \(c\pr a\).

q: Lemma 1-1 states that a preference relation on \(X\) has at least one maximal and one minimal element. Which hypothesis on \(X\) does it require?
options: No hypothesis: every preference relation has a maximal element
explain: The lemma needs \(X\) nonempty (an empty set has no members) and finite (the induction on \(|X|\)). On infinite sets it fails: \(\{1,2,3,\dots\}\) with \(\geq\) has no maximal element, even though the set is countable and closed in \(\R\).

q: Lemma 1-1 (maximal element) is proved by induction on \(|X|=n\). In the inductive step one removes \(y\), finds a maximal \(x\) of \(X\setminus\{y\}\), and argues: 'If \(x\pr y\), \(x\) is maximal in \(X\). If not, then \(y\succ x\).' Which property justifies 'if not \(x\pr y\), then \(y\succ x\)'?
explain: By completeness, if not \(x\pr y\) then \(y\pr x\); together with 'not \(x\pr y\)' this is exactly \(y\succ x\). Transitivity is used in the next step, to pass from \(y\succ x\) and \(x\pr z\) to \(y\pr z\).

q: In the inductive step of Lemma 1-1, suppose \(y\succ x\) where \(x\) is maximal in \(X\setminus\{y\}\). How does one conclude that \(y\) is maximal in \(X\)?
options: For every \(z\in X\setminus\{y\}\), \(y\succ x\) and \(x\pr z\) give \(y\pr z\) by transitivity; and \(y\pr y\)
By the induction hypothesis applied to \(X\)
Because \(y\) was chosen arbitrarily, it can be taken to be the best
explain: Maximality of \(x\) in \(X\setminus\{y\}\) gives \(x\pr z\) for all such \(z\); chaining with \(y\pr x\) via transitivity yields \(y\pr z\). Completeness alone only gives \(y\pr z\) or \(z\pr y\). The induction hypothesis applies to sets of size \(n-1\), not to \(X\).

q: Which of the following is a preference relation on an infinite set with no maximal element?
explain: There is no largest natural number, so nobody is at least as good as everything. On \([0,1]\) with \(\geq\), 1 is maximal; with \(\leq\) on the naturals, 1 is maximal; the lexicographic order on \([0,1]^2\) has maximal element \((1,1)\).

q: True or false: every preference relation on \(X=[0,1]\) has a maximal element.
explain: False. Compactness of \([0,1]\) is irrelevant without continuity. Example: rank \(x\in[0,1)\) by \(\geq\) and put \(1\) at the bottom (\(x\succ1\) for all \(x<1\)). This is complete and transitive (it is represented by \(u(x)=x\) for \(x<1\), \(u(1)=-1\)), but for every \(x<1\) some \(x'\in(x,1)\) is better, so nothing is maximal.

q: Proposition 1-1 states:
options: Every binary relation on a finite set can be represented by a utility function
Every preference relation on a finite set can be represented by a utility function
Every preference relation on a countable set can be represented by an integer-valued utility function
Every preference relation can be represented by a utility function
explain: Finite \(X\) plus completeness and transitivity is sufficient. Arbitrary binary relations cannot be represented (representability forces completeness and transitivity). PS1 (b) shows integer-valued representation can fail on a countable set, and Prop. 1-2 shows representation can fail on \([0,1]^2\).

q: In the proof of Prop. 1-1, \(Y_0=X\), \(M_1\) = minimal elements of \(Y_0\), \(Y_k=Y_{k-1}\setminus M_k\), \(M_{k+1}\) = minimal elements of \(Y_k\), and \(u(x)=k\) for \(x\in M_k\). Why is each \(M_k\) (while \(Y_{k-1}\neq\emptyset\)) nonempty, and why does the process stop?
options: Nonempty by Lemma 1-1 applied to the finite set \(Y_{k-1}\); it stops because \(X\) is finite and each step removes at least one element
Nonempty by completeness; it stops after exactly \(|X|\) steps
Nonempty by transitivity; it stops because utilities are bounded
Nonempty by definition; it stops after two steps
explain: Each \(Y_{k-1}\) is a nonempty finite set, so Lemma 1-1 gives a minimal element. Removing a nonempty \(M_k\) each round strictly shrinks the finite set, so after some \(K\leq|X|\) rounds it is empty. It takes exactly \(|X|\) rounds only when there are no ties.

q: Apply the 'peeling' construction of Prop. 1-1 to \(X=\{a,b,c,d\}\) with \(d\succ a\sim b\succ c\). What utility does it assign?
explain: \(M_1\) = minimal elements of \(X\) = \(\{c\}\) gets 1; removing it, \(M_2=\{a,b\}\) (indifferent, peeled together) gets 2; finally \(M_3=\{d\}\) gets 3. The first option breaks the tie \(a\sim b\); the second reverses the order (it peels maximal elements); the last makes \(d\sim a\).

q: True or false: in the peeling construction of Prop. 1-1, the largest utility value \(K\) equals the number of indifference sets of \(\pr\) in \(X\).
explain: True. Each round removes exactly the minimal elements of what remains, which form one indifference set (all minimal elements of a set are mutually indifferent). So the rounds correspond one-to-one to indifference classes, from worst to best, and the values used are \(1,\dots,K\).

q: Prop. 1-1 proof, Case 1: \(u(a)=u(b)=k\). Why does \(a\sim b\) follow?
options: Both are minimal in \(Y_{k-1}\), so \(b\pr a\) (as \(a\) is minimal and \(b\in Y_{k-1}\)) and \(a\pr b\) (as \(b\) is minimal and \(a\in Y_{k-1}\))
Because equal numbers always mean equal alternatives
By completeness, which gives \(a\pr b\) and \(b\pr a\)
explain: \(u(a)=u(b)=k\) means both lie in \(M_k\), the set of minimal elements of \(Y_{k-1}\). Minimality of \(a\) means \(y\pr a\) for all \(y\in Y_{k-1}\), in particular \(b\pr a\); symmetrically \(a\pr b\). Completeness gives only one of the two directions.

q: Prop. 1-1 proof, Case 2: \(u(a)>u(b)\). Then \(b\) is minimal in \(Y_{u(b)-1}\), so \(a\pr b\); and \(a\in Y_{u(b)-1}\) is not minimal there. Why does 'not \(b\pr a\)' follow?
options: If \(b\pr a\), then for every \(y\in Y_{u(b)-1}\), \(y\pr b\pr a\) gives \(y\pr a\) by transitivity, so \(a\) would be minimal there, a contradiction
Because \(u(a)>u(b)\) means \(a\neq b\), and preferences are antisymmetric
explain: \(b\) minimal means \(y\pr b\) for all \(y\) in that set; adding \(b\pr a\) and using transitivity would make \(a\) minimal too, so \(a\) would have been peeled at the same stage, contradicting \(u(a)>u(b)\). Completeness does not exclude both directions, preferences need not be antisymmetric, and \(a\) is removed later, not earlier.

q: PS1 (b): on the positive integers, \(x\succ y\) if (i) \(x\) odd and \(y\) even, (ii) both even and \(x<y\), or (iii) both odd and \(x>y\). Which statement is correct?
explain: Draw the ranking first: \(\cdots\succ7\succ5\succ3\succ1\succ2\succ4\succ6\succ\cdots\). Every odd beats every even, so \(1\succ2\); among odds bigger is better, so \(3\succ1\); among evens smaller is better, so \(2\succ4\). 1 is the worst odd, not the best.

q: PS1 (b) preference (odd \(\succ\) even; among evens smaller is better; among odds larger is better). Which statement about maximal/minimal elements is correct?
options: There is a maximal element (1) and a minimal element (2)
There is a minimal element (1) but no maximal element
There is a maximal element (2) but no minimal element
There is neither a maximal nor a minimal element
explain: The odds increase without bound at the top (no best odd), and the evens decrease without bound at the bottom (no worst even). The pair \(1\succ2\) sits in the middle of the ranking: 1 is the worst odd and 2 the best even, neither is extremal overall.

q: PS1 b(i): why can no utility function with nonnegative integer values represent the PS1 (b) preference?
options: Because \(u(1)>u(3)>u(5)>\cdots\) would be an infinite decreasing sequence
Because it would require \(u(2)>u(4)>u(6)>\cdots\geq0\), an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers, which is impossible
Because the preference is not transitive
Because the positive integers are uncountable
explain: Among evens, smaller is better, so \(u(2)>u(4)>\cdots\), each step down by at least 1; starting from the integer \(u(2)\), at most \(u(2)+1\) terms can stay \(\geq0\). Among odds the values increase (\(u(3)>u(1)\)), the preference is transitive, and the integers are countable.

q: PS1 b(ii): which real-valued function represents the PS1 (b) preference (odd \(\succ\) even; evens: smaller better; odds: larger better)?
explain: Odds get positive values increasing in \(x\), evens get negative values decreasing in \(x\), and every positive value exceeds every negative one. \(u=x\) ranks 2 above 1; the third option reverses everything; with \(x/2\) on evens, larger evens get higher values (wrong) and \(u(4)=2>1=u(1)\), so an even beats an odd.

q: PS1 b(ii), nonnegative version. Which function represents the PS1 (b) preference and takes only nonnegative values?
explain: For odds, \(1+\frac{x}{x+1}\in[1.5,2)\) increases in \(x\); for evens, \(\frac1{x+1}\in(0,1/3]\) decreases in \(x\); every odd value exceeds every even value. Option 2 orders the evens the wrong way (\(\frac{x}{x+1}\) increases in \(x\)) and gives \(u(2)=\frac23>\frac12=u(1)\); option 3 makes smaller odds better; option 4 makes larger evens better and ranks 2 above 1.

q: True or false: PS1 (b) shows that a preference relation on a countable set may have no real-valued utility representation.
explain: False. PS1 (b) rules out only nonnegative-integer-valued utilities; part (ii) builds a real-valued one. In fact every preference relation on a countable set has a real-valued representation. The real line has room to squeeze infinitely many values into a bounded interval; the nonnegative integers do not.

q: Lexicographic preference on \([0,1]^2\): first priority is a larger first coordinate, then a larger second coordinate. Which ranking is correct?
explain: The first coordinate decides unless tied: \(0.3>0.2\) so \((0.3,0.1)\) is best regardless of its small second coordinate. Between \((0.2,0.9)\) and \((0.2,0.3)\) the first coordinates tie, and \(0.9>0.3\) decides. Lexicographic preferences never trade the coordinates off.

q: Proposition 1-2 says the lexicographic preference on \(X=[0,1]^2\) is not represented by any utility function. Which basic property does this preference nevertheless satisfy?
options: It is a preference relation (complete and transitive), and it is even antisymmetric
It is complete and transitive but every indifference set is a line segment
explain: Any two points are ranked (compare first coordinates, then second), and the ranking chains, so it is a genuine preference relation; the failure of representation is not due to irrationality. Two distinct points are never indifferent, so it is antisymmetric and indifference sets are singletons.

q: Proof that the lexicographic preference on \([0,1]^2\) (or \(\R^2_+\)) has no utility \(u\). For each \(a\), the interval \(I_a=(u(a,0),u(a,1))\) is considered. What are the two key facts?
options: Each \(I_a\) is nonempty since \((a,1)\succ(a,0)\); and \(I_a\cap I_b=\emptyset\) for \(a\neq b\) since \(a>b\) implies \((a,0)\succ(b,1)\)
Each \(I_a\) is closed and bounded; and the \(I_a\) are nested
Each \(I_a\) has length 1; and their total length is infinite
explain: Nonemptiness: \(u(a,1)>u(a,0)\). Disjointness: if \(a>b\), every point with first coordinate \(a\) beats every point with first coordinate \(b\), in particular \(u(a,0)>u(b,1)\). Continuity of \(u\) is not assumed (the proof rules out any utility), and lengths are irrelevant.

q: Continuing the lexicographic proof: enumerate the rationals \(q_1,q_2,\dots\) and let \(f(a)\) be the first rational in \(I_a=(u(a,0),u(a,1))\). Where is the contradiction?
options: \(f\) is not well defined because some \(I_a\) contain no rational
\(f\) is a one-to-one map from the uncountable set \([0,1]\) into the countable set \(\mathbb{Q}\), which is impossible
explain: Every nonempty open interval contains a rational, so \(f\) is well defined. Since the intervals are disjoint, distinct \(a\neq b\) get distinct rationals: \(f\) is injective. An injection from an uncountable set into a countable one cannot exist. Intuition: the real line has no room for uncountably many disjoint gaps.

q: For which set \(X\) does the lexicographic preference (first coordinate first, then second, larger is better) admit a utility representation?
explain: With a finite first coordinate, \(u(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+x_2\) works: a unit step in \(x_1\) adds 2, more than the whole range 1 of \(x_2\). For \([0,1]\times\{0,1\}\) the proof still applies: uncountably many \(a\), each with nonempty disjoint \((u(a,0),u(a,1))\). The square and \(\R^2_+\) are Prop. 1-2 and the PS1 extra question.

q: True or false: the proof that lexicographic preferences on \([0,1]^2\) have no utility representation assumes that the utility function would be continuous.
explain: False. The argument uses only the representation property (\(u(a,1)>u(a,0)\) and \(u(a,0)>u(b,1)\) for \(a>b\)) and countability of \(\mathbb{Q}\). It therefore rules out every real-valued utility, continuous or not.

q: Proposition 1-3: if \(u\) represents \(\pr\) and \(f:\R\to\R\) is (strictly) increasing, then \(w=f\circ u\) represents \(\pr\). Which step of the one-line proof uses that \(f\) is strictly increasing?
explain: For strictly increasing \(f\), \(f(s)\geq f(t)\iff s\geq t\) in both directions. The first equivalence is the definition of \(w\), the third is the hypothesis that \(u\) represents \(\pr\). A weakly increasing (e.g. constant) \(f\) breaks the '\(\Leftarrow\)' direction of strict comparisons, creating spurious indifference.

q: Suppose \(u\) represents \(\pr\) and \(u\) can take negative values. Which function does NOT necessarily represent \(\pr\)?
explain: \(t\mapsto t^3\), \(t\mapsto2t+5\) and \(t\mapsto e^t\) are strictly increasing on \(\R\). \(t\mapsto t^2\) is not increasing on negative numbers: if \(u(x)=-1<0=u(y)\) then \(u(x)^2=1>0=u(y)^2\), reversing the ranking. Also invalid: \(-u\) and \(1/u\).

q: Cobb-Douglas \(u(x,y)=x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha}\) with \(0<\alpha<1\), \(\alpha\neq\tfrac12\). Which function does NOT represent the same preference on \(\R^2_{++}\)?
explain: \(\ln u\), \(u(x/2,y/2)=u/2\) and \(u^3\) are strictly increasing transformations of \(u\). Swapping exponents changes the preference: e.g. with \(\alpha=1/3\), \(u(1,8)=4>u(8,1)=2\), but \(x^{2/3}y^{1/3}\) gives \(2\) vs \(4\), reversing the ranking.

q: True or false: if \(u\) and \(w\) both represent the same preference relation \(\pr\) on \(X\), then there is a strictly increasing function \(f\) on \(u(X)\) with \(w=f\circ u\).
explain: True. Define \(f(u(x))=w(x)\); it is well defined because \(u(x)=u(y)\Rightarrow x\sim y\Rightarrow w(x)=w(y)\), and strictly increasing because \(u(x)>u(y)\Rightarrow x\succ y\Rightarrow w(x)>w(y)\). So utility is unique exactly up to strictly increasing transformations: it is ordinal.

\((3/2)^3-1^3=\frac{27}{8}-1=\frac{19}{8}\), while \(f(u(x))-f(u(y))=1-0=1\). So the comparison of differences flips (\(1<19/8\)) under a strictly increasing transformation: utility differences carry no meaning.

q: True or false: if \(u(\text{mapo tofu})=5\) and \(u(\text{hotpot})=2\) represent someone's preferences, we can conclude that one mapo tofu is better for her than two hotpots.
explain: False. Utility is ordinal: it only says mapo tofu \(\succ\) hotpot. The same preference is represented by values 5 and 4.99. Moreover a bundle 'two hotpots' is a different alternative whose ranking is not determined by these numbers. That reading is the hedonic (Bentham) interpretation, not the standard one.

q: What is the standard way economists interpret utility levels (Topic 1)?
options: As an objective measure of well-being (units of pleasure), following Bentham
As cardinal numbers whose differences measure intensity of preference
As a purely ordinal device: they encode only the ranking, like the Mohs hardness scale
As monetary values of the alternatives
explain: Utility numbers only encode the order of the underlying preference; any strictly increasing transformation is equally valid, so levels and differences have no meaning by themselves. Diamond (10) is not 'ten times harder' than talc (1) on the Mohs scale. The hedonic view is presented as the non-standard one.

q: A preference relation \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is continuous (Def. 4-1-3) if:
options: whenever \(x\succ y\), there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(a\succ b\) for every \(a\) within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(x\) and every \(b\) within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(y\)
whenever \(x\succ y\), every \(a\) close to \(x\) satisfies \(a\pr x\)
it is represented by some utility function
its indifference sets are straight lines
explain: Continuity says strict preference survives small perturbations of both bundles. It is not the same as having a utility (a discontinuous preference may still have a discontinuous utility), and it says nothing about the shape of indifference sets.

q: Which sequence shows that the lexicographic preference on \(\R^2_+\) (first coordinate first) is not continuous?
options: \((1+1/n,0)\succ(1,1)\) for all \(n\), but the limit \((1,0)\) satisfies \((1,1)\succ(1,0)\)
explain: Every \((1+1/n,0)\) beats \((1,1)\) because its first coordinate is larger, yet bundles arbitrarily close to \((1,0)\) are better than \((1,1)\) while \((1,0)\) itself is worse: strict preference does not survive the limit. In option 1 the limit keeps the ranking, option 3 is false (\((1,1/n)\succ(1,0)\)), and option 4 involves no limit.

q: Prop. 4-1-1: a preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) represented by a continuous utility is continuous; conversely (Debreu), every continuous preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) has a continuous utility representation. Which conclusion about the lexicographic preference follows?
options: It is continuous, since it is complete and transitive
It has a continuous utility but no discontinuous one
It is not continuous: if it were, Debreu's theorem would give a utility, contradicting Prop. 1-2
Nothing, because Debreu's theorem requires finite sets
explain: Contrapositive of the converse: no utility at all (Prop. 1-2 / PS1 extra) implies not continuous. Completeness and transitivity do not imply continuity. Debreu's theorem is about infinite sets like \(\R^2_+\); on finite sets Prop. 1-1 already gives representation.

q: True or false: if a preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) can be represented by some utility function, then it is continuous.
explain: False. Take \(u(x_1,x_2)=\lfloor x_1\rfloor\) (integer part). It represents a preference, but it is not continuous: \((1,0)\succ(0.5,0)\), while bundles \((1-\varepsilon,0)\) arbitrarily close to \((1,0)\) are indifferent to \((0.5,0)\). Prop. 4-1-1 needs a continuous utility.

q: PS1 (e): Firefly ranks lotteries \(p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)\) over (Win, Draw, Lose) by \(p\pr q\iff p_3<q_3\) or \([p_3=q_3\text{ and }p_2\leq q_2]\). Which statement is correct?
options: \(\pr\) is not complete, which is why it has no utility
\(\pr\) is complete and transitive, but not continuous, so it has no utility representation
explain: It is a genuine preference relation: compare \(p_3\), then \(p_2\), exactly like a lexicographic order. It is not continuous: \([\text{Draw}]\succ\lambda\,\text{Win}\oplus(1-\lambda)\,\text{Lose}\) for every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), so no mixture is indifferent to Draw. \(-p_3-p_2\) trades the coordinates off: \(q=(0.8,0.2,0)\succ p=(0.89,0,0.11)\) for Firefly (lower losing probability), but \(u(p)=-0.11>-0.2=u(q)\).

q: According to Definition 2-1, a choice function for a set \(X\) is
options: a map \(c:2^X\setminus\{\emptyset\}\to X\) assigning to every nonempty \(A\subseteq X\) a single member \(c(A)\in A\)
a map assigning to every nonempty \(A\subseteq X\) a nonempty subset \(c(A)\subseteq A\)
a complete and transitive binary relation on \(X\) describing what the individual likes
a map assigning to every \(A\subseteq X\), including \(\emptyset\), an element of \(X\)
explain: A choice problem is a nonempty subset of \(X\) and a choice function picks exactly one element of each choice problem, inside that problem. The second option is a choice correspondence (PS1 d), not a choice function. The third is a preference relation, a mental attitude rather than behaviour. The empty set is excluded because nothing can be chosen from it.

q: Definition 2-2: a choice function \(c\) is rationalizable if
options: the individual consciously maximizes a preference relation whenever she chooses
there is a utility function \(u\) such that \(c(A)\) maximizes \(u\) over \(X\)
there is a preference relation \(\pr\) such that for every choice problem \(A\), \(c(A)\) is a best element of \(A\) according to \(\pr\) (possibly tied with others)
there is a preference relation \(\pr\) such that for every choice problem \(A\), \(c(A)\) is the unique best element of \(A\) according to \(\pr\)
explain: The definition requires that \(c(A)\) be the unique best element of \(A\). If \"a best element\" were enough, total indifference would rationalize every choice function. Maximizing over \(X\) instead of over \(A\) ignores the menu. Rationalizability is an \"as if\" notion, so it does not require conscious maximization.

q: Why does Definition 2-2 require that \(c(A)\) be the unique best alternative in \(A\), rather than just a best alternative?
options: Because otherwise the relation in which all alternatives are indifferent would rationalize every choice function, so the concept would have no content
Because a choice function can never choose a tied alternative
Because uniqueness is needed for Property \(\alpha\) to be well defined
Because otherwise only transitive preferences could be used
explain: With total indifference every element of every menu is a best element, so any choice function would count as \"rationalizable\" and the definition would rule nothing out. Uniqueness is what gives the test its bite. Ties are handled separately with choice correspondences (PS1 d), where \(C(A)\) is the whole set of best elements.

q: Definition 2-3 (Property \(\alpha\)): a choice function \(c\) on \(X\) satisfies Property \(\alpha\) if
options: for all \(B\subset A\subseteq X\) with \(c(B)\in A\), \(c(A)=c(B)\)
for all \(B\subset A\subseteq X\) with \(c(A)\in B\), \(c(B)=c(A)\)
explain: Property \(\alpha\) is contraction consistency: if what you chose from the big menu \(A\) is still available in the smaller menu \(B\), you choose it again. The first option drops the condition \(c(A)\in B\), which cannot hold in general because \(c(A)\) may have been removed. The second is an expansion condition, and \(\alpha\) does not impose it. The third is path independence (OR Problem 2.5).

q: Property \(\alpha\) is also called
options: The weak axiom of revealed preference for budget sets
Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): removing unchosen alternatives should not change the choice
Expansion consistency: tied winners survive together when the menu grows
explain: The slides call \(\alpha\) Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives: eliminating some of the unchosen alternatives from \(A\) should not affect the choice of \(c(A)\). Expansion consistency is Property \(\beta\). WARP is the analogue for budget sets in Topic 4, and path independence is a different (stronger) property. Historically \(\alpha\) is Chernoff's Postulate 4.

q: For a choice correspondence \(C\) (with \(C(A)\) a nonempty subset of \(A\)), PS1 d calls \(C\) rationalizable if there is a preference relation \(\pr\) such that for every choice problem \(A\)
options: \(C(A)\) is a singleton consisting of the \(\pr\)-best element
\(C(A)\) contains at least one \(\pr\)-best element of \(A\)
explain: For correspondences, rationalizable means \(C(A)\) is exactly the set of all best elements: every best element is chosen, and only best elements are chosen. Inclusion alone, or \"contains a best element\", would allow dropping tied alternatives arbitrarily, and that is exactly what PS1 d(i) rules out. Singletons bring us back to choice functions.

q: For a choice correspondence \(C\), Property \(\beta\) (PS1 d(ii)) states: for all nonempty \(A\subseteq B\subseteq X\) and all \(x,y\in C(A)\),
explain: \(\beta\) governs expansions: if \(x\) and \(y\) are chosen together from the smaller menu \(A\) and \(x\) is still chosen from the bigger menu \(B\), then \(y\) must also be chosen from \(B\). Tied winners survive or fall together. Option 2 is just \(\alpha\) for correspondences (contraction). Option 3 would say chosen elements always survive expansion, which is false even for rational choice, since a better element may be added.

q: For a choice correspondence \(C\), Property \(\alpha\) (PS1 d) is the condition
options: for all \(A\subseteq B\) and \(x,y\in C(A)\): \(x\in C(B)\Rightarrow y\in C(B)\)
for all nonempty \(B\subseteq A\subseteq X\) and \(x\in B\): \(x\in C(A)\Rightarrow x\in C(B)\)
for all nonempty \(B\subseteq A\subseteq X\): \(C(B)\subseteq C(A)\)
for all nonempty \(B\subseteq A\subseteq X\): \(C(A)\cap B=C(B)\)
explain: \(\alpha\) for correspondences says a winner of the big menu that is still available in the smaller menu remains a winner there. It does not say that the smaller menu's winners were winners in the big menu (option 3), which fails for rational choice once a better element is added. Option 4 is too strong as stated (it fails whenever \(C(A)\cap B=\emptyset\)). Even restricted to a nonempty intersection, it is \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) together. Option 1 is \(\beta\).

q: Definition 2.4 (OR book, satisficing): \(X\) is finite, \(v:X\to\R\) is a valuation, \(v^*\) an aspiration level, \(O\) an ordering of \(X\). For \(A=\{a_1,\dots,a_K\}\) listed in the order \(O\), the satisficing choice \(c(A)\) is
options: the first \(a_k\) in the order \(O\) with \(v(a_k)\geq v^*\); if no such alternative exists, the last element \(a_K\)
the alternative in \(A\) with the highest \(v\)
the first \(a_k\) in the order \(O\) with \(v(a_k)\geq v^*\); if no such alternative exists, \(a_1\)
the last \(a_k\) in the order \(O\) with \(v(a_k)\geq v^*\); if none, the \(v\)-maximal element
explain: Simon's satisficing: examine the alternatives in the order \(O\) and stop at the first satisfactory one (\(v\geq v^*\)). If none is satisfactory, take the last one examined, \(a_K\). Choosing the \(v\)-maximal one when none is satisfactory is the variant in OR Problem 2.4. Choosing the overall \(v\)-maximum is plain maximization, not satisficing.

q: Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\). How many choice functions on \(X\) are there, and how many of them are rationalizable?
explain: Singletons leave no choice. Each of the three pairs has 2 possible choices and \(X\) has 3, so there are \(2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3=24\) choice functions. A rationalizable \(c\) corresponds to exactly one strict ordering of \(X\), and there are \(3!=6\) of these (OR Example 2.1). Answers that use 27 (\(3^3\)) or 8 miscount the menus.

q: Let \(|X|=4\). How many choice functions on \(X\) satisfy Property \(\alpha\)?
explain: \(X\) is finite, so Props 2-1 and 2-2 make Property \(\alpha\) equivalent to rationalizability. Each rationalizable \(c\) corresponds to exactly one strict ordering, and there are \(4!=24\) of them. 20736 \(=2^6\cdot3^4\cdot4\) is the total number of choice functions (6 pairs, 4 triples, 1 four-element menu).

q: True or false: if a choice function \(c\) is rationalizable, the preference relation that rationalizes it is unique.
explain: True. Any rationalizing \(\pr\) must make \(c(\{x,y\})\) the unique best element of \(\{x,y\}\), so \(x\succ y\) if \(c(\{x,y\})=x\) and \(y\succ x\) otherwise. The ranking of every pair is therefore pinned down by \(c\), and so is the whole relation (it must be a strict ordering). As OR notes, two individuals with different strict preferences have different choice functions.

q: In the course's notion of rationality, an individual who always chooses the alternative that causes her the greatest pain (measured in some fixed way) is
options: rational only if her choice set is infinite
irrational, because rational choice must serve her well-being
irrational, because her choices necessarily violate Property \(\alpha\)
rational, because the model only requires choosing the best alternative according to some preference relation, whatever its content
explain: Economics is \"not judgemental\": rationality means choosing a best element according to some preference relation, and nothing is assumed about what the preferences are. Maximizing pain is maximizing the preference \"more pain is better\", and this satisfies \(\alpha\). The slides add that, as outsiders, we do not observe preferences, only choices.

q: If the individual's preference is represented by a utility function \(u\), a rational individual facing menu \(A\) acts as if she solves
explain: Rational choice from a menu \(A\) means choosing a \(\pr\)-best element of \(A\). With a utility representation this is the constrained problem \(\max\{u(x):x\in A\}\). Maximizing over all of \(X\) ignores the constraint that only elements of \(A\) are available. For the induced choice to be single-valued, the maximizer in each \(A\) must be unique, for example when \(u\) is one-to-one.

q: Friedman's billiard-player quote is used in Topic 2 to support which idea?
options: Experts never violate Property \(\alpha\) because they compute optimal choices explicitly
Mental accounting explains why experts outperform novices
Choice functions on infinite sets cannot be rationalized
The \"as if\" justification: people need not consciously maximize a preference, it is enough that their behaviour can be described as if they did
explain: Friedman argues that a billiard player's shots can be predicted well by assuming he solves the physics equations, even though he does not. In the same way, modelling individuals as maximizers is justified if their behaviour looks as if they maximize, whether or not they are aware of their preferences. The point is not that experts compute explicitly; the quote says the opposite.

options: No: the pairwise choices form a cycle
explain: Pairs reveal \(a\succ b\), \(a\succ c\), \(b\succ c\). There is no cycle, so the ordering is \(a\succ b\succ c\), and \(c(X)=a\) is its top element. Every menu then picks its \(\succ\)-best element (OR Example 2.1). \(a\succ c\succ b\) is wrong because it would require \(c(\{b,c\})=c\). Option 2 confuses \(\alpha\): \(a\notin\{b,c\}\), so \(\alpha\) imposes nothing on that pair.

q: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(X)=a\), \(c(\{a,b\})=b\), \(c(\{a,c\})=a\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\). Which statement is correct?
options: Rationalizable, because the pairwise choices contain no cycle
Not rationalizable: \(\alpha\) fails at \(A=X\), \(B=\{a,b\}\), since \(c(X)=a\in B\) but \(c(B)=b\)
explain: The pairs give \(b\succ a\succ c\) with no cycle, but \(c(X)=a\) is not the top of that order. Formally, \(c(X)=a\in\{a,b\}\) yet \(c(\{a,b\})=b\neq a\), so \(\alpha\) fails and Prop 2-1 rules out rationalizability. The pair \(\{b,c\}\) is not a violation because \(a\notin\{b,c\}\). The trap: acyclic pairs are not enough, the big menu must also pick the top element.

options: No, but only because \(c(X)\) should be \(c\)
No: the pairwise choices are cyclic (\(a\succ b\succ c\succ a\)), and \(\alpha\) fails at \((X,\{a,c\})\)
explain: The pairs reveal \(a\succ b\), \(b\succ c\), \(c\succ a\), which is a cycle no transitive relation can produce. Concretely, \(c(X)=a\in\{a,c\}\) while \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), so \(\alpha\) fails. Changing \(c(X)\) cannot help: with cyclic pairs, any value of \(c(X)\) violates \(\alpha\) on one of the pairs that contains it.

q: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\). For how many of the three possible values of \(c(X)\) is \(c\) rationalizable?
explain: The pairs form the cycle \(a\succ b\succ c\succ a\). If \(c(X)=a\), \(\alpha\) fails on \(\{a,c\}\) (choice \(c\)). If \(c(X)=b\), it fails on \(\{a,b\}\) (choice \(a\)). If \(c(X)=c\), it fails on \(\{b,c\}\) (choice \(b\)). So no completion works. This is the money-pump choice function from slide 20.

q: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\), \(c(\{a,c\})=a\). Which value of \(c(X)\) makes \(c\) rationalizable?
options: Any value, since the pairs are acyclic
explain: The pairs reveal the strict ordering \(a\succ b\succ c\), and the only candidate rationalization is this ordering (it is unique). So \(c(X)\) must be its top element \(a\). With \(c(X)=b\), \(\alpha\) fails at \((X,\{a,b\})\); with \(c(X)=c\) it fails at \((X,\{a,c\})\). Acyclic pairs are necessary but not sufficient.

q: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(X)=b\), \(c(\{a,b\})=b\), \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\). Which preference rationalizes \(c\)?
explain: The pairs reveal \(b\succ a\), \(c\succ a\) and \(b\succ c\), so the ordering is \(b\succ c\succ a\). Its top element \(b\) equals \(c(X)\), so every menu picks its best element. \(b\succ a\succ c\) contradicts \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), and \(c\succ b\succ a\) contradicts \(c(\{b,c\})=b\).

q: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(X)=a\), \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{a,c\})=a\), \(c(\{b,c\})=c\). Does \(\alpha\) impose any restriction linking \(c(X)\) and \(c(\{b,c\})\)?
options: Yes: \(\alpha\) requires \(c(\{b,c\})=c(X)\), which is impossible here, so \(c\) is not rationalizable
No: \(c(X)=a\notin\{b,c\}\), so \(\alpha\) says nothing about that pair, and \(c\) is rationalizable by \(a\succ c\succ b\)
No, and \(c\) is not rationalizable because the pairwise choices are cyclic
explain: \(\alpha\) only constrains a subset \(B\) that still contains \(c(A)\). Since \(a\notin\{b,c\}\), the choice from \(\{b,c\}\) is unrestricted by \(c(X)\). The pairs reveal \(a\succ b\), \(a\succ c\), \(c\succ b\) with no cycle, so \(a\succ c\succ b\) rationalizes \(c\). A common mistake is to apply \(\alpha\) to every subset.

q: Let \(X=\{a,b,c,d\}\) and let \(c\) satisfy Property \(\alpha\) with \(c(X)=b\), \(c(\{a,c,d\})=d\), \(c(\{a,c\})=c\). Following the construction in the proof of Proposition 2-2, the rationalizing preference is
explain: The construction sets \(a_1=c(X)=b\), \(a_2=c(X\setminus\{b\})=c(\{a,c,d\})=d\), \(a_3=c(\{a,c\})=c\), and \(a_4=a\) is what remains. The ranking is \(a_1\succ a_2\succ a_3\succ a_4\), that is \(b\succ d\succ c\succ a\). The second option reverses it. The others put the elements in the wrong order of removal.

q: Continuing: \(c\) on \(X=\{a,b,c,d\}\) satisfies \(\alpha\), with \(c(X)=b\), \(c(\{a,c,d\})=d\), \(c(\{a,c\})=c\). What must \(c(\{a,d\})\) be?
options: Either, since \(\alpha\) restricts only menus that contain \(b\)
It is not determined by the given information
explain: \(\{a,d\}\subset\{a,c,d\}\) and \(c(\{a,c,d\})=d\in\{a,d\}\), so \(\alpha\) forces \(c(\{a,d\})=d\). Equivalently, the rationalizing order \(b\succ d\succ c\succ a\) ranks \(d\) above \(a\). \(\alpha\) applies to every pair \(B\subset A\), not only to subsets of \(X\) that contain \(c(X)\).

q: Suppose \(c\) is rationalizable and you observe only \(c(\{a,b,c,d\})=b\). What can you infer about the rationalizing preference \(\succ\)?
options: Nothing, since only binary choices reveal preferences
\(b\succ a\), \(b\succ c\), \(b\succ d\), and nothing yet about how \(a,c,d\) compare
explain: If \(\succ\) rationalizes \(c\), then \(c(A)\) is the unique best element of \(A\), so the chosen \(b\) is revealed strictly preferred to every other element of the menu. The choice says nothing about how the unchosen elements compare. Revealed preference does not need binary menus: \(\alpha\) then implies \(c(\{b,x\})=b\) for each \(x\).

q: Let \(X=\{1,2,3\}\) be ordered left to right. The median procedure (OR Example 2.2) chooses the median of an odd-sized menu and the leftmost of the two medians of an even-sized menu. Which pair \((A,B)\) shows that \(\alpha\) fails?
options: No pair: the median procedure satisfies \(\alpha\) on three elements
explain: \(c(\{1,2,3\})=2\). For \(B=\{1,2\}\), the leftmost median is 1, so \(c(B)=1\neq2\) although \(2\in B\), which violates \(\alpha\). For \(B=\{2,3\}\), \(c(B)=2\), consistent. \(B=\{1,3\}\) does not contain 2, so \(\alpha\) is silent there. The behaviour has a rationale (\"prefer the central option\"), but it is a preference over positions, not over \(X\).

q: OR's resolution of the median example: the behaviour becomes rationalizable if the alternatives are redefined as
options: pairs of candidates, chosen by majority vote
the same candidates, but with an infinite set \(X\)
positions relative to the median (median, one left of median, one right, ...), ranked median \(\succ\) one left \(\succ\) one right \(\succ\cdots\)
explain: The rationale \"always pick the central option\" is a preference over relative positions, not over the candidates. With \(Y=\{\)median, one left, one right, ...\(\}\), each menu becomes a set of positions, and the ordering median \(\succ\) one left \(\succ\) one right \(\succ\dots\) rationalizes the behaviour. The general lesson: \(\alpha\) failures often mean the alternatives were defined too coarsely.

q: Partygoer (slide 15): \(X=\{A,B_1,B_2\}\). Invited by \(A\) and \(B_1\), she goes to \(B_1\). Invited by all three, she goes to \(A\). Which statement is correct?
options: The behaviour is rationalizable by \(B_1\succ A\succ B_2\)
explain: \(\alpha\) is a contraction condition: start from the big menu, whose choice is \(A\), and shrink it to \(\{A,B_1\}\), which still contains \(A\). Then \(\alpha\) requires \(c(\{A,B_1\})=A\), but she picks \(B_1\). Option 3 states the logic in the wrong direction (expansion), which \(\alpha\) does not impose. \(\beta\) is a property of correspondences, irrelevant for single-valued choice.

q: What is the main lesson of the partygoer and steak-and-salmon examples?
options: People are irrational, so economic models of choice are useless
The meaning of an alternative can depend on what else is available. Redefining the alternatives (e.g. low-quality vs high-quality steak) can restore rationalizability
Property \(\alpha\) is not necessary for rationalizability
Choice functions must be defined on infinite sets
explain: In both examples one option (\(B_1\), or steak) means something different depending on the other options on the menu: snubbing \(B_2\), or a signal that the restaurant is first-rate. A choice function assumes an alternative is the same object in every menu. With richer alternatives, such as {high-quality steak, salmon, low-quality steak, snails, frog's legs}, a preference rationalizes the behaviour. \(\alpha\) remains necessary (Prop 2-1).

q: Steak and salmon (Luce and Raiffa): from {salmon, steak} the diner picks salmon. When told that snails and frog's legs (which he detests) are also available, he switches to steak. On \(X=\{\)salmon, steak, snails, frog's legs\(\}\):
options: \(c\) is rationalizable by steak \(\succ\) salmon \(\succ\) snails \(\succ\) frog's legs
\(\alpha\) fails only if he actually orders snails
\(\alpha\) holds, because the added dishes are never chosen
explain: From the full menu he picks steak, and steak is still available in {salmon, steak}, where he picks salmon. So \(\alpha\) is violated, and by Prop 2-1 no preference on \(X\) rationalizes him. The added dishes are never chosen, and that is exactly the IIA point: unchosen \"irrelevant\" alternatives changed the choice. OR's fix ranks high-quality steak \(\succ\) salmon \(\succ\) low-quality steak \(\succ\) snails \(\succ\) frog's legs.

q: Proposition 2-1 states that every rationalizable choice function satisfies Property \(\alpha\). Which hypothesis does it need?
options: The rationalizing preference must have a utility representation
None beyond rationalizability: it holds for any set \(X\)
explain: The proof only uses that \(c(A)\succ y\) for all \(y\in A\), hence for all \(y\) in any \(B\subset A\). Since \(c(A)\in B\), \(c(A)\) is the unique best element of \(B\), so \(c(B)=c(A)\). Nowhere does it use the size of \(X\) or a utility function. Finiteness is a hypothesis of Proposition 2-2 in the slides, not of 2-1.

q: Combining Propositions 2-1 and 2-2, for a single-valued choice function on a finite set \(X\):
options: \(c\) rationalizable \(\iff\) \(c\) satisfies \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and \(\alpha\) alone is not enough
explain: On finite \(X\), \(\alpha\) is necessary (2-1) and sufficient (2-2), so it is a complete behavioural test of rationality. \(\beta\) is automatically satisfied by single-valued choice and only matters for correspondences. Acyclic pairwise choices are necessary but not sufficient: the big menus must also pick the top element.

q: Proof of Proposition 2-1. Let \(\succ\) rationalize \(c\), let \(B\subset A\) and \(c(A)\in B\). Which chain of reasoning is correct?
options: \(c(B)\succ y\) for all \(y\in B\), so \(c(B)\succ c(A)\), hence \(c(B)=c(A)\)
\(c(A)\succ y\) for all \(y\in A\setminus\{c(A)\}\), hence for all \(y\in B\setminus\{c(A)\}\). Since \(c(A)\in B\), \(c(A)\) is the unique best element of \(B\), so \(c(B)=c(A)\)
By finiteness of \(X\) list the elements of \(A\) in order and remove them one by one
By transitivity of \(\succ\), \(c(B)\succ c(A)\succ y\) for all \(y\in A\)
explain: The key steps are that being best in \(A\) implies being best in any subset (since \(B\subset A\)), and that \(c(A)\in B\) makes \(c(A)\) a candidate in \(B\). Uniqueness of the best element then pins down \(c(B)=c(A)\). Option 1 is circular and wrong: it would need \(c(B)\succ c(A)\), which contradicts \(c(A)\) being best in \(A\supseteq B\). No finiteness is needed.

q: Proof of Proposition 2-2. Define \(a_1=c(X)\), \(a_2=c(X\setminus\{a_1\})\), \(a_3=c(X\setminus\{a_1,a_2\})\), ..., and \(a_1\succ a_2\succ\cdots\succ a_n\). For a menu \(A\), let \(a_m\) be the first member of \(A\) in this sequence. Why is \(A\subseteq\{a_m,a_{m+1},\dots,a_n\}\)?
options: Because \(a_1,\dots,a_{m-1}\) are not in \(A\) (by the choice of \(a_m\) as the first member of \(A\)), and \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) list all of \(X\)
Because Property \(\alpha\) implies \(A\) contains only elements ranked below \(a_m\)
explain: \(a_m\) is the earliest element of the list that lies in \(A\), so no earlier \(a_k\) belongs to \(A\). Since the list exhausts the finite \(X\), every element of \(A\) is among \(a_m,\dots,a_n\). This is pure bookkeeping; \(\alpha\) is used in the next step. Option 1 is the conclusion we want to prove, so assuming it is circular.

q: In the proof of Proposition 2-2, after establishing \(A\subseteq\{a_m,\dots,a_n\}\) and \(a_m\in A\), how does one conclude \(c(A)=a_m\)?
options: By construction \(c(\{a_m,\dots,a_n\})=a_m\), and since \(a_m\in A\subseteq\{a_m,\dots,a_n\}\), Property \(\alpha\) gives \(c(A)=a_m\)
By transitivity of \(\succ\), \(a_m\succ y\) for all \(y\in A\), so \(c(A)=a_m\) by definition of \(c\)
explain: \(\{a_m,\dots,a_n\}=X\setminus\{a_1,\dots,a_{m-1}\}\), and \(a_m\) was defined as the choice from this set. Apply \(\alpha\) with the big set \(\{a_m,\dots,a_n\}\) and the subset \(A\), which contains \(a_m\). Option 2 misapplies \(\alpha\): \(a_1\) need not be in \(A\). Option 3 is circular, since knowing that \(a_m\) is \(\succ\)-best does not tell us what \(c\) picks without \(\alpha\). Prop 2-1 is the converse direction.

q: PS1 c(i): which step of the slide proof of Proposition 2-2 fails when \(X\) is infinite?
options: The definition of a choice function, which requires \(X\) finite

The construction \(a_1=c(X)\), \(a_2=c(X\setminus\{a_1\}),\dots\): it never terminates and may not exhaust \(X\) (for instance, a sequence cannot exhaust an uncountable set), so the ranking may not include every alternative
The step showing \(\succ\) is complete on pairs that are listed
explain: With infinite \(X\) the removal procedure produces at most a sequence \(a_1,a_2,\dots\), which need not cover \(X\) (an uncountable \(X\) like \([0,1]\) cannot be covered). Unlisted alternatives are never ranked, so the relation is not complete, and a menu may have no \"first\" member in the list. Choice functions are well defined on infinite sets, and \(\alpha\) itself is not the problem.

q: True or false: Proposition 2-2 becomes false if \(X\) is infinite; there is a choice function on an infinite set that satisfies Property \(\alpha\) but is not rationalizable.
explain: False. PS1 c(ii) (OR Problem 2.7) shows the result still holds. Define \(x\pr_c y\iff c(\{x,y\})=x\). \(\alpha\) on triples gives transitivity, and \(\alpha\) on pairs \(\{x,a\}\subseteq A\) shows \(c(A)\) is the unique best element. Only the slide's proof technique (enumerating \(X\)) needs finiteness, not the theorem.

q: PS1 c(ii): for an arbitrary (possibly infinite) \(X\) and \(c\) satisfying \(\alpha\), which relation is used to prove rationalizability?
options: \(x\pr_c y\iff x\) appears before \(y\) in the list \(c(X),c(X\setminus\{c(X)\}),\dots\)
\(x\pr_c y\iff\) there is a menu \(A\) with \(c(A)=y\) and \(x\in A\)
explain: The pairwise relation \(x\pr_c y\iff c(\{x,y\})=x\) is defined for every pair, whatever the size of \(X\). The proof only looks at menus of size 2 and 3, which is why infinity does not matter. The list-based relation is the finite construction that breaks down. The last option reverses revealed preference: being available when \(y\) is chosen reveals \(y\) is preferred to \(x\).

q: PS1 c(ii), transitivity: suppose \(x\pr_c y\), \(y\pr_c z\) with \(x,y,z\) distinct, and let \(w=c(\{x,y,z\})\). Why can \(w\) not equal \(y\)?
options: Because \(y\pr_c z\) means \(y\) is chosen from \(\{y,z\}\), so \(y\) cannot be chosen from a larger set
Because by \(\alpha\) applied to \(\{x,y\}\subset\{x,y,z\}\), \(w=y\) would give \(c(\{x,y\})=y\), contradicting \(c(\{x,y\})=x\)
Because by \(\alpha\) applied to \(\{y,z\}\subset\{x,y,z\}\), \(w=y\) would give \(c(\{y,z\})=z\)
explain: If \(y\) were chosen from the triple, then since \(y\in\{x,y\}\), \(\alpha\) would force \(c(\{x,y\})=y\). But \(x\pr_c y\) means \(c(\{x,y\})=x\), a contradiction. Similarly \(w=z\) contradicts \(c(\{y,z\})=y\). So \(w=x\), and \(\alpha\) on \(\{x,z\}\) gives \(c(\{x,z\})=x\), that is \(x\pr_c z\). Option 1 is false: winning a small menu does not prevent winning a larger one.

q: PS1 c(ii), rationalization step: \(x=c(A)\) and \(a\in A\), \(a\neq x\). Why is \(x\) strictly (not just weakly) better than \(a\) under \(\pr_c\)?
options: Because \(\alpha\) gives \(c(\{x,a\})=x\), and since \(c\) is single-valued, \(c(\{x,a\})\neq a\), so \(a\pr_c x\) fails
explain: \(\alpha\) applied to \(\{x,a\}\subseteq A\) gives \(c(\{x,a\})=x\), so \(x\pr_c a\). Single-valuedness means the choice from \(\{x,a\}\) is \(x\) and not \(a\), so \(a\pr_c x\) is false and \(x\succ_c a\). Hence \(x\) is the unique best element, as Definition 2-2 requires. Finiteness and \(\beta\) play no role here.

q: OR Problem 2.2: \(c\) satisfies \(\alpha\), and \(A,B\) are menus with \(c(A)\in B\) and \(c(B)\in A\). To prove \(c(A)=c(B)\), the key step is to
options: apply \(\alpha\) to \(A\cup B\) and its subsets \(A\) and \(B\)
apply \(\alpha\) to \(A\cap B\subseteq A\), which contains \(c(A)\), and to \(A\cap B\subseteq B\), which contains \(c(B)\), giving \(c(A)=c(A\cap B)=c(B)\)
explain: \(c(A)\in A\cap B\subseteq A\), so \(\alpha\) gives \(c(A\cap B)=c(A)\). Symmetrically, \(c(B)\in A\cap B\subseteq B\) gives \(c(A\cap B)=c(B)\). Hence \(c(A)=c(B)\). Working with \(A\cup B\) fails because we know nothing about \(c(A\cup B)\). \(A\) and \(B\) need not be nested.

q: True or false: Property \(\alpha\) implies that if \(B\subset A\) and \(c(B)=x\), then \(c(A)=x\).
explain: False. \(\alpha\) is only a contraction condition, so adding alternatives can change the choice even for rational behaviour. Example: \(z\succ x\succ y\) gives \(c(\{x,y\})=x\) but \(c(\{x,y,z\})=z\). What \(\alpha\) does say is that if the new choice \(c(A)\) lies in \(B\), it must coincide with \(c(B)\).

q: True or false: on a finite \(X\), if the binary choices \(c(\{x,y\})\) contain no cycle, then \(c\) is rationalizable.
explain: False. Acyclic pairs give a candidate ordering, but the larger menus must also pick its top element. Example: \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\), \(c(\{a,c\})=a\), but \(c(\{a,b,c\})=b\). Then \(\alpha\) fails at \((X,\{a,b\})\). The correct test is Property \(\alpha\) on all pairs of nested menus.

q: PS1 d(i): \(X=\{x,y,z\}\), \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(\{x,z\})=\{x\}\), \(C(\{y,z\})=\{y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\) (singletons choose themselves). Which statement is correct?
options: \(C\) satisfies \(\alpha\) and is rationalizable by \(x\succ y\succ z\)
\(C\) satisfies \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and is rationalizable by \(x\sim y\succ z\)
explain: \(\alpha\) holds: the only element chosen from \(X\) is \(x\), and \(x\) is chosen from every subset containing it. In pairs, each chosen element is trivially chosen from its singleton. But a rationalizing \(\pr\) would need \(x\sim y\) (from \(C(\{x,y\})\)) and \(x\pr z\), hence \(y\pr z\) and \(y\in C(X)\), a contradiction. Option 1 states an expansion requirement, which is \(\beta\)'s territory, not \(\alpha\)'s.

q: PS1 d(ii): in the same correspondence (\(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(\{x,z\})=\{x\}\), \(C(\{y,z\})=\{y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\)), which sets and alternatives show that \(\beta\) fails?
explain: \(\beta\) needs two alternatives chosen together from a smaller set, and the only such set is \(\{x,y\}\). When the set grows to \(X\), \(x\) stays chosen but \(y\) is dropped, which violates \(\beta\). Option 2 has only one chosen element in \(A\), and a single winner being dropped is not a \(\beta\) violation (a better element may have been added). Option 4 has the sets in the wrong direction.

q: In PS1 d(i), what intuitively goes wrong?
options: Removing \(z\) changes the winner, an \(\alpha\) problem
\(x\) and \(y\) are tied, then adding \(z\) (which is worse than both) breaks the tie. A rational individual's tie cannot be broken by adding an alternative
\(z\) is never chosen, so it should not be in \(X\)
The relation \(x\pr_C y\iff x\in C(\{x,y\})\) is not transitive
explain: \(\alpha\) controls only shrinking menus, but here the problem appears when the menu expands: \(x\) and \(y\) tie in \(\{x,y\}\), yet in \(\{x,y,z\}\) only \(x\) survives. Under a preference, \(x\sim y\) means both are best whenever one is, so adding \(z\) cannot separate them. In fact \(\pr_C\) (\(x\sim y\succ z\)) is transitive here. What fails is that it does not reproduce \(C(X)\).

q: PS1 d(iii): to prove that \(\beta\) is necessary for rationalizability, take \(\pr\) rationalizing \(C\), \(A\subseteq B\), \(x,y\in C(A)\), \(x\in C(B)\). The key step is
options: \(y\pr x\) (since \(y\) is best in \(A\) and \(x\in A\)) and \(x\pr z\ \forall z\in B\); by transitivity \(y\pr z\ \forall z\in B\), so \(y\in C(B)\)
by completeness, \(y\pr x\) or \(x\pr y\), so \(y\in C(B)\)
\(x\pr y\) (since \(x\in C(A)\)) and transitivity gives \(x\in C(A)\)
explain: \(y\) best in \(A\) and \(x\in A\) give \(y\pr x\). \(x\) best in \(B\) gives \(x\pr z\) for all \(z\in B\). Transitivity yields \(y\pr z\) for all \(z\in B\), so \(y\) is a best element of \(B\), and rationalizability (\(C(B)\) is all best elements) puts \(y\in C(B)\). \(\alpha\) is a contraction property and cannot move \(y\) into a bigger set's choice. Completeness alone gives nothing.

q: PS1 d(iv): \(C\) satisfies \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), \(x\pr_C y\iff x\in C(\{x,y\})\). For transitivity with \(x\pr_C y\), \(y\pr_C z\), \(T=\{x,y,z\}\), \(w\in C(T)\): in the case \(w=y\), how do we get \(x\in C(T)\)?
options: \(\alpha\) gives \(y\in C(\{x,y\})\). Also \(x\in C(\{x,y\})\). Since \(y\in C(T)\) and \(\{x,y\}\subseteq T\), \(\beta\) gives \(x\in C(T)\)
It cannot be done; this case is a contradiction
explain: \(x\) and \(y\) are both chosen from \(\{x,y\}\) (\(x\) by assumption, \(y\) by \(\alpha\) since \(y\in C(T)\)). \(\beta\) says that if one of them survives in the larger \(T\), so does the other, hence \(x\in C(T)\). Then \(\alpha\) on \(\{x,z\}\subseteq T\) gives \(x\in C(\{x,z\})\), that is \(x\pr_C z\). Unlike the single-valued case, \(w=y\) is not a contradiction, since ties are allowed.

q: PS1 d(iv), transitivity, case \(w=z\in C(T)\) with \(x\pr_C y\), \(y\pr_C z\), \(T=\{x,y,z\}\). How many times is \(\beta\) used to reach \(x\in C(T)\)?
explain: \(\alpha\) gives \(z\in C(\{y,z\})\). With \(y\in C(\{y,z\})\) and \(z\in C(T)\), the first use of \(\beta\) gives \(y\in C(T)\). Then, with \(x,y\in C(\{x,y\})\) and \(y\in C(T)\), the second use of \(\beta\) gives \(x\in C(T)\). Finally \(\alpha\) gives \(x\in C(\{x,z\})\). The case \(w=x\) needs no \(\beta\), and the case \(w=y\) needs it once.

q: PS1 d(iv), showing \(\pr_C\) rationalizes \(C\). Which property is essential for the inclusion \(\{x\in A: x\pr_C y\ \forall y\in A\}\subseteq C(A)\), i.e. every \(\pr_C\)-best element is chosen?
options: \(\beta\) (together with \(\alpha\) to get \(z\in C(\{x,z\})\) for some \(z\in C(A)\))
explain: Take a \(\pr_C\)-best \(x\in A\) and any \(z\in C(A)\). \(\alpha\) gives \(z\in C(\{x,z\})\), and \(x\in C(\{x,z\})\) by definition. Since \(z\) survives in \(A\), \(\beta\) forces \(x\) to survive as well: \(x\in C(A)\). The other inclusion (chosen implies best) uses only \(\alpha\). In PS1 d(i) exactly this \(\beta\)-step fails: \(y\) is \(\pr_C\)-best in \(X\) but not chosen.

options: \(\pr_C\) is \(x\succ y\succ z\), and it rationalizes \(C\)
\(\pr_C\) is not transitive, and this is why \(C\) is not rationalizable
\(\pr_C\) is \(x\sim y\succ z\), a preference relation, but its best set on \(X\) is \(\{x,y\}\neq C(X)\)
explain: \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\) gives \(x\sim_C y\), and the other two pairs give \(x\succ_C z\) and \(y\succ_C z\). This is complete and transitive. Its best elements in \(X\) are \(x\) and \(y\), but \(C(X)=\{x\}\), so the rationalization step fails (the \(\beta\)-inclusion). A common wrong guess is that transitivity breaks.

Under \(x\sim y\succ z\) the best set of \(X\) is \(\{x,y\}\), of \(\{x,y\}\) it is \(\{x,y\}\), of \(\{x,z\}\) it is \(\{x\}\), and of \(\{y,z\}\) it is \(\{y\}\), matching \(C\) everywhere. \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both hold: the tied pair survives together in \(X\). \(x\succ y\succ z\) would give \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x\}\) and \(C(X)=\{x\}\).

options: Neither, and \(C\) is rationalizable by total indifference
explain: \(y\) is chosen from the big menu \(X\) and is available in \(\{x,y\}\), so \(\alpha\) requires \(y\in C(\{x,y\})\). It is not, so \(\alpha\) fails and \(C\) is not rationalizable. Total indifference would give \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\). Option 4 is wrong on the facts, since \(x\in C(X)\).

q: True or false: every single-valued choice function, viewed as a choice correspondence (\(C(A)=\{c(A)\}\)), satisfies Property \(\beta\).
explain: True, vacuously. \(\beta\) has bite only when two distinct alternatives \(x\neq y\) are both chosen from some \(A\). With singleton choice sets, \(x,y\in C(A)\) forces \(x=y\), and the implication is trivial. This is why \(\alpha\) alone characterizes rationalizability for choice functions (Prop 2-2), while correspondences need \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

q: True or false: on a finite \(X\), a choice correspondence satisfying Property \(\alpha\) is rationalizable.
explain: False. PS1 d(i) is a counterexample: \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(\{x,z\})=\{x\}\), \(C(\{y,z\})=\{y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\) satisfies \(\alpha\) but is not rationalizable. With ties, \(\beta\) (expansion consistency) is also needed. \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) together are necessary and sufficient.

q: True or false: if a choice correspondence \(C\) is rationalizable, then it satisfies both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
explain: True. \(\alpha\): an element that is best in \(A\) is best in any \(B\subseteq A\) containing it. \(\beta\) (PS1 d(iii)): if \(x,y\) are best in \(A\) and \(x\) is best in \(B\supseteq A\), then \(y\sim x\pr z\) for all \(z\in B\), so \(y\) is best in \(B\). Both proofs use transitivity and the definition of \(C(A)\) as the set of all best elements.

In \(\{a,b,d\}\), scanning alphabetically, \(a\) and \(b\) are unsatisfactory (\(v<0\)) and \(d\) has \(v=3\geq0\), so she stops at \(d\). In \(\{a,b\}\) nothing is satisfactory, so she takes the last one examined, \(b\). Picking \(a\) (the \(v\)-higher one) confuses satisficing with the Problem 2.4 variant.

q: Same satisficing data (\(O\) alphabetical, \(v^*=0\), \(v(a)=-1\), \(v(b)=-2\), \(v(c)=1\), \(v(d)=3\)). The OR proof of Proposition 2.3 builds which rationalizing preference?
explain: Put the satisfactory alternatives \(\{c,d\}\) on top in the order \(O\): \(c\succ d\). Below them put the unsatisfactory ones \(\{a,b\}\) in reverse \(O\) order: \(b\succ a\). Result: \(c\succ d\succ b\succ a\). Ranking by \(v\) fails because satisficing stops at the first satisfactory \(c\) even when the better \(d\) is available. Unsatisfactory ones are reversed because, when nothing is satisfactory, the last examined is chosen.

q: Satisficing with \(X=\{a,b,c,d\}\), \(O\) alphabetical, \(v^*=0\), \(v(a)=2\), \(v(b)=-1\), \(v(c)=-3\), \(v(d)=1\). Which preference rationalizes the choice function?
explain: Satisfactory: \(a,d\), in \(O\)-order \(a\succ d\). Unsatisfactory: \(b,c\), in reverse \(O\)-order \(c\succ b\). So the ranking is \(a\succ d\succ c\succ b\). Check: \(c(\{b,c\})\) has no satisfactory element, so she takes the last in \(O\), which is \(c\), consistent with \(c\succ b\). Ranking the unsatisfactory ones by \(v\) (\(b\succ c\)) is the common mistake. The last option is not even a relation.

q: OR Problem 2.3 (satisficing satisfies \(\alpha\)): let \(B\subset A\), \(c(A)\in B\), and suppose \(A\) contains a satisfactory alternative. Why is \(c(B)=c(A)\)?
options: Because \(c(A)\) has the highest \(v\) in \(A\), hence in \(B\)

Because \(c(A)\) is the first satisfactory element of \(A\) in the order \(O\). Every element of \(B\) that precedes it in \(O\) is also in \(A\), hence unsatisfactory, so \(c(A)\) is the first satisfactory element of \(B\) too
Because satisficing choice is path independent by definition
explain: Elements of \(B\) that come before \(c(A)\) in \(O\) lie in \(A\) before \(c(A)\), so all are unsatisfactory. \(c(A)\in B\) is satisfactory, so the scan of \(B\) stops exactly at \(c(A)\). If \(A\) has no satisfactory element, then neither does \(B\), and \(c(A)\), the \(O\)-last element of \(A\), is also \(O\)-last in \(B\). \(c(A)\) need not maximize \(v\).

q: OR Problem 2.4 (variant of satisficing): as satisficing, except that if no alternative is satisfactory she chooses the one with the highest \(v\) (assume \(v\) is one-to-one). Which preference rationalizes it?
options: Satisfactory alternatives in the order \(O\), then unsatisfactory alternatives in reverse \(O\)
Satisfactory alternatives in the order \(O\), then unsatisfactory alternatives ranked by decreasing \(v\)
explain: If a menu has a satisfactory element, she picks the first in \(O\), as before, so satisfactory ones go on top in the order \(O\). If not, she maximizes \(v\), so unsatisfactory ones are ranked by \(v\). Ranking everything by \(v\) is wrong whenever two satisfactory alternatives appear in the \"wrong\" \(v\)-order. Reverse \(O\) was the rule for the original satisficing, where the last examined is chosen.

q: OR Problem 2.1a: she has a strict ranking of candidates, orders the menu alphabetically, and moves down the list while each new candidate is better than the previous one, stopping at the first candidate who is better than the next (otherwise taking the last). With candidates \(a,b,c\) (alphabetical) and true ranking \(c\succ a\succ b\), which shows \(\alpha\) fails?
options: No violation: the procedure always picks the best candidate
explain: In \(\{a,b,c\}\), she compares \(a\) with \(b\). Since \(a\succ b\), \(a\) is better than the next, so she stops at \(a\). In \(\{a,c\}\), \(c\) is better than \(a\), so she moves on and takes the last, \(c\). So \(c(X)=a\in\{a,c\}\) but \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), and \(\alpha\) fails. Option 3 is wrong because \(c(\{a,b\})=a\). The procedure finds a local, not a global, best.

q: OR Problem 2.1b (round robin): teams 1, 2, 3 with 1 beating 2, 2 beating 3, 3 beating 1. From a menu she picks the team with most wins within the menu, breaking ties by lowest index. Which is correct?
explain: In \(\{1,2,3\}\) each team has one win, so the lowest index, 1, is chosen. In \(\{1,3\}\) team 3 beats 1, so it has more wins and is chosen. Since \(1\in\{1,3\}\) but \(c(\{1,3\})=3\), \(\alpha\) fails and the procedure is not rationalizable. Tie-breaking applies only when win counts are equal, which they are not in \(\{1,3\}\).

q: OR Problem 2.1d: she has two functions \(u,v\) on \(X\) (assume each is one-to-one). From \(A\) she takes the \(u\)-maximal element if its \(u\) value is at least 10; otherwise she takes the \(v\)-maximal element of \(A\). Is this rationalizable?
options: No: it combines two criteria, so it must violate \(\alpha\)
Yes, by ranking all alternatives by \(u\)
Yes, by ranking all alternatives by \(v\)
