Yes, by ranking alternatives with \(u\geq10\) on top in decreasing \(u\), then all others in decreasing \(v\)
explain: If \(A\) contains some \(x\) with \(u(x)\geq10\), the \(u\)-maximum of \(A\) has \(u\geq10\) and is chosen: it is the best of the top block. If not, all elements are in the bottom block and the \(v\)-maximum is chosen. So the two-block ranking rationalizes \(c\). Mixing criteria does not by itself break \(\alpha\). Problem 2.6 (\"caring up to a limit\") is the variant that is not rationalizable.

q: OR Problem 2.1e: alternatives are red or blue; she has a preference \(\succ\) and chooses the best alternative among those of the color more common in \(A\) (ties in counts: choose among red). With \(X=\{r,b_1,b_2\}\) (\(r\) red, \(b_i\) blue) and \(r\succ b_1\succ b_2\):
options: \(c(X)=r\) and the procedure is rationalizable by \(\succ\)
\(c(\{r,b_1\})\) is undefined because of the tie
explain: In \(X\), blue is more common (2 vs 1), so she picks the best blue, \(b_1\). In \(\{r,b_1\}\) the counts tie, so she chooses among red and picks \(r\). Since \(b_1=c(X)\in\{r,b_1\}\) but \(c(\{r,b_1\})=r\), \(\alpha\) fails. The tie rule makes the choice well defined.

q: OR Problem 2.6 (caring up to a limit): from \(A\) she finds the \(u\)-maximal \(x\). If \(v(x)\geq v^*\) she picks \(x\), otherwise the \(v\)-maximal element of \(A\). Let \(X=\{x,y,z\}\), \(u(x)>u(y)>u(z)\), \(v(x)=1\), \(v(y)=5\), \(v(z)=10\), \(v^*=3\). Which is correct?
options: \(c(X)=z\) and \(c(\{y,z\})=z\), so the procedure is rationalizable by \(z\succ y\succ x\)
explain: In \(X\) the \(u\)-max is \(x\) with \(v(x)=1<3\), so she takes the \(v\)-max, \(z\). In \(\{y,z\}\) the \(u\)-max is \(y\) with \(v(y)=5\geq3\), so she takes \(y\). Since \(z=c(X)\in\{y,z\}\) but \(c(\{y,z\})=y\), \(\alpha\) fails. Interpretation: she lets her friend (measured by \(u\)) have their way unless it costs her too much (\(v\) below \(v^*\)).

q: OR Problem 2.5b: path independence (\(c(A\cup B)=c(\{c(A),c(B)\})\) for disjoint \(A,B\)) implies \(\alpha\). Let \(B\subset A\) with \(c(A)\in B\). The key step is
options: note that \(c(B)\in A\) and \(c(A)\in B\), then apply transitivity
use Proposition 2-2 to get a preference, then apply Proposition 2-1

write \(A=B\cup(A\setminus B)\), a disjoint union with \(A\setminus B\neq\emptyset\). Then \(c(A)=c(\{c(B),c(A\setminus B)\})\in\{c(B),c(A\setminus B)\}\), and since \(c(A)\in B\) while \(c(A\setminus B)\notin B\), \(c(A)=c(B)\)
write \(A=B\cup B\) and apply path independence
explain: Split \(A\) into the disjoint pieces \(B\) and \(A\setminus B\), which is nonempty because \(B\) is a proper subset. Path independence says the overall choice is one of the two sub-winners. \(c(A)\) lies in \(B\), and \(c(A\setminus B)\) does not, so \(c(A)\) must be \(c(B)\). \(B\cup B\) is not a disjoint union. Using Prop 2-2 would be circular, since it presupposes \(\alpha\).

q: True or false: if \(c\) is induced by maximizing a preference relation (each menu has a unique best element), then \(c\) is path independent: \(c(A\cup B)=c(\{c(A),c(B)\})\) for disjoint \(A,B\).
explain: True (OR Problem 2.5a). The best element of \(A\cup B\) lies in \(A\) or in \(B\), so it is the best of that part, that is \(c(A)\) or \(c(B)\). Being best overall, it beats the other sub-winner, so it is chosen from \(\{c(A),c(B)\}\).

q: OR Problem 2.1c: pictures are filtered by ordered binary criteria \(1,\dots,L\). Reject those failing criterion 1, then (among the rest) those failing criterion 2, and so on, until one remains (any two pictures differ on some criterion). Is this rationalizable?
options: Yes, by counting the number of criteria met
Yes, by the lexicographic ordering of the criteria vectors: \(x\succ y\) if \(x\) meets the first criterion on which they differ
explain: The survivor of the elimination is the lexicographically best picture in the menu: at the first criterion where pictures differ, those meeting it win. This lexicographic order on a finite set is a strict preference, and it rationalizes \(c\). Counting criteria met is a different order: one picture can meet more criteria in total yet fail an earlier, more important one.

q: Money pump (slide 20): \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{a,c\})=c\), \(c(\{b,c\})=b\), and you hold \(a\). Which sequence of trades, each costing €1, returns you to \(a\) €3 poorer?
options: No sequence works, because \(a\) is chosen from \(\{a,b\}\)
explain: Holding \(a\), you prefer \(c\) (since \(c(\{a,c\})=c\)) and pay €1 to switch. Holding \(c\), you prefer \(b\) (since \(c(\{b,c\})=b\)) and pay €1. Holding \(b\), you prefer \(a\) (since \(c(\{a,b\})=a\)) and pay €1. You are back at \(a\), €3 poorer, and the cycle repeats. The order \(a\to b\) fails at the first step, because you would not pay to swap \(a\) for \(b\).

q: What is the purpose of the money pump argument in Topic 2?
options: It shows that rational individuals are always risk averse
It is a defence of assuming rationalizable (transitive, \(\alpha\)-consistent) choice: inconsistent choosers can be exploited repeatedly, so behaviour that harms the individual should not survive
It shows that framing effects disappear when money is involved
It proves that every choice function on a finite set satisfies \(\alpha\)
explain: The argument justifies the rationality assumption: someone with cyclic choices will pay for a sequence of swaps that leaves her where she began, poorer, and can be pumped indefinitely. The \"trader who thinks 2 + 3 = 6\" question makes the same point about survival in markets. OR notes that its force depends on the individual not noticing the exploitation. It is an argument, not a theorem about \(\alpha\).

q: OR shows a money pump exists for any choice function violating \(\alpha\): there are \(B\subset A\) with \(c(A)\in B\) and \(c(B)\neq c(A)\). Starting from \(c(A)\), the manipulation repeats which two steps?
options: (i) offer to replace \(c(A)\) by any element of \(B\setminus\{c(A)\}\), and she picks \(c(B)\); (ii) offer to replace \(c(B)\) by any element of \(A\setminus\{c(B)\}\), and she picks \(c(A)\)
(i) offer an element of \(A\setminus B\); (ii) offer an element of \(B\setminus A\)
(i) offer every element of \(X\); (ii) take back the chosen one
explain: Holding \(c(A)\) and offered the rest of \(B\), she effectively chooses from \(B\) and takes \(c(B)\neq c(A)\), paying something. Holding \(c(B)\) and offered the rest of \(A\), she chooses from \(A\) and returns to \(c(A)\), paying again. This repeats forever. \(B\setminus A\) is empty since \(B\subset A\).

q: True or false: according to OR, the money pump argument is a decisive proof that real individuals' choices are rationalizable.
explain: False. It is offered as a justification for assuming rationalizable choice, but OR stresses that its effectiveness depends on the manipulated individual not noticing the exploitation, and leaves it to the reader to judge its persuasiveness. The experiments in Section 2.6 show that real choices do sometimes violate rationality.

q: Attention (decoy) experiment: Camera A (rating 9.1, 6 MP), B (8.3, 9 MP), C (8.1, 7 MP). Results: from {A,B}, 48% A / 52% B; from {A,B,C}, 30% A / 68% B / 2% C. Which statement is correct?
options: The experiment shows a violation of transitivity in pairwise choices
C is dominated by A on both attributes
The data are consistent with \(\alpha\) for every individual, because almost nobody chooses C
C is dominated by B (lower rating and fewer megapixels), but not by A. Adding C shifts choices toward B, so an individual who picks A from {A,B} and B from {A,B,C} violates \(\alpha\)
explain: B (8.3, 9) beats C (8.1, 7) on both attributes. A has a higher rating than C but fewer megapixels (6 < 7), so A does not dominate C. For such an individual, \(c(\{A,B,C\})=B\in\{A,B\}\) while \(c(\{A,B\})=A\), which violates \(\alpha\). That almost nobody picks C is the point: an \"irrelevant\" unchosen alternative changes choices. Only pairwise data on a single pair is involved, so this is not a transitivity cycle.

q: Which two explanations do the slides give for the camera (decoy) result?
options: The availability of C directs attention to B, which dominates it; and B's dominance over C provides a reason to choose B that does not apply to A
People choose the median alternative, and megapixels are more important than ratings
explain: The slides give an attention explanation (C draws focus to the alternative that dominates it, B) and a reason-based explanation (dominating C gives a justification for choosing B). Both make the choice between A and B depend on an irrelevant alternative. Mental accounting is the theatre experiment.

q: Theatre experiment: (1) you lost a $40 ticket and can buy another; (2) you lost $40 in cash and can still buy the $40 ticket. 65% buy in (1) and 79% buy in (2). Why is this inconsistent with the standard model?
options: Because in both cases the options are the same: be $80 poorer and see the show, or be $40 poorer and not see it. A choice should depend only on the set of options, not on its description
Because the money pump can be applied
Because it violates Property \(\alpha\) on a three-element set
Because buying a second ticket is never rational
explain: The final outcomes coincide across the two framings, so a rational individual faces the same choice problem and should answer the same way. The difference suggests mental accounting: in (1) the ticket \"costs\" $80, while in (2) the lost cash is treated as unrelated. This challenges the assumption that choice depends only on the set of alternatives, not on how it is described. It is not an \(\alpha\) violation, since there is no nested menu.

q: Framing experiment (OR 2.6.2): roulette A (90% $0, 6% $45, 1% $30, 3% -$15) vs B (90% $0, 7% $45, 1% -$10, 2% -$15); about 51% choose A. Roulette C splits A's Yellow 3% into 1% and 2%; D splits B's Red 7% into 6% and 1%; 93% choose D. What does this show?
options: It is a violation of transitivity
People always prefer roulettes with more colours
A and C (and B and D) are the same lotteries described differently, yet choices differ: the presentation changes the procedure used (cancelling similar parts vs checking dominance)
Nothing, since A and C are different lotteries
explain: C is A with one outcome split into two contingencies, and D is B with one outcome split, so in outcomes A = C and B = D. D visibly dominates C, and 93% choose D, while only about 49% choose B over A. The different presentations lead people to simplify by cancelling similar components in the A/B problem and to apply dominance in the C/D problem. This is a framing effect: choice depends on the description, not just the alternatives.

q: Which experiment from Topic 2 is described in OR as conflicting with Property \(\alpha\), as opposed to challenging description-invariance (framing)?
options: Mental accounting (lost ticket vs lost cash)
explain: In the camera experiment, adding C to {A,B} changes choices between A and B, which is a nested-menu (\(\alpha\)) pattern. The roulette and theatre experiments present the same set of options in different descriptions, so they challenge the assumption that choice depends only on the set of alternatives. They contain no nested menus to which \(\alpha\) could apply.

q: \"Can a trader who thinks that 2 + 3 = 6 survive in our cruel world?\" (slide 21, OR Problem 2.8). The intended point is
options: Rationality requires correct arithmetic, so the trader violates completeness
Arithmetic errors are irrelevant in markets, since prices adjust
The trader satisfies Property \(\alpha\), so he survives

Like an agent with cyclic choices, a systematically inconsistent trader can be exploited by others (e.g. by repeatedly buying 2 and 3 separately and selling them as 6), so such behaviour tends not to survive. This is an evolutionary/market defence of consistency
explain: The question parallels the money pump: an inconsistency (paying for 6 what costs 5) can be arbitraged repeatedly, draining the trader. The argument is that market pressure weeds out such inconsistencies, supporting the assumption of rational behaviour. As with the money pump, its strength depends on others actually spotting and exploiting the mistake.

q: True or false: a choice function \(c\) on \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(c(\{a,b\})=a\), \(c(\{a,b,c\})=c\) necessarily violates Property \(\alpha\).
explain: False. \(\alpha\) applies to \(B=\{a,b\}\subset A=X\) only if \(c(X)\in B\), and here \(c(X)=c\notin\{a,b\}\). Adding \(c\) and switching to it is fully consistent with rationality, for example \(c\succ a\succ b\). The violation pattern would be: shrink the menu, the old choice is still available, and the choice changes.

q: Let \(Z=\mathbb{N}\) (the positive integers). According to Definition 3-1, which of the following is a lottery over \(Z\)?
explain: A lottery assigns positive probability to finitely many prizes, zero to all others, and the probabilities sum to 1. \(p(n)=2^{-n}\) sums to 1 but has infinite support, so it is not a lottery in the sense of Definition 3-1. A negative 'probability' is not allowed even if the total is 1, and probabilities summing to 0.8 are not a lottery.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) and \(p=\tfrac12\cdot\$100\oplus\tfrac12\cdot\$1\). What is \(\mathrm{supp}(p)\)?
explain: The support is the set of prizes with positive probability, \(\{z\in Z: p(z)>0\}\). Here \(p(\$10)=0\), so \(\$10\) is excluded. The support is a set of prizes, not of probabilities, and it contains every prize with positive probability, not only the best one.

q: Geometrically, what is the set \(\Lz\) when \(Z=\{z_1,z_2,z_3\}\)?
options: A triangle (2-dimensional simplex) whose vertices are the degenerate lotteries \([z_1],[z_2],[z_3]\)
explain: Each lottery is a vector \((p_1,p_2,p_3)\ge 0\) with \(p_1+p_2+p_3=1\): the simplex, drawn as a triangle with the sure prizes at the corners. With two prizes it is a segment. The orthant and the cube ignore the constraint that probabilities sum to 1.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\), \(p=\tfrac12\cdot[\$100]\oplus\tfrac12\cdot[\$1]\) and \(q=[\$10]\). What is the compound lottery \(r=\tfrac12\cdot p\oplus\tfrac12\cdot q\), written as \((r(\$100),r(\$10),r(\$1))\)?
explain: By Definition 3-3, \(r(z)=\tfrac12 p(z)+\tfrac12 q(z)\): \(\$100\): \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14\); \(\$10\): \(\tfrac12\cdot 1=\tfrac12\); \(\$1\): \(\tfrac14\). (1/2,1/2,1/2) does not sum to 1 (it forgets to multiply along branches), and (1/2,0,1/2) is just \(p\).

q: Let \(Z=\{W,D,L\}\), \(p=0.6\cdot W\oplus 0.4\cdot L\) and \(q=0.2\cdot W\oplus0.3\cdot D\oplus0.5\cdot L\). What is the compound lottery \(\tfrac12\cdot p\oplus\tfrac12\cdot q\)?
explain: Each prize gets \(\tfrac12 p(z)+\tfrac12 q(z)\): W: 0.3+0.1=0.4; D: 0+0.15=0.15; L: 0.2+0.25=0.45 (sum 1). The second option adds without weighting (sum 2); the others are arithmetic slips that do not even match the weighted formula.

q: In the model of the slides, a compound lottery \(\alpha_1\cdot p_1\oplus\dots\oplus\alpha_K\cdot p_K\) is itself an element of \(\Lz\), so the decision maker cares only about the reduced probabilities of the final prizes.
explain: Definition 3-3 defines the compound lottery as the simple lottery giving each \(z\) probability \(\sum_k\alpha_k p_k(z)\). Preferences are defined on \(\Lz\), so two-stage and one-stage lotteries with the same reduced probabilities are the same object. This is exactly what lets independence be stated with compound lotteries.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) with \(\$100\succ\$10\succ\$1\). A pessimist ranks lotteries by the worst prize with positive probability. Compare \(p=(0.9,0,0.1)\) and \(q=(0.5,0.5,0)\).
explain: The worst prize in the support of \(p\) is \$1, in the support of \(q\) it is \$10, and \(\$10\succ\$1\), so \(q\succ p\). An expected-value maximiser would pick \(p\) (90.1 vs 55), which is the tempting wrong answer. The pessimist's relation is complete, so the lotteries can always be compared.

options: \(p\sim q\) because both give a bad prize with positive probability
explain: \(G(p)=0.9>0.5=G(q)\), so \(p\succ q\). Only the total probability of good prizes matters; how the bad probability is split between \$10 and \$1 is irrelevant.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) and \(p\pr q\iff|\mathrm{supp}(p)|\le|\mathrm{supp}(q)|\) ('minimizing options'). Compare \(p=(0,0,1)\) and \(q=(0.5,0.5,0)\).
options: Undefined, since \(p\) gives the worst prize
explain: \(p=[\$1]\) has support size 1, \(q\) has support size 2, so \(p\succ q\). This individual ignores the prizes themselves and wants to be prepared for as few outcomes as possible. Getting \$1 for sure is the best kind of lottery for them.

q: Which statement is exactly Definition 3-2 (continuity of \(\pr\) over \(\Lz\))?
options: For any prizes \(a,b,c\), there is \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) with \([b]\sim\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\).
For any lotteries \(p,q\), the set \(\{r: r\pr p\}\) is open.
For any prizes \(a,b,c\) with \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\) there is \(\alpha\) with \(0<\alpha<1\) such that \([b]\sim\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\).
For any prizes \(a,b,c\) with \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\) there is \(\alpha\) with \(0<\alpha<1\) such that \([b]\succ\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\).
explain: Continuity asks that every strictly intermediate prize be exactly matched by some mixture of the better and worse prize. The strict version (\(\succ\)) is satisfied even by the pessimist. Dropping the hypothesis \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\) gives a condition that fails trivially (take \(b\) better than both \(a\) and \(c\)).

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) with \(\$100\succ\$10\succ\$1\). Why does the pessimist violate continuity?
options: Because the pessimist's relation is not transitive.
Because \([\$100]\sim[\$1]\) for a pessimist, so there is no strict triple.
For every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) the worst prize of \(\alpha\cdot\$100\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot\$1\) is \$1, so this mixture is strictly worse than \([\$10]\); no \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) gives indifference.
explain: Only \(\alpha=1\) removes \$1 from the support. So the value 'jumps' from \$1 to \$100 and never equals \$10. The pessimist does rank \([\$100]\succ[\$10]\succ[\$1]\), so there is a strict triple, and the relation is complete and transitive. The mixtures are worse than \([\$10]\), not better.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\), good \(=\{\$100\}\), bad \(=\{\$10,\$1\}\). Do the 'good and bad' preferences satisfy continuity?
options: No, because \(G\) takes only the values 0 and 1.
Yes, vacuously: \([\$10]\sim[\$1]\), so there are no prizes \(a,b,c\) with \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\).
No: \([\$100]\succ[\$10]\) but no mixture of \$100 and \$1 is indifferent to \([\$10]\).
explain: With two classes only, every degenerate lottery has \(G\in\{0,1\}\), and there is never a strict triple. The hypothesis of continuity is never met, so the property holds vacuously. Note that \(G\) takes any value in \([0,1]\) on non-degenerate lotteries. The first option assumes \(\$10\succ\$1\), which is false here.

q: Let \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) and \(p\pr q\iff|\mathrm{supp}(p)|\le|\mathrm{supp}(q)|\). Is this relation continuous?
options: No, because \(\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\) has support size 2 and is never indifferent to \([b]\).
No, because the relation is not complete.
Yes, vacuously, because all degenerate lotteries are indifferent (support size 1), so no strict triple \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\) exists.
explain: Continuity only says something about strict triples of sure prizes. Every sure prize has support size 1, so \([a]\sim[b]\sim[c]\) for all prizes and the condition is never triggered. The first option is true about mixtures but irrelevant, since the hypothesis fails. \(\alpha=1\) is not allowed (\(0<\alpha<1\)).

q: PS1(e): Firefly ranks war strategies \(p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)\) over (Win, Draw, Lose) by \(p\pr q\iff p_3<q_3\) or \([p_3=q_3\) and \(p_2\le q_2]\). Why is this relation not continuous?
options: \([\text{Win}]\succ[\text{Draw}]\succ[\text{Lose}]\), but every \(\alpha\cdot\text{Win}\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot\text{Lose}=(\alpha,0,1-\alpha)\) with \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) has a positive chance of losing, so \([\text{Draw}]\) is strictly better than all of them.
Because mixing with a third lottery can reverse the ranking of two lotteries.
explain: \([\text{Draw}]=(0,1,0)\) has \(p_3=0\) while every proper mixture of Win and Lose has \(p_3=1-\alpha>0\), so Draw always wins on the first criterion. No chance of winning compensates any risk of losing, which is exactly what continuity rules out. The relation is transitive and independent (PS1 e i, iii).

q: A preference is consistent with EU with \(v(a)=9\), \(v(b)=5\), \(v(c)=1\). For which \(\alpha\) is \([b]\sim\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\)?
explain: Solve \(9\alpha+1\cdot(1-\alpha)=5\), i.e. \(8\alpha=4\), \(\alpha=1/2\). In general \(\alpha=(v(b)-v(c))/(v(a)-v(c))\), as in the proof of Proposition 3-1. \(5/9=v(b)/v(a)\) is the trap: it ignores that \(v(c)\neq0\).

q: 'I would never accept even a 0.0000001 chance of death, whatever the reward.' Let \(a\)= alive and rich, \(b\)= alive as now, \(c\)= dead. Which axiom does this attitude violate?
explain: With \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\), the person finds \([b]\succ\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot c\) for every \(\alpha<1\), so no mixture is indifferent to \([b]\). This is a lexicographic 'infinitely bad prize', the same structure as Firefly. Nothing here concerns mixing with a common third lottery (independence), and the ranking can be complete and transitive.

q: Which is the 'working form' of the independence axiom used in the PS solutions?
options: For all \(p,q,r\in\Lz\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\): \(p\pr q\iff\alpha\cdot p\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot r\pr\alpha\cdot q\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot r\).
For all \(p,q,r\): if \(p\pr r\) and \(r\pr q\), then \(p\pr q\).
For all \(p,q,r\): \(p\pr q\iff p\oplus r\pr q\oplus r\), where \(\oplus\) adds probability vectors.
For all \(p,q\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\): \(p\pr q\implies\alpha\cdot p\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot q\pr q\), but not conversely.
explain: Mixing both lotteries with the same third lottery \(r\), with the same weight, does not change their ranking. \(\oplus\) is not vector addition (the sum would not be a lottery). The third option is a convexity-type statement, and the last one is transitivity.

q: Definition 3-4 in the slides is stated with prizes. Which statement matches it?
options: \([z_k]\pr\lambda\cdot a\oplus(1-\lambda)\cdot b\) iff the lottery \(\alpha_1\cdot z_1\oplus\dots\oplus\alpha_k\cdot z_k\oplus\dots\oplus\alpha_K\cdot z_K\) is weakly preferred to the same lottery with \(z_k\) replaced by the sub-lottery \(\lambda\cdot a\oplus(1-\lambda)\cdot b\).
Every lottery is indifferent to the lottery obtained by replacing \(z_k\) with \(\lambda\cdot a\oplus(1-\lambda)\cdot b\).
\([z_k]\pr[a]\) iff \(z_k\) can be replaced by \(a\) in every lottery.
explain: The two lotteries differ only in the \(k\)-th term, so they should be ranked the way that term is ranked. The definition is an 'iff', so it also preserves strict preference and indifference. The other options either drop the 'iff' with the sub-lottery comparison or invent conditions.

q: Why is independence considered natural for lotteries but not for consumption bundles (slide 25)?
options: Because lotteries have finite support, while bundles do not.

Lottery outcomes are mutually exclusive: the individual gets \(L\) or \(L''\) instead of each other, never together, so \(L''\) should not affect the comparison of \(L\) and \(L'\); goods in a bundle are consumed together and can be complements.
Because consumers' preferences over bundles are never transitive.
Because probabilities are always rational numbers.
explain: In a coin-toss compound lottery, the tails branch gives the same \(L''\) in both options, and in the heads branch the preferred lottery wins. Since \(L''\) is consumed instead of \(L\), not with it, it is irrelevant. For goods (coffee and cake) there is no such argument. The other options are false or irrelevant.

q: Let \([a]\succ[b]\). Consider \(p=0.6\cdot a\oplus0.4\cdot b\) and \(q=0.6\cdot b\oplus0.4\cdot b=[b]\). What does independence require, and how does a pessimist rank them?
options: Independence says nothing, since \(q\) is degenerate.
Independence requires \(p\sim q\); the pessimist agrees.
Independence requires \(p\succ q\); the pessimist has \(p\sim q\), since both have worst prize \(b\). So the pessimist violates independence.
Independence requires \(p\succ q\); the pessimist also has \(p\succ q\).
explain: \(p\) and \(q\) differ only in the prize that occurs with probability 0.6: \(a\) versus \(b\). Since \([a]\succ[b]\), independence forces \(p\succ q\). The pessimist only looks at the worst prize, \(b\) in both, so \(p\sim q\). A degenerate lottery is a perfectly valid object for independence.

q: Let \(\$100\succ\$10\succ\$1\) and take \(\alpha=\tfrac12\). Which triple \((p,q,r)\) shows that the pessimist violates the working form of independence?
options: No such triple exists; the pessimist satisfies independence
explain: In the correct triple, the worst prizes are \$10 vs \$1, so \(p\succ q\). After mixing with \([\$1]\), both supports contain \$1, so the mixtures are indifferent: strict preference became a tie, which the 'iff' forbids. In the second option the mixtures are \([\$100]\) and \(\tfrac12\$10\oplus\tfrac12\$100\) (worst \$100 vs \$10), so the ranking is preserved. In the third they are \([\$10]\) and \(\tfrac12\$1\oplus\tfrac12\$10\) (worst \$10 vs \$1), also preserved. The trick is to choose \(r\) so that mixing destroys the feature the person cares about (the worst prize).

q: Show that 'minimizing options' (\(p\pr q\iff|\mathrm{supp}(p)|\le|\mathrm{supp}(q)|\)) violates independence. Which of the following is a valid counterexample?
options: The relation is not complete, so independence is not defined.
\([a]\sim[b]\), but \(\tfrac12\cdot a\oplus\tfrac12\cdot b\) (two prizes) is strictly worse than \(\tfrac12\cdot b\oplus\tfrac12\cdot b=[b]\).
explain: Independence applied to \([a]\sim[b]\) requires \(\tfrac12 a\oplus\tfrac12 b\sim\tfrac12 b\oplus\tfrac12 b=[b]\). But the left side has support size 2 and \([b]\) has size 1, so \([b]\) is strictly preferred. Sure prizes are never strictly ranked by this individual, so the third option's premise is false. The relation is complete, since support sizes are integers.

q: Why do 'good and bad' preferences (\(p\pr q\iff G(p)\ge G(q)\)) satisfy independence?
options: Because they are monotonic, and monotonicity implies independence.
Because \(G\) takes only the values 0 and 1.

\(G\) is linear in probabilities: \(G(\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)r)=\alpha G(p)+(1-\alpha)G(r)\), so the common term cancels and the comparison of the mixtures is the comparison of \(G(p)\) and \(G(q)\).
explain: Linearity in probabilities is the key. In fact \(G\) is an expected utility with \(v=1\) on good prizes and \(v=0\) on bad ones. Continuity is a different axiom and does not give independence. \(G\) takes all values in \([0,1]\). Monotonicity does not imply independence (PS1 f), only the converse holds.

q: PS1(e) iii: Firefly's preference (minimise \(p_3\), then minimise \(p_2\)) is independent. What is the key step?
options: Mixing with \(r\) makes all lotteries indifferent.

Mixing with \(r\) at weight \(\alpha>0\) turns \(p_3,q_3\) into \(\alpha p_3+(1-\alpha)r_3\) and \(\alpha q_3+(1-\alpha)r_3\), ordered as \(p_3,q_3\). If \(p_3=q_3\), the same holds for the second coordinates.
Firefly's preference is continuous, and continuous preferences are independent.
Firefly's preference has an EU representation, so it is independent by Proposition 3-1.
explain: Each comparison criterion is an affine function of the probabilities, so mixing with a common \(r\) preserves each lexicographic comparison. Firefly is not continuous and has no EU (not even a real-valued) representation, so the second option is false. Mixing does not create indifference.

q: PS1(e): Firefly's lexicographic preference over (Win, Draw, Lose) cannot be represented by any expected utility. Which assumption of the EU theorem fails?
options: Only continuity (it is complete, transitive and independent)
explain: (i) Complete and transitive: compare \(p_3\), then \(p_2\), which are real numbers. (ii) Continuity fails: Draw beats every proper mixture of Win and Lose. (iii) Independence holds because each criterion is linear in probabilities. Lesson: lexicographic structure kills continuity.

q: Let \(Z=\{a,b,c\}\) and suppose \(p\pr q\iff p(a)^2\ge q(a)^2\). Which statement is correct?
options: The relation satisfies continuity (vacuously) and independence; it is consistent with EU with \(v(a)=1\), \(v(b)=v(c)=0\).
It is not a preference relation because \(p(a)^2\) is not an expected utility.
It violates independence because \(p(a)^2\) is not linear in probabilities.
It violates continuity because \([a]\succ[b]\) and no mixture of \(a\) and \(c\) is indifferent to \([b]\).
explain: Since \(p(a)\ge0\), \(p(a)^2\ge q(a)^2\iff p(a)\ge q(a)\). So the relation is the 'good and bad' preference with good = \(\{a\}\), which is EU. A non-linear utility can still represent an EU preference: what matters is the relation, not the formula. \([b]\sim[c]\), so there is no strict triple and continuity holds vacuously.

q: Which of the following preference relations over \(\Lz\), \(Z=\{a,b,c\}\), is consistent with expected utility?
explain: \(p(a)-p(c)=\sum_z p(z)v(z)\) with \(v(a)=1\), \(v(b)=0\), \(v(c)=-1\). The pessimist violates continuity and independence, minimizing options violates independence, and the lexicographic relation violates continuity. By Proposition 3-1, none of these three can be EU.

q: What does it mean for a preference \(\pr\) over \(\Lz\) to be monotonic (slides, Topic 3.1)?
options: More of every good is better.
For prizes \(a,b\) with \([a]\succ[b]\), lotteries \(\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\) are ranked by \(\alpha\): higher probability of the better prize is better.
If \(p\) gives at least as much money as \(q\) in every state, then \(p\pr q\).
explain: Monotonicity over lotteries only concerns lotteries supported on two prizes. The last option is monotonicity over bundles (Topic 4), and the first is a dominance idea. Because it only concerns two-prize lotteries, monotonicity is weak, which is why it does not imply independence.

q: Lemma 3-1 (independence implies monotonicity): assume \(\pr\) satisfies independence and \([a]\succ[b]\). Which conclusion does the lemma give?
options: \(\alpha>\beta\implies\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\pr\beta\cdot a\oplus(1-\beta)\cdot b\), but strictness can fail
\(\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\succ\beta\cdot a\oplus(1-\beta)\cdot b\implies[a]\succ[b]\) for all \(\alpha,\beta\)
explain: The lemma gives strict preference whenever \(\alpha>\beta\), using the hypothesis \([a]\succ[b]\) (strict). Strictness survives because independence is an 'iff' and so preserves strict comparisons. The other options either weaken the conclusion or reverse the roles of hypothesis and conclusion.

q: Proof of Lemma 3-1, step 1: let \(p=\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\) with \(\alpha>0\) and \([a]\succ[b]\). How does one show \(p\succ[b]\)?
options: By independence: replace \(a\) by \(b\) in the \(\alpha\)-weighted term; since \([a]\succ[b]\), \(p\succ\alpha\cdot b\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b=[b]\).
explain: The two lotteries differ only in the \(\alpha\)-weighted prize (\(a\) vs \(b\)), so independence transfers \([a]\succ[b]\) to \(p\succ[b]\). Continuity is not assumed in the lemma. The transitivity option assumes what needs to be proved.

q: Proof of Lemma 3-1, step 2: with \(p=\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\succ[b]\) and \(\alpha>\beta\), one writes \(\beta\cdot a\oplus(1-\beta)\cdot b\) as a mixture of \(p\) and \([b]\). Which mixture?
explain: The mixture \(\gamma\cdot p\oplus(1-\gamma)\cdot b\) gives \(a\) with probability \(\gamma\alpha\), so \(\gamma=\beta/\alpha\in[0,1)\). Then independence gives \(p=(\beta/\alpha)p\oplus(1-\beta/\alpha)p\succ(\beta/\alpha)p\oplus(1-\beta/\alpha)b\). \(\alpha/\beta>1\) is not a probability, and \(\beta\cdot p\) gives \(a\) with probability \(\alpha\beta\), not \(\beta\).

q: If a preference relation over \(\Lz\) is monotonic, then it satisfies independence.
explain: Lemma 3-1 only gives independence \(\Rightarrow\) monotonicity. PS1(f) builds a monotone preference that violates independence: it is EU on two-prize lotteries, where monotonicity looks, and does something odd on three-prize lotteries. 'Minimizing options' is another example, since it is vacuously monotone (no \([a]\succ[b]\)) yet violates independence.

q: PS1(f): on \(Z=\{a,b,c\}\) let \(U(p)=2p_1+p_2-10\,p_1p_2p_3\). Why is the induced preference monotonic?
options: A two-prize lottery has some \(p_i=0\), so the product term vanishes and \(U=2p_1+p_2\), an EU with \(v(a)=2,v(b)=1,v(c)=0\), which is monotone.
explain: Monotonicity only concerns two-prize lotteries, and on them \(U\) is exactly expected utility, which ranks \(\alpha\cdot x\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot y\) by \(\alpha\) when \(v(x)>v(y)\). \(U\) is not linear overall (the cubic term), and the preference is not independent, which is the whole point.

q: PS1(f) with \(U(p)=2p_1+p_2-10p_1p_2p_3\): \(\tfrac12 a\oplus\tfrac12 b\) has \(U=1.5\) and \(\tfrac12 a\oplus\tfrac12 c\) has \(U=1\). Mix each with \([c]\) at weight \(\tfrac12\). What are the utilities of \(\tfrac14 a\oplus\tfrac14 b\oplus\tfrac12 c\) and \(\tfrac14 a\oplus\tfrac34 c\)?
options: \(0.4375\) and \(0.25\), so the ranking is preserved
\(0.6875\) and \(0.5\), so the ranking is preserved
\(0.75\) and \(0.5\), so the ranking is preserved
\(0.4375\) and \(0.5\), so the ranking reverses and independence fails
explain: First: \(2\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac14-10\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12=0.5+0.25-0.3125=0.4375\). Second: \(2\cdot\tfrac14+0=0.5\) (no \(b\), so the product is 0). Before mixing the first was better (1.5 > 1), after mixing it is worse, so independence fails. 0.75 forgets the product term.

q: The official PS1(f) example ranks every lottery with at most two prizes above every three-prize lottery (two-prize ones by \(2p_1+p_2\), three-prize ones lexicographically by \((p_1,p_2)\)). Why does it violate independence?
options: \(\tfrac12 a\oplus\tfrac12 b\succ\tfrac12 a\oplus\tfrac12 c\), but mixing both with \([c]\) at \(\tfrac12\) gives \(\tfrac14 a\oplus\tfrac14 b\oplus\tfrac12 c\) (three prizes, bottom group), which is worse than \(\tfrac14 a\oplus\tfrac34 c\) (two prizes, top group).
Because two-prize lotteries are ranked by expected utility.
explain: Mixing with \(c\) adds a third prize to one lottery but not to the other, which throws it into the bottom group and reverses the ranking. The relation is complete, transitive and monotonic by construction. Ranking two-prize lotteries by EU is what makes it monotone, not what breaks independence.

q: A pessimist with \([a]\succ[b]\) ranks \(\alpha\cdot a\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot b\) for \(\alpha\in[0,1)\) all as indifferent to \([b]\). What follows via Lemma 3-1?
options: The pessimist is not monotonic, so it cannot be complete.
The pessimist is monotonic, so it satisfies independence.
Nothing: Lemma 3-1 applies only to continuous preferences.
The pessimist is not monotonic, so by the contrapositive of Lemma 3-1 it cannot satisfy independence.
explain: Take \(\alpha=0.6>\beta=0.3\): monotonicity demands strict preference, but the pessimist is indifferent. Lemma 3-1 says independence \(\Rightarrow\) monotonicity, so failing monotonicity proves that independence fails. The lemma does not assume continuity, and the pessimist is complete.

q: 'Minimizing options' preferences (\(p\pr q\iff|\mathrm{supp}(p)|\le|\mathrm{supp}(q)|\)) are monotonic.
explain: Monotonicity is a statement about prizes \(a,b\) with \([a]\succ[b]\). Here all sure prizes are indifferent (support size 1), so the condition is never triggered and monotonicity holds vacuously. Since this relation violates independence, it is also an example that monotonicity does not imply independence.

q: Definition 3-5: \(\pr\) on \(\Lz\) is consistent with expected utility if...
options: there is a concave \(v:Z\to\R\) such that \(U(p)=v(\sum_z p(z)z)\) represents \(\pr\).
there is \(v:Z\to\R\) such that \(U(p)=\sum_{z\in Z}p(z)v(z)\) represents \(\pr\); \(v\) is called the Bernoulli function.
\(p\pr q\iff E(p)\ge E(q)\), where \(E\) is the expected monetary value.
explain: EU requires a representation that is linear in the probabilities, with the weights \(v(z)\) attached to prizes. Any complete, transitive relation on a finite set has some utility, which is much weaker. Expected value is the special case \(v(z)=z\). \(v(E(p))\) is the utility of the mean, not expected utility.
\(U(p)=0.9\cdot1+0\cdot0.4+0.1\cdot0=0.9\). \(U(q)=0.5\cdot1+0.5\cdot0.4=0.7\). Hence \(p\succ q\). 1.1 comes from wrongly adding \(0.5+0.4+\dots\) without weighting \(v(\$10)\) by its probability.

q: Normalise \(v(a)=1\), \(v(c)=0\) and suppose \([b]\sim0.6\cdot a\oplus0.4\cdot c\). Under EU, compare \(p=(0.3,0.4,0.3)\) and \(q=[b]=(0,1,0)\) (order \(a,b,c\)).
explain: The indifference gives \(v(b)=0.6\cdot1+0.4\cdot0=0.6\). Then \(U(p)=0.3+0.4\cdot0.6+0=0.54\) and \(U(q)=0.6\). The distractor 0.4 takes \(v(b)\) from the weight on \(c\), and 0.66 comes from \(0.3+0.4\cdot0.9\).

q: EU with \(v(0)=0\), \(v(50)=6\), \(v(100)=10\). For which \(\lambda\) is \([50]\sim\lambda\cdot[100]\oplus(1-\lambda)\cdot[0]\)?
explain: \(10\lambda=6\), so \(\lambda=0.6\). The answer is not 0.5: 50 is the mean of a 50/50 lottery, but this \(v\) is concave (risk averse), so the person demands more than a 50% chance of 100 to give up 50 for sure.

q: Proposition 3-1 states that...
options: a continuous preference relation is consistent with EU.
a preference relation consistent with EU satisfies continuity and independence (the axioms are necessary for EU).
a preference relation consistent with EU is risk averse.
a preference relation that satisfies continuity and independence is consistent with EU.
explain: Proposition 3-1 is the 'easy' direction, EU \(\Rightarrow\) continuity + independence, and holds for any \(Z\). The converse, for finite \(Z\), is Proposition 3-2. Risk aversion corresponds to concavity of \(v\) and is a separate result (Topic 3.2).

q: Proof of Proposition 3-1 (independence part): EU compares \(\alpha_1 v(z_1)+\dots+\alpha_k v(z_k)+\dots\) with \(\alpha_1 v(z_1)+\dots+\alpha_k[\lambda v(a)+(1-\lambda)v(b)]+\dots\). Which steps reduce this to \(v(z_k)\ge\lambda v(a)+(1-\lambda)v(b)\)?
options: Cancel the common terms \(\alpha_j v(z_j)\), \(j\neq k\), then divide by \(\alpha_k>0\).
explain: Since \(U\) is linear in probabilities, the two sums differ only in the \(k\)-th term. Dividing by \(\alpha_k>0\) preserves the inequality, and \(U\) represents \(\pr\) on both sides, so the inequality is \([z_k]\pr\lambda a\oplus(1-\lambda)b\). No continuity, concavity or monotonicity is needed.

q: Proposition 3-2 (continuity + independence \(\Rightarrow\) EU) has a hypothesis on the set of prizes in the slides. Which?
explain: The slides prove the result for a finite \(Z\). Finiteness ensures a best prize \(M\) and a worst prize \(m\) exist, so every prize can be calibrated between them. Prizes need not be monetary, and the theorem also holds (trivially) with one or two prizes.

q: In the proof of Proposition 3-2 (case \([M]\succ[m]\)), how is \(v(z)\) defined for each prize \(z\), and which axiom guarantees it exists?
options: \(v(z)\) is the rank of \(z\) in the order \([z_1]\pr\dots\pr[z_K]\); it exists by transitivity.
\(v(z)\) is the monetary value of \(z\); it exists by completeness.
\(v(z)\) is the number with \([z]\sim v(z)\cdot M\oplus(1-v(z))\cdot m\); it exists by independence.
\(v(z)\) is the number with \([z]\sim v(z)\cdot M\oplus(1-v(z))\cdot m\); it exists by continuity.
explain: Continuity gives, for each \(z\) strictly between \(M\) and \(m\), a mixture of \(M\) and \(m\) indifferent to \([z]\). (For \(z\sim M\) or \(z\sim m\), take 1 or 0.) Independence is used later to substitute these equivalents inside a lottery. A rank is ordinal and would not give an EU representation.

q: In the proof of Proposition 3-2, why is the number \(v(z)\) with \([z]\sim v(z)\cdot M\oplus(1-v(z))\cdot m\) unique?
options: By monotonicity (Lemma 3-1): since \([M]\succ[m]\), two different weights on \(M\) give strictly ranked lotteries, so at most one can be indifferent to \([z]\).
It is not unique; any such number can be chosen.
By continuity, which states that \(\alpha\) is unique.
explain: Continuity only asserts existence. If \(\alpha>\beta\) both worked, then \(\alpha M\oplus(1-\alpha)m\succ\beta M\oplus(1-\beta)m\) by Lemma 3-1, contradicting transitivity of indifference with \([z]\). Uniqueness comes from monotonicity, which itself follows from independence.

q: In the proof of Proposition 3-2, after independence is applied \(K\) times to \(p=p(z_1)\cdot z_1\oplus\dots\oplus p(z_K)\cdot z_K\), \(p\) is indifferent to which lottery?
explain: Each prize \(z_k\) is replaced by \(v(z_k)M\oplus(1-v(z_k))m\). Reducing the compound lottery, \(M\) occurs with probability \(\sum_k p(z_k)v(z_k)\), which is exactly the expected utility. The unweighted sum need not even be at most 1, and max and product ignore how probabilities combine in compound lotteries.

q: Final step of Proposition 3-2: \(p\sim U(p)\cdot M\oplus(1-U(p))\cdot m\) and \(q\sim U(q)\cdot M\oplus(1-U(q))\cdot m\). Why is \(p\pr q\iff U(p)\ge U(q)\)?
options: Because \([M]\succ[m]\) and, by monotonicity (Lemma 3-1), lotteries over \(M\) and \(m\) are ranked by the probability of \(M\).
explain: Both lotteries are now two-prize lotteries over the same \(M\) and \(m\), so monotonicity ranks them by the weight on \(M\). Combined with the indifferences and transitivity, this gives the representation. This is why the strict case \([M]\succ[m]\) is treated separately from \([M]\sim[m]\).

q: In the proof of Proposition 3-2, what happens in the case \([M]\sim[m]\)?
options: All sure prizes are indifferent, so by independence \(p\sim[M]\) for every lottery \(p\); the choice \(v(z)=0\) for all \(z\) gives \(U\equiv0\), which represents \(\pr\).
One sets \(v(M)=1\) and \(v(m)=0\) as in the other case.
The preference cannot be represented by any utility.
Continuity fails, so the theorem does not apply.
explain: If the best and worst prizes are indifferent, every prize is indifferent to \(M\). Replacing prizes one at a time (independence) shows every lottery is indifferent to \([M]\). A constant \(U\) represents total indifference. Setting \(v(M)=1\neq v(m)=0\) would wrongly rank \([M]\succ[m]\). Continuity holds vacuously here.

q: Following the vNM construction, suppose \([z]\sim0.3\cdot M\oplus0.7\cdot m\). The lottery \(p=0.5\cdot M\oplus0.5\cdot z\) is indifferent to which lottery?
explain: With \(v(M)=1\) and \(v(z)=0.3\), the probability of \(M\) is \(0.5\cdot1+0.5\cdot0.3=0.65\). Formally, independence replaces \(z\) by \(0.3M\oplus0.7m\), and reducing gives \(M\) with probability \(0.5+0.15\). 0.15 forgets the direct \(M\) branch, and 0.8 adds \(0.5+0.3\) without weighting.

q: Which matching of axioms to their role in the proof of the EU theorem (Proposition 3-2) is correct?
options: Completeness creates \(v(z)\); transitivity gives uniqueness; continuity gives the final comparison.

Continuity creates the numbers \(v(z)\); independence lets each prize be replaced by its equivalent \(M\)/\(m\) gamble inside a lottery; monotonicity (from independence) turns the final comparison into a comparison of numbers.
Continuity is used only in the case \([M]\sim[m]\).
Independence creates the numbers \(v(z)\); continuity lets each prize be replaced inside a lottery; monotonicity is an extra axiom.
explain: This is the calibration idea: \(v(z)\) is 'the chance of the jackpot you would accept in place of \(z\)' (continuity). Substitution inside lotteries is exactly independence. Monotonicity, derived from independence via Lemma 3-1, both makes \(v(z)\) unique and ranks \(M\)/\(m\) gambles. In the case \([M]\sim[m]\), only independence is needed.

q: Let \(Z\) be finite and \(\pr\) on \(\Lz\) be continuous and monotonic. Then \(\pr\) is consistent with expected utility.
explain: Counterexample: PS1(f), \(U(p)=2p_1+p_2-10p_1p_2p_3\). It is monotonic, and continuous: \(\alpha a\oplus(1-\alpha)c\) has \(U=2\alpha\), which equals \(U([b])=1\) at \(\alpha=1/2\). But it violates independence, so by Proposition 3-1 it is not EU. Monotonicity is strictly weaker than independence.

q: The pessimist's preference over \(\Lz\) with \(Z=\{\$100,\$10,\$1\}\) and \(\$100\succ\$10\succ\$1\) cannot be represented by any expected utility function.
explain: By Proposition 3-1, every EU preference is continuous and independent, and the pessimist violates both. Note that the pessimist does have an ordinary (non-EU) utility, e.g. the value of the worst prize, so 'no EU' does not mean 'no utility'.

q: Firefly's lexicographic preference (PS1 e) shows that the continuity axiom cannot be dropped from Proposition 3-2: it is a complete, transitive and independent preference that is not consistent with EU.
explain: Firefly satisfies independence but not continuity, and it is not EU (it has no real-valued utility at all). So independence alone is not sufficient, and continuity is a genuinely needed hypothesis.

q: Proposition 3-1 (EU implies continuity and independence) requires the set of prizes \(Z\) to be finite.
explain: The proof of Proposition 3-1 only uses that \(U(p)=\sum_z p(z)v(z)\) is linear in probabilities and that lotteries have finite support, so it works for any \(Z\). Finiteness of \(Z\) is used in Proposition 3-2, to obtain a best and a worst prize.

q: \(v\) is a Bernoulli function for an EU representation of \(\pr\). Which of the following is necessarily also a Bernoulli function for \(\pr\)?
explain: Bernoulli functions are unique up to positive affine transformations \(w=\alpha v+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\). A negative \(\alpha\) reverses all rankings. Non-linear increasing transformations (cube, exponential) preserve the ranking of sure prizes but generally change the ranking of lotteries.

q: A Bernoulli function on \((z_1,z_2,z_3)\) is \(v=(0,1,4)\). Which \(w\) represents the same preferences over \(\Lz\)?
explain: \(w=3v+2\): \((3\cdot0+2,\,3\cdot1+2,\,3\cdot4+2)=(2,5,14)\). Test: the ratio of differences \((w_3-w_2)/(w_2-w_1)\) must equal \((4-1)/(1-0)=3\). For (2,5,14) it is 9/3=3. For (0,1,16), i.e. \(v^2\), it is 15. For (1,2,6) it is 4. (4,3,0) is \(-v+4\), with negative slope.

q: If \(v>0\) is a Bernoulli function for \(\pr\), then \(w=v^3\) is also a Bernoulli function for \(\pr\), since it preserves the ranking of all prizes.
explain: Preserving the order of sure prizes is not enough, because EU adds utility differences weighted by probabilities. E.g. \(v=(1,2,3)\): \([z_2]\sim\tfrac12 z_1\oplus\tfrac12 z_3\) (2 = 2), but with \(w=(1,8,27)\), \(8<14\), so the ranking changes. Only positive affine transformations are allowed.

q: Risk-neutral \(v(z)=z\) prefers \(\tfrac12\cdot\$0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot\$100\) to \([\$40]\). What happens with \(w(z)=\sqrt z\)?
options: EU becomes \(5\) versus \(\sqrt{40}\approx6.32\), so \([\$40]\) is preferred: the ranking flips, showing \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is not an admissible transformation.
EU becomes \(5\) versus \(6.32\), so the lottery is still preferred.
EU becomes \(\sqrt{50}\approx7.07\) versus \(6.32\), so the lottery is still preferred.
The ranking is unchanged because \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is increasing.
explain: \(\tfrac12\sqrt0+\tfrac12\sqrt{100}=5<\sqrt{40}\approx6.32\). Since the ranking flips, \(v\) and \(\sqrt v\) represent different preferences over lotteries. \(\sqrt{50}\) computes the utility of the mean, not the expected utility. Being increasing only preserves rankings of sure prizes.

q: If \(U(p)=\sum_z p(z)v(z)\) represents \(\pr\) on \(\Lz\), then \(\tilde U(p)=e^{U(p)}\) also represents \(\pr\) (although \(\tilde U\) is not of the expected-utility form).
explain: Any strictly increasing transformation of a utility function represents the same relation (Topic 1, ordinal). The cardinality restriction concerns the Bernoulli function \(v\): replacing \(v\) by \(e^{v}\) inside the sum is generally not allowed. Transforming the whole \(U(p)\) is fine.
\(v_2>0.10v_1+0.89v_2+0.01v_3\); subtracting \(0.89v_2\) gives \(0.11v_2>0.10v_1+0.01v_3\). The third option forgets the \(0.89v_2\) on the right. The common 0.89 chance of 0.5M cancels.

q: Allais: \(L_2=(0,0.11,0.89)\), \(L_2'=(0.10,0,0.90)\) over (2.5M, 0.5M, 0). Most people choose \(L_1=(0,1,0)\) over \(L_1'=(0.10,0.89,0.01)\) and \(L_2'\) over \(L_2\). Is this pattern consistent with EU?
options: No, because the pattern violates transitivity.
No: \(L_2'\succ L_2\) requires \(0.10v_1+0.01v_3>0.11v_2\), the exact opposite of what \(L_1\succ L_1'\) requires.
explain: \(L_2'\succ L_2\): \(0.10v_1+0.90v_3>0.11v_2+0.89v_3\iff0.10v_1+0.01v_3>0.11v_2\). Combined with \(0.11v_2>0.10v_1+0.01v_3\), this is a contradiction for every \(v\), so no risk attitude can explain it. Transitivity is not violated: the four lotteries are distinct objects.

q: The slides ask whether the Allais choices (\(L_1\succ L_1'\) and \(L_2'\succ L_2\)) are 'rational'. What is the right answer?
options: Yes in the Topic 1 sense: there is a complete, transitive ranking of \(\{L_1,L_1',L_2,L_2'\}\) consistent with them. But no expected utility is consistent with them.
Yes, and they are also consistent with EU for a risk-averse \(v\).
No, because no utility function can represent them.
explain: E.g. \(L_1\succ L_1'\succ L_2'\succ L_2\) is a preference relation on these four objects, so the choices are rationalisable. EU is a stronger requirement (independence) and it fails here. 'Rational' and 'EU' are different properties.

q: Which axiom does the Allais pattern violate, and what is the 'common consequence'?
options: Continuity; the common consequence is the prize 0.
Completeness; people cannot compare the lotteries.
Independence; the common consequence is a 0.11 chance of 0.5M.
Independence; \(L_1,L_1'\) share a 0.89 chance of 0.5M and \(L_2,L_2'\) share a 0.89 chance of 0. Removing it leaves the same comparison '0.11 of 0.5M' vs '0.10 of 2.5M + 0.01 of 0' in both pairs.
explain: Each pair is a mixture with weight 0.11 of the same two sub-lotteries (\([0.5M]\) vs \(\tfrac{10}{11}2.5M\oplus\tfrac1{11}0\)), with weight 0.89 on a common lottery that differs across pairs. Independence says the common slice cannot matter. People react to it because certainty is special. Nothing here involves continuity.

q: The slides list four reactions to the Allais paradox. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Conclude that people's choices over lotteries violate transitivity, so the theory of preferences must be abandoned
Weaken independence, or define preferences over richer objects (e.g. regret theory)
The paradox is of limited significance because it involves probabilities close to 0 and 1
Treat choice under uncertainty as reflective: correct mistakes that are inconsistent with independence
explain: The four reactions are (1) a mistake to be corrected, (2) limited importance (extreme probabilities), (3) richer domains such as regret theory, (4) giving up independence for something weaker. Transitivity is not at stake: the Allais choices are transitive.

q: Common ratio (OR): \(L_1\): \$4000 w.p. 0.2; \(R_1\): \$3000 w.p. 0.25; \(L_2\): \$4000 w.p. 0.8; \(R_2\): \$3000 for sure (zero otherwise). Which identity links the pairs?
explain: \(0.25\cdot0.8=0.2\), so \(L_1\) is \(L_2\) mixed with \([0]\) at weight 0.25, and \(R_1\) is \(R_2\) with the same weight. Because the same \(r=[0]\) and the same \(\alpha=0.25\) are used, independence requires \(L_1\pr R_1\iff L_2\pr R_2\). The second option uses different weights and breaks this argument. With weight 0.2, \(L_1\) would pay 4000 w.p. 0.16.

q: In the common-ratio experiment (\(L_1\): 4000 w.p. 0.2; \(R_1\): 3000 w.p. 0.25; \(L_2\): 4000 w.p. 0.8; \(R_2\): 3000 for sure), which pairs of strict choices are consistent with EU?
options: All four pairs, for a suitable \(v\)
explain: Since \(L_1=0.25L_2\oplus0.75[0]\) and \(R_1=0.25R_2\oplus0.75[0]\), independence forces the same choice in both pairs. Under EU: \(R_2\succ L_2\iff v(3000)>0.8v(4000)+0.2v(0)\iff0.25v(3000)+0.75v(0)>0.2v(4000)+0.8v(0)\iff R_1\succ L_1\). The popular pair (\(L_1\), \(R_2\)), chosen by 44% in Rubinstein's data, violates EU.

\(U(L_1)=0.5\), \(U(L_1')=0.1+0.89\cdot0.5=0.545\); \(U(L_2)=0.055\), \(U(L_2')=0.1\). Both comparisons reduce to \(0.11\cdot0.5=0.055\) vs \(0.1\), so an EU maximiser picks the primed lottery in both pairs (or the unprimed in both, for other \(v\)). The popular mixed pattern (second option) is impossible under EU.

q: The slides give two justifications for the widespread use of EU. Which pair is correct?
options: Technical: EU needs no assumptions. Normative: everyone is risk neutral.
Technical: EU is analytically very convenient. Normative: if one accepts the axioms (notably independence), the theorem can guide decisions under risk.
Empirical: experiments confirm EU. Technical: it is the only representable preference.
Normative: EU maximises expected money. Empirical: the Allais paradox supports it.
explain: Slide 39: EU is easy to work with (hence pervasive), and it is a guide to action for people who find it hard to think about risk but endorse independence. Experiments (Allais, common ratio) are evidence against EU as a description of behaviour, and EU does not imply risk neutrality.

q: A student claims: 'Independence fails for a preference \(\pr\) because \(p\succ q\) and \(\tfrac12 p\oplus\tfrac12 r\sim\tfrac12 q\oplus\tfrac12 r\).' Is this a valid disproof of independence?
options: No: one needs \(\alpha\) close to 1, not \(\alpha=\tfrac12\).
No: one must also show that continuity fails.
No: independence only requires the weak preference \(\tfrac12 p\oplus\tfrac12 r\pr\tfrac12 q\oplus\tfrac12 r\), which holds.
Yes: independence is an 'iff', so \(p\succ q\) must give strict preference between the mixtures. A tie is a violation.
explain: From \(p\succ q\) we have \(q\not\pr p\). Independence gives \(\tfrac12 q\oplus\tfrac12 r\pr\tfrac12 p\oplus\tfrac12 r\iff q\pr p\), and the tie makes the left side true. So \(q\pr p\), a contradiction. This is exactly how the pessimist and minimizing-options counterexamples work. One \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) suffices.

q: Why does the SEU framework (Topic 3.3) use acts instead of lotteries?
options: In situations like a horse race, the probabilities of outcomes are not objective or observable, so objects cannot be described as known probability distributions over prizes.
Because in SEU the individual is assumed risk neutral.
Because acts have infinitely many prizes.
Because lotteries cannot represent monetary bets.
explain: SuperEnalotto odds are objective (1 in 622,614,630), so a ticket is a lottery. A bet on horse A has no given probability: someone betting on one of 3 horses does not necessarily have a 1/3 chance. Acts specify the prize in each state and leave the probabilities to the decision maker's beliefs.

q: In SEU, the set of states of the world \(\Omega\) is...
options: an exclusive and exhaustive list of all possible realizations of the uncertain situation
a list of the events the decision maker considers likely
the set of all lotteries over prizes
the set of prizes the decision maker can receive
explain: States are mutually exclusive (exactly one occurs) and exhaustive (one must occur). Prizes are the set \(Z\), and the uncertainty about which state occurs replaces the objective probabilities of lotteries. States are not restricted to the 'likely' ones.

q: A race among three horses A, B, C (no ties). If a state of the world is a full finishing order, how many states are there?
explain: A state is a full ordering of the three horses: \(3!=6\) (ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA). 3 counts only the possible winners: that grouping is enough to evaluate bets on the winner, but it is not the state list on the slides.

q: Definition 3-11: given prizes \(Z\) and a finite set of states \(\Omega\), an act is...
options: a function \(f:\Omega\to Z\) assigning a prize to each state
a function \(f:Z\to[0,1]\) assigning probabilities to prizes
explain: An act is defined by the outcome it gives in each state, and \(F\) is the set of all such functions. A function \(Z\to[0,1]\) is a lottery, and a distribution over \(\Omega\) is the belief \(\pi\), which is part of the representation, not of the act.

q: Act \(g\) is 'a 10 euro bet at odds of 2 to 1 that Challenger (C) will win'. Which prizes does \(g\) give?
options: \(+10\) in states where C wins, \(-10\) otherwise
\(+30\) in states where C wins, \(-10\) otherwise
\(+20\) in states where C wins, \(0\) otherwise
\(+20\) in states where C wins, \(-10\) in all other states
explain: At 2 to 1 odds, a winning 10 euro stake gains 20, and a losing bet loses the 10 euro stake. So \(g(CAB)=g(CBA)=+20\) and \(g=-10\) in the four states where A or B wins. Even money (the act \(f\) on Ace) would pay \(+10\).

q: Act \(f\) = 10 euro even-money bet on Ace. Which expression is the SEU of \(f\)?
explain: SEU sums \(\pi(\omega)v(f(\omega))\) over states: \(f\) pays 10 in the two states where A wins and \(-10\) in the other four. Using 1/3 imposes objective, equal probabilities, which SEU does not do. The last option is \(v\) of the expected payoff, not the expected utility.

q: With linear \(v\), let \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_C\) be the subjective probabilities that Ace and Challenger win. When is \(f\) (10 even money on A) weakly preferred to \(g\) (10 at 2:1 on C)?
explain: \(U(f)=10\pi_A-10(1-\pi_A)=20\pi_A-10\). \(U(g)=20\pi_C-10(1-\pi_C)=30\pi_C-10\). So \(f\pr g\iff20\pi_A\ge30\pi_C\iff\pi_A/\pi_C\ge3/2\). The 2:1 odds on C compensate for C being less likely. A naive 'more likely horse' rule ignores the different payoffs.

q: Linear \(v\), subjective probabilities \(\pi_A=0.5\), \(\pi_B=0.2\), \(\pi_C=0.3\). \(f\): 10 even money on A; \(g\): 10 at 2:1 on C. Which is chosen and what are the SEUs?
explain: \(U(f)=20(0.5)-10=0\) and \(U(g)=30(0.3)-10=-1\). Equivalently \(\pi_A/\pi_C=5/3>3/2\). The distractor \(U(g)=1\) forgets that \(g\) loses 10 when C does not win, and 5 and 6 count only the winning branches.

q: Same bets (\(f\): 10 even money on A; \(g\): 10 at 2:1 on C), \(\pi_A=0.4\), \(\pi_C=0.25\), but now \(v(-10)=0\), \(v(10)=1\), \(v(20)=3\). What does the SEU maximiser choose, and how does this compare with linear \(v\)?
options: \(g\) in both cases, because C pays more
\(g\) (\(U(f)=0.4<U(g)=0.75\)), while with linear \(v\) she would choose \(f\) (\(\pi_A/\pi_C=1.6>1.5\)): tastes matter, not only beliefs
\(f\) in both cases, because the beliefs are the same
explain: \(U(f)=0.4\cdot1+0.6\cdot0=0.4\) and \(U(g)=0.25\cdot3+0.75\cdot0=0.75\), so \(g\). With linear \(v\): \(U(f)=20(0.4)-10=-2\), \(U(g)=30(0.25)-10=-2.5\), so \(f\). With the same beliefs, the convex \(v\) (it likes the big prize) flips the choice.

q: Which is Definition 3-11 (SEU representation of \(\pr\) on the set of acts \(F\))?
options: There exists \(\pi\) such that \(f\pr g\iff\max_\omega v(f(\omega))\ge\max_\omega v(g(\omega))\).
There exist \(v:Z\to\R\) and \(\pi:\Omega\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_\omega\pi(\omega)=1\) such that \(f\pr g\iff\sum_\omega\pi(\omega)v(f(\omega))\ge\sum_\omega\pi(\omega)v(g(\omega))\).
There exist \(v\) and objective probabilities \(\pi\) given by the modeller such that \(f\pr g\iff\sum_\omega\pi(\omega)f(\omega)\ge\sum_\omega\pi(\omega)g(\omega)\).
There exists \(v:Z\to\R\) such that \(f\pr g\iff\sum_\omega v(f(\omega))\ge\sum_\omega v(g(\omega))\).
explain: Both the utility \(v\) and the subjective probability \(\pi\) are part of the representation and are derived from preferences. The first option drops beliefs (equal weights), the second imposes objective probabilities and linear money utility, and the third is not an expectation.

q: Under EU (objective lotteries) versus SEU (acts), why might two decision makers choose differently?
options: Under both, only because of different tastes.
Under EU because of different beliefs; under SEU because of different tastes.
Under both, only because of different beliefs.
Under EU only because of different tastes \(v\); under SEU because of different tastes \(v\) and/or different beliefs \(\pi\).
explain: In EU the probabilities \(p(z)\) are part of the object, the same for everyone, so only \(v\) can differ. In SEU, \(\pi\) is subjective: two equally risk-neutral gamblers can bet on different horses because they disagree about who will win. That is why betting markets exist.

q: In the SEU model, the probabilities \(\pi(\omega)\) are objective quantities given to the decision maker, exactly as \(p(z)\) in a lottery.
explain: The 'S' stands for subjective: \(\pi\) represents the decision maker's beliefs and is part of the representation of her preferences over acts. Objective probabilities are the lottery (SuperEnalotto) case.

q: Suppose \(\pr\) on acts has an SEU representation with an increasing \(v\). If act \(f\) gives at least as much money as act \(g\) in every state, then \(f\pr g\).
explain: For every \(\omega\), \(v(f(\omega))\ge v(g(\omega))\). Multiplying by \(\pi(\omega)\ge0\) and summing gives \(U(f)\ge U(g)\). Statewise dominance is respected whatever the beliefs are.

q: When evaluating bets on which horse wins, the six finishing-order states can be grouped. What is the right grouping, and why?
options: Group all states into one event, since only the expected payoff matters.
Group states by which horse finishes last, since bets pay on the loser.

Group states by the winner (events \(\{ABC,ACB\}\), \(\{BAC,BCA\}\), \(\{CAB,CBA\}\)), since every act considered gives the same prize within each event. Only event probabilities like \(\pi_A=\pi(ABC)+\pi(ACB)\) matter.
States cannot be grouped; SEU requires all six probabilities to be equal.
explain: If two states give the same prize under every act being compared, only the total probability of the pair matters. The full 6-state list keeps the description exhaustive, but payoff-relevant events are enough for the computation. SEU does not impose equal probabilities.

q: Ellsberg-type urn (an extension of the SEU slides): 30 red balls and 60 balls that are black or yellow in unknown proportion. Many people prefer 'win if red' to 'win if black', and also 'win if black or yellow' to 'win if red or yellow' (same prize, same loss). Can these choices come from an SEU representation with \(v(\text{win})>v(\text{lose})\)?
options: No: the first choice requires \(\pi(R)>\pi(B)\), the second \(\pi(B)+\pi(Y)>\pi(R)+\pi(Y)\), i.e. \(\pi(B)>\pi(R)\), which is a contradiction.
No, because the choices violate transitivity.
explain: Each bet's SEU is \(\pi(\text{win event})v(\text{win})+(1-\pi(\text{win event}))v(\text{lose})\), increasing in the probability of the winning event, so the choices reveal comparisons of subjective probabilities. Yellow is common to both bets in the second pair and cancels, giving opposite inequalities. No belief, and no shape of \(v\), fits. This is an aversion to unknown probabilities (ambiguity), and the choices can still be transitive.

q: Let \(Z=\R_+\) and \(E[p]=\sum_z p(z)z\). According to Definition 3-7, a preference \(\pr\) on \(\Lz\) is risk-averse if:
options: \(\pr\) has an EU representation with a concave Bernoulli function v
explain: Def 3-7 says the degenerate lottery paying the mean for sure is at least as good as p, for all p. \(p\pr[E[p]]\) is risk-loving. 'For some p' is too weak: the definition requires consistency across all lotteries. Concavity of v is the EU characterisation (Prop 3-3), not the definition, which does not presume EU.

q: Which statement defines strict risk aversion (Definition 3-7)?
options: \([E[p]]\succ p\) for every non-degenerate lottery p
v is concave and strictly increasing
\([E[p]]\pr p\) for every lottery p, with \(\succ\) for at least one p
explain: Strictness can only bite on non-degenerate lotteries: if p is degenerate, \(p=[E[p]]\) and \([E[p]]\succ p\) is impossible, so 'for every p' is contradictory. 'Strict for at least one p' is weaker than the definition. Under EU, strict risk aversion is equivalent to strict concavity of v; mere concavity is not enough (v linear is concave).

q: A preference on money lotteries is risk-neutral (Definition 3-7) if:
options: \([E[p]]\pr p\) for every \(p\) and \(p\pr[E[p]]\) for some \(p\)
its Bernoulli function satisfies \(v'(z)=0\) for all z
explain: Risk neutrality means every lottery is indifferent to its mean for sure. Indifference among all lotteries is total indifference (it ignores the amount of money). Under EU, neutrality corresponds to linear v, i.e. \(v''=0\), not \(v'=0\) (which would make v constant).

q: Given a Bernoulli function v, the certainty equivalent \(c(p,v)\) of a lottery p (Definition 3-8) is defined by:
explain: c(p,v) is the sure amount of money that is indifferent to p, so its utility equals the lottery's expected utility; hence \(c=v^{-1}(U(p))\). The second option confuses money with utility (EU is in utils). \(v(E[p])\) is the utility of the mean, not an amount of money. The last option mixes units.

q: The risk premium of lottery p for an agent with Bernoulli function v is:
explain: The risk premium is how much expected money the agent gives up to remove the risk: mean minus certainty equivalent. It is positive for risk-averse agents. \(v(E[p])-U(p)\) is a gap in utils, not money, and it changes under rescaling of v. The others have the wrong sign or wrong reference point.

q: The Arrow-Pratt coefficient of absolute risk aversion of a twice-differentiable Bernoulli function v at z is:
explain: Definition 3-9: \(r_A=-v''/v'\). Using \(-v''\) alone fails because it is not invariant to positive affine transformations of v. The minus sign is there so that concave increasing v gives a positive number. \(-zv''/v'\) is relative risk aversion, which is not the slides' definition.

q: Lottery p first-order stochastically dominates lottery q (Definition 3-10) if:
options: \(\sum_z p(z)v(z)\ge\sum_z q(z)v(z)\) for some non-decreasing v
\(\sum_z p(z)v(z)\ge\sum_z q(z)v(z)\) for every concave non-decreasing v
explain: FOSD means every EU maximiser who likes more money (any risk attitude) weakly prefers p. Restricting to concave v gives a weaker notion (second-order dominance), which is not in the definition. A higher mean is only necessary. 'For some v' would make almost everything dominate.

q: Proposition 3-5 states that p FOSD q if and only if, with \(F_p,F_q\) the CDFs of p and q:
options: \(F_p(z)\le F_q(z)\) for every z in the support of p
explain: A lower CDF means a smaller chance of getting 'z or less' at every threshold, i.e. a bigger chance of getting more. \(F_p\ge F_q\) is the reverse (q dominates). The inequality must hold at every z, not only at p's support points. The integral condition is equivalent to \(E[p]\ge E[q]\), which is necessary but not sufficient.

q: Proposition 3-3. Suppose \(\pr\) has an EU representation with Bernoulli function v on money. Which list contains only statements equivalent to '\(\pr\) is risk-averse'?
options: v is strictly concave; \(r_A(z)>0\) for all z
v is increasing; \(c(p,v)\le E[p]\) for all p
v is concave; \(c(p,v)\le E[p]\) for all p
v is concave; \(c(p,v)\ge E[p]\) for all p
explain: Prop 3-3: risk-averse \(\iff\) v concave \(\iff\) \(c(p,v)\le E[p]\) for all p. Monotonicity of v says nothing about attitude to risk. \(c\ge E\) is risk-loving. Strict concavity is equivalent to strict risk aversion, which is stronger than risk aversion (linear v is risk-averse in the weak sense but not strictly).

q: Under EU, the bridge between 'risk-averse' and 'v concave' in Proposition 3-3 is the inequality:
options: \(\sum_z p(z)v(z)\ge v\big(\sum_z p(z)z\big)\) for all p
\(\sum_z p(z)v(z)\le v\big(\sum_z p(z)z\big)\) for all p (Jensen)
explain: Risk aversion under EU reads \(U(p)\le U([E[p]])=v(E[p])\): 'average of v is at most v of the average', which is Jensen's inequality and the defining property of a concave function. The reversed inequality characterises convex v (risk-loving). Quasiconcavity is much weaker: every increasing v on \(\R\) is quasiconcave.

q: To prove '(risk-averse) \(\Rightarrow\) (v concave)' under EU, which lottery do you plug into the definition \([E[p]]\pr p\)?
options: any lottery whose support has at least three prizes
\(p=\alpha\cdot x\oplus(1-\alpha)\cdot y\), giving \(\alpha v(x)+(1-\alpha)v(y)\le v(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\)
explain: The two-prize lottery with weights α, 1-α has mean \(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\), so risk aversion gives exactly the concavity inequality for every x, y, α. A degenerate lottery yields a triviality. A single specific lottery only checks one chord, not concavity everywhere.

q: In proving '(v concave) \(\Rightarrow\) \(c(p,v)\le E[p]\)', after Jensen gives \(v(c(p,v))=\sum p(z)v(z)\le v(E[p])\), which property of v lets you conclude \(c(p,v)\le E[p]\)?
options: v is continuous, so the inequality is preserved in the limit
v is strictly increasing, so \(v(a)\le v(b)\) implies \(a\le b\)
v is concave, so \(v(a)\le v(b)\) implies \(a\le b\)
explain: Comparing certainty equivalents always goes 'compare v-values, then undo v'. Undoing v requires (strict) monotonicity. Concavity alone does not let you invert an inequality (a concave function can be decreasing). Continuity is what makes c exist, but it is not the step that inverts the inequality.

q: True or false: under EU, a preference is strictly risk-averse if and only if its Bernoulli function v is strictly concave.
explain: True. This is stated on the slides: strict Jensen \(\sum p(z)v(z)<v(E[p])\) for every non-degenerate p is exactly strict concavity (take two-prize lotteries for one direction, strict Jensen for the other).

q: True or false: Definition 3-7 (risk-averse / neutral / loving) presupposes that the preference has an expected utility representation.
explain: False. The slides stress that the definition 'does not presume an EU formulation': it only compares p with the degenerate lottery \([E[p]]\). EU is added afterwards to get the characterisation via concavity of v (Prop 3-3).

q: True or false: every preference relation on money lotteries is either risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-loving.
explain: False. The definition demands consistency across all lotteries, so the classification is not exhaustive. Someone who refuses small fair bets but buys fair lottery tickets with tiny win probability prefers \([E[p]]\) for some p and p for others: none of the three. Under EU, a v that is concave on one region and convex on another is an example.

q: True or false: under EU, a risk-neutral agent has a Bernoulli function of the form \(v(z)=az+b\) with \(a>0\).
explain: True. Risk neutrality means \(\sum p(z)v(z)=v(E[p])\) for all p, i.e. v is both concave and convex, hence affine. With v increasing in money (more money is better), a > 0. Linear and affine are equivalent here because v is unique only up to positive affine transformations.

q: On the slides, strict concavity of v is interpreted as:
options: increasing marginal utility of money: each extra euro is worth more than the previous one
the agent dislikes money: more money lowers utility
decreasing marginal utility of money: the utility gain from an extra euro is smaller than the loss from one euro less, so a 50/50 bet of \(\pm\)1 euro is not worth taking
the agent is indifferent between any lottery and its expected value
explain: Concave v means v' decreases: gaining one euro raises utility by less than losing one euro lowers it, so the fair ±1 gamble lowers EU. Increasing marginal utility is convexity (risk-loving). 'Dislikes money' would be a decreasing v, which is about slope, not curvature. Indifference to the mean is risk neutrality.

q: Which Bernoulli function on \(Z=\R_+\) represents a risk-loving agent who still prefers more money to less?
explain: Risk attitude is about curvature, not slope, but more money must still be better, so we need v increasing and convex: \(z^2\) on \(\R_+\). \((10-z)^2\) is convex but decreasing (a common error in notes). \(\sqrt z\) is concave (averse). \(-z^2\) is concave and decreasing on \(\R_+\).

q: Geometrically, for a 50/50 lottery between prizes \(a<b\), the expected utility is the height at \(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\) of the chord joining \((a,v(a))\) and \((b,v(b))\). For a strictly concave v:
options: the curve lies above the chord, so \(v(\tfrac{a+b}{2})\) exceeds the EU and \(c(p,v)<\tfrac{a+b}{2}\)
the curve coincides with the chord, so \(c(p,v)=\tfrac{a+b}{2}\)
the curve lies below the chord, so \(c(p,v)>\tfrac{a+b}{2}\)
the curve lies above the chord, so \(c(p,v)>\tfrac{a+b}{2}\)
explain: Concave means the curve is above its chords, so the sure mean gives more utility than the gamble. To find c, read the EU level across to the curve: since the curve is above the chord, it reaches that height at a point to the left of the mean. So \(c<E[p]\). The last option gets the geometry right but the conclusion wrong.

q: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot 1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot 9\) (euros). Alice has \(v(z)=\ln z\). What is her certainty equivalent \(c(p,v)\)?
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12\ln1+\tfrac12\ln9=\tfrac12\ln 9=\ln 3\), so \(c=e^{\ln 3}=3\). 5 is the expected value (that would be risk-neutral Carlo). \(\ln 3\) is the expected utility, not the money amount: forgetting to invert v is the standard error.

q: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot 1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot 9\). Bianca has \(v(z)=z^2\). Her certainty equivalent and risk premium are:
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(81)=41\), so \(c=\sqrt{41}\approx6.40>5\). Risk premium \(=E[p]-c\approx 5-6.40=-1.40\): negative, she would pay to keep the risk. 41 is the EU in utils, not euros. A positive premium would indicate risk aversion.

q: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot 1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot 9\). An agent has \(v(z)=\sqrt z\). What is the risk premium of p?
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(3)=2\), so \(c=2^2=4\) and the premium is \(5-4=1\). 2 is the premium for \(v=\ln z\) (c = 3), which is more risk-averse. \(5-\sqrt5\) wrongly treats \(v(E[p])\) as a money amount.

q: Slide 11: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot9\). Alice is risk-averse and \(p\sim_A[x]\); Bianca is risk-loving and \(p\sim_B[y]\); Carlo is risk-neutral and \(p\sim_C[z]\). What can you conclude?
explain: x, y, z are certainty equivalents. Averse: \([5]\pr p\sim[x]\), so x is at most 5 (given more money is better). Loving gives \(y\ge5\). Neutral gives z = 5. Strict inequalities require strict risk aversion or loving, which is not given. The specific values 3 and √41 require knowing v (ln z, z²).

q: An agent with \(v(z)=\sqrt z\) faces \(p=\tfrac12\cdot 0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot 100\). What are \(c(p,v)\) and the risk premium?
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot10=5\), so \(c=5^2=25\), and premium \(=50-25=25\). 5 is the EU in utils. \(\sqrt{50}\) is \(v(E[p])\), the utility of the mean, not a money amount.

q: \(v(z)=z^{1/4}\), \(p=\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot16\). Compute \(c(p,v)\).
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12\cdot 16^{1/4}=\tfrac12\cdot2=1\), so \(c=1^4=1\). For comparison, with \(\sqrt z\) one gets \(U=2\), \(c=4\): the more concave \(z^{1/4}\) has the lower certainty equivalent, as Prop 3-4 predicts. 8 is the mean, 2 is \(16^{1/4}\).

q: Slides 14-15: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot3\) and \(v(z)=\ln z\). Which is correct?
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12\ln 3=\ln\sqrt3\), so \(c=\sqrt3\approx1.732<2\): some expected return is traded for certainty. \(\tfrac12\ln3\) is the EU in utils, not money. \(\ln 2\) is \(v(E[p])\).

q: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot4\) versus \(q=[1]\). Agent A has \(v(z)=z\), agent B has \(v(z)=\sqrt z\). Which is correct?
options: A strictly prefers p; B strictly prefers q
A is indifferent; B strictly prefers q
A strictly prefers p; B is indifferent between p and q
explain: A: \(U(p)=2>1=U(q)\). B: \(U(p)=\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12\cdot2=1=\sqrt1=U(q)\), so B is exactly indifferent (\(c(p,\sqrt{\cdot})=1\)). A more risk-averse agent (e.g. \(\ln(1+z)\) or \(z^{1/4}\)) would strictly prefer q. A higher mean does not imply that everyone prefers p, because p does not FOSD q.

q: CARA utility \(v(z)=-e^{-az}\) with \(a=\ln 2\), lottery \(p=\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot1\). Compute \(c(p,v)\).
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(-e^{-\ln2})=-\tfrac12-\tfrac14=-0.75\). Solve \(-e^{-ac}=-0.75\): \(c=-\ln(0.75)/a=-\ln0.75/\ln2\approx0.415<0.5\). 0.75 is \(|U(p)|\), not money, and the negative value has the sign wrong.

q: With \(v(z)=\ln z\), compare the risk premium of \(p_1=\tfrac12\cdot1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot9\) with that of \(p_2=\tfrac12\cdot12\oplus\tfrac12\cdot20\) (the same \(\pm4\) gamble, with 11 euros added).
options: Premium of \(p_2\) is larger, because the prizes are larger
Premium of \(p_1\) is 2; premium of \(p_2\) is \(16-\sqrt{240}\approx0.51\): smaller at higher wealth
Premium of \(p_1\) is 2; premium of \(p_2\) is \(16-\ln 240\approx 10.5\)
Both premia equal 2, because the gamble is the same
explain: \(c(p_2)=e^{\frac12(\ln12+\ln20)}=\sqrt{240}\approx15.49\), so the premium is \(\approx0.51\), against 2 for \(p_1\) (c = 3). With \(\ln z\), \(r_A=1/z\) falls with wealth (decreasing absolute risk aversion). Equal premia hold for CARA, not for ln. The last option forgets to exponentiate.

q: Wealth 100. With probability \(\tfrac12\) a loss of 64 occurs. \(v(z)=\sqrt z\). What is the maximum premium the agent would pay for full insurance (a policy that removes the loss completely)?
explain: Without insurance: \(U=\tfrac12\sqrt{100}+\tfrac12\sqrt{36}=8\), so \(c=64\). Full insurance at premium P gives \([100-P]\), which is acceptable iff \(100-P\ge64\), i.e. \(P\le36\). The expected loss is 32: the 4 euro gap is the risk premium (\(E=68\), \(c=64\)). 64 is the loss itself.

q: Compute the Arrow-Pratt coefficient of \(v(z)=\sqrt z\) at \(z=4\).
explain: \(v'=\tfrac12z^{-1/2}\), \(v''=-\tfrac14z^{-3/2}\), so \(r_A=-v''/v'=\frac{1}{2z}\); at z = 4 that is 1/8. \(1/4\) is \(1/z\) (the value for ln z). \(1/32\) is \(-v''(4)\) alone. The negative sign would mean risk-loving.

q: Which is the Arrow-Pratt coefficient of \(v(z)=-e^{-az}\), \(a>0\)?
options: \(a\) for every z (constant absolute risk aversion)
explain: \(v'=ae^{-az}\), \(v''=-a^2e^{-az}\), so \(r_A=a^2e^{-az}/(ae^{-az})=a\), independent of wealth (CARA). \(a^2\) forgets to divide by v'. \(a/z\) is the form for power utilities (CRRA).

q: For \(v(z)=z^{a}\) with \(0<a<1\) on \(z>0\), the Arrow-Pratt coefficient is:
explain: \(v'=az^{a-1}\), \(v''=a(a-1)z^{a-2}\), so \(r_A=-a(a-1)z^{a-2}/(az^{a-1})=(1-a)/z\). So a closer to 0 means more risk-averse, and \(a=\tfrac12\) gives \(1/(2z)\). \((a-1)/z\) has the sign wrong. The last option is \(-v''\), which is not scale-invariant.

q: Why does the Arrow-Pratt measure use \(-v''/v'\) instead of just \(-v''\)?
options: \(-v''\) is always negative for concave v
dividing by v' makes the measure invariant to every increasing transformation of v
v is unique only up to \(\alpha v+\beta\) (\(\alpha>0\)); \(v''\) scales with α while the ratio does not
\(v''\) may not exist, while \(v''/v'\) always exists
explain: Replacing v by \(\alpha v+\beta\) represents the same EU preference but multiplies v'' by α, so \(-v''\) is not a meaningful measure. The ratio cancels α. It is not invariant to arbitrary increasing transformations, and it should not be: those change risk attitudes. \(-v''\ge0\) for concave v, so the third option is false.
