q: True or false: \(v_1(z)=\sqrt z\) and \(v_2(z)=3\sqrt z+7\) have the same Arrow-Pratt coefficient at every z, and the same certainty equivalent for every lottery.
explain: True. \(v_2\) is a positive affine transformation of \(v_1\), so it represents the same EU preference. \(r_A=-v''/v'\) is unchanged because the factor 3 cancels. The certainty equivalent is unchanged because \(v_2(c)=3v_1(c)+7\) and \(E[v_2]=3E[v_1]+7\) define the same c.

q: True or false: if \(f\) is strictly increasing, then \(v\) and \(f\circ v\) give the same certainty equivalent for every lottery.
explain: False. Only positive affine transformations preserve EU preferences. Example: \(v(z)=z\) and \(f(t)=\sqrt t\). For \(\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot100\), v gives c = 50 but \(\sqrt z\) gives c = 25. Bernoulli functions are cardinal.

q: Proposition 3-4 says the following are equivalent ways to say '\(v_2\) is more risk-averse than \(v_1\)'. Which list is correct?
options: \(r_A(z,v_2)\ge r_A(z,v_1)\) for all z; \(v_2=\varphi\circ v_1\) for some increasing concave φ; \(c(p,v_2)\le c(p,v_1)\) for all p
\(r_A(z,v_2)\le r_A(z,v_1)\) for all z; \(v_2=\varphi\circ v_1\) for some increasing convex φ; \(c(p,v_2)\ge c(p,v_1)\) for all p
\(v_2''\le v_1''\) for all z; \(v_2\le v_1\); \(c(p,v_2)\le c(p,v_1)\) for all p
\(r_A(z,v_2)\ge r_A(z,v_1)\) for some z; \(v_2\) concave and \(v_1\) convex; \(c(p,v_2)\le E[p]\) for all p
explain: Prop 3-4: higher \(r_A\) everywhere \(\iff\) \(v_2\) is a concave increasing transformation of \(v_1\) \(\iff\) a lower certainty equivalent for every lottery. The second list is 'less risk-averse'. Comparing raw v'' or levels of v is meaningless because v is only unique up to affine transformations. 'For some z' is not a uniform comparison.

q: Compare \(v_1(z)=\sqrt z\) and \(v_2(z)=\ln z\) on \(z>0\).
options: \(v_2\) is more risk-averse: \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) with \(\varphi(t)=2\ln t\), increasing and concave
They are equally risk-averse, since both are concave
\(v_1\) is more risk-averse, because \(\sqrt z>\ln z\)
explain: \(\ln z=2\ln\sqrt z\), so \(\varphi(t)=2\ln t\), which is increasing and concave. Also \(r_A(z,\ln)=1/z\ge1/(2z)=r_A(z,\sqrt{\cdot})\) everywhere. Consistent check: for \(\tfrac12\cdot1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot9\), \(c_{\ln}=3<4=c_{\sqrt{}}\). The level comparison \(\sqrt z>\ln z\) says nothing about risk attitude.

options: They are equally risk-averse since both are power functions
explain: For \(z^a\), \(r_A=(1-a)/z\): \(\tfrac{2}{3z}\) vs \(\tfrac{1}{2z}\). Equivalently \(v_2=v_1^{2/3}\) with \(\varphi(t)=t^{2/3}\), increasing and concave. \(t^{3/2}\) goes the wrong way (it is convex and would give \(v_1\) from \(v_2\)). A smaller exponent means more concave.

q: Compare \(v_1(z)=z^2\) and \(v_2(z)=\sqrt z\) on \(z>0\) using Prop 3-4 definition (2).
options: \(v_1=\varphi(v_2)\) with \(\varphi(t)=t^4\) concave, so \(v_1\) is more risk-averse
\(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) with \(\varphi(t)=t^{1/4}\), increasing and concave, so \(v_2\) is more risk-averse
No φ exists, because one function is convex and the other concave
explain: \(\sqrt z=(z^2)^{1/4}\), and \(t^{1/4}\) is increasing and concave on \(t>0\). So \(v_2\) is more risk-averse. Indeed \(r_A\) is \(1/(2z)\) against \(-1/z\). Definition (2) does not require \(v_1\) to be concave: any v can be compared. \(t^4\) is convex, not concave.

q: Compare \(v_1(z)=-e^{-z}\) (CARA, \(a=1\)) and \(v_2(z)=\sqrt z\) on \(z>0\).
options: \(v_2\) is more risk-averse everywhere, since \(\sqrt z\) is unbounded
They are equally risk-averse, since both are concave and increasing
Neither is more risk-averse than the other for all z: \(r_A\) is 1 vs \(\frac{1}{2z}\), and the ranking flips at \(z=\tfrac12\)
explain: \(r_A(z,v_1)=1\) and \(r_A(z,v_2)=1/(2z)\). For \(z<\tfrac12\), \(\sqrt z\) is more averse. For \(z>\tfrac12\), CARA is more averse. Definition (1) needs the inequality at every z, so neither dominates. 'More risk-averse than' is not a complete relation.

q: True or false: for any two increasing, twice-differentiable Bernoulli functions \(v_1,v_2\), either \(v_1\) is more risk-averse than \(v_2\) or \(v_2\) is more risk-averse than \(v_1\) (in the sense of Prop 3-4).
explain: False. The relation is not complete. Example: \(v_1=-e^{-z}\) has \(r_A=1\), and \(v_2=\sqrt z\) has \(r_A=1/(2z)\). Which is bigger depends on whether z is below or above 1/2, so neither inequality holds for every z.

q: PS2 1c(ii): \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) with φ strictly increasing, concave, twice differentiable. The chain rule gives \(r_A(z,v_2)=-\dfrac{\varphi''(v_1(z))}{\varphi'(v_1(z))}\,v_1'(z)+r_A(z,v_1)\). Which facts make the first term \(\ge0\)?
explain: From \(v_2'=\varphi'(v_1)v_1'\) and \(v_2''=\varphi''(v_1)(v_1')^2+\varphi'(v_1)v_1''\), we get \(-v_2''/v_2'=-\frac{\varphi''}{\varphi'}v_1'+(-v_1''/v_1')\). With φ concave (\(\varphi''\le0\)), φ increasing (\(\varphi'>0\)) and \(v_1'>0\), the first term is non-negative. No assumption on the sign of \(v_1''\) is needed: \(v_1\) need not be concave.

q: PS2 1c(iii): \(v_2=\varphi\circ v_1\), φ strictly increasing and concave. Which chain proves \(c(p,v_2)\le c(p,v_1)\)?
explain: Use the definition of c twice and Jensen for the concave φ: \(E[\varphi(X)]\le\varphi(E[X])\). This gives \(v_2(c_2)\le v_2(c_1)\), and since \(v_2\) is strictly increasing, \(c_2\le c_1\). The reversed Jensen inequality is for convex φ. The third option confuses utils with money. The last option assumes \(v_1\) is risk-loving, which is not given.

q: PS2 1c(i): \(v_1(z)=z\) and \(v_2(z)=z\) for \(z\ge0\), \(v_2(z)=2z\) for \(z<0\). Which is correct?
options: They are equally risk-averse, because \(r_A(z,v_1)=r_A(z,v_2)=0\) wherever both are defined
\(v_2\) is more risk-averse: \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) with \(\varphi(t)=t\) for \(t\ge0\), \(2t\) for \(t<0\), increasing and concave
\(v_1\) is more risk-averse, because \(v_2\) has a larger slope for losses
\(v_2\) is risk-loving, since its slope changes from 2 to 1
explain: The slope drops from 2 to 1 at 0, so \(v_2\) is a concave kinked line (loss aversion). As \(v_1\) is the identity, \(\varphi=v_2\) is increasing and concave, so \(v_2\) is more risk-averse, and \(c(p,v_2)\le E[p]=c(p,v_1)\). The Arrow-Pratt coefficient is 0 except at the kink, where \(v_2\) is not differentiable. That is why definition (1) can't see this risk aversion, while (2) and (3) can.

q: With the kinked \(v_2(z)=z\) for \(z\ge0\), \(2z\) for \(z<0\), what is the certainty equivalent of \(p=\tfrac12\cdot(-1)\oplus\tfrac12\cdot(+1)\)?
explain: \(U(p)=\tfrac12(-2)+\tfrac12(1)=-\tfrac12\). Since \(-\tfrac12<0\), invert on the loss branch: \(2c=-\tfrac12\), so \(c=-\tfrac14\). The risk premium is \(0-(-\tfrac14)=\tfrac14>0\). \(-\tfrac12\) is the EU, which needs to be inverted with the slope-2 branch.

q: Why is the kinked \(v_2\) of PS2 1c(i) an example showing that Prop 3-4 definitions (2) and (3) are more general than definition (1)?
options: \(r_A\) is 0 wherever \(v_2\) is differentiable and undefined at the kink, so (1) cannot detect its risk aversion, while (2) and (3) still apply
explain: Definition (1) needs twice-differentiability. The kinked line is linear on each side (so \(v''=0\) there) and has no derivative at 0. All of its curvature sits at the kink, which (1) cannot see. The concave-transformation and certainty-equivalent definitions do not need derivatives. \(v_2\) is continuous, increasing and concave.

q: True or false: if \(v_2\) is more risk-averse than \(v_1\) (Prop 3-4) and \(v_1\) is risk-neutral, then \(v_2\) is risk-averse.
explain: True. By definition (3), \(c(p,v_2)\le c(p,v_1)=E[p]\) for every p (a risk-neutral agent's certainty equivalent is the mean), so by Prop 3-3 \(v_2\) is risk-averse. Equivalently \(v_2=\varphi(az+b)\) with φ concave is concave.

q: True or false: if \(v_2\) is more risk-averse than \(v_1\), then \(v_2\) must be concave.
explain: False. 'More risk-averse' is relative. \(v_1=z^3\) and \(v_2=z^2\) on \(z>0\): \(v_2=v_1^{2/3}\) with \(t^{2/3}\) concave and increasing, so \(v_2\) is more risk-averse than \(v_1\), yet \(v_2\) is convex (risk-loving).

options: Yes: CDFs at 1, 10, 100 are \(0,0.5,1\) for p and \(0.1,0.7,1\) for q, so \(F_p\le F_q\) everywhere
explain: Cumulate the probabilities: \(F_p=(0,0.5,1)\), \(F_q=(0.1,0.7,1)\). \(F_p\le F_q\) at every prize (and in between, since both are step functions), so p FOSD q. Comparing individual probabilities is not the test: compare cumulative sums. A higher mean (55 vs 36.1) is necessary but not sufficient.

options: p FOSD q, since p puts more weight on the top prize
q FOSD p, since q puts less weight on the bottom prize
explain: \(F_p=(0.2,0.5,1)\), \(F_q=(0.1,0.6,1)\). The CDFs cross, so neither dominates. (Both means equal 2.3.) Looking only at the top or bottom prize is not enough: the condition must hold at every threshold.

q: PS2 1b: \(p=\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot4\), \(q=[1]\). Which is correct?
options: q FOSD p, since q is riskless
Neither FOSD the other, even though \(E[p]=2>1=E[q]\)
explain: \(F_p(0)=\tfrac12>0=F_q(0)\), so p doesn't dominate. \(F_q(1)=1>\tfrac12=F_p(1)\), so q doesn't dominate. The CDFs cross. A risk-neutral agent prefers p and a very risk-averse one prefers q, so not everyone agrees. This shows that FOSD is incomplete and that a higher mean is not sufficient for FOSD.

q: True or false: first-order stochastic dominance is a complete relation on finite-support money lotteries.
explain: False. The CDFs of \(\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot4\) and \([1]\) cross, so neither dominates (PS2 1b(i)). FOSD is transitive (pointwise \(\le\) on CDFs), but not complete.

q: PS2 1b(i): why is FOSD transitive?
options: Because the CDFs of p and r cannot cross
Because every EU preference is transitive, so FOSD is a preference relation
\(F_p\le F_q\) and \(F_q\le F_r\) pointwise imply \(F_p\le F_r\) pointwise, by transitivity of \(\le\) on real numbers at each x
explain: Fix any x: \(F_p(x)\le F_q(x)\le F_r(x)\). Since this holds for every x, \(F_p\le F_r\), i.e. p FOSD r. Transitivity of expected value doesn't prove it (EV is only necessary for FOSD). FOSD is not a preference relation, because it is incomplete.

q: PS2 1b(ii)-(iii): let \(p\succeq_{EV}q\iff E[p]\ge E[q]\). Which is correct?
options: \(\succeq_{EV}\) is complete and transitive, and \(p\succeq_{EV}q\) is necessary but not sufficient for p FOSD q
\(\succeq_{EV}\) is transitive but not complete, like FOSD
\(\succeq_{EV}\) is complete and transitive, and \(p\succeq_{EV}q\) is sufficient but not necessary for p FOSD q
explain: \(E[\cdot]\) maps lotteries to real numbers, and \(\ge\) on \(\R\) is complete and transitive. (\(\succeq_{EV}\) is EU with \(v(z)=z\).) FOSD \(\Rightarrow\) higher mean: plug the non-decreasing \(v(z)=z\) into the definition. The converse fails: \(\tfrac12\cdot0\oplus\tfrac12\cdot4\) has a higher mean than [1] but doesn't dominate it.

q: What is the fastest proof that 'p FOSD q \(\Rightarrow\) \(E[p]\ge E[q]\)'?
options: Use Jensen's inequality for the concave function v
Apply Definition 3-10 with the non-decreasing function \(v(z)=z\)
Note that \(F_p\le F_q\) implies \(p(z)\ge q(z)\) for every z
explain: FOSD gives \(\sum p(z)v(z)\ge\sum q(z)v(z)\) for every non-decreasing v, and \(v(z)=z\) is non-decreasing, so \(E[p]\ge E[q]\). (Alternative: \(E[s]=a+\int_a^b(1-F_s(x))dx\), and a lower CDF gives more area above it.) The square root would give an EU comparison, not the mean. The last claim is false: CDF dominance does not imply pointwise dominance of probabilities.

q: For a lottery s with support in \([a,b]\) and CDF \(F_s\), the PS2 solution uses the formula:
explain: The mean is a plus the area above the CDF (below 1). Equivalently \(E[s]=b-\int_a^bF_s\). Check with \(s=[a]\): \(F_s=1\) on [a,b], which gives \(E=a\). So a lower CDF means a larger mean, which is the integral route to 'FOSD \(\Rightarrow\) higher mean'. The second option gives \(b-a\) for \(s=[a]\).

q: PS2 extra (a): \(p\sim U[0,1]\), \(q\sim U[0.5,1]\). Which is correct?
options: Neither dominates, since the supports overlap
q FOSD p only for risk-averse agents, since q has smaller variance
q FOSD p, since \(F_q(x)=\max\{0,2x-1\}\le x=F_p(x)\) on [0,1]; hence \(U(q)\ge U(p)\) for every increasing v
p FOSD q, since p has the larger support
explain: \(F_p(x)=x\). \(F_q(x)=0\) for \(x<0.5\) and \(2x-1\) on [0.5,1]. Since \(2x-1\le x\iff x\le1\), \(F_q\le F_p\) everywhere. By Prop 3-5, every non-decreasing v gives \(U(q)\ge U(p)\), whatever the risk attitude. Overlapping supports are no obstacle to dominance.

q: PS2 extra (b), pizza: price 10. Delivery costs +2, but if the pizza arrives cold (prob 1/50) it is free. Pick-up: no fee; late and cold w.p. 1/10; independently, w.p. 1/100 you are the 200th customer and it is free. Writing outcomes as temperature/price paid, which describes the pick-up lottery?
options: Hot/10: 0.9; Cold/10: 0.1; free w.p. 0.01 on top
explain: Independence means you multiply: hot and paid \(0.9\times0.99=0.891\); hot and free \(0.9\times0.01=0.009\); cold and paid \(0.1\times0.99=0.099\); cold and free \(0.1\times0.01=0.001\). These sum to 1. The third option double-counts probability, and the last one is the delivery lottery.

q: Pizza problem (outcome = temperature/price paid): delivery = (Hot/12 w.p. 0.98, Cold/0 w.p. 0.02); pick-up = (Hot/10 0.891, Hot/0 0.009, Cold/10 0.099, Cold/0 0.001). You only know that hot beats cold and cheaper beats dearer, other things equal. Can delivery FOSD pick-up under some ranking consistent with this?
options: No, because the two lotteries have different supports
Yes: delivery is hot with higher probability (0.98 vs 0.9)
No: Hot/0 is the unique best outcome, pick-up gives it w.p. 0.009 and delivery never does, so just below the top \(F_{\text{del}}=1>0.991=F_{\text{pick}}\)
explain: Hot/0 beats every other outcome by the two rules (hot and free). At the outcome just below it, delivery has cumulative probability 1, while pick-up has \(1-0.009=0.991\). Delivery's CDF is higher there, so it can never dominate. Ranking Hot/12 top violates 'cheaper is better' against Hot/0. Different supports don't prevent dominance.

q: Pizza problem (outcome = temperature/price paid): which ranking (worst to best), consistent with 'hot beats cold, cheaper beats dearer', makes pick-up FOSD delivery?
explain: With the first ranking, cumulative sums are pick-up 0, 0.099, 0.1, 0.991, 1 and delivery 0.98, 0.98, 1, 1, 1, so pick-up is lower everywhere. In the second ranking, delivery's CDF reaches 0.02 at Cold/0 while pick-up's is already 0.1, so pick-up does not dominate. The third ranking puts Cold/0 below Cold/10, which violates 'cheaper is better'. So does the last one.

q: True or false: if p FOSD q, then every risk-loving EU maximiser (with increasing v) weakly prefers p to q.
explain: True. FOSD requires \(\sum p v\ge\sum q v\) for every non-decreasing v, whatever its curvature. Risk-averse, neutral and risk-loving agents all agree. That is why FOSD is an 'objective' comparison of lotteries.

q: True or false: if every risk-averse EU maximiser (with increasing concave v) weakly prefers p to q, then p FOSD q.
explain: False. Take \(p=[5]\) and \(q=\tfrac12\cdot1\oplus\tfrac12\cdot9\). By Jensen every concave v gives \(v(5)\ge\tfrac12v(1)+\tfrac12v(9)\), so every risk-averter prefers p. But \(F_p(5)=1>\tfrac12=F_q(5)\), so p does not FOSD q, and a risk-lover prefers q. FOSD needs agreement among all increasing v, not only the concave ones.

q: True or false: if p FOSD q and \(E[p]=E[q]\), then \(p=q\).
explain: True. \(E[p]-E[q]=\int(F_q-F_p)\,dx\), and the integrand is \(\ge0\). A zero integral of a non-negative right-continuous step function forces \(F_p=F_q\), so the lotteries coincide. In particular, a non-degenerate lottery never FOSDs a different lottery with the same mean (e.g. a mean-preserving spread).

q: The slides distinguish 'comparing utility functions' from 'comparing payoff distributions'. Which pairing is right?
options: Both risk aversion and FOSD are subjective, because they depend on v
Risk aversion / Arrow-Pratt / certainty equivalent compare agents (subjective); FOSD compares lotteries (objective)
Both are objective properties of lotteries
FOSD compares agents; Arrow-Pratt compares lotteries
explain: Risk attitude is about the shape of a person's v. FOSD is a property of the two distributions themselves: p is better for every person who likes more money, so it does not depend on whose v it is (it quantifies over all non-decreasing v).

q: PS2 1a: wealth w, loss D with probability p. The agent pays x for insurance and gets \(\lambda x\) if the accident occurs. What are final wealths in the two states?
explain: The premium x is paid in both states. The payout \(\lambda x\) arrives only after an accident. Forgetting that the premium is paid in the accident state is a common slip. The insurer's expected profit is \(x-p\lambda x\).

q: PS2 1a(i): fair insurance, \(\lambda=1/p\). What is the agent's expected wealth as a function of x?
explain: \(p(w-x-D+\lambda x)+(1-p)(w-x)=w-x-pD+p\lambda x=w-pD\), because \(p\lambda=1\). Fair insurance changes only the risk, not the mean. So a risk-averse agent picks the x that removes all risk.

q: Wealth 100, loss 64 with probability \(\tfrac14\), fair insurance (\(\lambda=4\)), and the agent is risk-averse. What is the optimal x, and what is final wealth?
options: \(x=16\); final wealth 100 without accident and 84 with accident
explain: Full insurance needs \(\lambda x=D\), so \(x=D/\lambda=pD=16\). Wealth is \(100-16=84\) without an accident and \(100-16-64+64=84\) with one. This sure amount equals the mean \(w-pD=84\), and a risk-averse agent weakly prefers it to every other x (all of which have the same mean). \(x=64\) confuses premium with coverage.

q: PS2 1a(i): why is \(x=pD\) optimal for a risk-averse agent under fair insurance?
options: Because v is strictly concave, so U(x) is strictly increasing
Every x gives a lottery with mean \(w-pD\); \(x=pD\) gives \([w-pD]\) for sure, and risk aversion means \([E[q]]\pr q\) for each such lottery q
Because the first-order condition \(U'(x)=0\) holds at \(x=pD\) for every v
explain: The argument uses only Definition 3-7: all feasible choices share the same mean, and one of them is the degenerate lottery at that mean, which is weakly preferred to all the others. It needs neither differentiability nor EU. Expected wealth is the same for every x, so 'maximises expected wealth' cannot single it out.

q: PS2 1a(ii): unfair insurance, \(p\lambda<1\), v differentiable. With \(U(x)=p\,v(w-D+(\lambda-1)x)+(1-p)v(w-x)\), what is \(U'(D/\lambda)\)?
explain: \(U'(x)=p(\lambda-1)v'(w-D+(\lambda-1)x)-(1-p)v'(w-x)\). At \(x=D/\lambda\) both wealths equal \(w-D/\lambda\), so the v' terms are the same and \(U'=[p\lambda-p-1+p]v'=(p\lambda-1)v'<0\). A negative slope at full insurance means buying slightly less raises EU, so the optimum has \(\lambda x<D\).

q: True or false: with unfair insurance (\(p\lambda<1\)), a risk-neutral agent buys zero insurance.
explain: True. With \(v(z)=z\), \(U(x)=w-pD+(p\lambda-1)x\), which is strictly decreasing in x, so \(x=0\). PS2 1a(ii) asks for strict risk aversion to show under-insurance. The risk-neutral case is the extreme where the agent buys nothing.

q: True or false: with unfair insurance (\(p\lambda<1\)), a strictly risk-averse agent may still buy a strictly positive amount of insurance.
explain: True. PS2 1a(ii) only shows \(\lambda x<D\), 'possibly zero'. For example, with \(v=\ln\), \(w=100\), \(D=50\), \(p=\tfrac12\), \(\lambda=1.8\) (\(p\lambda=0.9\)), the optimum is \(x=18.75>0\). Whether x is zero or positive depends on how unfair the price is and on how risk-averse the agent is.

q: \(v(z)=\ln z\), \(w=100\), \(D=50\), \(p=\tfrac12\), \(\lambda=1.8\) (unfair: \(p\lambda=0.9\)). The first-order condition \(\frac{p(\lambda-1)}{w-D+(\lambda-1)x}=\frac{1-p}{w-x}\) gives:
explain: \(\frac{0.4}{50+0.8x}=\frac{0.5}{100-x}\), so \(40-0.4x=25+0.4x\) and \(x=18.75\). Final wealths: 65 after an accident, 81.25 otherwise. This is partial insurance, as PS2 1a(ii) predicts. Full insurance (\(x=D/\lambda\)) would require fair pricing.

q: True or false: if insurance is favourable to the buyer (\(p\lambda>1\)) and x is restricted to \([0,D/\lambda]\), a strictly risk-averse EU maximiser (differentiable concave v) chooses full insurance \(x=D/\lambda\).
explain: True. U is concave in x (a sum of concave functions of affine functions of x), so U' is non-increasing. \(U'(D/\lambda)=(p\lambda-1)v'(w-D/\lambda)>0\), so U' > 0 on the whole interval and the maximum is at the upper bound. Without the cap, she would over-insure.

q: Wealth 100 and \(v(z)=\ln z\). The agent can bet any \(b\in[0,100)\) on an event with probability 0.6: she wins b if it happens and loses b otherwise. Optimal b?
explain: \(U(b)=0.6\ln(100+b)+0.4\ln(100-b)\). The FOC \(\frac{0.6}{100+b}=\frac{0.4}{100-b}\) gives \(60-0.6b=40+0.4b\), so \(b=20\) (a fraction \(2\pi-1\) of wealth). She bets a positive amount because the bet has positive expected value. She doesn't bet everything because ln is concave (and \(\ln 0=-\infty\)).

q: Wealth w, differentiable strictly increasing concave v. A bet of size b wins b w.p. π and loses b w.p. 1-π, with \(\pi>\tfrac12\). Why is the optimal b strictly positive?
options: Because the bet FOSDs not betting
\(U'(0)=\pi v'(w)-(1-\pi)v'(w)=(2\pi-1)v'(w)>0\), so a small bet raises EU
Because a risk-averse agent prefers the lottery to its expected value
explain: \(U(b)=\pi v(w+b)+(1-\pi)v(w-b)\). At b = 0 both v' are evaluated at w, so the curvature of v has no first-order effect. Any bet with positive expected value is accepted in small amounts (local risk neutrality). The bet does not FOSD [w]: it can lose. U is concave in b, not convex.

q: A loss-averse agent has \(v(g)=g\) for gains \(g\ge0\) and \(v(g)=2g\) for losses (relative to current wealth). She can take a bet that wins b w.p. π and loses b w.p. 1-π. For which π does she accept a small bet b > 0?
options: For no π, since she is risk-averse
explain: EU of the bet is \(\pi b-2(1-\pi)b=b(3\pi-2)\), which is positive iff \(\pi>2/3\). Unlike the differentiable case, the kink makes her refuse small bets with positive expected value (first-order risk aversion). This is the PS2 1c(i) function, applied to gains and losses.

q: True or false: for any continuous strictly increasing v, the certainty equivalent of a finite lottery exists, is unique, and lies between the smallest and the largest prize.
explain: True. \(U(p)\) lies between \(v(\min z)\) and \(v(\max z)\). By the intermediate value theorem some c in \([\min z,\max z]\) has \(v(c)=U(p)\), and strict monotonicity makes it unique. So \(c(p,v)=v^{-1}(U(p))\) is well defined.

q: True or false: with CARA utility \(v(z)=-e^{-az}\), adding a sure amount w to every prize of a lottery raises its certainty equivalent by exactly w, so the risk premium does not depend on wealth.
explain: True. \(E[-e^{-a(w+z)}]=e^{-aw}E[-e^{-az}]\), so \(-e^{-a c'}=e^{-aw}(-e^{-ac})\) gives \(c'=w+c\). The risk premium \(E-c\) is unchanged. This matches \(r_A=a\) being constant. For ln z (\(r_A=1/z\)) the premium falls with wealth.

q: True or false: if v is increasing and concave on \(\R_+\), then for \(p=\tfrac12\cdot a\oplus\tfrac12\cdot b\) the risk premium is at most \(\tfrac{|b-a|}{2}\).
explain: True. With v increasing, \(c(p,v)\ge\min\{a,b\}\), and concavity gives \(c\le E[p]=\tfrac{a+b}{2}\). So the premium \(E[p]-c\le\tfrac{a+b}{2}-\min\{a,b\}=\tfrac{|b-a|}{2}\). The certainty equivalent can never fall below the worst prize.

q: In Topic 4.1 the set of alternatives is \(X=\R^2_+\). Why does the model use \(\R^2_+\) rather than \(\mathbb N^2\) (whole units only)?
options: Because consumers can actually buy fractions of every good
Modeling convenience: continuous quantities make tradeoffs easy to describe and analyse
Because preferences on \(\mathbb N^2\) can never be represented by a utility function
Because monotonicity cannot be defined on \(\mathbb N^2\)
explain: The slides answer the '1/2 T-shirt?' question with 'modeling convenience'. Nobody claims half a car is meaningful; continuous quantities just make tradeoffs tractable. Preferences on the countable set \(\mathbb N^2\) always have a utility representation, and monotonicity is perfectly definable there, so those options are false.

q: For a preference relation \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\), the indifference set of bundle \(a\) is
explain: The indifference set is the set of bundles indifferent to \(a\); the collection of all indifference sets is the partition induced by the equivalence relation \(\sim\). \(\{y: y\pr a\}\) is the upper contour set (used for convexity), and \(\{y:y\succ a\}\) is the strict upper contour set.

q: Definition 4-1-2: \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is monotone if
options: \(x_1\ge y_1, x_2\ge y_2\Rightarrow x\pr y\), and \(x_1>y_1, x_2>y_2\Rightarrow x\succ y\)
\(x_1\ge y_1, x_2\ge y_2, x\ne y\Rightarrow x\succ y\)
explain: Monotonicity has two parts: weakly more of both is at least as good, and strictly more of both is strictly better. The second option is the definition of strong monotonicity. The third fails even for \(x=y\) (irreflexive), and the fourth would compare bundles with more of one and less of the other, which no definition does.

q: Which condition defines strong monotonicity of \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\)?
options: \(x_1\ge y_1\), \(x_2\ge y_2\) and \(x\ne y\Rightarrow x\succ y\)
explain: Strong monotonicity: more of at least one good and no less of the other makes the bundle strictly better. The first two options are the two halves of ordinary monotonicity. The last one would say only the total quantity matters, which describes a specific preference (perfect substitutes with equal weights), not a property.

q: Definition 4-1-3 (continuity): \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is continuous if
options: whenever \(x\succ y\) there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(a\succ b\) for every \(a\) within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(x\) and every \(b\) within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(y\)
whenever \(x\sim y\) there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(a\sim b\) for all \(a,b\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(x,y\)
for every \(x\) there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that all bundles within \(\varepsilon\) of \(x\) are indifferent to \(x\)
it is represented by some utility function
explain: Continuity says strict preferences survive small perturbations of both bundles (distance is Euclidean). The indifference version is false for any strongly monotone preference, and the third would make indifference sets thick. Having a utility function is not enough: lexicographic-like or Example 4.3 preferences show utility representations may be discontinuous or nonexistent.

q: Definition 4-1-4: \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is convex if
options: every indifference set is a convex set
explain: Convexity: if \(a\) is at least as good as \(b\), every bundle on the segment from \(a\) to \(b\) is at least as good as \(b\) (the worse endpoint). Requiring the mix to beat \(a\) is too strong (it fails for \(u=x_2\) with \(a=(0,2), b=(0,1)\)). Mixes being indifferent and convex indifference sets describe linear (or thick) indifference sets, not convexity in general: the indifference curve \(x_1x_2=1\) is not a convex set.

q: Which is the definition of a strictly convex preference relation on \(\R^2_+\)?
options: \(a\pr b\) and \(a\ne b\Rightarrow \lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\succ b\) for all \(\lambda\in(0,1)\)
explain: Strict convexity: for distinct \(a\pr b\), every interior point of the segment is strictly better than \(b\). The first option only covers strict preference \(a\succ b\), so it says nothing about indifferent bundles, which is exactly where strict convexity bites (no flat parts on indifference curves). The last option is just convexity (endpoints add nothing).

q: Definition 4-1-5: \(u:\R^2_+\to\R\) is quasiconcave if, for all bundles \(a,b\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
explain: Quasiconcavity says a mix is never worse than the worse endpoint. The first option is concavity (stronger). '\(\ge\max\)' would force \(u\) to be constant along segments essentially, and '\(\le\max\)' is quasiconvexity.

q: Lexicographic preferences (Example 4.6, good 1 has priority) are defined by: \(x\pr y\) iff
explain: Good 1 is compared first; good 2 only breaks ties in good 1. The first option is the incomplete dominance order. The third is the 'sum first, then good 1' preference from PS2 extra d(iii). The last option is wrong because '\(x_1\ge y_1\)' alone would make \((1,0)\sim(1,5)\), i.e. good 2 would never matter.

q: Example 4.3: the consumer cares only about increasing good 1 until its quantity exceeds 10, then only about good 2. Which utility function represents these preferences?
explain: Below 10 only \(x_1\) matters; once \(x_1>10\), every bundle beats every bundle with \(x_1\le10\) and only \(x_2\) matters, so we add 11 to push those utilities above 10. Option 3 fails because \((11,0)\) would get 0 < u(5,0)=5. Option 1 values good 2 below 10, and option 4 values good 1 above 10.

q: For Example 4.3 (good 1 up to 10, then only good 2; \(u=x_1\) if \(x_1\le10\), \(u=11+x_2\) if \(x_1>10\)), what do indifference sets look like?
options: L-shaped curves with kinks on the line \(x_1=10\)
Vertical segments for \(x_1\le10\), and horizontal half-lines open on the left (starting at \(x_1=10\)) for utility levels above 10
explain: For \(x_1\le10\) utility is \(x_1\), so the indifference sets are vertical lines \(x_1=c\). For \(x_1>10\) utility is \(11+x_2\), so the sets are \(\{x: x_1>10, x_2=k\}\): horizontal half-lines that do not include their endpoint at \(x_1=10\). There are no kinked L shapes (those belong to min), and single points belong to lexicographic preferences.

q: Which statement about indifference sets of a preference relation \(\pr\) (complete and transitive) on \(\R^2_+\) is correct?
options: Every indifference set is a convex set when \(\pr\) is convex
Two distinct indifference sets can intersect at a single point
Every indifference set is a curve
The indifference sets form a partition of \(X\)
explain: Indifference sets are the equivalence classes of \(\sim\), which is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so they partition \(X\): distinct sets are disjoint (no crossing). They need not be curves: lexicographic preferences have single-point indifference sets, and non-monotone preferences can have thick ones. Convexity is about upper contour sets, not indifference sets (the curve \(x_1x_2=1\) is not a convex set).

q: Consider \(u(x)=x_2\) (only good 2 is valued, Example 4.2). Which is true?
explain: More of both goods weakly raises \(x_2\), and strictly more of both strictly raises it, so it is monotone. But \((2,1)\sim(1,1)\) even though \((2,1)\ge(1,1)\) with \((2,1)\ne(1,1)\), so strong monotonicity fails. Strong monotonicity implies monotonicity, so option 3 can never be true for any preference.

q: Every strongly monotone preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) is monotone.
explain: If \(x\ge y\): either \(x=y\) and \(x\pr y\) by reflexivity, or \(x\ne y\) and strong monotonicity gives \(x\succ y\). If \(x\) has strictly more of both goods, then \(x\ne y\), so again \(x\succ y\). Both parts of monotonicity hold.

q: For \(u(x)=v_1x_1+v_2x_2\), which condition on \((v_1,v_2)\) is necessary and sufficient for the preference to be strongly monotone?
explain: If \(v_1=0\), adding good 1 leaves utility unchanged, so \((2,1)\sim(1,1)\) breaks strong monotonicity (similarly for \(v_2=0\)). With both positive, any weak increase in both with at least one strict raises \(u\) strictly. Nonnegative weights with \(v_1+v_2>0\) only guarantee ordinary monotonicity.

q: Is the preference represented by \(u(x)=\max\{x_1,x_2\}\) monotone? Strongly monotone?
options: Monotone but not strongly monotone, e.g. \((1,\tfrac12)\sim(1,0)\)
explain: If \(x\ge y\) then \(\max\) of \(x\) is at least \(\max\) of \(y\), strictly if both coordinates are strictly larger, so it is monotone. But raising the smaller good does nothing: \((1,\tfrac12)\sim(1,0)\). The pairs in options 3 and 4 are not ordered by \(\ge\), so they say nothing about monotonicity (they are the witnesses of non-convexity).

q: Is the preference represented by \(u(x)=x_1-x_2\) monotone?
options: No: \((1,1)\) has weakly more of both goods than \((1,0)\) but \((1,1)\prec(1,0)\)
No, because it is not continuous
explain: Good 2 is a bad here: adding it lowers utility, so \((1,1)\ge(1,0)\) yet \(u(1,1)=0<1=u(1,0)\), violating the first part of monotonicity. Linearity gives convexity and continuity, not monotonicity. The preference is continuous, so the last option is false.

q: Ideal bundle (Example 4.5) with \(x^*=(5,5)\) and \(x\pr y\) iff \(|x_1-5|+|x_2-5|\le|y_1-5|+|y_2-5|\). Which pair witnesses that the preference is NOT monotone?
options: \((5,5)\succ(6,6)\) although \((6,6)\) has strictly more of both goods
explain: Monotonicity (part b) requires a bundle with strictly more of both goods to be strictly better, but \((6,6)\) is at distance 2 from the ideal, \((5,5)\) at distance 0. Indifference between unordered bundles (options 2 and 4) is consistent with monotonicity, and \((5,5)\succ(4,4)\) is what monotonicity predicts.

q: If \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is monotone, then no indifference set contains an open disk (a ball of positive radius).
explain: Any open disk contains two bundles \(x,y\) with \(x_1>y_1\) and \(x_2>y_2\) (e.g. its centre and a point slightly up and to the right). Part (b) of monotonicity gives \(x\succ y\), so they cannot both be in the same indifference set. Hence monotone preferences have 'thin' indifference sets, although they may still contain horizontal or vertical pieces.

q: Cobb-Douglas \(u(x)=x_1x_2\) on all of \(\R^2_+\). Which statement is correct?
options: Monotone, but not strongly monotone on \(\R^2_+\): \((0,5)\sim(0,1)\)
explain: If \(x\ge y\) then \(x_1x_2\ge y_1y_2\), strictly when both coordinates are strictly larger, so it is monotone. On the axes utility is 0, so adding good 2 to \((0,1)\) gives \((0,5)\sim(0,1)\): strong monotonicity fails on the boundary (it does hold on the interior). \((0,5)\sim(0,1)\) violates only strong monotonicity, and \((1,4)\sim(4,1)\) is a pair of unordered bundles.

q: PS3 1b: \(u(x)=\min\{x_1+2x_2,\ 2x_1+3x_2-10\}\). Which statement is correct?
options: \(u\) is continuous and strictly increasing in each good, and the preference is convex
\(u\) is strictly increasing in each good but not continuous at the kink
The preference is monotone but not convex, because \(u\) has a kink
\(u\) is continuous but not monotone, because it can take negative values
explain: Each expression is continuous and strictly increasing in both goods, and the minimum of such functions inherits both properties (raising \(x_1\) raises both expressions, hence the min). It is the minimum of two linear (concave) functions, so it is concave and the preference is convex by Prop 4-1-4. Negative values do not matter (only the ranking does), and kinks break differentiability, not continuity or convexity.

q: For \(u(x)=\min\{x_1+2x_2,\ 2x_1+3x_2-10\}\) (PS3 1b), on which set of bundles are the two expressions equal, and which is the minimum below it?
options: On \(x_1+x_2=10\); below that line \(2x_1+3x_2-10\) is the smaller one
On \(x_1+x_2=10\); below that line \(x_1+2x_2\) is the smaller one
explain: Setting \(x_1+2x_2=2x_1+3x_2-10\) gives \(x_1+x_2=10\). The difference \((2x_1+3x_2-10)-(x_1+2x_2)=x_1+x_2-10\) is negative when \(x_1+x_2<10\), so below the line the second expression is the minimum and above it the first one is. Option 2 reverses the comparison.

q: Proposition 4-1-1 states:
options: Every utility function representing a continuous preference is continuous
Every continuous preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) is monotone
A preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) that can be represented by a continuous utility function is continuous
A preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) has a utility representation iff it is convex
explain: Prop 4-1-1 goes from a continuous utility to a continuous preference. The converse (Debreu) also holds: some continuous utility exists, but not every representation must be continuous. Continuity says nothing about monotonicity, and convexity is unrelated to the existence of a utility function.

q: In the proof of Prop 4-1-1, \(x\succ y\) and \(u\) is continuous. The proof sets \(\varepsilon=\tfrac13(u(x)-u(y))\) and picks \(\delta\) so that \(u(a)>u(x)-\varepsilon\) on the \(\delta\)-ball around \(x\) and \(u(b)<u(y)+\varepsilon\) on the \(\delta\)-ball around \(y\). Which choice of \(\varepsilon\) would make the argument FAIL?
explain: The chain is \(u(a)>u(x)-\varepsilon\ge u(y)+\varepsilon>u(b)\), so we need \(2\varepsilon\le u(x)-u(y)\). With \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\) of the gap the middle step is an equality and the chain is still strict, so \(\tfrac13\) is just a safe choice. With \(\varepsilon\) equal to the whole gap, \(u(x)-\varepsilon=u(y)<u(y)+\varepsilon\) and nothing can be concluded.

q: If \(u\) represents a continuous preference relation on \(\R^2_+\), then \(u\) must be continuous.
explain: Debreu's theorem says that SOME continuous representation exists, not that all of them are continuous. Take the continuous \(u=x_1+x_2\) and compose it with the increasing but discontinuous \(f(t)=t\) for \(t<1\), \(f(t)=t+1\) for \(t\ge1\). Then \(f\circ u\) represents the same continuous preference but jumps on the line \(x_1+x_2=1\).

q: Lexicographic preferences (good 1 first) are not continuous. Which pair gives a correct witness?
options: \(x=(1,2)\succ y=(1,0)\), but \(a=(1-\tfrac{\delta}{2},2)\), within \(\delta\) of \(x\), satisfies \(a\prec y\) for every \(\delta>0\)
explain: A tiny loss of good 1 outweighs any amount of good 2, so bundles arbitrarily close to \(x\) fall below \(y\): the strict preference \(x\succ y\) does not survive small perturbations. Options 2 and 3 show perturbations that preserve the ranking, which is consistent with continuity. Option 4 starts from indifference, which the definition does not constrain.

q: PS2 extra d(iii): the consumer cares first about \(x_1+x_2\); if sums are equal, she prefers more good 1. Which witness shows this preference is NOT continuous?
explain: \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) have the same sum, so good 1 decides and \((2,1)\succ(1,2)\). But \((1,2+\varepsilon)\), arbitrarily close to \((1,2)\), has a larger sum and beats \((2,1)\): the strict ranking flips under a tiny perturbation. Options 2 and 4 show rankings that survive perturbation, and \((1,0)\sim(0,1)\) is false here (\((1,0)\succ(0,1)\)).

q: Which of the following preferences on \(\R^2_+\) is NOT continuous?
options: Example 4.3: good 1 up to 10, then good 2
explain: In Example 4.3, \(x=(10.5,0)\) has \(u=11\) and \(y=(10,5)\) has \(u=10\), so \(x\succ y\). But \((10+\delta/2,5)\), within \(\delta\) of \(y\), has \(u=16\) and beats \(x\): the strict ranking flips, because utility jumps at \(x_1=10\). The other three are given by continuous formulas, hence continuous by Prop 4-1-1.

q: PS2 extra d(ii): balanced bundles (\(x_1=x_2\)) beat unbalanced ones; among balanced, more is better; among unbalanced, more good 2 is better. Which witness shows it is NOT continuous?
explain: \((2+\varepsilon,2)\) is unbalanced, so it is worse than every balanced bundle including \((1,1)\), although it is arbitrarily close to \((2,2)\succ(1,1)\). Option 2 is the witness against monotonicity, and option 3 is the witness against convexity. Option 4 is true but harmless: \((1,3)\sim(2,3)\) just reflects that only \(x_2\) matters among unbalanced bundles.

q: Comment after Prop 4-1-1: if \(\pr\) is continuous and \(a\succ b\succ c\), then
options: \(b\) lies on the segment between \(a\) and \(c\)
explain: Continuity gives an intermediate-value property along the segment from \(a\) to \(c\): moving from a bundle better than \(b\) to one worse than \(b\), some bundle in between is indifferent to \(b\). This parallels the continuity axiom for lotteries in Topic 3. Nothing forces the midpoint to be the indifferent point, nor \(b\) to lie on the segment, and continuity alone cannot make a mix beat \(a\).

q: OR Problem 4.3: \(\pr\) is monotone and continuous, represented by an increasing continuous \(u\). Show that for every \(x\) there is a balanced bundle \(y=(t,t)\) with \(y\sim x\). What is the key argument?
options: Convexity: the midpoint of \(x\) and \((x_2,x_1)\) is balanced and indifferent to \(x\)

With \(m=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\), \(M=\max\{x_1,x_2\}\): monotonicity gives \((m,m)\preceq x\preceq(M,M)\), and the intermediate value theorem applied to the continuous \(t\mapsto u(t,t)\) on \([m,M]\) gives \(t\) with \(u(t,t)=u(x)\)
explain: Monotonicity sandwiches \(x\) between two balanced bundles, and continuity of \(u\) along the diagonal fills the gap by the intermediate value theorem. Convexity is not assumed and would not give indifference anyway. The specific choice \(t=(x_1+x_2)/2\) is right only for some preferences (e.g. perfect substitutes with equal weights), not in general.

q: Every complete and transitive preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) can be represented by a utility function.
explain: Lexicographic preferences are complete and transitive but have no utility representation (Prop 1.2 / PS1 extra). On an uncountable set like \(\R^2_+\), representation needs something more, such as continuity (Debreu). On a countable set the statement would be true.

q: Proof that lexicographic preferences have no utility function: suppose \(u\) represents them and let \(I_a=(u(a,0),u(a,1))\) for each \(a\ge0\). Which pair of facts drives the contradiction?
options: Each \(I_a\) is non-empty because \((a,1)\succ(a,0)\), and \(I_a\cap I_b=\emptyset\) for \(a\ne b\) because every bundle with more good 1 beats every bundle with less; choosing a rational in each \(I_a\) gives a one-to-one map from an uncountable set into \(\mathbb Q\)
Each \(I_a\) is bounded, and a bounded set of reals has a maximum
The intervals \(I_a\) are nested, so their intersection is a single point
\(u\) must be discontinuous, and discontinuous functions cannot represent preferences
explain: The two sentences that make the proof work are why the intervals are non-empty and why they are disjoint. Picking a rational \(q_a\in I_a\) gives an injection \(a\mapsto q_a\) from \([0,\infty)\) (uncountable) into \(\mathbb Q\) (countable), which is impossible. The intervals are disjoint, not nested, and discontinuous functions can represent preferences (Example 4.3), so the last option is wrong.

q: Slide 27 proves that lexicographic preferences are convex. Assume \(a\pr b\) and \(a_1=b_1\). How does the proof conclude \(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\pr b\)?
options: Then \(a_2\ge b_2\), so the mix has good 1 equal to \(b_1\) and good 2 equal to \(\lambda a_2+(1-\lambda)b_2\ge b_2\)
Then the mix has strictly more good 1 than \(b\)
By continuity, the mix is indifferent to \(b\)
By concavity of the lexicographic utility function
explain: With equal good 1, \(a\pr b\) forces \(a_2\ge b_2\), and the mix keeps good 1 at \(b_1\) while its good 2 is a weighted average of \(a_2\) and \(b_2\), hence \(\ge b_2\). The 'strictly more good 1' argument is the other case (\(a_1>b_1\)). Continuity fails for this preference and there is no utility function, so the last two options cannot be used.

q: Lexicographic preferences on \(\R^2_+\) are strictly convex.
explain: Let \(a\pr b\), \(a\ne b\), \(\lambda\in(0,1)\). If \(a_1>b_1\), the mix has good 1 strictly above \(b_1\), so it is strictly better. If \(a_1=b_1\), then \(a_2>b_2\) (as \(a\ne b\)), so the mix has the same good 1 and strictly more good 2: strictly better again. This is consistent with each indifference set being a single point.

q: Every strongly monotone and convex preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) is continuous.
explain: Lexicographic preferences are strongly monotone and (even strictly) convex, yet not continuous. Monotonicity and convexity restrict the direction and shape of the ranking but cannot rule out 'jumps' caused by one good having absolute priority.

q: PS2 extra d(iii): 'sum first, then good 1'. Which set of properties is correct?
options: Strongly monotone, not continuous, convex; no utility function exists
explain: Adding any good raises the sum, so it is strongly monotone. Like lexicographic preferences, each indifference set is a single point and no utility function exists; continuity fails (\((2,1)\succ(1,2)\) but \((1,2+\varepsilon)\succ(2,1)\)). It is convex: if \(x\pr y\), the mix's sum is at least \(y\)'s, and with equal sums its good 1 is at least \(y_1\). \(x_1+x_2\) does not represent it, since that function treats \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) as indifferent.

q: Proposition 4-1-3: \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is convex if and only if
options: for every \(x^*\), the lower contour set \(\{x\in X: x^*\pr x\}\) is convex
\(\pr\) is represented by a concave utility function
for every \(x^*\), the upper contour set \(\{x\in X: x\pr x^*\}\) is convex
explain: Convexity of the preference is equivalent to convexity of every upper contour set (the 'at least as good as' sets). Lower contour sets of convex preferences need not be convex (\(\{x: x_1x_2\le1\}\) is not convex), and neither need indifference sets be. A concave representation is sufficient (Prop 4-1-4) but not necessary.

q: Proof of Prop 4-1-3, 'only if': \(\pr\) convex, \(a,b\in\{x: x\pr x^*\}\). The proof says 'without loss assume \(a\pr b\)', then \(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\pr b\pr x^*\). Which properties of \(\pr\) justify the WLOG step and the final conclusion?
explain: Completeness ensures \(a\pr b\) or \(b\pr a\), so we may rename the bundles. Convexity gives the mix \(\pr b\), and transitivity combines \(\text{mix}\pr b\) with \(b\pr x^*\) to get \(\text{mix}\pr x^*\). Neither monotonicity nor continuity is assumed in Prop 4-1-3.

q: Proof of Prop 4-1-3, 'if': every upper contour set is convex and \(a\pr b\). How does the proof obtain \(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\pr b\)?
options: Use the upper contour set of \(b\): both \(a\) (since \(a\pr b\)) and \(b\) (reflexivity) belong to it, so by convexity of this set the mix does too
Apply the definition of convex preferences directly
Use the lower contour set of \(a\), which contains \(b\)
Use the upper contour set of \(a\): \(b\) belongs to it
explain: The right set is \(\{x: x\pr b\}\): it contains \(a\) by assumption and \(b\) by reflexivity, so convexity of the set puts the mix in it, i.e. \(\text{mix}\pr b\). \(b\) is generally not in the upper contour set of \(a\), lower contour sets are not assumed convex, and using the definition of convex preferences would assume what is to be proved.

q: If \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is convex, then every lower contour set \(\{x: x^*\pr x\}\) is convex.
explain: Take \(u=x_1x_2\), which represents convex preferences. The lower contour set \(\{x: x_1x_2\le1\}\) contains \((4,0)\) and \((0,4)\) but not their midpoint \((2,2)\), where \(u=4\). Prop 4-1-3 characterises convexity by UPPER contour sets only.

q: If \(\pr\) is convex, then every indifference set of \(\pr\) is a convex set.
explain: For \(u=x_1x_2\) the indifference set \(\{x_1x_2=1\}\) contains \((1,1)\) and \((4,\tfrac14)\) but not their midpoint \((2.5,0.625)\), where \(u\approx1.56\). Convexity concerns upper contour sets: the region on and above each curve is convex, the curve itself is not. Indifference curves are 'bowed toward the origin', not convex sets.

q: OR motivates convexity with candidates on a left-right line, ordered D, A, C, B, E. A voter who cares only about positions prefers A to B. Which conclusion does the convexity intuition support?
options: She prefers C to B, since moving part of the way from B toward A should also be an improvement
explain: If moving from B to A is an improvement, going part of the way (to C, between them) should be too: this is exactly '\(a\pr b\Rightarrow\) mix \(\pr b\)'. The comparison of A with C is open (it depends on whether C or A is her favourite), D versus A is open too. E is on the other side of B, and the natural conclusion is B over E, not E over B.

q: Which situation is the best example of a VIOLATION of convex preferences?
options: A traveller indifferent between a week in Rome and a week in Tokyo who finds half a week in each strictly worse than either
A consumer who values only good 2
A consumer indifferent between 10 coffees and 10 croissants who strictly prefers 5 coffees and 5 croissants
A consumer with perfect substitutes preferences
explain: Convexity says the mix is at least as good as the worse endpoint. Splitting a holiday so the mix is worse than both endpoints contradicts this. The coffee-croissant consumer displays the taste for variety that convexity describes. Preferences that value only good 2 or treat goods as perfect substitutes are convex (linear utilities are concave).

q: Is the preference represented by \(u=\max\{x_1,x_2\}\) convex?
options: Yes: its indifference curves are L-shaped like those of min
No, because it is not continuous
explain: The upper contour set \(\{x: \max\{x_1,x_2\}\ge1\}\) contains \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) but not their midpoint, where max is \(\tfrac12\). The L-shapes of max point toward the origin (the reverse of min), and max of linear functions is convex, not concave. The function is continuous.

q: Which of the following utility functions represents a NON-convex preference relation?
explain: \(x_1^2+x_2^2\) has quarter-circle indifference curves bowed away from the origin: \((1,0)\sim(0,1)\succ(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\). \(\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) is concave, \(\min\{2x_1,x_2\}\) is concave (min of linear functions), and \(x_1-x_2\) is linear, so all three represent convex preferences by Prop 4-1-4, even though \(x_1-x_2\) is not monotone.

q: Ideal bundle with \(x^*\) and \(u(x)=-(|x_1-x_1^*|+|x_2-x_2^*|)\) (OR Problem 4.6). Which is correct?
options: Continuous and convex, but not monotone
Continuous but not convex, because indifference sets are diamonds
Convex but not continuous, because \(|\cdot|\) has kinks
explain: \(u\) is continuous (sum of absolute values), and the distance \(|x_1-x_1^*|+|x_2-x_2^*|\) is a convex function, so \(u=-\)distance is concave and the preference is convex by Prop 4-1-4. The diamond-shaped indifference sets surround the ideal point and their upper contour sets (filled diamonds) are convex. Kinks break differentiability, not continuity, and moving past \(x^*\) makes the consumer worse off, so monotonicity fails.

q: Which property does the preference represented by \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) LACK?
explain: \((1,1)\sim(2,1)\) and their midpoint \((1.5,1)\) is indifferent to both, not strictly better, so strict convexity fails (the indifference curves have flat pieces). Min is monotone, continuous (a continuous formula, Prop 4-1-1) and convex (concave, or the direct argument of PS2 extra g).

q: PS2 extra g: prove \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) gives a convex preference. Take \(x\pr y\) and \(m=\min\{y_1,y_2\}\). What is the key step?
options: \(\min\) is a linear function, so \(u(\text{mix})=\lambda u(x)+(1-\lambda)u(y)\)
\(\min\) is continuous, so the mix is indifferent to \(y\)
\(x_1,x_2\ge\min\{x_1,x_2\}\ge m\) and \(y_1,y_2\ge m\), so each coordinate of \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\) is an average of numbers \(\ge m\), hence \(\ge m\); so \(u(\text{mix})\ge m=u(y)\)
\(\min\) is strictly increasing in each good, so the mix is better
explain: All four coordinates involved are at least \(m\), so both coordinates of the mix are at least \(m\) and its min is at least \(u(y)\). Min is not linear (it is only concave: \(\min\) of the mix \(\ge\) the weighted average), it is not strictly increasing in each good, and continuity says nothing about convexity.

q: PS2 extra f(ii): \(u=x_2+g(x_1)\) with \(g\) concave and increasing; assume \(b\pr a\). The proof writes \(u(\lambda b+(1-\lambda)a)=\lambda b_2+(1-\lambda)a_2+g(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)a_1)\ge\lambda u(b)+(1-\lambda)u(a)\ge u(a)\). Where is the concavity of \(g\) used?
options: In the last inequality \(\lambda u(b)+(1-\lambda)u(a)\ge u(a)\)
In the first inequality: \(g(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)a_1)\ge\lambda g(b_1)+(1-\lambda)g(a_1)\)
It is not used: any increasing \(g\) works
explain: The \(x_2\) part is linear and passes through with equality; concavity of \(g\) supplies the first inequality. The last inequality uses \(u(b)\ge u(a)\), not concavity. Without concavity the result can fail: \(g(x_1)=x_1^2\) gives \(u=x_2+x_1^2\), and \((2,0)\sim(0,4)\) but the midpoint \((1,2)\) has \(u=3<4\).

q: PS2 extra f(i): for quasilinear \(u=x_2+g(x_1)\), how are the indifference sets related?
options: They are vertical translations of each other: \(x_2=k-g(x_1)\)
They all pass through the origin
They are horizontal translations of each other
They are radial expansions (scalings) of each other
explain: Each indifference set is \(x_2=k-g(x_1)\); changing \(k\) shifts the same curve up or down. Hence the slope (MRS) at a given \(x_1\) is the same on every curve: it depends only on \(x_1\). Radial scaling describes homothetic preferences (e.g. Cobb-Douglas), and horizontal translations would arise for \(x_1+h(x_2)\).

q: PS2 extra d(ii) 'balanced first'. Which witness shows it is NOT convex?
explain: \((2,2)\) is balanced, so it beats the unbalanced \((0,4)\). The midpoint \((1,3)\) is unbalanced with less good 2 than \((0,4)\), so it is worse than \((0,4)\), the worse endpoint: convexity fails. Option 2 is the non-monotonicity witness, option 3 the non-continuity witness, and option 4 is false (\((2,2)\succ(1,1)\)).

q: Slides 31-32: \(a=(10,10)\), \(b=(11,10-\beta)\), \(c=(12,10-\beta-\gamma)\) with \(a\sim b\sim c\). Under strong monotonicity and convexity, \(\beta\ge\gamma\). Suppose \(\beta<\gamma\). Which step yields the contradiction?
options: \(\tfrac12a+\tfrac12c\) equals \(b\), so it is indifferent to \(b\)
\(b\succ a\) by strong monotonicity because \(b\) has more good 1
By continuity there is a bundle between \(a\) and \(c\) indifferent to \(b\)
\(\tfrac12a+\tfrac12c=(11,10-\tfrac12(\beta+\gamma))\) has less good 2 than \(b\), so by strong monotonicity it is \(\prec b\); but convexity gives \(\tfrac12a+\tfrac12c\pr c\sim b\)
explain: If \(\beta<\gamma\) then \(\beta<\tfrac12(\beta+\gamma)\), so the midpoint has the same good 1 as \(b\) but strictly less good 2: strong monotonicity makes it strictly worse than \(b\). Convexity (with \(a\sim c\)) makes it at least as good as \(c\sim b\). Contradiction. The midpoint equals \(b\) only when \(\beta=\gamma\), continuity is not used, and \(b\) has less good 2 than \(a\), so strong monotonicity cannot compare them.

q: A consumer with strongly monotone and convex preferences has \((10,10)\sim(11,7)\sim(12,c_2)\). Which value of \(c_2\) is IMPOSSIBLE?
explain: Here \(\beta=3\) and \(\gamma=7-c_2\). Diminishing MRS requires \(\beta\ge\gamma\), i.e. \(c_2\ge4\). With \(c_2=3\), \(\gamma=4>3\): the midpoint of \((10,10)\) and \((12,3)\) is \((11,6.5)\), which is worse than \((11,7)\) by strong monotonicity, contradicting convexity. \(c_2=4\) (linear indifference curve) is allowed.

q: In economic terms, convexity of (strongly monotone) preferences is equivalent to
options: diminishing marginal rate of substitution: the more good 1 you have, the less good 2 you are willing to give up for one more unit of good 1
increasing marginal rate of substitution: the more good 1 you have, the more good 2 you give up for an extra unit of good 1
constant marginal utility of each good
diminishing marginal utility of each good, i.e. concave \(u\)
explain: Convexity means the indifference curve flattens as \(x_1\) grows: good 1 measured in units of good 2 becomes less valuable. This is about the rate of substitution (ordinal), not about diminishing marginal utility of a particular \(u\) (cardinal): \(x_1^2x_2^2\) has increasing marginal utilities yet represents convex preferences.

q: Proposition 4-1-4: a preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) represented by a concave function is convex. Which statement about the converse is correct?
options: The converse holds if the preference is also continuous
The converse holds if the preference is strongly monotone
The converse holds: every convex preference is represented by a concave function
The converse fails: a convex preference may be represented by non-concave functions, and there may be no concave representation at all
explain: The slides note 'convexity of \(\pr\) does not imply \(u\) is concave; there may not be any concave utility function representing a particular convex \(\pr\)'. For example \((\min\{x_1,x_2\})^2\) is not concave but represents the convex min preference. Adding continuity or monotonicity does not rescue the converse; the exact characterisation uses quasiconcavity (Prop 4-1-5).

q: Proof of Prop 4-1-4: \(u\) concave represents \(\pr\), \(a\pr b\). The chain is \(u(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\ge\lambda u(a)+(1-\lambda)u(b)\ge u(b)\). What justifies the SECOND inequality?
explain: The first inequality is concavity. The second is just arithmetic: a weighted average of \(u(a)\) and \(u(b)\) is at least \(u(b)\) when \(u(a)\ge u(b)\), which comes from the representation. No monotonicity or continuity is needed.

q: Proposition 4-1-5: suppose \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\) is represented by \(u\). Then
explain: Convexity of the preference is exactly quasiconcavity of any utility representation (PS2 2a). Concavity is only sufficient. Quasiconvexity would correspond to convex LOWER contour sets, and continuity is unrelated to convexity.

q: PS2 2a, direction 'convex \(\Rightarrow\) \(u\) quasiconcave'. Take any \(a,b\) and \(\lambda\). What is the crucial first step?
options: Assume \(a\sim b\), since otherwise the claim is trivial
Assume WLOG \(u(a)\ge u(b)\), so \(a\pr b\) and \(\min\{u(a),u(b)\}=u(b)\); then convexity gives \(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\pr b\), i.e. \(u(\text{mix})\ge u(b)\)
Use continuity of \(u\) to pass to the limit \(\lambda\to1\)
explain: Ordering the two bundles turns the min into the smaller one, so the definitions line up word for word. Assuming concavity begs the question (and is false in general). The claim is not trivial when \(a\not\sim b\), and no continuity is needed.

q: PS2 2a, direction 'quasiconcave \(\Rightarrow\) convex'. Let \(a\pr b\). Which reasoning is correct?
options: \(u(a)\ge u(b)\), so quasiconcavity gives \(u(\text{mix})\ge u(a)\), so the mix \(\pr a\)
\(u(a)\ge u(b)\), so \(\min\{u(a),u(b)\}=u(b)\); quasiconcavity gives \(u(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\ge u(b)\), so the mix \(\pr b\)
Quasiconcavity implies concavity, so Prop 4-1-4 applies
explain: The min equals \(u(b)\), and quasiconcavity delivers exactly what convexity requires. It does not give \(u(\text{mix})\ge u(a)\) (that would be '\(\ge\max\)'). The weighted-average inequality is concavity, which quasiconcavity does not provide, and quasiconcave functions need not be concave.

q: If \(u\) is quasiconcave and \(f:\R\to\R\) is strictly increasing, then \(f\circ u\) is quasiconcave.
explain: \(u(\text{mix})\ge\min\{u(a),u(b)\}\) implies \(f(u(\text{mix}))\ge f(\min\{u(a),u(b)\})=\min\{f(u(a)),f(u(b))\}\) since \(f\) is increasing. This is why quasiconcavity, unlike concavity, is an ordinal property, and why Prop 4-1-5 holds for every representation of \(\pr\).

q: If \(u\) is concave and \(f\) is strictly increasing, then \(f\circ u\) is concave.
explain: Concavity is cardinal and is destroyed by increasing transformations: \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) is concave but \(u^2=(\min\{x_1,x_2\})^2\) is not (along the diagonal it equals \(t^2\)). Both represent the same convex preference. That is why the slides warn that convexity of \(\pr\) does not imply that a given representation is concave.

q: Which utility function is quasiconcave but NOT concave on \(\R^2_+\)?
explain: \(x_1^{0.7}x_2^{0.7}\) equals \(t^{1.4}\) on the diagonal, which is strictly convex, so \(u\) is not concave; but it is an increasing transformation of the concave \(\sqrt{x_1x_2}\), hence quasiconcave. Cobb-Douglas with exponents summing to less than 1 (\(0.3+0.3\)) is concave, and \(\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) and min are concave.

q: The preference represented by \(u=(x_1+x_2)^2\) is not convex, because \(u\) is a convex function.
explain: \(u=(x_1+x_2)^2\) is an increasing transformation of \(x_1+x_2\) on \(\R^2_+\), so it represents perfect-substitutes preferences, which are convex (upper contour sets are half-planes intersected with \(\R^2_+\)). Convexity of the preference depends on quasiconcavity of \(u\), and \((x_1+x_2)^2\) is quasiconcave even though it is a convex function.

q: Consider \(u=x_1x_2\) on all of \(\R^2_+\). Is the preference strictly convex?
options: Yes, on all of \(\R^2_+\), because its indifference curves are hyperbolas
No: \((0,1)\sim(0,5)\), and the mix \((0,3)\) is indifferent to them, not strictly better
No, because it is not monotone
explain: All bundles on the axes have utility 0, so the indifference set at level 0 contains segments, and mixing \((0,1)\) and \((0,5)\) gives a bundle that is not strictly better. On the interior the indifference curves are strictly convex hyperbolas, so strict convexity holds there. Non-concavity is irrelevant (quasiconcavity is what matters), and \(x_1x_2\) is monotone.

q: If \(\pr\) is represented by a strictly concave function \(u\), then \(\pr\) is strictly convex.
explain: Let \(a\pr b\), \(a\ne b\), \(\lambda\in(0,1)\). Strict concavity gives \(u(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)>\lambda u(a)+(1-\lambda)u(b)\ge u(b)\), so the mix is strictly better than \(b\). This is the strict analogue of Prop 4-1-4's proof.

q: Which preference is convex but NOT strictly convex?
explain: Perfect substitutes have straight indifference lines: \((3,0)\sim(0,2)\) and their midpoint \((1.5,1)\) is also indifferent, not strictly better. \(\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) and the log sum are strictly concave, so strictly convex; lexicographic preferences are strictly convex too (each indifference set is a single point).

q: Which preference is monotone, continuous and convex, but NOT strongly monotone?
explain: Min is monotone, continuous (Prop 4-1-1), convex (concave), but \((2,1)\sim(1,1)\). Max is monotone but not strongly monotone and not convex. Lexicographic preferences are strongly monotone and convex but not continuous. \(x_1^2+x_2^2\) is strongly monotone, continuous, not convex.

q: PS2 extra d(i): 'prefers bundles further from the origin (Euclidean distance)'. Which description is correct?
options: No utility exists; strongly monotone, not continuous, convex
explain: The distance itself (or its square) represents the preference; indifference curves are quarter circles bowed away from the origin, so \((1,0)\sim(0,1)\succ(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\): not convex. It is continuous and strongly monotone on \(\R^2_+\). \(|x_1|+|x_2|\) uses the wrong distance, and \(-\)distance would describe a consumer who wants to be close to the origin.

q: OR Definition 4.6: a monotone and convex \(\pr\) is differentiable if for every bundle \(z\) there is a pair \((v_1(z),v_2(z))\ne(0,0)\) of nonnegative 'local valuations' such that for all \((\delta_1,\delta_2)\):
options: \(v_1\delta_1+v_2\delta_2>0\Rightarrow z+(\delta_1,\delta_2)\succ z\) for every size of change
\(v_1(z)=\partial u/\partial x_1\) and \(v_2(z)=\partial u/\partial x_2\) for every representation \(u\)
explain: Local valuations describe small changes: a direction is an improvement for small enough steps exactly when its valuation-weighted value is positive. The condition is local (\(\varepsilon\) small), not for changes of any size. Partial derivatives are one pair of local valuations when \(u\) has continuous partials (OR Prop 4.4), but the definition does not mention \(u\), and only the ratio \(v_1/v_2\) matters.

q: For \(u(x)=x_1x_2\), which is a pair of local valuations at bundle \(z=(z_1,z_2)\) (OR Prop 4.4)?
explain: With continuous partial derivatives, the partials \(\partial u/\partial x_1=x_2\) and \(\partial u/\partial x_2=x_1\) form a pair of local valuations, so \((z_2,z_1)\). The classic slip is to write \((z_1,z_2)\). \((1,1)\) would be perfect substitutes with equal weights.

q: Lexicographic preferences on \(\R^2_+\) are differentiable in the sense of OR Definition 4.6.
explain: The only candidate is \((1,0)\) (or a positive multiple), since any change with \(\delta_1>0\) is an improvement and any with \(\delta_1<0\) is not. But for \((\delta_1,\delta_2)=(0,1)\) we get \(1\cdot0+0\cdot1=0\), although \(z+\varepsilon(0,1)\succ z\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). So the 'iff' fails and the preference is not differentiable.

q: For \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\), at which bundles does the preference fail to be differentiable?
options: At bundles on the diagonal \(x_1=x_2\) (the kinks)
explain: At a kink \(z=(t,t)\), \(t>0\), improvements require increasing both goods, and no single line separates them as Definition 4.6 requires: e.g. \(v=(1,1)\) would label \((1,-\tfrac12)\) an improvement, which it is not. Off the diagonal, say \(x_1>x_2\), only good 2 matters locally and \((0,1)\) is a valid pair of local valuations.

q: With differentiable utility, \(MRS(x)=u_1(x)/u_2(x)\) is minus the slope of the indifference curve. Compute the MRS of \(u=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\) at \(x=(2,1)\).
explain: \(MRS=\dfrac{\tfrac13x_1^{-2/3}x_2^{2/3}}{\tfrac23x_1^{1/3}x_2^{-1/3}}=\dfrac{x_2}{2x_1}=\dfrac{1}{4}\) at \((2,1)\). Inverting the ratio gives 4, forgetting the exponents gives \(x_2/x_1=\tfrac12\).

q: For quasilinear \(u=x_2+\sqrt{x_1}\), what is the MRS at \((4,10)\), and what does it depend on?
options: \(\tfrac{10}{4}\); it depends only on the ratio \(x_2/x_1\)
explain: \(MRS=u_1/u_2=\dfrac{1/(2\sqrt{x_1})}{1}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt4}=\tfrac14\). It does not involve \(x_2\): consistent with indifference curves being vertical translations of each other. Dependence only on \(x_2/x_1\) characterises homothetic preferences such as Cobb-Douglas.

q: The marginal rate of substitution \(u_1/u_2\) of a differentiable utility function is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(f\circ u\) for a differentiable \(f\) with \(f'>0\).
explain: By the chain rule both partials are multiplied by \(f'(u(x))\), which cancels in the ratio. The MRS is minus the slope of the indifference curve, an ordinal object, so it depends only on the preference, not on the chosen representation. This is why taking logs of Cobb-Douglas before computing the MRS is allowed.

q: A preference relation on \(\R^2_+\) is called homothetic if \(x\sim y\Rightarrow\alpha x\sim\alpha y\) for all \(\alpha>0\). Which preference is NOT homothetic?
explain: Cobb-Douglas, Leontief and linear utilities are homogeneous, so scaling indifferent bundles keeps them indifferent. For the quasilinear \(x_2+\sqrt{x_1}\): \((1,0)\sim(0,1)\) but \((4,0)\) has \(u=2\) while \((0,4)\) has \(u=4\). Equivalently, its MRS \(1/(2\sqrt{x_1})\) is not constant along rays from the origin.

q: For Leontief preferences \(u=\min\{2x_1,x_2\}\), where are the kinks of the indifference curves?
explain: The kink is where the two arguments are equal: \(2x_1=x_2\). Off this ray, the extra amount of the 'excess' good is wasted. Placing the kink at \(x_1=2x_2\) is the common inversion mistake. In general, for \(\min\{ax_1,bx_2\}\) the kinks lie on \(ax_1=bx_2\).

q: OR Problem 4.7: \(\pr_A\) favours good 1 more than \(\pr_B\) if for all \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\): \((x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_A x\Rightarrow(x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_B x\). Why does \(\pr_A\) (from \(2x_1+x_2\)) favour good 1 more than \(\pr_B\) (from \(x_1+x_2\))?
options: Under A, giving up \(\varepsilon\) of good 1 is acceptable only if \(\delta\ge2\varepsilon\), which implies \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\), so it is acceptable under B too
Because A's MRS (2) is smaller than B's (1)
Under B, giving up \(\varepsilon\) of good 1 requires \(\delta\ge2\varepsilon\)
explain: \((x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_A x\iff-2\varepsilon+\delta\ge0\iff\delta\ge2\varepsilon\), and that implies \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\), which is the condition under B. Comparing utility levels across different preferences is meaningless (option 2). A's MRS is 2, which is larger than B's 1, and the requirement \(\delta\ge2\varepsilon\) belongs to A, not B.

q: OR Problem 4.7: \(\pr_A\) favours good 1 more than \(\pr_B\) if for all \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\), \((x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_A x\Rightarrow(x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_B x\). A lexicographic preference with priority on good 1 favours good 1 more than any strongly monotone preference does.
explain: Under lexicographic preferences, giving up any \(\varepsilon>0\) of good 1 makes the bundle strictly worse, whatever \(\delta\) is added. So the premise \((x_1-\varepsilon,x_2+\delta)\pr_A x\) is never satisfied and the implication holds (vacuously) for every comparison preference \(\pr_B\). Intuitively, no preference can value good 1 more than one that refuses any trade away from it.

q: Which set is the Walrasian (competitive) budget set \(B_{p,w}\) for prices \(p\gg 0\) and wealth \(w\gt 0\) (two goods)?
explain: Definition 4-2-0: \(B_{p,w}=\{x\in X: p\cdot x\le w\}\) with \(X=\R^2_+\), i.e. all non-negative bundles that cost at most w. The set with equality is the budget line (hyperplane), only the frontier. Dropping non-negativity would allow negative consumption, which is outside the consumption set.

q: Let \(p=(2,1)\) and \(w=8\). Which description of the budget line is correct?
explain: The intercepts are \(w/p_1=4\) on the \(x_1\)-axis and \(w/p_2=8\) on the \(x_2\)-axis. With \(x_1\) on the horizontal axis the slope is \(-p_1/p_2=-2\): giving up one unit of good 1 frees 2 euros, which buy 2 units of good 2. Writing the intercepts the other way round (\(w/p_2\) on the \(x_1\)-axis) is the usual mistake.

q: Starting from \(p=(2,1)\), \(w=8\), the price of good 1 falls to \(p_1=1\) with \(p_2\) and \(w\) unchanged. How does the budget line move?
options: It pivots around the \(x_2\)-intercept \((0,8)\), becoming flatter
It does not move, because only relative prices matter
It pivots around the \(x_1\)-intercept \((4,0)\), becoming steeper
It shifts out parallel to itself
explain: The \(x_2\)-intercept \(w/p_2=8\) does not depend on \(p_1\), so it stays put, while the \(x_1\)-intercept moves out from 4 to 8: the line rotates around \((0,8)\) and the slope goes from \(-2\) to \(-1\). A parallel shift happens when w changes (or all prices change in the same proportion). Relative prices did change here, so the line must move.

q: To show that \(B_{p,w}\) is convex, take \(x,y\in B_{p,w}\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Which step is the key one?
options: Since preferences are convex, \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\pr x\)
Since \(p\gg0\), the budget set is compact, hence convex
Since \(x\) and \(y\) are on the budget line, so is every convex combination
explain: Cost is linear in the bundle, so the cost of the mixture is the mixture of the costs, which is at most w; non-negativity is also kept by averaging. Convexity of preferences has nothing to do with the budget set, which depends only on p and w. Compactness does not imply convexity, and x, y need not be on the budget line.

q: According to the slides, a Walrasian demand function is:
options: the solution of the utility maximisation problem for a continuous, monotone preference
a function that assigns to each budget set the bundle on the budget line closest to the origin
a function assigning to each bundle the cheapest price vector at which it is affordable
a function that assigns to each budget set \(B_{p,w}\) one of its members, \(x(p,w)\in B_{p,w}\)
explain: A Walrasian demand function just picks a member of each budget set. The slides stress that the definition does NOT assume demand comes from maximising a preference relation (examples: buy only the cheaper good, half of wealth on each good, and so on). Utility maximisation is one way to generate demand, studied in Topic 4.3.

q: True or false: By definition, a Walrasian demand function \(x(p,w)\) is the result of the consumer maximising some preference relation over \(B_{p,w}\).
explain: False. The slides say explicitly that the definition does not assume maximisation; any rule that picks a member of each budget set qualifies. Whether such a rule can be rationalized by a preference is exactly the question WARP helps to answer. For example, the demand \(x=wp/\|p\|^2\) (PS3 4e) is a Walrasian demand function but no preference rationalizes it.

q: A Walrasian demand function is homogeneous of degree zero (HD0) if:
explain: Definition 4-2-1: scaling all prices and wealth by the same \(\alpha\gt0\) leaves demand unchanged. The justification is that \(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}=B_{p,w}\): the set of feasible bundles is literally the same, and choice should depend only on that set. The option with \(\alpha x\) is degree-one homogeneity; scaling only prices or only wealth changes the budget set.

q: Walras' law for a Walrasian demand function \(x(p,w)\) states that:
options: the value of aggregate excess demand is zero at equilibrium prices
explain: Definition 4-2-2: the consumer fully spends her wealth, \(p\cdot x=w\). The weak inequality holds for every demand function by definition (the choice is a member of the budget set), so it is not an extra property. The aggregate-excess-demand version is Walras' law for an economy (Topic 5.2); the last option is HD0.

q: Consider \(x_1(p,w)=\dfrac{p_2}{p_1+p_2}\cdot\dfrac{w}{p_1}\), \(x_2(p,w)=\dfrac{\beta p_1}{p_1+p_2}\cdot\dfrac{w}{p_2}\) with \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Which is correct?
options: It satisfies HD0 but not Walras' law
It satisfies Walras' law but not HD0
It satisfies both HD0 and Walras' law
explain: Replacing \(p,w\) by \(\alpha p,\alpha w\), every \(\alpha\) cancels, for any \(\beta\), so HD0 holds. Expenditure is \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2=w\cdot\frac{p_2+\beta p_1}{p_1+p_2}\), which equals w only if \(\beta=1\); for \(\beta\lt1\) it is strictly below w, so money is left unspent and Walras' law fails.

q: For the demand \(x_1=\dfrac{p_2}{p_1+p_2}\cdot\dfrac{w}{p_1}\), \(x_2=\dfrac{\beta p_1}{p_1+p_2}\cdot\dfrac{w}{p_2}\), total expenditure \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2\) equals:
explain: \(p_1x_1=\frac{p_2w}{p_1+p_2}\) and \(p_2x_2=\frac{\beta p_1w}{p_1+p_2}\); adding gives \(w(p_2+\beta p_1)/(p_1+p_2)\). It equals w iff \(\beta=1\) and it is less than w for \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Answering \(\beta w\) wrongly applies \(\beta\) to the whole budget, but only good 2's spending is scaled.

q: Which of the following demand functions satisfies Walras' law but is NOT homogeneous of degree zero?
explain: For the last one, \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2=\frac{p_1w+w}{p_1+1}=w\), so Walras holds; but scaling gives \(x_1=\frac{\alpha w}{\alpha p_1+1}\ne\frac{w}{p_1+1}\) in general, because the constant 1 is not scaled (numerator degree 1, denominator not homogeneous). The first two are HD0 and satisfy Walras; the third is HD0 but spends only \(2w/3\).

q: Which of the following demand functions is homogeneous of degree zero but violates Walras' law?
explain: \(\left(\frac{w}{3p_1},\frac{w}{3p_2}\right)\) is HD0 (ratios of degree-one terms) and spends \(\frac{2}{3}w\lt w\). The second is HD0 and satisfies Walras. In the third and fourth the constant \(-1\) is not scaled, so they fail HD0 (and both do satisfy Walras: e.g. \(p_1(\frac{w}{p_1}-1)+p_2\frac{p_1}{p_2}=w\)).

q: Slide 10, example 4: the consumer buys as much as he can of good 1 up to 7 units and spends any remaining wealth on good 2, so \(x_1=\min\{7,w/p_1\}\), \(x_2=\max\{0,(w-7p_1)/p_2\}\). What is \(x(p,w)\) at \(p=(2,1)\), \(w=20\)?
explain: \(w/p_1=10\gt7\), so \(x_1=7\), costing 14; the remaining 6 euros buy \(6/p_2=6\) units of good 2. The bundle \((10,0)\) ignores the 7-unit cap. \((7,13)\) forgets to subtract the cost of good 1, and \((7,6)\) indeed costs exactly 20 (Walras).

q: Which of the four slide-10 demand rules (1: buy only the cheaper good, split wealth equally if prices are equal; 2: same quantity of each good, spend everything; 3: half of wealth on each good; 4: good 1 up to 7 units, rest on good 2) fail homogeneity of degree zero?
options: Only rule 4, because the cap of 7 units is not scaled
Only rule 1, because it uses a price comparison
explain: All four are HD0 and satisfy Walras' law. Rule 1 depends on prices only through \(p_1\lt p_2\), which is unchanged when both prices are multiplied by \(\alpha\gt0\). Rule 4 uses \(w/p_1\) and \((w-7p_1)/p_2\), both unchanged by scaling; the cap 7 is a quantity, not money, so it does not need to be scaled.

q: Rule 2 on slide 10 (\"the consumer chooses the same quantity of each good and spends all his wealth\") gives which demand?
explain: Set \(x_1=x_2=t\) and impose \(p_1t+p_2t=w\), so \(t=w/(p_1+p_2)\). Option \(w/2\) ignores prices (fails HD0). \((w/2p_1,w/2p_2)\) is rule 3 (half of wealth on each good), which gives equal spending, not equal quantities.

q: Which utility function rationalizes slide-10 rule 3 (\"the consumer spends half of his wealth on each good\")?
explain: \(u=x_1x_2\) is Cobb-Douglas with equal exponents, whose demand is \(x_i=w/(2p_i)\): spending share 1/2 on each good. \(\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) gives equal quantities (rule 2). \(x_1+x_2\) buys only the cheaper good (rule 1, up to tie-breaking). \(\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) gives the spending ratio \(p_2/p_1\) (PS3 1a), not equal shares.

q: PS3 1a: a consumer spends all her wealth, and the ratio of spending on good 1 to spending on good 2 is \(p_2/p_1\). What is her demand for good 1?
explain: From \(p_1x_1/(p_2x_2)=p_2/p_1\) we get \(p_2x_2=\frac{p_1}{p_2}p_1x_1\); substituting into \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2=w\) gives \(p_1x_1\frac{p_1+p_2}{p_2}=w\), so \(x_1=\frac{p_2w}{p_1(p_1+p_2)}\). This is exactly the slide-13 demand with \(\beta=1\), and it is rationalized by \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\). The option with \(p_1\) on top is \(x_2\).

q: PS3 1a: to show that \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) rationalizes the demand \(x_1=\frac{p_2w}{p_1(p_1+p_2)}\), \(x_2=\frac{p_1w}{p_2(p_1+p_2)}\), what is the key condition at the (interior, unique) optimum?
options: The cheaper good is bought exclusively
explain: \(\partial u/\partial x_i=1/(2\sqrt{x_i})\), so \(MRS=\sqrt{x_2}/\sqrt{x_1}\); setting it equal to \(p_1/p_2\) gives \(x_2=(p_1/p_2)^2x_1\), and the binding budget yields the given demand. The optimum is interior because the square root has infinite slope at 0. The condition \(x_2/x_1=p_1/p_2\) is the Cobb-Douglas one, which gives equal spending shares instead.

q: Following the slides, good i is normal at \((p,w)\) if:
explain: The wealth effect for good i is \(\partial x_i/\partial w\); the good is normal if it is \(\ge0\) and inferior if it is \(\lt0\). So a zero wealth effect counts as normal under the slides' (weak) definition. Conditions on \(\partial x_i/\partial p_i\) are about price effects: a positive own-price effect defines a Giffen good.

q: Good i is a Giffen good at \((p,w)\) if:
explain: A Giffen good is one whose demand rises when its own price rises, holding the other price and wealth fixed. A negative wealth effect defines an inferior good: inferiority is necessary for Giffen behaviour in rational demand but not sufficient. A positive cross-price effect is about substitutes, and a negative own-price effect is the ordinary law of demand.

q: Fix \(w\) and \(p_1\). The locus of bundles demanded as \(p_2\) ranges over all positive values is called:
explain: The offer curve traces demand as one price varies with wealth and the other price fixed (slide 16). The wealth expansion path instead traces demand as w varies at fixed prices. The budget hyperplane is \(\{x: p\cdot x=w\}\) for given (p, w).
