q: Slide 19: \(p_1=\bar p_1\) and \(w\) are fixed and \(p_2\) falls from \(p_2\) to \(p_2'\) to \(p_2''\). On the offer curve, the chosen \(x_2\) rises from the first to the second price, but falls between \(p_2'\) and \(p_2''\). What can you conclude?
options: Good 2 is inferior but not Giffen
The demand function violates Walras' law
Good 2 is a Giffen good at \((\bar p_1,p_2',w)\)
explain: Between \(p_2'\) and \(p_2''\) the price of good 2 falls and demand for good 2 falls too, so \(\partial x_2/\partial p_2\gt0\) there: good 2 is Giffen at \((\bar p_1,p_2',w)\), and the offer curve bends back. Inferiority is a statement about wealth changes and cannot be read directly from a price change. Nothing in the figure says money is left unspent.

q: In the slides' potato story, a poor consumer eats a lot of potatoes. When the price of potatoes falls, his potato consumption may fall. What drives this?
options: A violation of WARP: the consumer is irrational
A violation of Walras' law: he no longer spends all his money
The wealth effect: he is effectively richer and switches to more desirable foods, potatoes being an inferior good
The substitution effect: potatoes are now relatively more expensive
explain: A cheaper price raises real wealth; with more real wealth a poor consumer buys other foods that also prevent hunger, so demand for the low-quality good falls. This requires potatoes to be inferior with a strong wealth effect that beats the substitution effect (which goes the other way, toward more potatoes). Nothing irrational happens: Giffen behaviour is consistent with WARP.

q: According to the slides, when does the assumption that demand is normal (both goods normal at every \((p,w)\)) make most sense?
options: When goods are large aggregates such as food or shelter
When goods are narrowly defined, such as one specific kind of shoes
When the consumer is very poor
Only when demand comes from a quasilinear utility
explain: The slides point out that normality is plausible for broad aggregates (more wealth, more food, more shelter), but not for disaggregated goods, where cheap low-quality varieties are often inferior. Very poor consumers are where inferior and even Giffen goods (the potato story) appear.

q: For Cobb-Douglas demand \(x_1=\alpha w/p_1\), \(x_2=(1-\alpha)w/p_2\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), which statement is correct?
options: Good 1 is inferior because \(\partial x_1/\partial p_1\lt0\)
Both goods are normal, neither is Giffen, and the cross-price effect \(\partial x_1/\partial p_2\) is zero
Good 1 is normal but good 2 is inferior
Good 1 is Giffen at low prices
explain: \(\partial x_1/\partial w=\alpha/p_1\gt0\) and \(\partial x_2/\partial w=(1-\alpha)/p_2\gt0\): both normal. \(\partial x_1/\partial p_1=-\alpha w/p_1^2\lt0\): not Giffen. \(x_1\) does not depend on \(p_2\), so the cross-price effect is 0. A negative own-price effect says nothing about inferiority, which is about wealth.

q: Demand from \(u=\ln x_1+x_2\) (interior case) is \(x_1=p_2/p_1\), \(x_2=w/p_2-1\). Using the slides' definitions, good 1 is:
options: inferior, since its demand does not rise with wealth
explain: \(\partial x_1/\partial w=0\ge0\), so good 1 is normal under the slides' weak definition (inferior needs a strictly negative wealth effect). \(\partial x_1/\partial p_1=-p_2/p_1^2\lt0\), so it is not Giffen. Calling a zero wealth effect inferior is the trap.

q: With \(p_2\) and \(w\) fixed, a consumer buys \(x_1=3\) when \(p_1=1\) and \(x_1=3.2\) when \(p_1=1.1\) (her demand is differentiable in between). Which conclusion is justified?
options: Good 1 is a substitute for good 2
Good 1 is Giffen somewhere between these prices
explain: Demand for good 1 rose although its own price rose, with wealth and the other price fixed, so \(\partial x_1/\partial p_1\gt0\) at some price in between: Giffen behaviour. In fact, for rational demand a Giffen good must be inferior, so 'normal' is the wrong conclusion. Uncompensated price data alone cannot show a WARP violation, since Giffen goods are compatible with WARP.

q: True or false: If good 1 is inferior at \((p,w)\), then it is a Giffen good at \((p,w)\).
explain: False. Inferiority means the wealth effect \(\partial x_1/\partial w\lt0\). To be Giffen, the wealth effect of the price change must be strong enough to beat the (negative) substitution effect. Most inferior goods still have downward-sloping demand. The implication goes the other way for rational demand: Giffen requires inferior.

q: True or false: For a demand function generated by a rational consumer (so it satisfies WARP and hence the compensated law of demand), a good that is normal at \((p,w)\) cannot be Giffen at \((p,w)\).
explain: True. A price rise has a substitution effect (compensated, \(\le0\) by the compensated law of demand) plus a wealth effect: the consumer is poorer, so for a normal good demand falls (or stays the same). Both push \(x_i\) down, so \(\partial x_i/\partial p_i\le0\). This is why the slides' Giffen story needs an inferior good with a strong wealth effect.

q: A price change affects the consumer in two ways. Which pair does the slides' analysis distinguish?
options: It changes nominal wealth, and it changes the number of goods
It changes WARP, and it changes Walras' law
It changes the relative cost of the goods, and it changes real wealth
It changes preferences, and it changes the consumption set
explain: Slide 26: a price change alters relative costs (substitution) and changes real wealth (purchasing power). Slutsky compensation adjusts wealth so that the old bundle is just affordable, which removes the real-wealth effect so that WARP can be linked to the relative-price effect alone.

q: A Walrasian demand function \(x(p,w)\) satisfies WARP if, for any \((p,w)\) and \((p',w')\):
options: if \(p\cdot x(p',w')\le w\) and \(x(p',w')\ne x(p,w)\), then \(p'\cdot x(p,w)\gt w'\)
if \(p\cdot x(p',w')\le w\), then \(p'\cdot x(p,w)\le w'\)
if \(p\cdot x(p',w')\gt w\) and \(x(p',w')\ne x(p,w)\), then \(p'\cdot x(p,w)\le w'\)
explain: Definition 4-2-3: if \(x'=x(p',w')\) was affordable when \(x=x(p,w)\) was chosen (and differs from it), then x is revealed preferred to \(x'\), so x must not be affordable at \((p',w')\). The second option reverses the conclusion. The last one is too strong: x may be affordable at \((p',w')\) as long as \(x'\) was not affordable at \((p,w)\).

q: Which statement is equivalent to WARP for a demand function \(x(\cdot)\)?
options: Demand never changes when prices change
For any two situations, we cannot have both \(p\cdot x(p',w')\le w\) and \(p'\cdot x(p,w)\le w'\) with \(x(p,w)\ne x(p',w')\)
For any two situations, at least one of the two chosen bundles is affordable in the other situation
The consumer always spends all her wealth
explain: WARP rules out exactly the case where the two different choices are each affordable in the other situation (each would be revealed preferred to the other). If neither, or only one, is affordable in the other situation, there is no conflict. Spending all wealth is Walras' law, a different property.

q: WARP for demand functions is the analogue of which earlier condition for choice functions (Topic 2)?
explain: Topic 2 tested rationality of choice functions with property \(\alpha\); Topic 4.2 does the same with budget sets as the menus, and the test is WARP. Both say: if x is chosen while y is available, y should not be chosen in another situation where x is also available. Independence belongs to choice under uncertainty (Topic 3).

q: Observations (Walras' law holds, so wealth equals spending): at \(p=(1,2)\) the consumer buys \(x=(2,4)\); at \(p'=(2,1)\) she buys \(x'=(4,2)\). Does this violate WARP?
options: Yes, because the bundles are mirror images, which violates HD0
Yes: \(p\cdot x'=8\le10=w\) and \(p'\cdot x=8\le10=w'\), with \(x\ne x'\)
No: the two bundles cost the same at both price vectors
explain: \(w=p\cdot x=2+8=10\) and \(w'=p'\cdot x'=8+2=10\). The cross costs are \(p\cdot x'=4+4=8\le10\) and \(p'\cdot x=4+4=8\le10\): each chosen bundle was affordable when the other was chosen, so each is revealed preferred to the other, a WARP violation. HD0 has nothing to do with it, since the two budgets are not scalar multiples of each other.

q: Observations (Walras' law holds): at \(p=(1,1)\) the consumer buys \(x=(3,1)\); at \(p'=(1,2)\) she buys \(x'=(2,1)\). Which is correct?
options: WARP holds: \(x'\) is affordable at \((p,w)\) (cost 3 ≤ 4), but \(x\) is not affordable at \((p',w')\) (cost 5 > 4)
WARP cannot be checked without knowing the utility function
WARP is violated, since both bundles are affordable at \(p\)
WARP holds because neither bundle is affordable in the other situation
explain: \(w=4\), \(w'=2+2=4\). \(p\cdot x'=3\le4\): x is revealed preferred to \(x'\). \(p'\cdot x=3+2=5\gt4\): x was not affordable when \(x'\) was chosen. Only one direction of revealed preference occurs, so there is no conflict. Both bundles being affordable at the same p is irrelevant; what matters is cross-affordability.

q: Three observations (Walras' law holds): A: \(p=(1,1)\), \(x=(4,2)\); B: \(p=(1,2)\), \(x=(2,3)\); C: \(p=(3,1)\), \(x=(1,4)\). Which pair violates WARP?
explain: Wealths: \(w_A=6\), \(w_B=8\), \(w_C=7\). A–B: \(x_B\) costs 5 ≤ 6 at A and \(x_A\) costs 8 ≤ 8 at B: violation. A–C: \(x_C\) costs 5 ≤ 6 at A but \(x_A\) costs 14 > 7 at C: fine. B–C: \(x_C\) costs 9 > 8 at B and \(x_B\) costs 9 > 7 at C: fine. Note that 'on the budget line' (8 ≤ 8) counts as affordable.

q: A consumer buys \(x=(4,2)\) at \(p=(1,2)\), \(w=8\) and \(x'=(2,4)\) at \(p'=(2,1)\), \(w'=8\) (Cobb-Douglas with equal shares). Is WARP violated for this pair?
options: Yes, because both bundles cost 8 somewhere
No: \(p\cdot x'=10\gt8\) and \(p'\cdot x=10\gt8\), so neither bundle is affordable in the other situation
No, because \(x'\) is affordable at \((p,w)\) but \(x\) is not affordable at \((p',w')\)
explain: \(p\cdot x'=2+8=10\gt8\) and \(p'\cdot x=8+2=10\gt8\). Neither bundle was available when the other was chosen, so there is no revealed preference at all and nothing to contradict. Demand from a utility with unique optima always satisfies WARP, so this is no surprise.

q: True or false: If \(x(p,w)=x(p',w')\) for two different price-wealth pairs, WARP is violated.
explain: False. WARP only restricts pairs with \(x(p',w')\ne x(p,w)\). Choosing the same bundle from two different budget sets that both contain it is perfectly consistent (as in PS3 1b(vi), where the compensated bundle stays (5, 5)).

q: True or false: Suppose prices are the same in two observations, \(p=p'\), wealth rises from \(w\) to \(w'\gt w\), and the demand function satisfies Walras' law. Then these two observations cannot violate WARP, whatever bundles are chosen.
explain: True. With Walras' law, \(p\cdot x'=p'\cdot x'=w'\gt w\), so \(x'\) was never affordable at \((p,w)\); one cross-affordability condition fails, so WARP cannot be violated. This is the nested-budget logic behind Beatty and Crawford's finding that even random choosers pass the test.

q: A consumer who does not necessarily spend all her wealth chooses \(x=(3,3)\) at \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=10\), and \(x'=(4,2)\) at \(p'=(2,1)\), \(w'=10\). Using the WARP definition with the given wealths, which is correct?
options: No violation, because \(x\) does not exhaust the budget
WARP is not defined when Walras' law fails
Violation: \(p\cdot x'=6\le10\) and \(p'\cdot x=9\le10\), with \(x\ne x'\)
explain: The definition uses the wealths w, w', not the amounts spent. \(p\cdot x'=4+2=6\le10\) and \(p'\cdot x=6+3=9\le10\): each chosen bundle was affordable in the other situation and they differ, so WARP fails. WARP is defined for any Walrasian demand function; Walras' law is only needed for Proposition 4-2-2 and for the shortcut \(w=p\cdot x\).

q: A demand function \(x(p,w)\) is rationalized by a preference relation \(\pr\) when \(x(p,w)\) is the unique \(\pr\)-best bundle in every \(B_{p,w}\). Which statement is correct?
options: Such a demand always satisfies WARP
Such a demand must be linear in w
Such a demand never has inferior goods
Such a demand always satisfies the ordinary law of demand
explain: If \(x'\) is affordable when x is chosen and \(x\ne x'\), uniqueness gives \(x\succ x'\); if x were also affordable when \(x'\) is chosen, then \(x'\succ x\), a contradiction. So rationalizable demand satisfies WARP, which is why failing WARP proves non-rationalizability. Rational demand can have inferior and even Giffen goods (PS3 1b), and need not be linear in wealth.

q: PS3 4e: the consumer chooses the bundle where the budget line meets the ray from the origin orthogonal to it. What is this demand?
explain: The line \(p\cdot x=w\) has normal vector p, so the orthogonal ray is \(\{tp: t\ge0\}\). Setting \(p\cdot(tp)=w\) gives \(t=w/\|p\|^2\), so \(x=wp/\|p\|^2\). The first option is the equal-quantities ray (the 45-degree line), which is not orthogonal unless \(p_1=p_2\).

q: For the PS3 4e demand \(x(p,w)=wp/\|p\|^2\), what is \(x\) at \(p=(2,1)\), \(w=3\)?
explain: \(\|p\|^2=4+1=5\), so \(x=\frac35(2,1)=(6/5,3/5)\). Check: \(2\cdot\frac65+\frac35=\frac{15}{5}=3=w\). The bundle lies in the direction of p, so it has more of good 1, the more expensive good, which is the odd feature that leads to the WARP failure.

options: \(p\cdot x'=9/5\le2\) and \(p'\cdot x=3\le3\): WARP fails, so no preference relation (monotone or not) rationalizes this demand
WARP fails, but a non-monotone preference can still rationalize it
WARP holds, so the demand is rationalizable by a monotone preference
WARP fails only because the demand violates Walras' law
explain: \(x'\) costs \(6/5+3/5=9/5\le2\) at the first budget, and x costs \(2+1=3\le3\) at the second (exactly on the line counts). Each was chosen while the other was affordable and they differ, so WARP fails. Since any demand rationalized by a preference with unique optima satisfies WARP, no preference at all, monotone or not, rationalizes it. The demand does satisfy Walras' law.

q: Which properties does the PS3 4e demand \(x(p,w)=wp/\|p\|^2\) have?
options: HD0 and Walras' law, but not WARP
Walras' law and WARP, but not HD0
explain: \(x(\alpha p,\alpha w)=\alpha w\,\alpha p/(\alpha^2\|p\|^2)=x(p,w)\): HD0. \(p\cdot x=w\|p\|^2/\|p\|^2=w\): Walras. But the pair \(((1,1),2)\), \(((2,1),3)\) gives cross-affordable different bundles, so WARP fails. HD0 and Walras together do not imply WARP.

q: PS3 4f: show that a Walrasian demand function satisfying WARP is homogeneous of degree zero. What is the key fact used?
options: Walras' law gives \(\alpha p\cdot x=\alpha w\), so \(x\) is unchanged
The compensated law of demand with \(\Delta p=(\alpha-1)p\)
\(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}=B_{p,w}\), so \(x(p,w)\) and \(x(\alpha p,\alpha w)\) are each affordable in the other situation; WARP then forces them to be equal
explain: For \(\alpha\gt0\), \(\alpha p\cdot x\le\alpha w\iff p\cdot x\le w\), so the two budget sets coincide. Both choices lie in this common set, hence each is affordable when the other is chosen; if they differed, WARP would be violated. So HD0 is a consequence of WARP, not an extra assumption. No Walras' law or preference is needed.

q: True or false: A Walrasian demand function can satisfy WARP while failing homogeneity of degree zero.
explain: False (PS3 4f). Since \(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}=B_{p,w}\), the two choices \(x(p,w)\) and \(x(\alpha p,\alpha w)\) are each affordable in the other situation; if they were different, WARP would be violated. So WARP implies HD0.

options: 9: \(x^2\) was not affordable when \(x^1\) was chosen
explain: \(p^1\cdot x^2=2\cdot2+1\cdot1+2\cdot2=9\gt8\), so \(x^2\) was not affordable at budget 1 and nothing is revealed between \(x^1\) and \(x^2\) from this observation. The affordable entries are \(p^1\cdot x^3=8\), \(p^2\cdot x^1=8\), \(p^3\cdot x^2=8\), giving \(x^1\) over \(x^3\), \(x^2\) over \(x^1\) and \(x^3\) over \(x^2\).

q: PS3 4h (three goods, three observations): each pair satisfies WARP, but \(x^1\) is revealed preferred to \(x^3\), \(x^3\) to \(x^2\), and \(x^2\) to \(x^1\). What is the lesson?
options: These choices can be rationalized because each pair satisfies WARP
The cycle shows that the demand violates Walras' law
WARP checks only pairs; a revealed-preference cycle through three observations is not excluded, so the choices are inconsistent with any rational preference even though WARP holds
The cycle shows that the demand is not HD0
explain: In each pair only one bundle is affordable in the other's budget (the off-diagonal 9s), so WARP holds pairwise. But \(x^1\succ x^3\succ x^2\succ x^1\) (strict, as choices are unique) contradicts transitivity. Ruling out such cycles needs the strong axiom (SARP); with three or more goods WARP is not enough. All bundles cost 8 at their own prices, so Walras' law holds.

q: True or false: With three or more goods, every demand function satisfying WARP (and Walras' law) is rationalized by some rational preference relation.
explain: False. PS3 4h gives three observations in three goods where every pair satisfies WARP, yet the revealed preferences form a cycle \(x^1\to x^3\to x^2\to x^1\), which no transitive preference can produce. WARP is a pairwise condition and does not rule out longer cycles; the strong axiom does.

q: A Slutsky-compensated price change from \((p,w)\) to new prices \(p'\) sets new wealth to:
options: the wealth that keeps utility at its old level
explain: Slutsky compensation gives exactly enough wealth for the old bundle to be just affordable at the new prices: \(w'=p'\cdot x(p,w)\), equivalently \(\Delta w=\Delta p\cdot x(p,w)\) under Walras' law. Keeping utility constant is Hicksian compensation (Topic 4.3), which gives (weakly) less money because the consumer can substitute. Keeping \(w'=w\) is an uncompensated change.

q: At \(p=(1,2)\), \(w=10\) the consumer buys \(x=(4,3)\). Prices change to \(p'=(2,2)\). What is the Slutsky-compensated wealth \(w'\)?
explain: \(w'=p'\cdot x=2\cdot4+2\cdot3=14\). Equivalently \(\Delta w=\Delta p\cdot x=(1,0)\cdot(4,3)=4\), so \(w'=10+4\). Doubling wealth to 20 would compensate for doubling all prices, but only \(p_1\) doubled.

q: Proposition 4-2-2 (WA and compensated price changes) requires which hypotheses on \(x(p,w)\)?
options: x is generated by a continuous, monotone, convex preference
x is HD0 and satisfies Walras' law
x is differentiable and all goods are normal
explain: The statement: suppose x is homogeneous of degree zero and satisfies Walras' law; then x satisfies WARP iff the compensated law of demand holds. No preference or utility is assumed; this is a statement about demand functions. Walras' law is used directly in the proof (\(p'\cdot x'=w'\) and \(p\cdot x=w\)).

q: Proposition 4-2-2 says that (for x HD0 with Walras' law) WARP holds if and only if, for every compensated change from \((p,w)\) to \((p',w')=(p',p'\cdot x(p,w))\):
options: \(x_i(p',w')\le x_i(p,w)\) for every good i with \(p_i'\gt p_i\)
explain: The compensated law of demand \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x\le0\), with strict inequality when demand changes: prices and quantities move in opposite directions on average. The third option uses uncompensated wealth w, and the ordinary law is not implied by WARP. The last option is a good-by-good statement, stronger than the inner-product condition when several prices change at once.

q: Proof of the 'only if' part of Proposition 4-2-2. Write \(x=x(p,w)\), \(x'=x(p',w')\) with \(w'=p'\cdot x\), and \((p'-p)\cdot(x'-x)=p'\cdot(x'-x)-p\cdot(x'-x)\). Why is the first term zero?
options: By Walras' law \(p'\cdot x'=w'\) and the compensation \(p'\cdot x=w'\)
explain: Walras' law at the new situation gives \(p'\cdot x'=w'\), and compensation is defined by \(p'\cdot x=w'\); subtracting, \(p'\cdot(x'-x)=0\). WARP is used for the second term. HD0 is a hypothesis of the proposition but this step does not use it; and \(x'\ne x\) is the case being considered.

q: Proof of the 'only if' part of Proposition 4-2-2 (with \(x=x(p,w)\), \(x'=x(p',w')\ne x\), \(w'=p'\cdot x\)). How is the second term \(p\cdot(x'-x)\gt0\) obtained?
options: \(x'\) is affordable at \((p,w)\), so by WARP \(x\) is not affordable at \((p',w')\)
\(x\) is affordable at \((p',w')\) by compensation, so by WARP \(x'\) is not affordable at \((p,w)\): \(p\cdot x'\gt w=p\cdot x\)
By the law of demand, \(x'\) has less of every good whose price rose
explain: Compensation makes x exactly affordable at \((p',w')\) and \(x'\) was chosen there, so \(x'\) is revealed preferred to x; WARP then says x' must not be affordable at \((p,w)\): \(p\cdot x'\gt w\). With Walras \(w=p\cdot x\), so \(p\cdot(x'-x)\gt0\) and the total is \(0-(\text{positive})\lt0\). The first option has the roles reversed: x is affordable at the new situation by construction, so it cannot be the conclusion.

q: Which part of Proposition 4-2-2 is proved in the slides, and which is left out of the exam?
options: Neither part is proved; the proposition is stated without proof
The 'if' part is proved; the 'only if' part is left to MWG
Both parts are proved in the slides
The 'only if' part (WARP ⇒ compensated law) is proved; the 'if' part is in MWG and not examined
explain: Slide 29 proves 'only if': assuming WARP, the compensated law of demand holds. Slide 30 says the 'if' part is skipped (MWG chapter 2, p. 31) and will not be covered in the exam.

q: Compensated law of demand with only one price change: \(\Delta p=(\Delta p_1,0)\) with \(\Delta p_1\lt0\), and the bundle changes. What does \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x\lt0\) imply?
options: Nothing about good 1, only about total spending
\(\Delta x_1\gt0\): the compensated demand for good 1 rises when its price falls
explain: \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x=\Delta p_1\Delta x_1\lt0\) with \(\Delta p_1\lt0\) forces \(\Delta x_1\gt0\). This is the law of demand once the wealth effect is neutralised by compensation (slide 32). The inequality says nothing about good 2, since its price did not change.

q: True or false: If a demand function satisfies WARP (and HD0 and Walras' law), then the ordinary (uncompensated) law of demand holds: \(\partial x_i/\partial p_i\le0\) for every good.
explain: False. WARP (with HD0 and Walras) is equivalent to the compensated law of demand, not the uncompensated one (slide 33). Without compensation the wealth effect remains and, for an inferior good, can outweigh the substitution effect. PS3 1b is a utility-maximising (so WARP-satisfying) consumer with a Giffen good.

q: True or false: The existence of a Giffen good shows that the consumer's demand violates WARP.
explain: False. Giffen behaviour is about uncompensated price changes, and WARP only implies the compensated law of demand. In PS3 1b the consumer maximises a utility function (so WARP holds), yet good 1 is Giffen for \(1\lt p_1\lt4/3\).

q: At \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=10\) the consumer buys \(x=(5,5)\). Price of good 1 rises to \(p'=(2,1)\) with Slutsky compensation, \(w'=15\). Which new choice (all satisfying Walras' law at \((p',w')\)) would violate WARP?
explain: For \((6,3)\): \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x=(1,0)\cdot(1,-2)=1\gt0\), against the compensated law. Directly: it costs 9 ≤ 10 at \((p,w)\) and the old bundle costs 15 ≤ 15 at \((p',w')\), so both are cross-affordable. \((4,7)\) and \((3,9)\) give \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x=-1,-2\lt0\); \((5,5)\) gives 0, allowed because the bundle did not change.

q: Cobb-Douglas demand \(x=(w/(2p_1),w/(2p_2))\), \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=8\), so \(x=(4,4)\). \(p_1\) rises to 2. What are the uncompensated and the Slutsky-compensated demands for good 1?
explain: Uncompensated: \(x_1=8/(2\cdot2)=2\). Compensation: \(w'=p'\cdot x=2\cdot4+1\cdot4=12\), so \(x_1=12/4=3\) (and \(x_2=6\)). Check: \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x=(1,0)\cdot(-1,2)=-1\lt0\). The fall from 4 to 3 is the substitution effect and the further fall from 3 to 2 is the wealth effect (good 1 is normal). \(w'=16\) would double all wealth although only one price doubled.

q: Why does the slides' Proposition 4-2-2 need compensated price changes to link WARP with a law of demand?
options: Because HD0 fails for uncompensated changes
Because WARP is only defined for compensated price changes
Because Walras' law fails for uncompensated changes
Because without compensation the old bundle may not be affordable at the new prices, so WARP gives no restriction, and the wealth effect can dominate
explain: Compensation makes the old bundle exactly affordable in the new situation, which is what lets WARP bite: the new choice must then be unaffordable at the old budget. Without compensation (e.g. a price rise with fixed w), the old bundle may be out of reach, nothing is revealed, and an inferior good can show Giffen behaviour. WARP, Walras and HD0 are defined for all (p, w).

q: Proposition 4-2-2: why is the inequality \((p'-p)\cdot(x'-x)\le0\) only required to be strict when \(x'\ne x\)?
options: Because WARP allows the consumer to be indifferent
Because if \(x'=x\), then \(\Delta x=0\) and the product is exactly 0
Because compensation is only defined when the bundle changes
explain: If the consumer buys the same bundle after the compensated change, \(\Delta x=0\) and the inner product is 0, so strictness is impossible. This is exactly PS3 1b(vi): \((0.1,0)\cdot(0,0)=0\le0\). When the bundle changes, the proof shows the inner product is strictly negative.

q: PS3 1b: \(u=\min\{x_1+2x_2,\ 2x_1+3x_2-10\}\), \(p_2=2\), \(w=16\). For \(1\lt p_1\lt4/3\) the optimum is on the line \(x_1+x_2=10\), giving \(x_1=4/(2-p_1)\). What are the optimal bundles at \(p_1=1.2\) and \(p_1=1.3\)?
explain: At \(p_1=1.2\): \(x_1=4/0.8=5\), \(x_2=10-5=5\). At \(p_1=1.3\): \(x_1=4/0.7=40/7\approx5.71\), \(x_2=30/7\approx4.29\). Both are on the budget: \(1.3\cdot\frac{40}7+2\cdot\frac{30}7=\frac{112}{7}=16\). The price of good 1 rose and its demand rose: good 1 is Giffen.

q: PS3 1b(iii): with \(w=16\), \(p_2=2\) and the binding budget \(x_2=8-\frac{p_1}{2}x_1\), the two pieces become \(f=16+(1-p_1)x_1\) and \(g=14+(2-\frac32p_1)x_1\). For \(1\lt p_1\lt4/3\), why is the optimum where \(f=g\)?
options: Because \(f\) is strictly decreasing and \(g\) strictly increasing in \(x_1\), so \(\min\{f,g\}\) is maximised at their crossing
Because both pieces decrease in \(x_1\), so the consumer buys only good 2
Because the MRS equals the price ratio at the crossing
Because both pieces increase in \(x_1\), so the consumer buys only good 1
explain: \(1-p_1\lt0\) makes f decreasing and \(2-\frac32p_1\gt0\) (since \(p_1\lt4/3\)) makes g increasing. For small \(x_1\) the minimum is g (rising), for large \(x_1\) it is f (falling), so the minimum peaks where they cross, on \(x_1+x_2=10\). The utility is kinked there, so a tangency/MRS argument does not apply.

q: PS3 1b(v): for \(1\lt p_1\lt4/3\), \(p_2=2\) and wealth \(w\) in the interior range, demand for good 1 is \(x_1=\frac{20-w}{2-p_1}\). Which is correct?
options: Valid for \(10p_1\lt w\lt20\); good 1 is normal, since \(x_1\gt0\)
Valid for \(0\lt w\lt20\); good 1 is normal
Valid for \(10p_1\lt w\lt20\); good 1 is inferior, since \(\partial x_1/\partial w=-1/(2-p_1)\lt0\)
explain: \(x_1\gt0\) needs \(w\lt20\); \(x_2=10-x_1\gt0\) needs \(x_1\lt10\), i.e. \(20-w\lt10(2-p_1)\iff w\gt10p_1\). On that range \(\partial x_1/\partial w=-1/(2-p_1)\lt0\): more wealth, less good 1, so good 1 is inferior. That is the wealth effect behind the Giffen behaviour in (iv).

q: PS3 1b(vi): start at \(p_1=1.2\), \(p_2=2\), \(w=16\) with bundle \((5,5)\). \(p_1\) rises to 1.3 with Slutsky compensation. What are the new wealth and new bundle?
explain: \(w'=1.3\cdot5+2\cdot5=16.5\), which lies in \((10p_1,20)=(13,20)\), so \(x_1=(20-16.5)/0.7=5\) and \(x_2=5\). The compensated law holds with equality: \((0.1,0)\cdot(0,0)=0\le0\). \((40/7,30/7)\) is the uncompensated choice at \(w=16\).

q: PS3 1b(vii): without compensation \(x_1\) goes from 5 to \(40/7\) when \(p_1\) rises from 1.2 to 1.3; with compensation it stays at 5. How is the difference \(5/7\) explained?
options: It is the substitution effect, which is positive because good 1 is Giffen
It is a rounding error; with exact arithmetic both demands are 5
It is a WARP violation of size \(5/7\)
It is the wealth effect: without compensation the consumer is 0.5 poorer, and since good 1 is inferior, \(\Delta x_1=0.5/0.7=5/7\)
explain: The uncompensated consumer has 16 instead of 16.5. With \(\partial x_1/\partial w=-1/0.7\), losing 0.5 raises \(x_1\) by \(0.5/0.7=5/7=40/7-5\). The substitution effect is zero here (the compensated bundle is unchanged), so the whole rise is the inferior-good wealth effect. No WARP violation occurs.

q: PS3 1b(vii): \(x=(5,5)\) is chosen at \((p_1,p_2,w)=(1.2,2,16)\) and \(x'=(40/7,30/7)\) at \((1.3,2,16)\). Why is there no WARP violation although the ordinary law of demand fails?
options: Because \(x'\) costs \(108/7\le16\) at the first budget (so x is revealed preferred to \(x'\)), but x costs \(16.5\gt16\) at the second budget, so it was not affordable when \(x'\) was chosen
Because \(x\) and \(x'\) cost the same at both price vectors
Because WARP only applies when prices of both goods change
Because neither bundle is affordable in the other situation
explain: \(1.2\cdot\frac{40}7+2\cdot\frac{30}7=\frac{48+60}{7}=\frac{108}7\approx15.4\le16\), and \(1.3\cdot5+2\cdot5=16.5\gt16\). Only one direction of revealed preference occurs, so the choices are consistent. WARP only implies the compensated law of demand, which holds here; the consumer maximises a utility, so she is rational.

q: PS3 1b(i): \(u=\min\{x_1+2x_2,2x_1+3x_2-10\}\) with \(p\gg0\). Why does the optimal bundle exhaust the budget (so demand satisfies Walras' law)?
options: Because every Walrasian demand function satisfies Walras' law
Because u is strictly increasing in each good: if \(p\cdot x\lt w\), raising \(x_1\) a little stays affordable and strictly raises u
Because u is continuous, so Weierstrass gives an optimum on the boundary
explain: Both pieces strictly increase in each good, so the minimum does too; any bundle with money left over can be improved, contradicting optimality. Weierstrass (continuity plus a compact budget set) gives existence, not that the budget binds. Walras' law is not automatic for demand functions in general (see the slide-13 demand with \(\beta\lt1\)).

q: Beatty and Crawford (2011) study Spanish household expenditure data. Which description matches the slides?
options: 3,134 households, 1985–1997, expenditures on aggregates such as food; 95.7% pass the rationality test
Danish consumers over 1985–1997; 95.7% fail the test
3,134 households, laboratory experiment with individual goods; 4.5% pass
explain: The data are a government expenditure survey of 3,134 Spanish households, 1985–1997, recorded for aggregates like 'food', and 95.7% pass. Danish consumers, New York dairy farmers, children and capuchin monkeys come from previous studies that also found predominantly rational behaviour. 4.5 is the gap in pass rates between real and random households.

q: In Beatty and Crawford (2011), simulated households with the same budget sets but random choices pass the rationality test at a rate:
options: only 4.5 percentage points below the real households' pass rate
explain: Randomly choosing households, simulated on the computer with the real budget sets, pass at a rate only 4.5 points below the observed 95.7%. So the high pass rate is not a 'triumph of economic theory': the test has little power on these data.

q: Why do even random choosers pass the revealed-preference test in Beatty and Crawford's data?
options: Because budget sets are mostly nested: price fluctuations are small and income variations large, so whatever is chosen satisfies the axiom
Because the data are for individual goods, not aggregates
Because random choice is a special case of utility maximisation
Because Spanish prices fluctuated wildly, making all bundles affordable
explain: With small price changes and large income changes, one budget set typically contains the other. Under Walras' law the choice on the larger budget's line is unaffordable at the smaller budget, so WARP cannot fail whatever the household picks. A test needs crossing budget lines to have power.

q: What lessons do the slides draw from Beatty and Crawford (2011)?
options: Random choice models should replace the economic model
WARP is a logically invalid test of rationality
Approaching data through the theory is likely to be successful, but that does not tell us much about people's 'true' rationality
People are fully rational, so economic theory is confirmed
explain: The slides say: (1) looking at data through the theory is likely to succeed, (2) but this says little about true rationality. They still defend the economic approach: it lets us attribute preferences to people and assess how well markets serve them, which is useful for policy, rather than switching to a random-choice model.

q: True or false: In Topic 4.2, homogeneity of degree zero and Walras' law are derived as consequences of utility maximisation.
explain: False. In Topic 4.2 they are properties a demand function may or may not satisfy, and Proposition 4-2-2 assumes them. In Topic 4.3 (Prop 4-3-2) they become results of the UMP: HD0 for any utility, and Walras' law when preferences are monotone. Separately, PS3 4f shows that WARP alone implies HD0.

q: True or false: Proposition 4-2-2 applies to the demand \(x_1=\frac{p_2}{p_1+p_2}\frac{w}{p_1}\), \(x_2=\frac{\beta p_1}{p_1+p_2}\frac{w}{p_2}\) with \(\beta=1/2\).
explain: False. The proposition requires HD0 and Walras' law. This demand is HD0, but with \(\beta=1/2\) it spends \(w(p_2+p_1/2)/(p_1+p_2)\lt w\), so Walras' law fails and the hypotheses are not met.

q: True or false: If a demand function satisfies HD0 and Walras' law, then it satisfies WARP.
explain: False. The PS3 4e demand \(x=wp/\|p\|^2\) is HD0 and satisfies Walras' law, but the observations \(((1,1),2)\) and \(((2,1),3)\) give two different bundles, each affordable in the other's budget. HD0 and Walras are only the background assumptions under which WARP is equivalent to the compensated law of demand.

q: A consumer buys \(x=(2,2)\) at \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=4\), and at \(p'=(2,2)\), \(w'=8\) buys \(x'=(1,3)\). Which is correct?
options: No problem: the second budget is larger in money terms
WARP is violated (and so is HD0): the two budget sets are identical, so each bundle is affordable when the other is chosen
explain: \(B_{(2,2),8}=B_{(1,1),4}\): the same budget set. Both bundles cost 4 at p and 8 at p', so each is cross-affordable and they differ: WARP fails. This is the PS3 4f logic: WARP implies HD0, so a demand violating HD0 must violate WARP. Walras' law holds in both observations.

q: Which of the following is the utility maximization problem (UMP) as stated in Definition 4-3-1?
explain: The UMP maximizes utility over the budget set \(B_{p,w}=\{x\in\R^2_+:p\cdot x\le w\}\) with strictly positive prices and positive wealth. The constraint is an inequality; that it binds (Walras' law) is a result, not part of the definition. The min problem is the EMP, and \(u(x)-p\cdot x\) is a quasilinear 'surplus' problem, not the UMP.

q: The Walrasian demand correspondence \(x(p,w)\) is defined as
options: the set of bundles that exhaust the budget, \(\{x: p\cdot x=w\}\)
the maximal utility value attainable at \((p,w)\)
the set of optimal bundles of the UMP at \((p,w)\gg 0\)
the set of cheapest bundles reaching a given utility level
explain: \(x(p,w)\) assigns to each \((p,w)\gg0\) the set of solutions of the UMP; when it is single-valued it is the Walrasian demand function. The maximal utility value is the indirect utility \(v(p,w)\); the cheapest bundles reaching \(\bar u\) form the Hicksian demand \(h(p,\bar u)\). The budget line is only where optima lie under monotonicity.

q: The indirect utility function \(v(p,w)\) is
options: the value of the UMP: \(v(p,w)=u(x)\) for any \(x\in x(p,w)\)
the minimal wealth needed to reach utility \(u\)
the utility level that the consumer would reach after Hicksian compensation
explain: \(v(p,w)\) is the value function of the UMP: the utility of any optimal bundle (all optimal bundles give the same utility, so it is well defined). The minimal wealth to reach a utility level is the expenditure function \(e(p,u)\).

q: For a differentiable utility \(u\) with \(u_2(x)>0\), the marginal rate of substitution at \(x\) is
options: \(MRS(x)=u_2(x)/u_1(x)\), equal to the slope of the budget line
\(MRS(x)=u_1(x)/u_2(x)\), equal to minus the slope \(dx_2/dx_1\) of the indifference curve through \(x\)
explain: Totally differentiate \(u(x)=c\): \(u_1dx_1+u_2dx_2=0\), so \(-dx_2/dx_1=u_1/u_2\). The MRS is the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up good 2 for good 1. It equals \(p_1/p_2\) only at an interior optimum, not everywhere.

q: The expenditure minimization problem (EMP) is
explain: The EMP finds the minimal wealth needed to reach utility at least \(\bar u\): objective and constraint of the UMP swap roles. The choice variable is the bundle \(x\), not prices. With \(u(x)\le\bar u\) the answer would trivially be \(x=0\).

q: Hicksian wealth compensation for a price change from \(p\) to \(p'\), starting at wealth \(w\) and utility \(\bar u=v(p,w)\), is
explain: Hicksian compensation gives exactly the extra money needed to keep utility at \(\bar u\) at the new prices: \(e(p',\bar u)-w\). The option \(p'\cdot x(p,w)-w\) is Slutsky compensation (enough to buy the old bundle), which is weakly larger. \(e(p,\bar u)-w=0\) by duality.

q: How does Hicksian (compensated) demand \(h(p,\bar u)\) differ from Walrasian demand \(x(p,w)\) as prices vary?
options: \(h\) keeps money wealth fixed and lets utility vary; \(x\) keeps utility fixed
\(h\) keeps the old bundle affordable; \(x\) keeps utility fixed
They coincide for every \((p,w)\) and every \(\bar u\)
\(h\) keeps the utility level fixed and lets money vary; \(x\) keeps money wealth fixed and lets utility vary
explain: Slide 44: \(h(p,\bar u)\) is the demand that would arise if wealth were simultaneously adjusted to keep utility at \(\bar u\); Walrasian demand keeps money wealth fixed. Keeping the old bundle affordable is Slutsky compensation. They coincide only when \(w=e(p,\bar u)\).

q: Proposition 4-3-1 guarantees that the UMP has a solution under which hypotheses?
explain: With \(p\gg0\) the budget set is closed and bounded, hence compact, and a continuous function attains a maximum on a compact set (Weierstrass). A zero price makes the budget set unbounded; monotonicity alone does not give a maximum without continuity; quasiconcavity matters for uniqueness, not existence.

q: In the proof of Proposition 4-3-1 (existence of a UMP solution), where exactly is the assumption \(p\gg 0\) used?
options: To make the budget set bounded, so that (being also closed) it is compact
To make the budget set closed
To make the budget constraint bind at the optimum
To make the utility function continuous on the budget set
explain: Closedness of \(\{x\ge0:p\cdot x\le w\}\) holds for any \(p\) (weak inequalities, continuous functions). Boundedness needs \(p_i>0\): then \(x_i\le w/p_i\). If \(p_1=0\), any amount of good 1 is affordable and the set is unbounded. Binding of the budget is Walras' law, which uses monotonicity.

q: True or false: if \(u\) is continuous and strictly increasing, \(p_1=0\), \(p_2>0\) and \(w>0\), the UMP still has a solution because the budget set is closed.
explain: False. With \(p_1=0\) the budget set \(\{x\ge0: p_2x_2\le w\}\) is closed but unbounded in \(x_1\), so it is not compact. With \(u\) strictly increasing in \(x_1\), any bundle can be improved by adding good 1 for free, so no maximum exists. Closedness alone is not enough for Weierstrass.

q: True or false: if \(u\) is not continuous, the UMP may fail to have a solution even with \(p\gg 0\).
explain: True. Continuity is needed for Weierstrass. Example: \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=1\), \(u(x)=x_1+x_2\) if \(x_1+x_2<1\) and \(u(x)=0\) otherwise. Utility approaches 1 inside the budget set but the supremum 1 is never attained, so there is no maximizer.

q: Suppose \(\pr\) is continuous, monotone and strictly convex, and \(p\gg 0\), \(w>0\). What can we say about the UMP?
options: It has a solution, but it may have several solutions
It has exactly one solution, and that solution is always interior
It may have no solution unless preferences are also differentiable
It has exactly one solution, so \(x(p,w)\) is a function
explain: Continuity and \(p\gg0\) give existence. Strict convexity gives uniqueness: if \(x\ne y\) were both optimal, \(\frac12x+\frac12y\) is affordable (the budget set is convex) and strictly preferred to \(x\), a contradiction. Strict convexity does not rule out corners (e.g. \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+x_2\) can have \(x_1^*>0,x_2^*=0\)), and differentiability is irrelevant.

q: Proof of uniqueness of the UMP solution under strict convexity: suppose \(x\ne y\) are both optimal at \((p,w)\). Which step completes the contradiction?
options: By monotonicity, \(x+y\) is strictly better than \(x\) and affordable
By continuity, \(\lambda x\) for \(\lambda<1\) is affordable and as good as \(x\)
\(z=\tfrac12x+\tfrac12y\) satisfies \(p\cdot z\le w\) and, by strict convexity, \(z\succ x\), contradicting optimality of \(x\)
By Walras' law \(p\cdot x=p\cdot y=w\), so \(x=y\)
explain: The budget set is convex, so the midpoint is affordable; \(x\sim y\) and strict convexity give \(z\succ x\). The bundle \(x+y\) is generally not affordable (it costs \(2w\)). Walras' law only places both on the budget line; many distinct bundles cost exactly \(w\).

q: True or false: convex (but not strictly convex), continuous and monotone preferences guarantee that the Walrasian demand is single-valued.
explain: False. Perfect substitutes \(u=x_1+x_2\) are convex, continuous and monotone, but when \(p_1=p_2\) every bundle on the budget line is optimal: \(x(p,w)\) is a correspondence. Weak convexity only makes the set of optima convex; strict convexity is needed for uniqueness.

q: Proposition 4-3-2: for a continuous \(u\) representing a monotone \(\pr\) on \(\R^2_+\), the Walrasian demand satisfies
options: homogeneity of degree one in \((p,w)\) and Walras' law
homogeneity of degree zero in \(p\) only and \(p\cdot x\le w\)
the ordinary law of demand and Walras' law
homogeneity of degree zero in \((p,w)\) and Walras' law \(p\cdot x=w\) for all \(x\in x(p,w)\)
explain: HD0: \(x(\alpha p,\alpha w)=x(p,w)\) because the budget set is unchanged. Walras' law: the budget binds at every optimum, by monotonicity. The ordinary law of demand is not implied (Giffen goods, PS3 1b). HD0 in \(p\) alone is the property of Hicksian demand.

q: In the proof that UMP demand is homogeneous of degree zero, which assumption on \(u\) is needed?
options: Monotonicity, so that the budget binds
Continuity, so that a solution exists
Strict convexity, so that the solution is unique
None: \(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}=B_{p,w}\), so the problem and hence its solutions are unchanged
explain: \(\{x:\alpha p\cdot x\le\alpha w\}=\{x:p\cdot x\le w\}\) for \(\alpha>0\), so the UMP is literally the same problem. The slides stress that this property needs no assumption on \(u\), and that in Topic 4-2 homogeneity was an assumption while here it is a result.

q: The proof of Walras' law for UMP demand supposes \(p\cdot x<w\) for some optimal \(x\). Which bundle and which property yield the contradiction?
options: \(y=\lambda x\) with \(\lambda<1\) is cheaper and, by continuity, as good as \(x\)
\(y=(x_1+\varepsilon,x_2+\varepsilon)\) with small \(\varepsilon>0\) is still affordable and, by monotonicity, \(y\succ x\)
\(y=\frac12 x+\frac12 x'\) is affordable and, by convexity, \(y\succ x\)
\(y=(x_1+\varepsilon,x_2)\) is affordable and, by continuity, \(y\succ x\)
explain: If money is left over, a slightly bigger bundle in both goods is still affordable, and monotonicity (more of every good is strictly better) makes it strictly better, contradicting optimality. Shrinking \(x\) by \(\lambda<1\) is the trick used for 'no excess utility' in the EMP, which relies on continuity. Convexity plays no role in Walras' law.

q: True or false: Walras' law for the UMP (\(p\cdot x=w\) at every optimum) requires the preference to be convex.
explain: False. The proof uses only monotonicity: if \(p\cdot x<w\), add \(\varepsilon\) of each good, stay affordable and strictly improve. Non-convex monotone preferences like \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) still exhaust the budget (at a corner).

q: Proposition 4-3-3 (differentiable \(u\), monotone \(\pr\), \(u_2(x)>0\), \(x\in x(p,w)\)). Which set of conditions is correct?
options: \(MRS=p_1/p_2\) at every optimum, interior or not
explain: At \(x_1=0\) the consumer would like to sell good 1 but cannot: the value of good 1 relative to good 2 is at most its relative price, \(MRS\le p_1/p_2\). At \(x_2=0\) she buys only good 1 and would buy more if she could sell good 2: \(MRS\ge p_1/p_2\). The swapped inequalities are the classic trap.

q: In the proof of Proposition 4-3-3, utility is restricted to the budget line via \(g(t)=u\big(t,(w-p_1t)/p_2\big)\), \(0\le t\le w/p_1\). What is \(g'(t)\)?
explain: By the chain rule, \(g'(t)=u_1+u_2\cdot\frac{d}{dt}\frac{w-p_1t}{p_2}=u_1-\frac{p_1}{p_2}u_2\). Setting it to zero at an interior max and dividing by \(u_2>0\) gives \(MRS=p_1/p_2\). The last option has the right sign of zero but is not the derivative.

q: In the proof of Proposition 4-3-3, why does \(x_2^*=0\) imply \(MRS(x^*)\ge p_1/p_2\)?
options: \(t=w/p_1\) maximizes \(g\) at the right endpoint, so the left derivative \(g'_-(w/p_1)=u_1-\frac{p_1}{p_2}u_2\ge 0\)
\(t=0\) maximizes \(g\) at the left endpoint, so \(g'_+(0)\le 0\)
\(t=w/p_1\) maximizes \(g\) at the right endpoint, so \(g'_-(w/p_1)\le 0\)
\(g\) is concave, so \(g'(t)=0\) everywhere on the budget line
explain: \(x_2=0\) means all wealth goes to good 1: \(t=w/p_1\), the right endpoint. For small \(h>0\), \(g(t)-g(t-h)\ge0\), so \((g(t)-g(t-h))/h\ge0\) and the left derivative is \(\ge 0\); divide by \(u_2>0\). The left-endpoint case \(t=0\) corresponds to \(x_1=0\) and gives \(\le 0\).

q: True or false: if \(x^*\) satisfies \(MRS(x^*)=p_1/p_2\) and \(p\cdot x^*=w\), then \(x^*\) solves the UMP, for any differentiable monotone utility.
explain: False. Prop 4-3-3 gives necessary conditions only. With non-convex preferences, e.g. \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\), the tangency point on the budget line is a minimum of utility along the line; the optimum is at a corner. Sufficiency needs convexity (quasiconcave \(u\)).

q: True or false: for \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) the optimal bundle is characterized by \(MRS=p_1/p_2\).
explain: False. Leontief utility is not differentiable at the kink \(x_1=x_2\), where the optimum lies, so Prop 4-3-3 (which assumes differentiability) does not apply. The optimum is found from 'no waste' \(x_1=x_2\) plus the budget: \(x_1=x_2=w/(p_1+p_2)\).

q: Economic intuition for the tangency condition: at a bundle on the budget line with \(x_1,x_2>0\) and \(MRS(x)>p_1/p_2\), the consumer should
options: buy more of good 2 and less of good 1
stay put, since the budget binds
buy more of good 1 and less of good 2
explain: MRS is how much good 2 she is willing to give for one unit of good 1; \(p_1/p_2\) is how much the market requires. If willingness exceeds the market rate, trading good 2 for good 1 along the budget line raises utility. She stops at tangency or when \(x_2\) hits 0 (then \(MRS\ge p_1/p_2\) remains).

q: True or false: for Cobb-Douglas utility \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\), \(0<\alpha<1\), the UMP solution is always interior when \(p\gg0,\ w>0\).
explain: True. If either good is zero, \(u=0\), while the interior bundle \((\alpha w/p_1,(1-\alpha)w/p_2)\) gives \(u>0\). Equivalently, marginal utility of a good is infinite as its quantity tends to 0, so corners are never optimal.

q: Solve \(\max\ x_1x_2\) s.t. \(2x_1+x_2\le 4\). The optimal bundle and maximal utility are
explain: \(MRS=x_2/x_1=p_1/p_2=2\Rightarrow x_2=2x_1\). Budget: \(2x_1+2x_1=4\Rightarrow x_1=1,\ x_2=2\), \(u=2\). CD shortcut with \(\alpha=\frac12\): spend half of 4 on each good, \(x_1=2/2\), \(x_2=2/1\). \((2,1)\) costs 5 and is unaffordable.

q: For \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\), \(0<\alpha<1\), the Walrasian demand is
explain: FOC of \(\max x_1^\alpha(w-p_1x_1)^{1-\alpha}\) simplifies to \(\alpha(w-p_1x_1)=(1-\alpha)p_1x_1\), so \(x_1=\alpha w/p_1\) and \(x_2=(1-\alpha)w/p_2\). The consumer spends the constant share \(\alpha\) of wealth on good 1. Swapping \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\) is a common slip.
Share \(1/3\) of 60 = 20 on good 1: \(x_1=20/2=10\); share \(2/3\) = 40 on good 2: \(x_2=40/4=10\). Check: \(2\cdot10+4\cdot10=60\). \((20,5)\) swaps the shares; \((15,7.5)\) splits wealth equally.

q: \(u=x_1x_2^3\), \(p=(1,3)\), \(w=24\). The Walrasian demand is
explain: \(x_1x_2^3\) is a monotone transformation of \(x_1^{1/4}x_2^{3/4}\), so \(\alpha=1/4\). \(x_1=\frac14\cdot24/1=6\), \(x_2=\frac34\cdot24/3=6\). Check \(6+18=24\). \((18,2)\) uses share \(3/4\) on good 1; \((6,2)\) leaves money unspent.

q: For \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\), which statement about the Walrasian demand is FALSE?
options: Spending on each good is a constant share of wealth, whatever the prices
Good 1 can be a Giffen good when \(\alpha\) is small
Demand for good 1 does not depend on \(p_2\)
explain: \(x_1=\alpha w/p_1\) is strictly decreasing in \(p_1\) for every \(\alpha\), so no Giffen behaviour. The other statements are true: \(p_1x_1=\alpha w\) (constant share), \(x_1\) independent of \(p_2\) (zero cross-price effect), and \(\partial x_i/\partial w>0\) (normal).

q: Indirect utility for \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\) is
explain: Plug demand into \(u\): \((\alpha w/p_1)^\alpha((1-\alpha)w/p_2)^{1-\alpha}=\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}w/(p_1^\alpha p_2^{1-\alpha})\). Prices must be in the denominator (v is nonincreasing in prices). The constant \(\alpha^{-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{\alpha-1}\) belongs to the expenditure function, and the wealth exponent is \(\alpha+(1-\alpha)=1\).

Demand: \(x_1=\frac12\cdot8/1=4\), \(x_2=\frac12\cdot8/4=1\), so \(v=\sqrt{4\cdot1}=2\). Formula check: \(v=w/(2\sqrt{p_1p_2})=8/(2\cdot2)=2\). Note \(u=x_1x_2\) would give 4: v depends on the representation.

q: Solve \(\max\ x_1+x_2\) s.t. \(p_1x_1+p_2x_2\le w\) when \(p_1<p_2\).
explain: The goods are perfect substitutes one-for-one, so buy only the cheaper one. Check with Prop 4-3-3: \(MRS=1>p_1/p_2\), consistent with the corner \(x_2^*=0\) (\(MRS\ge p_1/p_2\)). The equal-split bundle is the Cobb-Douglas answer; the last option is the Leontief answer.

q: \(u=2x_1+x_2\), \(p=(3,1)\), \(w=12\). The optimal bundle and \(v(p,w)\) are
explain: Compare utility per euro: good 1 gives \(2/3\), good 2 gives \(1/1=1\). Spend everything on good 2: \(x_2=12\), \(u=12\). Equivalently \(MRS=2<p_1/p_2=3\), the condition for the corner \(x_1=0\). All-good-1 gives only \(2\cdot4=8\).

q: For \(u=x_1+x_2\) with \(p_1=p_2=p\), the Walrasian demand is
options: the whole budget line \(\{x\ge0: x_1+x_2=w/p\}\) (a correspondence)
empty, since the problem has no solution
explain: With equal prices every bundle on the budget line gives \(u=w/p\), so all are optimal. Demand is a correspondence, not a function. Existence still holds (continuity, \(p\gg0\)); uniqueness fails because preferences are convex but not strictly.

q: Indirect utility for \(u=x_1+x_2\) is
explain: All wealth buys the cheaper good, giving \(w/\min\{p_1,p_2\}\) units, each worth one util. \(w/(p_1+p_2)\) is the Leontief \(\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) answer, and \(w/(2\sqrt{p_1p_2})\) is for \(\sqrt{x_1x_2}\).

q: \(u=\min\{x_1,2x_2\}\), \(p=(1,2)\), \(w=12\). The Walrasian demand is
explain: No waste at the optimum: \(x_1=2x_2\). Budget: \(2x_2+2x_2=12\Rightarrow x_2=3,\ x_1=6\); \(u=6\). General formula for \(\min\{ax_1,bx_2\}\): \(x_1=bw/(bp_1+ap_2)=24/4=6\). \((4,4)\) has \(\min\{4,8\}=4\), wasting good 2.

q: For \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\), the indirect utility and expenditure function are
explain: Buy equal amounts: \(x_1=x_2=w/(p_1+p_2)\), so \(v=w/(p_1+p_2)\). To reach \(\bar u\) you need \(h=(\bar u,\bar u)\), costing \((p_1+p_2)\bar u\). Duality check: \(e(p,v(p,w))=w\). The min-price formulas are for perfect substitutes.

q: \(u=x_2+\ln x_1\) (quasilinear), \(p=(2,4)\), \(w=10\). The Walrasian demand is
explain: Interior tangency: \(MRS=\frac{1/x_1}{1}=\frac{p_1}{p_2}=\frac12\Rightarrow x_1=2\), independent of \(w\). Cost of good 1: 4 \(\le 10\), so the rest buys good 2: \(x_2=(10-4)/4=1.5\). \((2.5,1.25)\) is the Cobb-Douglas half-split.

q: \(u=x_2+\ln x_1\), \(p=(2,4)\), \(w=3\). The Walrasian demand is
explain: Tangency would require \(x_1=p_2/p_1=2\), costing 4 > 3, so it is infeasible (\((2,-0.25)\) has negative \(x_2\)). Corner: all wealth on good 1, \(x_1=1.5\), \(x_2=0\). Check Prop 4-3-3 for \(x_2=0\): \(MRS=1/1.5=2/3\ge p_1/p_2=1/2\). ✓

q: For quasilinear utility \(u=x_2+g(x_1)\) with \(g\) strictly concave and an interior optimum, an increase in wealth
options: is split between the goods in fixed shares
leaves \(x_1\) unchanged and is spent entirely on good 2
explain: Tangency \(g'(x_1)=p_1/p_2\) pins down \(x_1\) without reference to \(w\); the budget then gives \(x_2=(w-p_1x_1)/p_2\). So the wealth effect on good 1 is zero once \(w\ge p_1x_1\). Below that threshold the optimum is the corner \(x_2=0\).

q: \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\), \(p=(1,2)\), \(w=6\). The Walrasian demand is
explain: Preferences are not convex, so tangency gives a minimum along the budget line. Compare corners: \((6,0)\) gives 36, \((0,3)\) gives 9. The tangency point \((1.2,2.4)\) (where \(MRS=x_1/x_2=p_1/p_2=1/2\)) gives \(1.44+5.76=7.2\), the minimum.

q: PS3 1(a): with \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\), the Walrasian demand for good 1 is
explain: Interior (infinite marginal utility at 0): \(MRS=\sqrt{x_2}/\sqrt{x_1}=p_1/p_2\Rightarrow x_2=(p_1/p_2)^2x_1\). Budget: \(p_1x_1+\frac{p_1^2}{p_2}x_1=w\Rightarrow x_1=\frac{p_2w}{p_1(p_1+p_2)}\). Then \(p_1x_1/p_2x_2=p_2/p_1\): spending ratio equals \(p_2/p_1\), the demand to be rationalized.

q: With \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\), \(p=(1,2)\), \(w=12\), the demand is
explain: \(x_1=\frac{2\cdot12}{1\cdot3}=8\), \(x_2=\frac{1\cdot12}{2\cdot3}=2\). Check budget \(8+4=12\) and tangency \(\sqrt{2}/\sqrt{8}=\frac12=p_1/p_2\). \((6,3)\) is the Cobb-Douglas half split; \((4,4)\) costs 12 but violates tangency.

Along the budget \(x_2=8-\frac{p_1}{2}x_1\): \(f=16+(1-p_1)x_1\) is decreasing and \(g=14+(2-\frac32p_1)x_1\) is increasing, so the min peaks where \(f=g\), i.e. \(x_1+x_2=10\). Then \(x_1+8-\frac{p_1}2x_1=10\Rightarrow x_1=\frac{4}{2-p_1}\).

q: PS3 1(b): with \(p_2=2\), \(w=16\), the optimum is \(x_1=4/(2-p_1)\). Comparing \(p_1=1.2\) and \(p_1=1.3\), what do we find?
options: \(x_1\) rises from 5 to 40/7: good 1 is a Giffen good
\(x_1\) falls from 5 to 30/7: the law of demand holds
\(x_1\) rises from 5 to 40/7, which shows the consumer violates WARP
explain: \(4/0.8=5\) and \(4/0.7=40/7\approx5.71\). Own price up, own demand up: Giffen. This contradicts neither rationality nor WARP: the consumer maximizes a utility, and WARP only implies the compensated law of demand.

q: PS3 1(b)(v): with \(p_2=2\), \(1<p_1<4/3\) and wealth \(w\) in the interior range, demand is \(x_1=\frac{20-w}{2-p_1}\). Over which range of \(w\) does this hold, and is good 1 normal or inferior?
explain: Interior needs \(x_1>0\iff w<20\) and \(x_2=10-x_1>0\iff x_1<10\iff w>10p_1\). \(\partial x_1/\partial w=-1/(2-p_1)<0\): inferior. Inferiority with a strong wealth effect is what makes the Giffen behaviour possible.

q: PS3 1(b)(vi): start at \(p=(1.2,2)\), \(w=16\), optimum \((5,5)\). \(p_1\) rises to 1.3 and wealth is adjusted so that \((5,5)\) is just affordable. The adjusted wealth and new optimum are
explain: \(1.3\cdot5+2\cdot5=16.5\). Then \(x_1=(20-16.5)/(2-1.3)=5\), \(x_2=5\). Compensated law: \((p'-p)\cdot(x'-x)=(0.1,0)\cdot(0,0)=0\le0\) holds. The whole uncompensated increase \(5/7\) is the inferior-good wealth effect.

q: Proposition 4-3-4: for continuous \(u\) representing monotone \(\pr\), the indirect utility \(v(p,w)\) is
options: homogeneous of degree one in \((p,w)\), strictly increasing in \(w\), strictly decreasing in each \(p_i\)
homogeneous of degree zero in \(p\), nondecreasing in \(w\), nonincreasing in each \(p_i\)
homogeneous of degree zero in \((p,w)\), strictly increasing in \(w\) and nonincreasing in \(p_1\) and \(p_2\)
homogeneous of degree one in \(p\), strictly increasing in \(w\) and in each \(p_i\)
explain: HD0 in \((p,w)\) follows from \(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}=B_{p,w}\). Higher wealth enlarges the budget set (and with monotonicity strictly raises utility, since the budget binds); a higher price shrinks it, so \(v\) cannot rise. Prices are only 'nonincreasing': e.g. raising the price of a good not consumed may leave \(v\) unchanged. HD1 in \(p\) is the expenditure function's property.

q: True or false: the indirect utility function is always strictly decreasing in each price.
explain: False. Prop 4-3-4 says only 'nonincreasing'. Example: \(u=x_1+x_2\), \(p_1<p_2\). The consumer buys only good 1, so a small rise in \(p_2\) leaves \(v=w/p_1\) unchanged.

q: Why is \(v(p,w)\) strictly (not just weakly) increasing in \(w\) under Proposition 4-3-4's assumptions?
options: Because the budget set at \(w'\) contains the one at \(w\), and inclusion of sets implies strictly higher maxima
Because \(v\) is homogeneous of degree zero
Because \(u\) is continuous, so \(v\) is continuous in \(w\)
If \(w'>w\), the optimum \(x\) at \(w\) leaves money unspent at \(w'\), so adding \(\varepsilon\) of each good is affordable and strictly better by monotonicity
explain: Set inclusion alone only gives \(v(p,w')\ge v(p,w)\). Strictness uses monotonicity, as in the Walras' law proof: at \(w'\) the old optimum is strictly inside the budget, and a slightly larger bundle is affordable and strictly preferred.

q: Let \(v\) be the indirect utility for \(u\), and let \(\tilde u=f(u)\) with \(f\) strictly increasing. Which is correct?
options: Walrasian demand is unchanged, and the indirect utility is unchanged
Walrasian demand is unchanged, and the new indirect utility is \(\tilde v=f(v)\)
explain: \(\tilde u\) represents the same preferences, so the UMP has the same solutions. The value changes: \(\tilde v(p,w)=\tilde u(x(p,w))=f(u(x(p,w)))=f(v(p,w))\). So \(x\) does not depend on the representation, but \(v\) does (slide 25).

q: \(u=\ln x_1+\ln x_2\). The indirect utility is
explain: \(\ln x_1+\ln x_2=\ln(x_1x_2)\) is Cobb-Douglas with \(\alpha=\frac12\): \(x=(w/2p_1,w/2p_2)\). So \(v=\ln\frac{w}{2p_1}+\ln\frac{w}{2p_2}=\ln\frac{w^2}{4p_1p_2}\). \(w^2/(4p_1p_2)\) is \(v\) for \(x_1x_2\); \(w/(2\sqrt{p_1p_2})\) is \(v\) for \(\sqrt{x_1x_2}\). Same demand, different \(v\) (\(f(v)\) rule).

q: Solve \(\min\ 2x_1+x_2\) s.t. \(x_1x_2\ge 2\). The solution and minimal expenditure are
explain: Tangency \(x_2/x_1=2\Rightarrow x_2=2x_1\); constraint \(2x_1^2=2\Rightarrow x_1=1,x_2=2\); cost \(2+2=4\). This is the same bundle as the UMP \(\max x_1x_2\) s.t. \(2x_1+x_2\le4\), illustrating duality: \(w=4\) reaches \(u=2\), and reaching \(u=2\) costs 4. \((\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\) costs \(3\sqrt2\approx4.24>4\).

q: Proposition 4-3-6: the Hicksian demand correspondence \(h(p,\bar u)\) satisfies
options: homogeneity of degree zero in \((p,\bar u)\) and \(u(x)\ge\bar u\) with strict inequality possible
homogeneity of degree one in \(p\) and no excess utility
homogeneity of degree zero in \(p\) and no excess utility: \(u(x)=\bar u\) for all \(x\in h(p,\bar u)\)
homogeneity of degree zero in \(p\) and Walras' law \(p\cdot x=\bar u\)
explain: Scaling prices does not change which bundle is cheapest, so \(h(\alpha p,\bar u)=h(p,\bar u)\). And the utility constraint binds (by continuity). This parallels HD0 and Walras' law for Walrasian demand. HD1 in \(p\) is the property of \(e\), not \(h\).

q: Proof of 'no excess utility' in the EMP: suppose \(x\in h(p,\bar u)\) with \(u(x)>\bar u\). Which argument gives the contradiction, and which assumption does it use?
options: Take \(x'=\alpha x\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) close to 1: by continuity \(u(x')\ge\bar u\), and \(p\cdot x'<p\cdot x\)
Take \(x'=x+\varepsilon(1,1)\): by monotonicity \(u(x')>u(x)\), and \(x'\) is cheaper
Take \(x'=\frac12x+\frac12y\) for another optimum \(y\): by convexity \(u(x')>\bar u\)
Since \(p\gg0\), the feasible set is compact, so \(u(x)=\bar u\)
explain: Shrinking the bundle slightly keeps utility above \(\bar u\) (continuity, since \(u(x)>\bar u\) strictly) while strictly lowering cost (\(p\gg0\), \(x\ne0\)). This contradicts minimality. Adding goods raises cost, so the first distractor is backwards; the slides say the property 'follows from the continuity of u'.

q: For \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\), the Hicksian demand for good 1 is
explain: Tangency: \(x_2=\frac{(1-\alpha)p_1}{\alpha p_2}x_1\). Plug into \(x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}=\bar u\): \(x_1\big(\frac{(1-\alpha)p_1}{\alpha p_2}\big)^{1-\alpha}=\bar u\), so \(h_1=\big(\frac{\alpha p_2}{(1-\alpha)p_1}\big)^{1-\alpha}\bar u\), decreasing in \(p_1\). It depends on prices only through \(p_2/p_1\), so it is HD0 in \(p\). \(\alpha\bar u/p_1\) mimics the Walrasian formula.

q: For \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\), the correct expenditure function is
explain: The constant must be the reciprocal of \(v\)'s constant \(\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}\) so that \(e(p,v(p,w))=w\). Slide 43 prints \(\alpha^\alpha\) (a typo): with \(\alpha=\frac12\), \(p=(2,1)\), \(\bar u=\sqrt2\) it gives 2, but the true minimal cost (bundle (1,2)) is 4; the corrected formula gives \((\tfrac12)^{-1/2}(\tfrac12)^{-1/2}\sqrt2\cdot1\cdot\sqrt2=2\cdot2=4\). Prices must be in the numerator: \(e\) is HD1 and nondecreasing in \(p\).

q: \(u=\sqrt{x_1x_2}\), \(p=(1,4)\), \(\bar u=3\). The Hicksian demand and \(e(p,\bar u)\) are
explain: \(\alpha=\frac12\): \(h_1=\sqrt{p_2/p_1}\,\bar u=2\cdot3=6\), \(h_2=\sqrt{p_1/p_2}\,\bar u=\frac12\cdot3=1.5\). Check \(\sqrt{6\cdot1.5}=3\). Cost \(6+4\cdot1.5=12=2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u\). \((3,3)\) reaches \(u=3\) but costs 15.

q: EMP with perfect substitutes: \(\min\ x_1+3x_2\) s.t. \(x_1+2x_2\ge 6\). The solution is
explain: Cost per util: good 1 costs \(1/1=1\), good 2 costs \(3/2=1.5\). Use only good 1: \(x_1=6\), cost 6. In general \(e=\bar u\min\{p_1/a,p_2/b\}\) for \(u=ax_1+bx_2\). \((0,3)\) also reaches 6 but costs 9.

q: EMP with Leontief utility: \(\min\ 3x_1+x_2\) s.t. \(\min\{2x_1,x_2\}\ge 4\). The solution is
explain: Need \(2x_1\ge4\) and \(x_2\ge4\); the cheapest is \(x_1=2,x_2=4\) (no waste, no excess utility), cost \(6+4=10\). \((4/3,4)\) gives \(\min\{8/3,4\}<4\), infeasible. Prices do not affect the Leontief Hicksian demand.

q: \(u=x_2+\ln x_1\), \(p\gg0\), \(\bar u\ge\ln(p_2/p_1)\). The expenditure function is
explain: Tangency \(1/x_1=p_1/p_2\) gives \(h_1=p_2/p_1\); no excess utility gives \(h_2=\bar u-\ln(p_2/p_1)\ge0\). Cost: \(p_1\frac{p_2}{p_1}+p_2h_2=p_2+p_2(\bar u-\ln\frac{p_2}{p_1})\). Check \(p=(1,1),\bar u=2\): \(h=(1,2)\), \(e=3\). \(p_1e^{\bar u}\) is the cost of reaching \(\bar u\) with good 1 only, which ignores the tangency condition.

q: Proposition 4-3-7: for continuous \(u\) representing monotone \(\pr\), the expenditure function \(e(p,\bar u)\) is
options: homogeneous of degree zero in \(p\), strictly increasing in \(\bar u\), nondecreasing in each \(p_i\)
homogeneous of degree one in \((p,\bar u)\), nondecreasing in \(\bar u\), strictly increasing in each \(p_i\)
homogeneous of degree one in \(p\), strictly decreasing in \(\bar u\), nonincreasing in each \(p_i\)
homogeneous of degree one in \(p\), strictly increasing in \(\bar u\), nondecreasing in \(p_1\) and \(p_2\)
explain: Doubling all prices doubles the cost of the same cheapest bundle: HD1 in \(p\). Reaching more utility costs strictly more; raising a price cannot lower the minimal cost. These parallel \(v\)'s properties (HD0, increasing in \(w\), nonincreasing in \(p\)).

q: In the proof that \(e\) is homogeneous of degree one in \(p\), the key observation is
options: the budget set \(B_{\alpha p,\alpha w}\) equals \(B_{p,w}\)

the constraint set \(\{x:u(x)\ge\bar u\}\) does not depend on prices, so the same bundle minimizes \(\alpha p\cdot x\) and \(p\cdot x\), giving \(e(\alpha p,\bar u)=\alpha p\cdot x=\alpha e(p,\bar u)\)
explain: Prices enter only the objective. Multiplying the objective by \(\alpha>0\) does not change the minimizers and scales the minimum by \(\alpha\). The budget-set identity is the argument for HD0 of \(x\) and \(v\). No homogeneity of \(u\) is assumed.

q: Proof that \(e\) is nondecreasing in \(p_1\): let \(p_1'\ge p_1\), \(p_2'=p_2\), and let \(x'\) be optimal in the EMP at \(p'\). Which chain of inequalities is used?
options: \(e(p',\bar u)=p'\cdot x'\le p\cdot x'\le e(p,\bar u)\)
\(e(p',\bar u)=p\cdot x'\ge p'\cdot x'\ge e(p,\bar u)\)
\(e(p',\bar u)=p'\cdot x'= p\cdot x'= e(p,\bar u)\)
\(e(p',\bar u)=p'\cdot x'\ge p\cdot x'\ge e(p,\bar u)\)
explain: \(p'\cdot x'\ge p\cdot x'\) because \(x_1'\ge0\) and \(p_1'\ge p_1\). And \(x'\) is feasible at \(p\) (the constraint set does not depend on prices), so its cost at \(p\) is at least the minimum \(e(p,\bar u)\). This is exactly PS3 4(g)(i).

q: Proof that \(e\) is strictly increasing in \(\bar u\): suppose \(\bar u'<\bar u''\) but \(e(p,\bar u')\ge e(p,\bar u'')\), with optimal bundles \(x'\), \(x''\). Which step yields the contradiction?
options: Shrink \(x''\) to \(\alpha x''\), \(\alpha<1\) close to 1: by continuity \(u(\alpha x'')>\bar u'\) and \(p\cdot\alpha x''<p\cdot x''\le p\cdot x'\), contradicting optimality of \(x'\)
Scale up \(x'\) to \(\alpha x'\), \(\alpha>1\): it reaches \(\bar u''\) at lower cost than \(x''\)
By monotonicity \(x''\succ x'\), so \(x''\) costs more
By no excess utility, \(u(x')=\bar u'\), hence \(p\cdot x'<p\cdot x''\) directly
explain: \(u(x'')\ge\bar u''>\bar u'\), so a slightly shrunk \(x''\) still exceeds \(\bar u'\) (continuity) and is strictly cheaper than \(x''\), hence strictly cheaper than \(x'\). So \(x'\) was not the cheapest way to reach \(\bar u'\). 'More preferred implies more costly' is not a valid step by itself.

q: True or false: the expenditure function is strictly increasing in each price \(p_i\).
explain: False. Only nondecreasing. With \(u=x_1+x_2\) and \(p_1<p_2\), \(e=p_1\bar u\): a small rise in \(p_2\) leaves \(e\) unchanged because good 2 is not bought.

q: True or false: the expenditure function is homogeneous of degree one in \((p,\bar u)\) jointly.
explain: False. It is HD1 in \(p\) only. For \(u=\sqrt{x_1x_2}\), \(e=2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u\), so \(e(\lambda p,\lambda\bar u)=\lambda^2e(p,\bar u)\). And since \(\bar u\) depends on the utility representation, no homogeneity in \(\bar u\) can hold in general.

q: Proposition 4-3-5 (part 1): if \(x\) is optimal in the UMP at \((p,w)\), \(w>0\), then
options: \(x\) is optimal in the EMP with required utility \(w\), and the minimal expenditure is \(u(x)\)
\(x\) is optimal in the EMP with required utility \(u(x)\), and the minimal expenditure is at most \(w\), possibly strictly less
\(x\) is optimal in the EMP only if preferences are strictly convex
\(x\) is optimal in the EMP with required utility \(u(x)\), and the minimal expenditure is exactly \(w\)
explain: The UMP optimum is the cheapest way to reach its own utility level, and it costs exactly \(w\) (Walras' law). If some bundle reached \(u(x)\) for less than \(w\), we could add a bit of each good, stay within \(w\) and beat \(x\) by monotonicity. No convexity is needed.

q: Proposition 4-3-5 (part 2) states: if \(x\) is optimal in the EMP with required utility \(\bar u\), then \(x\) is optimal in the UMP with wealth \(p\cdot x\), and the maximal utility is \(\bar u\). Which extra hypothesis on \(\bar u\) is imposed?
options: \(\bar u\) is an integer level of utility
explain: If \(\bar u\le u(0)\), the bundle 0 solves the EMP at zero cost, and wealth \(p\cdot0=0\) is not an admissible UMP (which needs \(w>0\)). The condition \(\bar u>u(0)\) ensures \(e(p,\bar u)>0\). \(\bar u>0\) is not the right condition since \(u(0)\) may be any number.

q: Which list contains exactly the four duality identities linking UMP and EMP (for \(\bar u>u(0)\), \(w>0\))?
explain: The cheapest way to reach the utility attainable with \(w\) costs exactly \(w\); with exactly the money needed for \(\bar u\), the best attainable is \(\bar u\). The demand identities follow: Hicksian demand is Walrasian demand at the compensated wealth \(e(p,\bar u)\), and Walrasian demand is Hicksian demand at the attained utility \(v(p,w)\).

q: Given the expenditure function \(e(p,\bar u)=2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u\), use duality to find \(v(p,w)\).
explain: \(e(p,v(p,w))=w\Rightarrow 2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,v=w\Rightarrow v=w/(2\sqrt{p_1p_2})\): invert \(e\) in its utility argument. This is indeed \(v\) for \(\sqrt{x_1x_2}\). \(w^2/(4p_1p_2)\) is \(v\) for \(x_1x_2\), whose expenditure function would be \(2\sqrt{p_1p_2\bar u}\).

q: \(u=\sqrt{x_1x_2}\). Initially \(p=(1,1)\), \(w=8\), so \(x=(4,4)\) and \(\bar u=4\). Then \(p_2\) rises to 4. Which is correct?
explain: Walrasian: \(x_1=4/1=4\), \(x_2=4/4=1\) (utility drops to 2). Hicksian: \(h_1=\sqrt{4}\cdot4=8\), \(h_2=\sqrt{1/4}\cdot4=2\), cost \(8+8=16\), so the consumer needs 8 more. \((4,4)\) costing 20 is Slutsky compensation (the old bundle); with \(w'=20\) she would choose \((10,2.5)\) with \(u=5>4\), over-compensated.

q: Same example: \(u=\sqrt{x_1x_2}\), \(p_2\) rises from 1 to 4 with \(p_1=1\), \(w=8\). Demand for good 2 goes \(4\to1\) (Walrasian), and the Hicksian demand at \(\bar u=4\) goes \(4\to2\). How does the total change \(-3\) decompose?
explain: The Hicksian move \(4\to2\) holds utility fixed: the pure substitution effect, \(-2\) (nonpositive, by the compensated law of demand). The rest, \(2\to1\), is due to the loss of purchasing power: the wealth effect \(-1\) (good 2 is normal). The substitution effect can never be positive for an own price.

q: Comparing Hicksian and Slutsky compensation after a price rise, which is true?
options: Hicksian compensation is always at least as large as Slutsky compensation
Slutsky compensation (enough to buy the old bundle) is at least as large as Hicksian compensation, because the consumer can substitute and reach the old utility more cheaply
Slutsky compensation keeps utility exactly constant
explain: The old bundle still reaches \(\bar u\), so \(e(p',\bar u)\le p'\cdot x(p,w)\): Hicksian \(\le\) Slutsky. In the \(\sqrt{x_1x_2}\) example, Hicksian needs 16 while Slutsky gives 20, and the Slutsky-compensated consumer reaches \(u=5>4\).

q: Proposition 4-3-8 (compensated law of demand): if \(h(p,\bar u)\) is single-valued for all \(p\gg0\), then for all \(p',p''\)
explain: Prices and compensated quantities move in opposite directions; in particular own-price effects of Hicksian demand are nonpositive. The comparable statement for Walrasian demand with fixed \(w\) is false (Giffen goods). The last inequality has the wrong direction: \(h(p'')\) is the cheapest at \(p''\).

q: Proof of Prop 4-3-8: which two inequalities are subtracted?
options: \(p''\cdot h(p'',\bar u)\le p''\cdot h(p',\bar u)\) and \(p'\cdot h(p',\bar u)\le p'\cdot h(p'',\bar u)\)
\(p''\cdot h(p'',\bar u)\ge p''\cdot h(p',\bar u)\) and \(p'\cdot h(p',\bar u)\ge p'\cdot h(p'',\bar u)\)
\(u(h(p'',\bar u))\ge u(h(p',\bar u))\) and \(u(h(p',\bar u))\ge u(h(p'',\bar u))\)
\(p''\cdot h(p'',\bar u)= w\) and \(p'\cdot h(p',\bar u)=w\)
explain: Each Hicksian bundle reaches \(\bar u\), so each is feasible in the other EMP; each is cheapest at its own prices. Subtracting the second from the first: \(p''\cdot(h''-h')-p'\cdot(h''-h')\le0\), i.e. \((p''-p')\cdot(h''-h')\le0\). No wealth level is fixed in the EMP, so the last option is wrong.

q: Apply Prop 4-3-8 when only \(p_1\) changes: \(p''=(p_1'',p_2)\), \(p'=(p_1',p_2)\) with \(p_1''>p_1'\). What follows?
explain: \((p''-p')=(p_1''-p_1',0)\), so the inequality reduces to \((p_1''-p_1')(h_1''-h_1')\le0\), i.e. \(h_1''\le h_1'\). The proposition by itself says nothing about \(h_2\) here.

q: True or false: a good can be Giffen for Hicksian (compensated) demand.
explain: False. By Prop 4-3-8 the own-price effect of Hicksian demand is nonpositive: there are no Giffen goods in compensated demand. Giffen behaviour (PS3 1b) is a Walrasian phenomenon, driven by a strong inferior-good wealth effect.

q: (Standard MWG result, beyond the slides.) Shephard's lemma states \(h_i(p,\bar u)=\partial e(p,\bar u)/\partial p_i\). Check it for \(e=2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u\): \(\partial e/\partial p_1\) equals
explain: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial p_1}2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{p_2}}{2\sqrt{p_1}}\bar u=\sqrt{p_2/p_1}\,\bar u\). This matches \(h_1=\big(\frac{\alpha p_2}{(1-\alpha)p_1}\big)^{1-\alpha}\bar u\) with \(\alpha=\frac12\).

q: (Standard MWG result, beyond the slides.) Roy's identity: \(x_1(p,w)=-\frac{\partial v/\partial p_1}{\partial v/\partial w}\). For \(v=\frac{w}{2\sqrt{p_1p_2}}\) this gives
explain: \(\partial v/\partial p_1=-\frac{w}{4p_1^{3/2}p_2^{1/2}}\), \(\partial v/\partial w=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{p_1p_2}}\). Ratio with the minus sign: \(\frac{w}{4p_1^{3/2}p_2^{1/2}}\cdot2\sqrt{p_1p_2}=\frac{w}{2p_1}\), the Cobb-Douglas demand with \(\alpha=\frac12\).

q: True or false: \(x(p,w)=h(p,v(p,w))\) for every \(p\gg0\), \(w>0\) (continuous \(u\), monotone \(\pr\)).
explain: True (slide 44, from Prop 4-3-5 part 1). The UMP optimum at \((p,w)\) is also the cheapest way to reach \(v(p,w)\), so the Walrasian demand equals the Hicksian demand at utility level \(v(p,w)\).

q: True or false: \(e(p,v(p,w))<w\) is possible when preferences are not convex.
explain: False. Duality \(e(p,v(p,w))=w\) uses only continuity and monotonicity (Prop 4-3-5). If some bundle reached \(v(p,w)\) for less than \(w\), adding a little of each good would be affordable and strictly better, contradicting the definition of \(v\). Convexity is not used.

q: \(u=x_1^{1/2}x_2^{1/2}\), \(p=(2,1)\). Which wealth \(w\) makes the UMP optimum equal to the Hicksian demand \(h(p,\sqrt2)\)?
explain: By duality \(h(p,\bar u)=x(p,e(p,\bar u))\) and \(e=2\sqrt{p_1p_2}\,\bar u=2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=4\). Check: \(x(p,4)=(1,2)\) with \(u=\sqrt2\). \(w=2\) is what the misprinted slide-43 constant would give.

q: In the jungle model, a society \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i)_{i\in N}\rangle\) requires which of the following?
options: N and H finite with the same number of members, and a strict preference \(\succ_i\) over houses for each i
N finite, H possibly infinite, and strict preferences over allocations
N and H finite with the same number of members, and a utility function over houses for each i that may have ties
N and H finite, \(|H|\ge|N|\), and weak preferences \(\succeq_i\) over houses
explain: Definition 5-1-1: finite N, finite H with as many houses as individuals, and a strict preference for each individual over houses (no individual is indifferent between two houses). Preferences are over the individual's own house, not over whole allocations (that would be the externalities variant). Allowing ties is a PS variant, not the base model.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an assignment from an allocation in a society \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i)\rangle\)?
options: An assignment gives each house an individual; an allocation gives each individual a house
They are the same notion; the slides use the two words interchangeably
An assignment is any function \(a:N\to H\); an allocation is an assignment in which each house is assigned to exactly one individual
An allocation is any function \(a:N\to H\); an assignment must be a bijection
explain: Definition 5-1-2: an assignment is any function from N to H (two people could be mapped to the same house); an allocation is an assignment where each house goes to exactly one individual. Since \(|N|=|H|\), an allocation is a bijection between N and H.

q: The power relation \(\rhd\) of a jungle is assumed to be
options: complete and transitive only, so ties in power are allowed
explain: Definition 5-1-3: \(\rhd\) is complete, transitive and antisymmetric. Completeness plus antisymmetry means no two distinct individuals are equally powerful, so individuals can be lined up \(1\rhd2\rhd\dots\rhd n\). Dropping antisymmetry (ties in power) is the PS3 extra question 4b variant.

q: An allocation \(a^*\) is an equilibrium of the jungle \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i),\rhd\rangle\) if and only if
options: there are no \(i,j\in N\) with \(i\rhd j\) and \(a^*(j)\succ_i a^*(i)\)
there are no \(i,j\in N\) with \(j\rhd i\) and \(a^*(j)\succ_i a^*(i)\)
no allocation b satisfies \(b(i)\succeq_i a^*(i)\) for all i with strict preference for some i
every individual occupies his favourite house
explain: Definition 5-1-4: nobody prefers the house of a weaker individual to his own. Only houses of weaker individuals matter, because those are the only ones i can take. Option C is Pareto stability, a different concept; option D is too strong (in general not everyone can get his favourite).

q: Cave game: individuals 1,2,3,4, caves A,B,C,D, strict rankings (best to worst) 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. An allocation is written as (cave of 1, cave of 2, cave of 3, cave of 4). With power \(1\rhd2\rhd3\rhd4\), what is the (unique) jungle equilibrium?
explain: Serial dictatorship in order of power: 1 takes B; 2 picks from {A, C, D} with ranking B, D, A, C, so D; 3 picks from {A, C}: A; 4 gets C. Result (B, D, A, C). (C, D, A, B) is the clan outcome, which is Pareto stable but not an equilibrium for this power order.

q: Cave game: individuals 1,2,3,4, caves A,B,C,D, strict rankings (best to worst) 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. An allocation is written as (cave of 1, cave of 2, cave of 3, cave of 4). With power \(4\rhd3\rhd2\rhd1\) (the reverse order), what is the jungle equilibrium?
explain: Serial dictatorship: 4 takes B; 3 takes A; 2 picks from {C, D}: D (ranked above C); 1 gets C. So (C, D, A, B), exactly the clan outcome of Round 2. This illustrates OR Prop 8.5: the Pareto stable clan outcome is the equilibrium for a suitable power relation.

q: Cave game: individuals 1,2,3,4, caves A,B,C,D, strict rankings (best to worst) 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. An allocation is written as (cave of 1, cave of 2, cave of 3, cave of 4). With power \(2\rhd1\rhd3\rhd4\), what is the jungle equilibrium?
explain: 2 takes B; 1 picks from {A, C, D}: C (ranking B, C, D, A); 3 picks from {A, D}: A; 4 gets D. So (C, B, A, D). (C, B, D, A) would require 3 to take D while A is available, which contradicts 3's ranking A first.

q: Cave game: individuals 1,2,3,4, caves A,B,C,D, strict rankings (best to worst) 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. An allocation is written as (cave of 1, cave of 2, cave of 3, cave of 4). With power \(1\rhd2\rhd3\rhd4\), consider the starting allocation (D, A, C, B). Which statement is correct?
options: It is not an equilibrium: e.g. \(1\rhd4\) and 1 prefers B (held by 4) to his own cave D
It is not an equilibrium, and the only individual who wants to move is 2
It is not an equilibrium, because 4 prefers D to B
It is an equilibrium, because no two-person swap is mutually acceptable
explain: 1 holds D, ranks B above D, and B is held by the weaker 4: a violation of Definition 5-1-4 (3 also wants B from the weaker 4). Option D confuses jungle equilibrium with immunity to mutually acceptable swaps. Option C is irrelevant: 4 is the weakest, and in fact 4 ranks B first.
