q: Cave game: individuals 1,2,3,4, caves A,B,C,D, strict rankings (best to worst) 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. An allocation is written as (cave of 1, cave of 2, cave of 3, cave of 4). With power \(1\rhd2\rhd3\rhd4\), is the allocation (B, C, A, D) a jungle equilibrium?
options: No: 3 prefers B to A and can take it from 1
No: 2 prefers D, held by the weaker 4, to C
Yes: 1 and 3 hold their favourite caves
Yes: 4 is the weakest and cannot take anything
explain: 2 ranks B D A C, holds C, and D is held by the weaker 4, so (2, 4) is a violating pair. Option A is wrong because 1 is stronger than 3, so 3 cannot take B. Checking only some individuals (options C, D) is not enough; every i must be checked against all weaker j.

q: Proposition 5-1-1 (existence) states that for any jungle \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i),\rhd\rangle\)
options: the allocation generated by serial dictatorship for any ordering is an equilibrium
any Pareto stable allocation is an equilibrium
the allocation generated by serial dictatorship for the ordering \(\rhd\) is an equilibrium
an equilibrium exists provided preferences are monotone and continuous
explain: The existence proof is constructive: run serial dictatorship using the power order itself. Serial dictatorship for an arbitrary ordering gives a Pareto stable allocation (Prop 5-1-3) but not, in general, an equilibrium for \(\rhd\). Monotonicity and continuity are exchange-economy assumptions.

q: In the proof that the serial-dictatorship allocation a (for the order \(\rhd\)) is an equilibrium, the key observation for stability is:
options: a(i) is i's best house among all houses not assigned to individuals stronger than i, which includes every house held by a weaker individual
every individual weakly prefers a(i) to his initial house
a(i) is i's favourite house in H
a(i) is the house that the weakest individual likes least
explain: When i chooses, only the houses of stronger individuals have been removed, so every house held by a weaker j was still available; i took his best, so \(a(i)\succ_i a(j)\) (strict since houses differ and preferences are strict). Option C is false except for the strongest individual. Feasibility (#H = #N, each house assigned once) is the other half of the proof.

q: Which assumptions are essential for Proposition 5-1-2 (every jungle has a UNIQUE equilibrium)?
options: That the individuals reach the equilibrium through a dynamic process
Strict preferences and a power relation with no ties (antisymmetric)
explain: With an indifferent individual (PS3 2a) or two equally powerful individuals (PS3 4b) a jungle can have several equilibria. The two-person examples: 1 indifferent between A and B gives (A, B) and (B, A) as equilibria; equal power with the same tastes also gives both. The dynamic process is a separate question.

q: Uniqueness proof (Prop 5-1-2): label \(1\rhd2\rhd\dots\rhd n\), let a and b be distinct equilibria and \(i^*\) the strongest individual with \(a(i^*)\neq b(i^*)\). Let k be the individual with \(a(k)=b(i^*)\). Why must k be weaker than \(i^*\)?
options: If k were stronger, then \(b(k)=a(k)=b(i^*)\), so two individuals would share a house in b, impossible since b is an allocation
Because k must be the weakest individual
explain: All individuals stronger than \(i^*\) hold the same houses in a and b. If k (who holds b(i*) in a) were stronger, he would also hold b(i*) in b, together with \(i^*\): contradiction. Also \(k\ne i^*\) since \(a(i^*)\ne b(i^*)\). So \(i^*\rhd k\), and equilibrium of a gives \(a(i^*)\succ_{i^*}b(i^*)\).

q: Uniqueness proof (Prop 5-1-2), continued: from 'a is an equilibrium and \(i^*\rhd k\) with \(a(k)=b(i^*)\)' we get \(a(i^*)\succ_{i^*}b(i^*)\). The symmetric argument gives \(b(i^*)\succ_{i^*}a(i^*)\). Where exactly is strictness of preferences used?
options: Strictness is not used: the proof works with ties in preferences
To show that k is weaker than i*
To guarantee that serial dictatorship is well defined for the order of a
To pass from 'i* does not strictly prefer b(i*) to a(i*)' to 'i* strictly prefers a(i*) to b(i*)', since the two houses differ
explain: Equilibrium only says \(i^*\) does NOT strictly prefer b(i*) to a(i*), i.e. \(a(i^*)\succeq_{i^*}b(i^*)\). With strict preferences and distinct houses this becomes strict, and the two strict inequalities contradict each other. With ties both could be indifferences, and the contradiction disappears, which is why ties allow multiple equilibria.

q: True or false: in a jungle (strict preferences, strict power order), every allocation obtained by serial dictatorship for SOME ordering of the individuals is an equilibrium of that jungle.
explain: False. Only the serial-dictatorship allocation for the power order \(\rhd\) is the equilibrium (and it is unique). In the cave game with \(1\rhd2\rhd3\rhd4\), the order 4, 3, 2, 1 gives (C, D, A, B), which is not an equilibrium since 1 takes B from 4. Other orderings give Pareto stable allocations, not equilibria.

q: True or false: in a jungle, the strongest individual always occupies his favourite house in equilibrium.
explain: True. The strongest individual can take any house (everyone else is weaker), so if he did not hold his favourite he would take it. Equivalently, he moves first in serial dictatorship. The same is not true of other individuals.

q: The jungle equilibrium is a static concept. PS3 (extra 4c) studies a dynamic process: at stage 0 all houses are vacant; at each stage everyone goes to his best house among those vacant or held by weaker individuals (or himself); ties at a house are won by the strongest. What is the result?
options: It converges only if preferences are identical
It converges, but possibly to a Pareto dominated allocation
It converges at the latest at stage \(|N|\) to the jungle equilibrium; by induction, after stage t individuals \(1,\dots,t\) hold their serial-dictatorship houses
explain: Induction: once individuals \(1,\dots,t\) hold \(h_1,\dots,h_t\), they keep them (nobody stronger contests them), and individual t+1's available set is exactly \(H\setminus\{h_1,\dots,h_t\}\), so he goes to \(h_{t+1}\) and wins it. After n stages everyone holds his serial-dictatorship house, the unique equilibrium, which is Pareto stable.

q: PS3 2a: a jungle where preferences need not be strict. N = {1, 2}, H = {A, B}, \(1\rhd2\), individual 1 is indifferent between A and B, individual 2 prefers A to B. Equilibrium means no \(i\rhd j\) with \(a(j)\succ_i a(i)\). Which allocations (house of 1, house of 2) are equilibria?
explain: Only 1 could move (he is stronger), and he is indifferent, so he never strictly prefers 2's house. Both allocations are equilibria, so uniqueness fails without strictness. Note (A, B) is Pareto dominated by (B, A) (1 indifferent, 2 better off): with ties an equilibrium need not even be Pareto stable (OR problem 8.1b).

q: PS3 2a(i): why can the standard serial dictatorship procedure not be applied directly when preferences are not strict, and what is the fix?
options: Because some individuals may become homeless; fix by adding houses
Because the procedure may not terminate; fix by limiting it to |N| steps
Because the power relation becomes incomplete; fix by adding a random power order
Because an individual's 'best house among those left' may not be unique; fix by letting each individual take any weakly best remaining house, breaking ties arbitrarily
explain: The procedure says 'give \(i_k\) his best house in \(H\setminus\{h_1,\dots,h_{k-1}\}\)', which is ill-defined if there is a tie at the top. The modified procedure picks any weakly best remaining house. It still yields an equilibrium (each \(i_k\) weakly prefers his house to every later house), but different tie-breaks can give different equilibria.

q: PS3 extra 4b: power is complete and transitive but not antisymmetric; only a STRICTLY stronger individual can displace another; preferences are strict. N = {1, 2}, H = {A, B}, 1 and 2 equally powerful, 1 prefers A to B and 2 prefers B to A. Which statement is correct?
options: (B, A) is an equilibrium but is Pareto dominated by (A, B), so with ties in power an equilibrium need not be Pareto stable
(B, A) is not an equilibrium because 1 can take A from 2
explain: Nobody is strictly stronger, so nobody can evict anybody: every allocation, including (B, A), is an equilibrium. But (A, B) gives both their favourite, so (B, A) is not Pareto stable. At least one equilibrium is Pareto stable: serial dictatorship with arbitrary tie-breaking (either order gives (A, B)), by Prop 5-1-3.

q: In the society \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i)\rangle\), allocation b Pareto dominates allocation a if
options: the strongest individual prefers b to a
\(b(i)\succeq_i a(i)\) for all \(i\in N\) and \(b(i)\succ_i a(i)\) for some \(i\in N\)
explain: Definition 5-1-6: everyone weakly better, someone strictly better. An allocation is Pareto stable (= Pareto optimal = Pareto efficient) if no allocation Pareto dominates it. Option B is strict domination for everyone, a stronger requirement. Power plays no role in the definition.

q: Clan game, Round 1, starting from (D, A, C, B) in the cave game (rankings 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D). Why is no two-person swap accepted?
options: Because player 4 holds his favourite cave and blocks every proposal
Every one of the six possible swaps makes at least one of the two players worse off
Because (D, A, C, B) is Pareto stable
Because power prevents weaker players from proposing
explain: Check: 1↔2 gives 1 A (worst); 1↔3 gives 3 D (worse than C); 1↔4 gives 4 D; 2↔3 gives 2 C (worst); 2↔4 gives 4 A (worse than B); 3↔4 gives 4 C (worse than B). But (D, A, C, B) is NOT Pareto stable: the three-way rotation to (C, D, A, B) makes 1, 2, 3 better and 4 unchanged. Immunity to pairwise swaps is weaker than Pareto stability.

q: Cave game rankings 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. Starting from (D, A, C, B) (caves of 1, 2, 3, 4), which reallocation Pareto dominates it?
explain: (C, D, A, B): 1 gets C (better than D), 2 gets D (better than A), 3 gets A (his favourite, better than C), 4 keeps B. Everyone weakly better, three strictly. (B, D, A, C) and (D, B, A, C) are Pareto stable but make 4 worse off (he loses B), so they do not dominate. (A, D, C, B) gives 1 his worst cave.

q: Cave game rankings 1: B C D A; 2: B D A C; 3: A B C D; 4: B C A D. How many of the 24 allocations are Pareto stable?
options: 1 (only the jungle equilibrium (B, D, A, C))
explain: Exhaustive check gives exactly 5: (B, D, A, C), (C, B, A, D), (C, B, D, A), (C, D, A, B), (D, B, A, C). These are exactly the serial-dictatorship outcomes over all 24 orderings (Prop 5-1-3 and OR Prop 8.5). For example (C, B, D, A) arises from order 2, 4, 1, 3. Pareto stability does not select a unique allocation.

q: Proposition 5-1-3 states:
options: For any society and any ordering of the individuals, the serial-dictatorship allocation is Pareto stable
The serial-dictatorship allocation Pareto dominates every other allocation
For any society, the serial-dictatorship allocation is Pareto stable only if the ordering is the power order
Every Pareto stable allocation is the serial-dictatorship allocation for the power order
explain: Pareto stability does not involve power, and the result holds for any ordering. The converse direction (every Pareto stable allocation comes from SOME ordering) is OR Prop 8.5, not 'the power order'. Option B is false: Pareto stable allocations are generally not comparable with each other.

q: Proof of Prop 5-1-3: a is the serial-dictatorship allocation for the order \(1,\dots,n\), and b Pareto dominates a. Let i be the FIRST individual in the order with \(b(i)\neq a(i)\). What gives the contradiction?
options: i is the last individual, who has no choice
b(i) must be i's favourite house
b(i) is held by someone stronger in a
b(i) is not among \(a(1),\dots,a(i-1)\) (those individuals hold the same houses in b), so b(i) was available when i chose; hence \(a(i)\succ_i b(i)\), contradicting \(b(i)\succeq_i a(i)\)
explain: Because \(b(k)=a(k)\) for all \(k\lt i\) and b is an allocation, b(i) differs from all those houses, so it was in i's choice set; i picked his best, and houses differ, so strict preference for a(i). That violates 'everyone weakly better in b'. Such an i exists because b ≠ a.

q: Proposition 5-1-4 (the jungle equilibrium is Pareto stable) is proved by chaining which results?
options: Existence (5-1-1) and the first welfare theorem
Lemma: in every Pareto stable allocation someone gets his favourite house
Uniqueness (5-1-2): the equilibrium is the serial-dictatorship allocation for \(\rhd\) (5-1-1), which is Pareto stable (5-1-3)
The dynamic process converges to a Pareto stable allocation
explain: The jungle has exactly one equilibrium (5-1-2); serial dictatorship for \(\rhd\) produces an equilibrium (5-1-1), so the equilibrium is that allocation; and every serial-dictatorship allocation is Pareto stable (5-1-3). Uniqueness is what lets us identify the arbitrary equilibrium with the serial-dictatorship one.

q: True or false (prove or disprove): in a jungle, every Pareto stable allocation is the equilibrium for the given power relation.
explain: False. In the cave game with \(1\rhd2\rhd3\rhd4\), the clan outcome (C, D, A, B) is Pareto stable but not an equilibrium: \(1\rhd4\) and 1 prefers B (held by 4) to C. Equilibrium implies Pareto stable (5-1-4), but not the reverse.

q: True or false: in the cave game, the jungle outcome (B, D, A, C) Pareto dominates the clan outcome (C, D, A, B).
explain: False. Player 1 prefers the jungle outcome (B over C), but player 4 prefers the clan outcome (B over C for him too). Players 2 and 3 get the same caves. Since one is better and one is worse off, neither Pareto dominates the other; both are Pareto stable.

q: OR Proposition 8.5 (a social planner who controls the power relation): for a society \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i)\rangle\) and an allocation a,
options: a is an equilibrium for some power relation only if everyone gets his favourite house
if a is Pareto stable then a is the equilibrium for the power relation that ranks individuals alphabetically
a is an equilibrium for every power relation if and only if it is Pareto stable
if a is Pareto stable, there is a power relation \(\rhd\) such that a is the unique equilibrium of the jungle \(\langle N,H,(\succ_i),\rhd\rangle\)
explain: Combined with 5-1-4, an allocation is the equilibrium for some power relation iff it is Pareto stable. The power relation must be constructed from a (it is not arbitrary). An observed allocation over which nobody quarrels is consistent with being a jungle outcome.

q: The proof of OR Prop 8.5 (every Pareto stable allocation is a jungle equilibrium for some power relation) relies on a lemma. Which one, and how is it used?
options: Every Pareto stable allocation is unique; so any power relation works
Every allocation is Pareto dominated by a serial-dictatorship allocation; reverse the order
In every Pareto stable allocation at least one individual gets his favourite house; make him the strongest, remove him and his house, note the restricted allocation is still Pareto stable, and repeat
The weakest individual always gets his worst house; put him last and repeat
explain: Lemma (OR 8.1): if nobody held his favourite, follow 'i's favourite is held by the next person' arrows until a cycle appears; rotating houses along the cycle makes everyone on it strictly better, so a was not Pareto stable. The construction then ranks individuals in the order they are peeled off; each holds his best house among those of weaker individuals, so a is an equilibrium, unique by 5-1-2.

q: Society: N = {1, 2, 3}, H = {x, y, z}, rankings 1: y x z; 2: y z x; 3: x y z. Which allocation (house of 1, 2, 3) is the jungle equilibrium for power \(3\rhd1\rhd2\)?
explain: Serial dictatorship: 3 takes x; 1 picks from {y, z}: y; 2 gets z. So (y, z, x). (z, y, x) is the equilibrium for \(2\rhd3\rhd1\), and (x, y, z) for \(2\rhd1\rhd3\).

q: Society: N = {1, 2, 3}, H = {x, y, z}, rankings 1: y x z; 2: y z x; 3: x y z. Which allocation (house of 1, 2, 3) is NOT Pareto stable?
explain: In (y, x, z), 2 holds x (his worst) and 3 holds z (his worst); swapping gives 2 z and 3 x, both strictly better, 1 unchanged. The other three are serial-dictatorship outcomes (orders 2-1-3, 1-2-3, 2-3-1), hence Pareto stable; an exhaustive check shows they are the only Pareto stable allocations.

q: True or false: in any society, an allocation in which no individual occupies his favourite house cannot be Pareto stable.
explain: True (OR Lemma 8.1). Start from anyone, go to the holder of his favourite house, then to the holder of that person's favourite, and so on; by finiteness a cycle appears. Giving each person on the cycle his favourite (the house of the next person) makes all of them strictly better, others unchanged: a Pareto improvement.

q: OR problem 8.2 (comparative statics): two jungles have the same society, and their power orders differ only in that two ADJACENT individuals i and j swap positions (i moves up, j moves down). Which statement is necessarily true?
options: Individuals stronger than both i and j get the same houses in both jungles, and i is weakly better off after moving up
j is always strictly worse off
Every individual gets the same house in both jungles
Individuals weaker than both i and j always get the same houses in both jungles
explain: Serial dictatorship runs identically up to the swapped positions, so stronger individuals are unaffected. Moving up enlarges i's choice set, so he is weakly better off (j weakly worse). Weaker individuals can be affected: e.g. 1: A B C, 2: A C B; order 1,2,3 gives 1 A, 2 C, 3 B, while order 2,1,3 gives 2 A, 1 B, 3 C. j need not be strictly worse (if i and j want different houses nothing changes).

q: OR problem 8.3 (manipulability): a computer computes the jungle equilibrium from the known power relation and the preference rankings that individuals REPORT. Which is true?
options: The strongest individual can gain by misreporting
Truth-telling is optimal only if everyone else tells the truth
The weakest individual can gain by misreporting
No individual can do better than reporting truthfully, whatever the others report
explain: The outcome is serial dictatorship in power order. When i's turn comes, the set of remaining houses depends only on the reports of stronger individuals, not on i's own report; truthful reporting gives i his true best house in that set. So truth-telling is a dominant strategy (the mechanism is strategy-proof).

q: OR problem 8.4: jungle with insufficient housing (fewer houses than individuals; allocation maps N to \(H\cup\{\text{homeless}\}\), no two individuals share a house; strict preferences with any house preferred to homelessness). Which is the natural equilibrium notion and existence argument?
options: An equilibrium does not exist because someone must be homeless
No i is stronger than j with a(j) ≻_i a(i), where a(j) is a house; serial dictatorship in power order (houses run out, the remaining weakest individuals are homeless) gives an equilibrium
Any allocation in which the strongest individuals have houses is an equilibrium
Equilibrium requires everyone to have a house, so it exists only when |H| = |N|
explain: Equilibrium: nobody prefers a house occupied by a weaker individual (or a vacant one) to his own situation. Serial dictatorship in power order still works: each of the strongest |H| individuals takes his best remaining house, the others are homeless and cannot take any house since all houses are held by stronger individuals. Option C ignores preferences among the housed individuals.

q: Jungle with externalities (OR 8.6): preferences are over whole allocations, and \(i\rhd j\) lets i force j to exchange houses. Which is true?
options: An equilibrium may fail to exist, and equilibria may fail to be Pareto stable
Existence holds but equilibrium may not be Pareto stable
Existence and Pareto stability of equilibrium both still hold
explain: OR Example 8.3: three houses on a circle, 1 wants to be 2's clockwise neighbour and 2 wants to be 1's; both cannot hold, so no equilibrium. Example 8.4: three allocations where everyone has his favourite neighbour are all equilibria, but two are Pareto dominated by the third. The basic results need people to care only about their own house.

q: Which statement about Pareto stability, as discussed in the slides, is correct?
options: A Pareto stable allocation is fair

Pareto stability assumes that an available Pareto improvement will be implemented; if two different improvements b and c of a exist and people disagree, bargaining may stall even though a is not Pareto stable
Pareto stability selects a unique allocation
Pareto stability depends on the power relation
explain: The slides note this second possible source of instability. Pareto stability does not imply fairness (the strongest gets everything he wants in a jungle) nor uniqueness (5 Pareto stable allocations in the cave game), and it is defined without reference to power.

q: True or false: if every individual in a jungle has a different favourite house, then the equilibrium is the same for every power relation and it gives everyone his favourite house.
explain: True. In serial dictatorship, whatever the order, each individual's favourite house has not been taken by anyone earlier (it is nobody else's favourite and earlier individuals took their own favourites), so everyone gets his favourite. This allocation is then the unique equilibrium for any power relation.

q: An exchange economy \(\langle N,(\succeq_i)_{i\in N},e\rangle\) (Definition 5-2-1) requires:
options: finite N; strictly convex preferences over \(\R^2_+\); endowments with every individual owning a positive amount of each good
finite N; for each i a monotone and continuous preference over \(\R^2_+\); an initial allocation e with \(\sum_i e_k(i)\gt0\) for k = 1, 2
infinite N; monotone preferences; positive prices
finite N; Cobb-Douglas utilities; endowments summing to (1, 1)
explain: Definition 5-2-1: monotone and continuous preferences over bundles of two goods, and the total endowment of each good is positive. Individual endowments may contain zeros (e.g. Ann owns only apples). Convexity is not part of the definition; it appears only as a condition for continuous demand.

q: In the exchange economy, a price system is
options: a pair of strictly positive numbers
a pair of nonnegative numbers different from (0, 0)
a pair of numbers summing to 1
explain: Definition 5-2-2: \(p=(p_1,p_2)\ge0\), \(p\ne(0,0)\). A zero price is allowed by the definition (e.g. OR Example 10.2 has a CE at (0, 1)), but with monotone preferences a free good is demanded without limit, so zero prices are often ruled out in a CE. Normalising to sum 1 is possible but not the definition.

q: Given price system p, the budget set of individual i in the exchange economy is
explain: Wealth is the value of the endowment, \(w_i(p)=p\cdot e(i)\), so it changes with prices (unlike Topic 4). The endowment itself is always affordable: the individual can choose not to trade. Option C forbids trade altogether.

q: Why are the price systems p and \(\lambda p\) (\(\lambda\gt0\)) equivalent in an exchange economy?
options: Because demand is homogeneous of degree one in prices
Because the total endowment is fixed
Because scaling prices scales both the value of every bundle and the value of every endowment by \(\lambda\), so each budget set \(B(\lambda p,e(i))=B(p,e(i))\) is unchanged
explain: \(\lambda p\cdot x\le\lambda p\cdot e(i)\iff p\cdot x\le p\cdot e(i)\). Only relative prices (the exchange rate \(p_1/p_2\)) matter, so if (p, a) is a CE so is \((\lambda p,a)\); we can normalise \(p_2=1\). Doubling both prices in the market game changes nobody's choice.

q: In an exchange economy, an assignment a is an allocation if
explain: Definition 5-2-3: the bundles add up exactly to the total endowment of each good (feasibility with equality, no free disposal). Option D is individual rationality, which holds in a CE but is not the definition. Option B is the budget-exhaustion condition used in Prop 5-2-1.

q: A pair (p, a) is a competitive equilibrium of \(\langle N,(\succeq_i),e\rangle\) if
options: for every i, a(i) is optimal for \(\succeq_i\) in \(B(p,e(i))\), and a is an allocation
for every i, a(i) is optimal in \(B(p,e(i))\); feasibility is not required
every individual weakly prefers a(i) to e(i), and a is an allocation
a is Pareto stable and p is any price system
explain: Definition 5-2-4 has two conditions: optimality of choices at common prices and feasibility (markets clear). (p, a) fails to be a CE iff someone is not optimising or some market does not clear. Option C is weaker: 'agreeing to trade' does not mean each person chose his best affordable bundle.

q: Market game: Ann owns (6, 0), Bob owns (0, 6); \(u_{Ann}=x_1^{2/3}x_2^{1/3}\), \(u_{Bob}=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\). What is the competitive equilibrium (with \(p_2=1\))?
explain: Apple market: \(4+2/r=6\Rightarrow r=1\). Bananas: \(2r+4=6\) also clears (as Prop 5-2-1 guarantees). So Ann gets (4, 2) and Bob (2, 4): Ann exchanges 2 apples for 2 bananas. Option C swaps the bundles, which is not optimal for either (Ann values apples more).

q: Market game (Ann (6, 0), Bob (0, 6), \(u_{Ann}=x_1^{2/3}x_2^{1/3}\), \(u_{Bob}=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\)). The aggregate excess demand for apples at prices (r, 1) is
explain: \(z(r)=d_{Ann}+d_{Bob}-6=4+2/r-6=2/r-2\). It is continuous on \((0,\infty)\), positive for r < 1, negative for r > 1, and zero at r = 1. This is exactly the aggregate condition used in PS3 extra 4a.

q: Same utilities as the market game, \(u_1=x_1^{2/3}x_2^{1/3}\), \(u_2=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\), but endowments \(e(1)=(1,0)\), \(e(2)=(0,100)\). With \(p_2=1\), what is the CE?
explain: Wealths: \(w_1=p_1\), \(w_2=100\). Apple demands: \(\frac23\) and \(\frac{100}{3p_1}\). Clearing \(\frac23+\frac{100}{3p_1}=1\Rightarrow p_1=100\). Then a(1) = (2/3, (1/3)·100) and a(2) = (1/3, (2/3)·100). The one scarce apple is worth 100 plentiful bananas.

q: Two individuals: \(u_1=x_1^{1/2}x_2^{1/2}\), \(e(1)=(4,0)\); \(u_2=x_1^{1/4}x_2^{3/4}\), \(e(2)=(0,6)\). With \(p_2=1\), find the competitive equilibrium price \(p_1\) and allocation.
Both individuals have \(u=x_1x_2\); \(e(1)=(1,2)\), \(e(2)=(3,2)\). With \(p_2=1\), what is the CE?
explain: Wealths \(w_1=p_1+2\), \(w_2=3p_1+2\); each spends half on good 1: \(\frac{p_1+2}{2p_1}+\frac{3p_1+2}{2p_1}=\frac{4p_1+4}{2p_1}=4\Rightarrow p_1=1\). Then \(w_1=3\Rightarrow(1.5,1.5)\), \(w_2=5\Rightarrow(2.5,2.5)\). Equal split (A) is Pareto stable but not affordable for 1 at these prices.

q: OR Example 10.3: both have \(u=x_1x_2\), \(e(1)=(\alpha,0)\), \(e(2)=(0,\beta)\), \(\alpha,\beta\gt0\). What is the competitive equilibrium (with \(p_2=1\))?
explain: Each spends half his wealth on each good: \(a(1)=(\alpha/2,p_1\alpha/2)\), \(a(2)=(\beta/(2p_1),\beta/2)\). Good-1 clearing \(\alpha/2+\beta/(2p_1)=\alpha\Rightarrow p_1=\beta/\alpha\). Then \(a(1)=(\alpha/2,\beta/2)=a(2)\). Zero prices are impossible (unbounded demand), so this is the only CE.

q: \(u_1=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\), \(e(1)=(2,0)\); \(u_2=x_1x_2\), \(e(2)=(0,2)\). With \(p_2=1\), what is the competitive equilibrium?
options: No CE exists because Leontief preferences are not strictly monotone
explain: Person 1 (wealth \(2p_1\)) buys equal amounts: \(x_1=x_2=2p_1/(p_1+1)\). Person 2 (wealth 2): \(x_1=1/p_1\), \(x_2=1\). Good 1: \(\frac{2p_1}{p_1+1}+\frac1{p_1}=2\iff2p_1^2+p_1+1=2p_1^2+2p_1\iff p_1=1\). Bundles (1, 1) and (1, 1); good 2: 1 + 1 = 2.

q: \(u_1=2x_1+x_2\), \(e(1)=(0,4)\); \(u_2=x_1x_2\), \(e(2)=(4,0)\). With \(p_2=1\), what is the competitive equilibrium?
explain: Person 2 always demands \(x_1=\frac12\cdot4p_1/p_1=2\), so person 1 must demand 2 units of good 1. If \(p_1\lt2\), 1 spends all on good 1: \(4/p_1=2\Rightarrow p_1=2\), contradiction; if \(p_1\gt2\), 1 buys no good 1. So \(p_1=2\), where 1 is indifferent and picks (2, 0) (cost 4). Person 2: wealth 8, bundle (2, 4). Option D is not feasible for good 1 demand by person 2.

q: OR Example 10.2: both have \(u=\min\{x_1,x_2\}\), \(e(1)=(\alpha,0)\), \(e(2)=(0,\beta)\). Which statement is correct?
options: If \(\alpha\gt\beta\), the CE price of good 1 is \(\alpha/\beta\)
No CE exists for any \(\alpha,\beta\) because preferences are not strictly convex
A CE always exists with \(p_1=p_2\) and both individuals at \((\alpha/2,\beta/2)\)
If \(\alpha=\beta\), every price system with \(p_1,p_2\gt0\) is a CE price system; if \(\alpha\gt\beta\), there is no CE with both prices positive, but there is one with \(p=(0,1)\)
explain: With \(p\gg0\) the demands are \(x^1=\frac{p_1\alpha}{p_1+p_2}(1,1)\), \(x^2=\frac{p_2\beta}{p_1+p_2}(1,1)\); both clearing equations have the same left-hand side, so they need \(\alpha=\beta\), and then any \(p\gg0\) works. If \(\alpha\gt\beta\), good 1 is in surplus and gets price 0. With complements a free good is not demanded without limit, so a zero price is possible.

q: PS3 3a: \(n^A\) individuals of type A with \(u_A=x_2\), \(e_A=(\alpha,0)\); \(n^B\) of type B with \(u_B=x_1\), \(e_B=(0,\beta)\). What are the CE?
options: Any \(p\gg0\); each A keeps \((\alpha,0)\), each B keeps \((0,\beta)\)
\(p=\lambda(n^B\beta,\,n^A\alpha)\), \(\lambda\gt0\); each A gets \((0,n^B\beta/n^A)\), each B gets \((n^A\alpha/n^B,0)\)
\(p=\lambda(n^A\alpha,\,n^B\beta)\); each A gets \((0,\beta)\), each B gets \((\alpha,0)\)
explain: A zero price is impossible (the type that wants the free good demands without limit). Type A sells everything for good 2: \((0,p_1\alpha/p_2)\); type B: \((p_2\beta/p_1,0)\). Good 1: \(n^Bp_2\beta/p_1=n^A\alpha\iff p_2/p_1=n^A\alpha/(n^B\beta)\). So prices are proportional to \((n^B\beta,n^A\alpha)\): one allocation, a ray of prices. Option C has the ratio inverted and ignores group sizes.

q: PS3 3b: two individuals with \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) (non-convex). Which describes an individual's demand at \(p\gg0\) with wealth W?
options: Spend everything on the cheaper good: \((W/p_1,0)\) if \(p_1\lt p_2\), \((0,W/p_2)\) if \(p_2\lt p_1\), either corner if \(p_1=p_2\)
Spend everything on the more expensive good
explain: The utility is convex, so on the budget triangle its maximum is at a corner: compare \((W/p_1)^2\) and \((W/p_2)^2\); the larger is for the cheaper good. The interior point (C) is actually the MINIMUM on the budget line. Demand jumps between corners at \(p_1=p_2\), so it is not continuous.

q: PS3 3b: two individuals with \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\), \(e(1)=e(2)=(2,1)\). Does a CE exist?
options: No: a CE needs \(p_1=p_2\); then each has wealth 3 and buys (3, 0) or (0, 3), so total demand is (6, 0), (3, 3) or (0, 6), never the supply (4, 2)
Yes, at p = (1, 1) with no trade
No, because total endowment of each good is not positive
Yes, at p = (2, 1) with each buying (0, 5)
explain: If \(p_1\lt p_2\) nobody buys good 2 although its supply is positive (and vice versa), so CE prices must be equal. At p = (1, 1) each wants all wealth (3) in one good; no combination gives (4, 2). No trade is not optimal because (2, 1) gives 5 < 9. Non-convexity breaks continuity of demand, so Prop 5-2-2 cannot be used.

q: PS3 3b(iv): two individuals with \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) and endowments with \(e_k(1)+e_k(2)\gt0\). For which endowments does a CE exist?
explain: Prices must be equal, p = (1, 1); individual i has wealth \(s_i=e_1(i)+e_2(i)\) and buys \((s_i,0)\) or \((0,s_i)\). Both buying the same good leaves the other market with zero demand, so one buys each good. 1 buys good 1: \(s_1=e_1(1)+e_1(2)\iff e_1(2)=e_2(1)\); 1 buys good 2: \(s_2=e_1(1)+e_1(2)\iff e_1(1)=e_2(2)\). Option B fails: e(1) = e(2) = (2, 1) has no CE.

q: Proposition 5-2-1: let \(p\gg0\) and let a be an assignment with \(p\,a(i)=p\,e(i)\) for all i. Then
explain: If everyone exhausts his budget and prices are strictly positive, clearing of one market implies clearing of the other (Walras' law for the economy). It does not say that either market clears, nor that the bundles are optimal. With L goods: if L − 1 markets clear, the last clears provided its price is positive.

q: In the proof of Prop 5-2-1, summing \(p\,a(i)=p\,e(i)\) over i gives \(p_1\big(\sum_ia_1(i)-\sum_ie_1(i)\big)=-p_2\big(\sum_ia_2(i)-\sum_ie_2(i)\big)\). Why is \(p\gg0\) needed?
options: To divide: if, say, \(p_2=0\), the right side is 0 regardless of the good-2 excess demand, so clearing of good 1 says nothing about good 2
It is not needed; the result holds for any price system
To make budget sets compact so that optimal bundles exist
explain: With \(p_1,p_2\gt0\), one bracket is zero iff the other is. If, say, \(p_2=0\), the right side is zero whatever the good-2 excess demand, so clearing of good 1 says nothing about good 2. Compactness of budget sets matters for the existence of optimal bundles, not for this identity; and the identity holds for any assignment exhausting budgets, continuous or not.

q: True or false: in the exchange economy with two goods, if every individual chooses an optimal bundle at prices \(p\gg0\) (preferences monotone) and the market for good 1 clears, then (p, chosen bundles) is a competitive equilibrium.
explain: True. Monotonicity makes every optimal bundle exhaust the budget (\(p\,a(i)=p\,e(i)\)), so Prop 5-2-1 applies: good 2 clears too, and optimality holds by assumption. This is why the recipe clears only one market.

q: Proposition 5-2-2 (existence of CE) assumes, with \(d_i(p_1)\) the demand for good 1 at prices \((p_1,1)\):
options: each \(d_i\) is differentiable and decreasing in \(p_1\)
each \(d_i\) is continuous; for some low \(p_1\), \(d_i(p_1)\gt e_1(i)\) for ALL i; for some high \(p_1\), \(d_i(p_1)\lt e_1(i)\) for ALL i
preferences are Cobb-Douglas and endowments strictly positive
aggregate excess demand is strictly decreasing
explain: The three assumptions are continuity of each individual demand and the low-price / high-price conditions for every individual. They imply that aggregate excess demand z is continuous, positive somewhere and negative somewhere. No monotonicity of z or differentiability is required, and the CE need not be unique.

q: In the proof of Prop 5-2-2, which mathematical theorem guarantees a price at which the market for good 1 clears?
options: The Intermediate Value Theorem applied to the continuous excess demand \(z(p_1)=\sum_i[d_i(p_1)-e_1(i)]\), which is positive for low and negative for high \(p_1\)
explain: z is continuous (sum of continuous functions), positive for small \(p_1\) and negative for large \(p_1\), so by the IVT \(z(p_1^*)=0\) for some \(p_1^*\) (possibly several). Optimality holds by definition of \(x_i\), and good 2 clears by Prop 5-2-1.

q: True or false: the market game (Ann (6, 0), Bob (0, 6), \(u_{Ann}=x_1^{2/3}x_2^{1/3}\), \(u_{Bob}=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\)) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 5-2-2.
explain: False. \(d_{Ann}(p_1)=4\lt6=e_1(\text{Ann})\) for every \(p_1\), so Ann never demands more apples than she owns at any low price; and \(d_{Bob}=2/p_1\gt0=e_1(\text{Bob})\) always. Yet a CE exists (r = 1): the assumptions are sufficient, not necessary. Only the aggregate z needs to cross zero.

q: PS3 extra 4a asks to weaken Prop 5-2-2 so that it covers the market game. Which weakened hypothesis works?
options: At least one individual demands more than his endowment at some price
Aggregate excess demand \(z(p_1)=\sum_i[d_i(p_1)-e_1(i)]\) is continuous, positive for some \(p_1\) and negative for some (higher) \(p_1\)
explain: The proof only uses these three properties of the aggregate z, then the IVT and Prop 5-2-1. The original assumptions imply them by summation, so this is strictly weaker. In the game \(z(r)=2/r-2\) is continuous, positive for r < 1 and negative for r > 1.

q: Why can Prop 5-2-2 not be used to prove existence in PS3 3b (\(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\))?
options: Because non-convex preferences make demand jump between corners at \(p_1=p_2\), so \(d_i\) is not continuous
Because the endowments are not strictly positive
Because the total endowment is zero
explain: \(x_1^2+x_2^2\) is monotone and continuous, but demand is (W/p_1, 0) for \(p_1\lt p_2\) and (0, W/p_2) for \(p_1\gt p_2\): a discontinuous jump. The IVT argument needs continuity. Indeed for e(1) = e(2) = (2, 1) no CE exists, while for e(1) = (α, 0), e(2) = (0, β) one does.

q: Proposition 5-2-3 (first welfare theorem) states:
options: Every competitive equilibrium allocation of an exchange economy is Pareto stable
Every Pareto stable allocation is a CE allocation for some endowment
Every exchange economy has a Pareto stable CE
Every CE allocation maximises the sum of utilities
explain: Every CE allocation is Pareto stable: 'the invisible hand is efficient'. Option B is the second-welfare-type direction, which is not this proposition. Existence is a separate result (5-2-2), and Pareto stability is not utilitarian maximisation.

q: First welfare theorem proof: (p, a) is a CE and y is a feasible allocation with \(y(i)\succeq_ia(i)\) for all i. Why is \(p\,y(i)\ge p\,e(i)\) for every i?
options: If \(p\,y(i)\lt p\,e(i)\), then for small \(\varepsilon\gt0\), \(y(i)+(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) is affordable and, by monotonicity, strictly better than y(i), hence than a(i), contradicting optimality of a(i)
Because a(i) is on the budget line
explain: This is the step that uses monotonicity (local non-satiation): any bundle at least as good as the optimum cannot be strictly cheaper than the budget. Feasibility of y is used later when summing. Convexity is never used in the proof.

q: First welfare theorem proof: for the individual j with \(y(j)\succ_ja(j)\), why is \(p\,y(j)\gt p\,e(j)\)?
options: Because otherwise y(j) would be affordable and strictly better than a(j), contradicting optimality of a(j) in \(B(p,e(j))\)
Because y(j) contains more of both goods than e(j)
explain: Revealed preference: a strictly better bundle than the optimal choice must be unaffordable. Summing over individuals, \(p\sum_iy(i)\gt p\sum_ie(i)\), contradicting \(\sum_iy(i)=\sum_ie(i)\) (feasibility of y), which forces equal values.

q: Which assumptions are actually used in the proof of the first welfare theorem (Prop 5-2-3)?
options: Existence of a CE via the IVT
Cobb-Douglas utilities and strictly positive endowments
Monotone preferences, optimal choice at common prices, feasibility of the dominating allocation, and no externalities (each person cares only about his own bundle)
explain: The proof uses monotonicity (to get \(p\,y(i)\ge p\,e(i)\)), optimality of choices, and feasibility (\(\sum y=\sum e\)). Implicitly preferences are over one's own bundle; the externality example shows the result fails otherwise. Convexity and continuity are not needed.

q: Externality example: endowments (1, 0) and (0, 1). Individual 1's utility is \(a_1(1)+a_2(1)-2a_2(2)\); individual 2's is \(2a_1(2)+3a_2(2)\). Each takes the other's consumption as given. At p = (1, 1), no trade is a 'CE'. Which allocation shows this outcome is not Pareto stable?
explain: Status quo: \(u_1=1-2\cdot1=-1\), \(u_2=3\). At b: \(u_1=0+0.5-2\cdot0.5=-0.5\gt-1\) and \(u_2=2+1.5=3.5\gt3\): both better, so the first welfare theorem fails with externalities. Option D gives \(u_2=2\lt3\); option A gives \(u_2=2.5\lt3\); option B gives \(u_2=1.5\lt3\).

q: True or false: if the initial allocation e is Pareto stable, then in every competitive equilibrium there is no trade, i.e. a = e.
explain: False. Since e(i) is affordable, \(a(i)\succeq_ie(i)\); Pareto stability of e then forces \(a(i)\sim_ie(i)\) for all i, but bundles can differ. Example: both have \(u=x_1+x_2\), e(1) = (1, 0), e(2) = (0, 1); at p = (1, 1) the swapped bundles (0, 1), (1, 0) are optimal and feasible. Trade happens, but nobody gains.

q: In any competitive equilibrium (p, a) of an exchange economy, which of the following must hold for every individual i?
options: \(a(i)\) contains positive amounts of both goods
explain: The endowment is always in the budget set, and a(i) is optimal there, so \(a(i)\succeq_ie(i)\) (individual rationality). Strict improvement need not hold (e.g. if e is Pareto stable), there may be no trade, and corner bundles are possible (e.g. PS3 3a).

q: OR Prop 10.3 (reopening trade): (p, a) is a CE of \(\langle N,(\succeq_i),e\rangle\). Is (p, a) a CE of the economy \(\langle N,(\succeq_i),a\rangle\) where the endowments are the equilibrium bundles?
options: Yes: since \(p\,a(i)=p\,e(i)\), the budget sets \(B(p,a(i))\) and \(B(p,e(i))\) coincide, so a(i) is still optimal, and a is an allocation
Only if preferences are strictly convex
explain: Optimal bundles exhaust the budget (monotonicity), so the budget line passes through both e(i) and a(i), and the same set is available. Hence a(i) remains optimal and feasibility is trivial. Reopening trade does not undo the equilibrium.

q: In the Edgeworth box of the market game (6 apples, 6 bananas; \(u_{Ann}=x_1^{2/3}x_2^{1/3}\), \(u_{Bob}=x_1^{1/3}x_2^{2/3}\)), what is true at the CE point Ann (4, 2), Bob (2, 4)?
options: The endowment point is also Pareto stable
Ann's MRS is 2 and Bob's is 1/2
The point lies on the box diagonal, so it is the only Pareto stable allocation
Both MRS equal the price ratio \(p_1/p_2=1\), and the budget line through the endowment is tangent to both indifference curves
explain: \(MRS_{Ann}=\frac{2/3}{1/3}\cdot\frac{x_2}{x_1}=2\cdot\frac24=1\); \(MRS_{Bob}=\frac{1/3}{2/3}\cdot\frac{x_2}{x_1}=\frac12\cdot\frac42=1\). Both equal \(p_1/p_2=1\). The endowment (6, 0)/(0, 6) is not Pareto stable (trade benefits both). There are many Pareto stable allocations (the contract curve), not only this one.

q: Two individuals both with \(u=x_1x_2\); total endowment (4, 4). Which allocation is Pareto stable?
explain: Interior Pareto stable allocations need equal MRS: \(x_2^1/x_1^1=x_2^2/x_1^2\), which with total (4, 4) means \(x_1^1=x_2^1\) (the diagonal). (3, 3)/(1, 1) is on it. (1, 3)/(3, 1): MRS 3 vs 1/3, so trading improves both. (4, 0)/(0, 4) gives both utility 0, dominated by (2, 2)/(2, 2).

q: True or false: every exchange economy (monotone, continuous preferences) has a competitive equilibrium.
explain: False. PS3 3b(iii): two individuals with \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) (monotone and continuous but not convex) and e(1) = e(2) = (2, 1) have no CE. Prop 5-2-2 gives only sufficient conditions.

q: True or false: the competitive equilibrium of an exchange economy is always unique (up to scaling of prices).
explain: False. The excess demand function may cross zero several times (OR Figure 10.2), and in OR Example 10.2 with \(\alpha=\beta\) and \(\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) preferences every positive price system is a CE price with different allocations. Contrast the jungle, where the equilibrium is unique.

q: Why must CE prices be strictly positive in PS3 3a (type A: \(u=x_2\), type B: \(u=x_1\))?
options: Because if a price were zero, the type that values that good would demand an unbounded amount of it, so no optimal bundle exists
Because the definition of a price system requires \(p\gg0\)
Because Walras' law fails at zero prices
explain: The definition allows zero prices (only (0, 0) is excluded). But if \(p_2=0\), type A wants unlimited good 2; if \(p_1=0\), type B wants unlimited good 1. With monotone preferences in the good that is free, demand is unbounded. Complements (min) are an exception: there a zero price can occur.

q: OR Definition 10.5 / Prop 10.5: a coalition S can improve upon allocation a if some bundles \((b(i))_{i\in S}\) with \(\sum_{i\in S}b(i)=\sum_{i\in S}e(i)\) satisfy \(b(i)\succ_ia(i)\) for all \(i\in S\); the core is the set of allocations no coalition can improve upon. Which is true?
options: The core coincides with the set of Pareto stable allocations
Whether an allocation is in the core does not depend on endowments
Every CE allocation is in the core; the proof mirrors the first welfare theorem summed over S only
CE allocations are generally not in the core
explain: If S could improve, each \(b(i)\) is strictly better than the optimal a(i), so \(p\,b(i)\gt p\,e(i)\); summing over S contradicts \(\sum_Sb=\sum_Se\). The core depends on endowments and is (weakly) smaller than the Pareto stable set: OR Example 10.4 has a Pareto stable allocation, preferred by all to their endowment, that is not in the core.

q: Comparing the jungle (5.1) and the exchange economy (5.2), which statement is correct?
options: The jungle equilibrium is Pareto stable but CE allocations are not
Both always have a unique equilibrium
The jungle equilibrium always exists and is unique; a CE exists only under conditions and need not be unique; both equilibrium notions are Pareto stable (the CE one absent externalities)
CE allocations are fair, jungle equilibria are not
explain: Jungle: existence via serial dictatorship, uniqueness with strict preferences and power. Exchange economy: existence via IVT under conditions; multiplicity possible. Props 5-1-4 and 5-2-3 give Pareto stability. Neither result establishes fairness or that all Pareto stable allocations are the same.

q: Both individuals have \(u=x_1+x_2\); e(1) = (1, 0), e(2) = (0, 1). Which pair is a competitive equilibrium?
explain: At p = (1, 1) both have wealth 1 and are indifferent along the budget line, so the swap is optimal and feasible (no trade is also a CE). At p = (2, 1) individual 1 (wealth 2) would buy 2 units of good 2, not keep (1, 0). At p = (1, 2), individual 1 buys only good 1, not (0.5, 0.5). At p = (1, 0) good 2 is free and demanded without limit.

q: True or false: an individual in an exchange economy can never benefit from destroying part of his endowment before trade opens.
explain: False. OR Example 10.2: with \(\min\{x_1,x_2\}\) preferences, e(1) = (α, 0), e(2) = (0, β) and α > β, the CE price is (0, 1) and individual 1's good is worthless. Destroying good 1 down to some γ < β flips the price to (1, 0), and individual 1 is better off. The phenomenon can occur with positive prices too.

q: Second-welfare-type comment (OR comment after Prop 10.4, slides 'Pareto-stable endowments'): suppose an authority redistributes goods to make the endowment equal to a Pareto stable allocation a, then opens trade. If (p, b) is a CE of the new economy, then
options: \(b(i)\sim_ia(i)\) for every i, and (p, a) is also a CE
some individual is strictly better off than at a
explain: Each a(i) is affordable, so \(b(i)\succeq_ia(i)\); if someone were strictly better, b would Pareto dominate the Pareto stable a. So everyone is indifferent, and a(i) is then also optimal in his budget set, making (p, a) a CE. Trade does not undo the redistribution, though bundles may change among indifferent ones.

q: PS1 Q(a)(i) — step 1/3: Is there a binary relation \(R\) on a set \(X\) that is both symmetric and antisymmetric?
options: Yes, but only the empty relation, which is not a genuine binary relation
Only if \(X\) has a single element
No: symmetry and antisymmetry contradict each other whenever \(R\) is nonempty
explain: Equality is symmetric (\(x=y\Rightarrow y=x\)) and antisymmetric (\(x=y\) and \(y=x\) give \(x=y\)). The two properties are compatible: they only force \(R\) to live on the diagonal. The empty relation also works (and is a legitimate relation), but it is not the only one, and \(X\) can be any set, e.g. \(\R\).

q: PS1 Q(a)(i) — step 2/3: Let \(R\) be symmetric and antisymmetric and suppose \(xRy\). What follows?
options: \(xRx\) for every \(x\), so \(R\) must be reflexive
\(x=y\): symmetry gives \(yRx\), then antisymmetry gives \(x=y\), so \(R\) is contained in the diagonal
\(x\neq y\), since antisymmetry forbids two-way pairs
explain: From \(xRy\), symmetry gives \(yRx\); antisymmetry applied to \(xRy\) and \(yRx\) gives \(x=y\). So every pair in \(R\) is of the form \((x,x)\). Nothing forces every \((x,x)\) to be in \(R\) (the empty relation is a valid example), so reflexivity does not follow, nor completeness.

q: PS1 Q(a)(i) — step 3/3: Equality on \(\R\) answers (a)(i), but the relation \(\le\) on \(\R\) does not.
explain: True. \(\le\) is antisymmetric (\(x\le y\), \(y\le x\Rightarrow x=y\)) but not symmetric (\(1\le2\) but not \(2\le1\)). Only relations contained in the diagonal (equality, the empty relation, subsets of the diagonal) are both symmetric and antisymmetric.

q: PS1 Q(a)(ii) — step 1/3: Is there a binary relation that is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric? Which example does the answer key give?
options: No: every relation is either symmetric or antisymmetric
explain: \(R=\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\}\) is not symmetric (\((1,3)\in R\), \((3,1)\notin R\)) and not antisymmetric (\((1,2),(2,1)\in R\) with \(1\ne2\)). \(\le\) is antisymmetric; \(\{(1,2),(2,1)\}\) is symmetric. 'Neither' is not the negation of 'one of them', so such relations exist.

q: PS1 Q(a)(ii) — step 2/3: For \(R=\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\}\) on \(\{1,2,3\}\), which fact proves that \(R\) is NOT antisymmetric?
options: \(R\) is not transitive: \((2,1),(1,2)\in R\) but \((2,2)\notin R\)
explain: Antisymmetry says \(xRy\) and \(yRx\) imply \(x=y\); the pair 1, 2 violates it. The fact \((1,3)\in R,(3,1)\notin R\) is the witness for non-symmetry, the other half of the answer. Reflexivity and transitivity are irrelevant to this question. (Note: the answer key's 'even though 1 = 2' is a conversion error for \(1\ne2\).)

q: PS1 Q(a)(ii) — step 3/3: What is the smallest number of elements \(X\) must have for a relation on \(X\) to be neither symmetric nor antisymmetric?
explain: Non-antisymmetry needs a two-way pair \((a,b),(b,a)\) with \(a\ne b\). Non-symmetry needs a one-way pair \((c,d)\), \(c\ne d\) (diagonal pairs are their own reverse). With two elements the only off-diagonal pairs are \((1,2),(2,1)\), and both are used by the two-way pair, so a third element is required.

q: PS1 Q(a)(iii) — step 1/3: The 'easy proof' that symmetry + transitivity imply reflexivity says: fix \(x\), take \(y\) with \(xRy\); then \(yRx\) by symmetry and \(xRx\) by transitivity. Why is it spurious?
options: Symmetry only applies to distinct elements
It is not spurious; the three properties are redundant
It assumes that some \(y\) with \(xRy\) exists, which need not be the case
explain: Each step is valid once a \(y\) with \(xRy\) is given; the hidden assumption is the existence of such a \(y\). If \(x\) is related to nothing, the argument never starts and \(xRx\) is not derived. Transitivity and symmetry do apply when \(y=x\).

q: PS1 Q(a)(iii) — step 2/3: Which relation is a counterexample showing that symmetry and transitivity do not imply reflexivity?
options: The empty relation on a nonempty set \(X\)
explain: On nonempty \(X\), the empty relation is symmetric and transitive vacuously (no pairs to check) but not reflexive (\(xRx\) fails for any \(x\)). Equality is reflexive; \(\le\) is not symmetric; on \(X=\emptyset\) the empty relation is vacuously reflexive too, so it is not a counterexample.

q: PS1 Q(a)(iii) — step 3/3: On \(X=\{a,b\}\), the relation \(R=\{(a,a)\}\) is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive.
explain: True. The only pair is \((a,a)\), whose reverse is itself (symmetric), and chains \(aRa,aRa\) give \(aRa\) (transitive). But \((b,b)\notin R\): \(b\) is related to nothing, which is exactly where the 'easy proof' breaks.

q: PS1 Q(b)(i) — step 1/3: On the positive integers, \(x\) is preferred to \(y\) if (i) \(x\) odd and \(y\) even, (ii) both even and \(x<y\), (iii) both odd and \(x>y\). Which is the ranking (best on the left)?
explain: All odds beat all evens; among odds larger is better (so there is no best element), among evens smaller is better (so 2 is the best even and there is no worst element). Writing the ranking first is the playbook's advice: it shows immediately that the evens form an infinite strictly descending chain \(2\succ4\succ6\succ\cdots\).

q: PS1 Q(b)(i) — step 2/3: Same preference on the positive integers (odds ranked above evens; odds: larger better; evens: smaller better). If \(u\) with nonnegative integer values represented it, which chain must hold?
explain: Among evens, smaller is better, so \(2\succ4\succ6\succ\cdots\) and \(u\) must be strictly decreasing along the evens, while staying \(\ge0\). An increasing integer chain \(u(1)<u(3)<\cdots\) is perfectly possible (integers are unbounded above), so it gives no contradiction. \(1\succ2\) holds but \(2\succ3\) is false (3 is odd).

q: PS1 Q(b)(i) — step 3/3: Why is \(u(2)>u(4)>u(6)>\cdots\ge0\) impossible when \(u\) takes nonnegative integer values?
options: Because the positive integers have no largest element
Because a utility function must be injective
A strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers starting at \(u(2)\) has at most \(u(2)+1\) terms
explain: Each step down loses at least 1, so after \(u(2)+1\) steps the value would be negative. The chain is infinite, contradiction. Boundedness above and injectivity are not the issue; the absence of a largest integer is why there is no best odd number, not why integer utility fails.

q: PS1 Q(b)(ii) — step 1/3: Same preference (odds above evens; odds: larger better; evens: smaller better). Which real-valued \(u\) represents it?
explain: Check the three clauses: odd values \(\ge1>0>\) even values (clause i); for evens, \(-x\) is larger for smaller \(x\) (clause ii); for odds, \(x\) is larger for larger \(x\) (clause iii). \(1/x\) on odds would make 1 the best odd, reversing clause (iii); the first distractor reverses everything.

q: PS1 Q(b)(ii) — step 2/3: The nonnegative representation is \(u(x)=1+\frac{x}{x+1}\) for odd \(x\) and \(u(x)=1-\frac{x}{x+1}=\frac1{x+1}\) for even \(x\). Why does it work?
options: Odd values decrease and even values increase in \(x\)
Odd and even values overlap, but ties are allowed
Odd values are \(\ge 1.5\) and increase in \(x\); even values are \(\le1/3\) and decrease in \(x\)
It takes integer values, so it fixes the problem found in (b)(i)
explain: \(\frac{x}{x+1}\) is increasing in \(x\), so \(1+\frac{x}{x+1}\in[1.5,2)\) is increasing on odds (\(x=1\) gives 1.5), and \(\frac1{x+1}\le\frac13\) for even \(x\ge2\), decreasing. So every odd beats every even and both within-class orders are right. The values are not integers, and there are no ties.

q: PS1 Q(b)(ii) — step 3/3: The nonnegative real-valued utility found in (b)(ii) contradicts the impossibility shown in (b)(i).
explain: False. (b)(i) only rules out nonnegative INTEGER values. Real numbers in \((0,1)\) admit infinite strictly decreasing sequences, e.g. \(1/3>1/5>1/7>\cdots>0\), so there is no conflict.

q: PS1 Q(c)(i): Prop. 2.2 (finite \(X\): every choice function with property \(\alpha\) is rationalizable) is proved by listing \(a_1=c(X)\), \(a_2=c(X\setminus\{a_1\})\), … and ranking \(a_1\succ a_2\succ\cdots\). Which step fails for infinite \(X\)?
options: The ranking produced is not transitive
\(c(X)\) is not defined when \(X\) is infinite
Property \(\alpha\) cannot hold on an infinite set
The list need not exhaust \(X\), so the resulting ranking need not cover every alternative
explain: The construction removes one alternative per step; on an infinite set it never terminates, and even a sequence indexed by all positive integers may leave elements out (e.g. if \(X\) is uncountable). \(c(X)\) is defined (a choice function chooses from every nonempty subset), \(\alpha\) can hold, and the list itself is transitively ordered.

q: PS1 Q(c)(ii) — step 1/4: Keep choice single-valued but let \(X\) be infinite. Does Proposition 2.2 (property \(\alpha\) ⇒ rationalizable) remain true?
options: Yes, with a different proof based on choices from pairs
No: the failure of the enumeration step gives a counterexample
explain: The failing step was a feature of that proof, not of the result. Defining the relation from pairwise choices works for any \(X\). \(\beta\) is needed only for multi-valued choice correspondences (PS1 d).

q: PS1 Q(c)(ii) — step 2/4: For a single-valued choice function \(c\) with property \(\alpha\) on an infinite \(X\), which relation should you define to rationalize \(c\)?
options: \(x\succsim_c y\iff x\) appears before \(y\) in the list \(c(X),c(X\setminus\{c(X)\}),\dots\)
explain: Pairwise choice defines a complete relation (the pair choice is one of the two). The enumeration-based relation is exactly what fails on infinite sets, and '\(x=c(X)\)' only ranks one element. The last option is the reverse order.

q: PS1 Q(c)(ii) — step 3/4: With \(x\succsim_c y\iff c(\{x,y\})=x\), to show transitivity take distinct \(x,y,z\) with \(x\succsim_c y\), \(y\succsim_c z\) and \(w=c(\{x,y,z\})\). Why is \(w=y\) impossible?
options: Because \(y\) is the middle element, it can never be chosen from a triple
explain: \(\alpha\): if \(w=c(A)\) and \(w\in B\subset A\) then \(w=c(B)\). With \(w=y\) and \(B=\{x,y\}\) we get \(c(\{x,y\})=y\ne x\). Similarly \(w=z\) contradicts \(y\succsim_c z\) via \(B=\{y,z\}\). So \(w=x\), and \(\alpha\) on \(\{x,z\}\) gives \(x\succsim_c z\).

q: PS1 Q(c)(ii) — step 4/4: The proof that \(\succsim_c\) is complete and transitive only compares choices from menus with at most three elements, which is why the cardinality of \(X\) does not matter.
explain: True. Completeness uses pairs, transitivity uses a triple and its pairs, and rationalization compares \(c(A)\) with each \(a\) through the pair \(\{c(A),a\}\). No step enumerates \(X\), so finiteness is never used.

q: PS1 Q(d)(i) — step 1/4: \(X=\{x,y,z\}\), \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(\{x,z\})=\{x\}\), \(C(\{y,z\})=\{y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\), singletons choose themselves. To verify property \(\alpha\) (\(x\in C(A)\), \(x\in B\subseteq A\Rightarrow x\in C(B)\)) for \(A=X\), what must you check?
explain: Only \(x\) is chosen from \(X\), so \(\alpha\) requires \(x\) to be chosen from every subset containing it: true for \(\{x,y\}\), \(\{x,z\}\), \(\{x\}\). The pairs' choices are chosen from their singletons trivially, so \(\alpha\) holds. \(C(\{x,y\})\subseteq C(X)\) is false (it is what \(\beta\)-type reasoning would demand) and is not part of \(\alpha\).

q: PS1 Q(d)(i) — step 2/4: Same \(C\) on \(\{x,y,z\}\). Suppose a preference \(\pr\) rationalizes \(C\). What does \(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\) imply?
explain: Both elements are best in \(\{x,y\}\): \(x\pr y\) and \(y\pr x\), i.e. indifference. A strict preference would make only one of them chosen.

q: PS1 Q(d)(i) — step 3/4: Same \(C\) (\(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\)). If \(\pr\) rationalizes it, \(y\pr x\) and \(x\in C(X)\) gives \(x\pr z\). What does transitivity give next?
options: \(y\pr z\), so \(y\) is a best element of \(X\)
explain: \(y\pr x\) and \(x\pr z\) give \(y\pr z\). Together with \(y\pr x\) and \(y\pr y\), \(y\) is weakly better than every element of \(X\).

q: PS1 Q(d)(i) — step 4/4: Having shown that \(y\) is a best element of \(X=\{x,y,z\}\) under any rationalizing \(\pr\), how does the proof end?
options: Rationalization requires \(y\in C(X)\), but \(C(X)=\{x\}\): contradiction, so no \(\pr\) rationalizes \(C\)
explain: A rationalizable \(C(A)\) contains ALL best elements of \(A\), so \(y\in C(X)\) is forced, contradicting \(C(X)=\{x\}\). \(\alpha\) holds for this \(C\) (step 1), so the contradiction is with rationalizability, not with \(\alpha\).

q: PS1 Q(d)(ii) — step 1/2: Property \(\beta\): for \(A\subseteq B\) and \(x,y\in C(A)\), \(x\in C(B)\Rightarrow y\in C(B)\). For the \(C\) above (\(C(\{x,y\})=\{x,y\}\), \(C(\{x,z\})=\{x\}\), \(C(\{y,z\})=\{y\}\), \(C(X)=\{x\}\)), which sets show the violation?
explain: \(\beta\) needs two alternatives chosen TOGETHER from the small set; only \(\{x,y\}\) has two chosen elements. \(C(\{x,z\})\) and \(C(\{y,z\})\) are singletons, so \(\beta\) says nothing about them (\(y\) dropping out of \(C(B)\) alone is not a \(\beta\) violation).

q: PS1 Q(d)(ii) — step 2/2: Property \(\beta\) restricts what happens when a menu SHRINKS, while property \(\alpha\) restricts what happens when it EXPANDS.
explain: False, it is the other way round. \(\alpha\): a chosen element stays chosen in smaller menus (shrinking). \(\beta\): if two elements are chosen together from a small menu and one stays chosen in a larger menu, so does the other (expanding).

q: PS1 Q(d)(iii) — step 1/3: To prove that \(\beta\) is necessary for rationalizability, what exactly must you show?
options: One example of a rationalizable \(C\) that satisfies \(\beta\)
If \(\pr\) rationalizes \(C\), \(A\subseteq B\), \(x,y\in C(A)\) and \(x\in C(B)\), then \(y\in C(B)\)
explain: 'Necessary' means rationalizable ⇒ \(\beta\). Assume a rationalizing \(\pr\) and derive \(\beta\) for arbitrary sets. The converse (sufficiency) is part (iv) and needs \(\alpha\) too. One example cannot prove a 'for all' statement.

q: PS1 Q(d)(iii) — step 2/3: \(\pr\) rationalizes \(C\), \(A\subseteq B\), \(x,y\in C(A)\), \(x\in C(B)\). Which first inference is correct?
options: \(y\pr z\) for all \(z\in B\), because \(y\in C(A)\)
\(y\pr x\), because \(y\) is best in \(A\) and \(x\in A\)
explain: \(y\in C(A)\) means \(y\pr a\) for all \(a\in A\), in particular \(a=x\). It does not directly compare \(y\) with elements of \(B\setminus A\). \(x\in C(B)\) is an assumption here, not something \(\alpha\) provides (and \(\alpha\) goes from large to small menus).

q: PS1 Q(d)(iii) — step 3/3: With \(y\pr x\) and \(x\pr z\) for every \(z\in B\) (since \(x\in C(B)\)), which property of \(\pr\) finishes the proof that \(y\in C(B)\)?
explain: Transitivity gives \(y\pr z\) for every \(z\in B\), so \(y\) is a best element of \(B\), hence \(y\in C(B)\). Preferences need not be antisymmetric (indeed \(x\sim y\) here).

q: PS1 Q(d)(iv) — step 1/4: \(C\) satisfies \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\); define \(x\succsim_C y\iff x\in C(\{x,y\})\). Why is \(\succsim_C\) complete?
options: \(C(\{x,y\})\) is nonempty, so it contains \(x\) or \(y\)
explain: A choice correspondence assigns a nonempty subset to every menu, so at least one of \(x\succsim_C y\), \(y\succsim_C x\) holds. Neither \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) nor finiteness is needed for completeness.

q: PS1 Q(d)(iv) — step 2/4: Transitivity of \(x\succsim_C y\iff x\in C(\{x,y\})\): given \(x\succsim_C y\), \(y\succsim_C z\), \(T=\{x,y,z\}\), \(w\in C(T)\). In the hardest case \(w=z\), which chain gives \(x\in C(\{x,z\})\)?
options: Since \(w=z\), \(z\succsim_C x\), so the claim fails in this case
explain: \(z\in C(T)\) and \(\alpha\) give \(z\in C(\{y,z\})\); with \(y\in C(\{y,z\})\) (from \(y\succsim_C z\)) \(\beta\) lifts \(y\) into \(C(T)\). Then \(x,y\in C(\{x,y\})\) and \(y\in C(T)\) lift \(x\) into \(C(T)\) by \(\beta\), and \(\alpha\) brings it down to \(\{x,z\}\). Completeness alone does not put \(x\) in \(C(\{x,z\})\).

q: PS1 Q(d)(iv) — step 3/4: To show \(\succsim_C\) rationalizes \(C\), first show: if \(x\in C(A)\) then \(x\succsim_C y\) for all \(y\in A\). Which property is used?
explain: \(x\in C(A)\) and \(x\in\{x,y\}\subseteq A\) give \(x\in C(\{x,y\})\) by \(\alpha\) (immediate if \(A=\{x,y\}\)). This is the 'chosen ⇒ best' inclusion.

q: PS1 Q(d)(iv) — step 4/4: Converse inclusion: \(x\in A\) with \(x\succsim_C y\) for all \(y\in A\); pick \(z\in C(A)\). Then \(x,z\in C(\{x,z\})\). Which property gives \(x\in C(A)\)?
options: \(\beta\) (with the small set \(\{x,z\}\), the large set \(A\), and \(z\in C(A)\))
explain: \(z\in C(\{x,z\})\) by \(\alpha\), and \(x\in C(\{x,z\})\) by definition of \(\succsim_C\). Since \(z\) stays chosen in the larger set \(A\), \(\beta\) forces \(x\in C(A)\). So \(C(A)\) is exactly the set of \(\succsim_C\)-best elements: \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are jointly sufficient.

q: PS1 Q(e) — step 1/5: Firefly: \(p\pr q\iff p_3<q_3\) or [\(p_3=q_3\) and \(p_2\le q_2\)], where \(p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)\) = (Win, Draw, Lose). Compare \(p=(0.5,0.5,0)\) and \(q=(0.9,0,0.1)\).
explain: First criterion: probability of losing. \(p_3=0<0.1=q_3\), so \(p\succ q\) regardless of the much higher win chance of \(q\). Lexicographic relations are complete, so 'incomparable' is impossible.

q: PS1 Q(e)(i) — step 2/5: Is Firefly's lexicographic relation (\(p\pr q\iff p_3<q_3\) or [\(p_3=q_3\), \(p_2\le q_2\)]) complete and transitive?
options: Neither, since it has no utility representation
explain: Complete: compare \(p_3,q_3\); if equal, \(p_2,q_2\) are reals and one is \(\le\) the other. Transitive: \(p_3\le q_3\le r_3\); a strict inequality gives \(p_3<r_3\), otherwise all equal and \(p_2\le q_2\le r_2\). Having no utility representation does not make a relation irrational.

q: PS1 Q(e)(ii) — step 3/5: Firefly (minimise P(Lose), then P(Draw)). With \([\text{Win}]\succ[\text{Draw}]\succ[\text{Lose}]\), for which \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) is \(\lambda\cdot\text{Win}\oplus(1-\lambda)\cdot\text{Lose}\sim[\text{Draw}]\)?
options: For no \(\lambda\): every such mixture is \((\lambda,0,1-\lambda)\), with a positive chance of losing, so \([\text{Draw}]\) is strictly better
\(\lambda=1/3\), by symmetry of the three outcomes
explain: \([\text{Draw}]=(0,1,0)\) has \(p_3=0<1-\lambda\) for every \(\lambda<1\). No win probability compensates any risk of losing, so continuity fails. This is the axiom that breaks.

q: PS1 Q(e)(iii) — step 4/5: Why does Firefly's preference satisfy independence (\(p\pr q\iff\lambda p\oplus(1-\lambda)r\pr\lambda q\oplus(1-\lambda)r\), \(\lambda\in(0,1)\))?
options: It does not satisfy independence: mixing with \(r\) can create ties
Because it can be represented by an expected utility function
The mixed third coordinates \(\lambda p_3+(1-\lambda)r_3\), \(\lambda q_3+(1-\lambda)r_3\) are ordered as \(p_3,q_3\); if \(p_3=q_3\) they tie and the second coordinates compare as \(p_2,q_2\)
explain: Mixing adds the same \((1-\lambda)r_k\) to both sides and scales by \(\lambda>0\), which preserves strict order and ties coordinate by coordinate, so each lexicographic stage is preserved. It has no EU (indeed no utility) representation and is not continuous.

q: PS1 Q(e) — step 5/5: Firefly's preference has no expected utility representation. Which assumption of the Expected Utility Theorem fails?
explain: (i) It is a preference relation; (iii) independence holds; (ii) continuity fails. Lexicographic structure kills continuity (same pattern as the lexicographic order on \(\R^2_+\)).

q: PS1 Q(f) — step 1/4: Is there a monotonic preference over \(\Lz\) that does not satisfy independence? What is the key insight?
options: No: every monotonic preference has an EU representation
No: monotonicity plus completeness implies independence
Yes: monotonicity only compares lotteries over the same two prizes, so be EU there and do something different on three-prize lotteries
Yes: any preference that is not continuous works
explain: Monotonicity: for \(a\succ b\), \(\alpha>\beta\) implies \(\alpha a\oplus(1-\alpha)b\succ\beta a\oplus(1-\beta)b\). It is silent on lotteries with full support on three prizes, which leaves room to violate independence.

q: PS1 Q(f) — step 2/4: Study-guide example: \(Z=\{a,b,c\}\), \(U(p)=2p_1+p_2-10p_1p_2p_3\). Why is the induced preference monotonic?
options: Because the term \(-10p_1p_2p_3\) is always negative
On a two-prize lottery one probability is 0, so \(U=2p_1+p_2\), an EU with \(v(a)=2,v(b)=1,v(c)=0\)
explain: Monotonicity only involves lotteries over two prizes, where the product term vanishes and \(U\) coincides with an expected utility, which is monotone. \(U\) is not linear (that would force independence) and is not increasing in \(p_3\).

q: PS1 Q(f) — step 3/4: With \(U(p)=2p_1+p_2-10p_1p_2p_3\): \(\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12b\) has \(U=1.5\) and \(\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12c\) has \(U=1\). Mixing each half-half with \([c]\): what is \(U(\tfrac14a\oplus\tfrac14b\oplus\tfrac12c)\)?
explain: \(2\cdot\tfrac14+\tfrac14-10\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12=0.75-0.3125=0.4375\). The other mixture is \(\tfrac14a\oplus\tfrac34c\) with \(U=0.5\) (two prizes, no product term). So \(0.4375<0.5\): the ranking flips, violating independence. 0.75 forgets the product term.

q: PS1 Q(f) — step 4/4: In the official example, lotteries with at most two prizes rank above all three-prize lotteries (two-prize ones by \(2p_1+p_2\), three-prize ones lexicographically). \(\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12b\succ\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12c\), but after mixing each half-half with \(c\) the order reverses. Why?
options: Because monotonicity fails for the mixtures
Because mixing with \(c\) lowers both lotteries equally
\(\tfrac14a\oplus\tfrac14b\oplus\tfrac12c\) has three prizes, while \(\tfrac14a\oplus\tfrac34c\) has two, so the second is in the top class
explain: Mixing \(\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12c\) with \(c\) keeps support \(\{a,c\}\), but mixing \(\tfrac12a\oplus\tfrac12b\) with \(c\) creates full support, dropping it to the bottom class. The weirdness is placed exactly where monotonicity does not look.

q: PS1 Extra — step 1/3: To prove the lexicographic order on \(\R^2_+\) (\(x\pr y\iff x_1>y_1\) or [\(x_1=y_1\), \(x_2\ge y_2\)]) has no utility, suppose \(u\) represents it. What does \((a,1)\succ(a,0)\) give for each \(a\in[0,1]\)?
explain: Strict preference gives \(u(a,1)>u(a,0)\), so the interval between them is nonempty and contains a rational. Saying why the intervals are nonempty is one of the two key sentences of the proof.

q: PS1 Extra — step 2/3: Lexicographic order on \(\R^2_+\), intervals \(I_a=(u(a,0),u(a,1))\). Why are \(I_a\) and \(I_b\) disjoint for \(a>b\)?
options: \((a,0)\succ(b,1)\), so \(u(a,0)>u(b,1)\): all of \(I_a\) lies above all of \(I_b\)
explain: With \(a>b\) the first coordinate decides: \((a,0)\succ(b,1)\). Hence \(u(b,0)<u(b,1)<u(a,0)<u(a,1)\). No continuity is assumed (and \((a,1)\succ(b,1)\), not \(\sim\)).

q: PS1 Extra — step 3/3: Choosing a rational \(f(a)\in I_a\) for every \(a\in[0,1]\) (with disjoint intervals \(I_a\)) gives what contradiction?
options: \(f\) is one-to-one from the uncountable \([0,1]\) into the countable \(\mathbb Q\)
\(f\) is onto \(\mathbb Q\), which is impossible
explain:
Disjoint intervals receive different rationals, so \(f(a)
e f(b)\) for \(a
e b\). An injection from an uncountable set into a countable one cannot exist. (The answer key's 'hence \(f(a)=f(b)\)' is a typo for \(f(a)
eq f(b)\).)

q: PS2 Q1(a)(i) — step 1/3: Wealth \(w\), loss \(D\) with probability \(p\); paying \(x\) for insurance pays \(\lambda x\) in case of accident. What are the wealths in the two states?
explain: The premium \(x\) is paid in both states; the payout \(\lambda x\) arrives only after the accident. Always start from the state-by-state wealth.

q: PS2 Q1(a)(i) — step 2/3: Insurance with \(\lambda=1/p\) (zero expected profit): accident wealth \(w-x-D+x/p\) (prob. \(p\)), no-accident wealth \(w-x\). What is the expected wealth?
explain: \(p(w-x-D+x/p)+(1-p)(w-x)=w-x-pD+x=w-pD\). Fair insurance does not change the mean, only the spread.

q: PS2 Q1(a)(i) — step 3/3: Fair insurance (\(\lambda=1/p\)), mean wealth \(w-pD\) for every \(x\). Why is \(x=pD\) optimal for a risk-averse individual?
options: At \(x=pD\) both states give \(w-pD\) for sure, and a risk-averse person weakly prefers the sure mean to any lottery with that mean
Because a risk-averse person always buys the maximum coverage \(D/\lambda\)
explain: Accident wealth \(w-pD-D+D=w-pD\) equals no-accident wealth. Every choice has mean \(w-pD\), and risk aversion means \([E[p]]\pr p\). Expected wealth is the same for all \(x\); and here \(D/\lambda=pD\), but the argument is risk aversion, not 'maximum coverage'.

q: PS2 Q1(a)(ii) — step 1/3: \(U(x)=p\,v(w-D+(\lambda-1)x)+(1-p)\,v(w-x)\) on \([0,D/\lambda]\). What is \(U'(D/\lambda)\)?
explain: \(U'(x)=p(\lambda-1)v'(w-D+(\lambda-1)x)-(1-p)v'(w-x)\). At \(x=D/\lambda\) both arguments equal \(w-D/\lambda\), so \(U'=[p\lambda-p-1+p]v'=(p\lambda-1)v'\). It is zero only for fair insurance \(p\lambda=1\).

q: PS2 Q1(a)(ii) — step 2/3: With \(p\lambda<1\) and \(v'>0\), \(U'(D/\lambda)=(p\lambda-1)v'(w-D/\lambda)\). What do you conclude?
options: \(U'(D/\lambda)>0\): she would like more than full insurance
\(U'(D/\lambda)<0\): reducing \(x\) slightly below full insurance raises expected utility, so any optimum has \(\lambda x<D\)
explain: A negative slope at the right endpoint of \([0,D/\lambda]\) means the endpoint is not a maximum. Strict risk aversion (concave \(v\)) makes \(U\) concave, so the argument is clean.

q: PS2 Q1(a)(ii) — step 3/3: The argument shows that with unfair insurance (\(p\lambda<1\)) a strictly risk-averse individual buys a strictly positive but partial amount, \(0<\lambda x<D\).
explain: False. It only shows \(\lambda x<D\) (less than full insurance). Zero insurance is possible, as the problem itself says: whether \(x>0\) depends on \(U'(0)\), which the argument does not sign.

q: PS2 Q1(b)(i) — step 1/3: \(p\succeq_{FOSD}q\iff F_p(x)\le F_q(x)\) for all \(x\). How is transitivity shown?
options: It is not transitive because CDFs can cross
\(F_p\le F_q\le F_r\) pointwise gives \(F_p\le F_r\) pointwise
By a numerical example with three lotteries
explain: Transitivity of \(\le\) on the reals, applied at each \(x\). An example cannot prove a 'for all' claim; expected values do not characterise FOSD; crossing CDFs break completeness, not transitivity.

q: PS2 Q1(b)(i) — step 2/3: To show FOSD is not complete, take \(p=\tfrac12[0]\oplus\tfrac12[4]\) and \(q=[1]\). Which comparison shows that \(p\) does NOT FOSD \(q\)?
explain: \(p\) dominating \(q\) needs \(F_p\le F_q\) everywhere; at 0 it fails. The comparison at 1 shows instead that \(q\) does not dominate \(p\). The mean comparison favours \(p\) and is irrelevant for showing non-dominance.

q: PS2 Q1(b)(i) — step 3/3: With \(p=\tfrac12[0]\oplus\tfrac12[4]\), \(q=[1]\), which comparison shows that \(q\) does NOT FOSD \(p\)?
explain: \(q\) dominating \(p\) needs \(F_q\le F_p\) everywhere; at \(x=1\), \(F_q=1>1/2\). The CDFs cross, so neither dominates: FOSD is incomplete. Using means alone would be the 'higher mean ⇒ FOSD' mistake in reverse.

q: PS2 Q1(b)(iii) — step 1/2: Why is \(E[p]\ge E[q]\) NECESSARY for \(p\succeq_{FOSD}q\) (finite supports in \([a,b]\))?
explain: The integral formula expresses the mean through the CDF; a smaller CDF gives a larger integrand. (Equivalently: FOSD implies higher EU for every increasing \(v\), take \(v(z)=z\).) The reverse implication is false, and an example cannot prove necessity.

q: PS2 Q1(b)(iii) — step 2/2: Why is \(E[p]\ge E[q]\) NOT sufficient for \(p\succeq_{FOSD}q\)?
options: Because FOSD is complete while \(\succeq_{EV}\) is not
explain: Reusing the part (i) counterexample, as the problem suggests: higher mean but \(F_p(0)=1/2>0=F_q(0)\). The last option is a case where both hold, which proves nothing about sufficiency. \(\succeq_{EV}\) is complete and transitive; FOSD is the incomplete one.

q: PS2 Q1(c)(i) — step 1/4: Compare \(v_1(z)=z\) and \(v_2(z)=z\) for \(z\ge0\), \(2z\) for \(z<0\). Which is more risk-averse?
options: They are equally risk-averse since \(r_A=0\) wherever defined
explain: \(v_2\) is concave (slope 2 then 1) and \(v_1\) is linear (risk neutral). \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) with concave \(\varphi\), and \(c(F,v_2)\le E[z]=c(F,v_1)\) for every \(F\). Arrow–Pratt being 0 off the kink is misleading, see next step.

q: PS2 Q1(c)(i) — step 2/4: \(v_2(z)=z\) (\(z\ge0\)), \(2z\) (\(z<0\)). Why can't the Arrow–Pratt coefficient settle the comparison with \(v_1(z)=z\)?
options: Because \(r_A\) only applies to bounded utilities
\(r_A=-v''/v'\) is 0 wherever \(v_2\) is differentiable, and \(v_2\) is not differentiable at the kink \(z=0\) where all the curvature sits
explain: Both functions are piecewise linear, so \(v''=0\) away from 0. The concavity is concentrated in the kink, which \(r_A\) cannot see. Use \(\varphi\) or certainty equivalents instead (playbook: 'with kinks, use \(\varphi\) or CE').

q: PS2 Q1(c)(i) — step 3/4: With \(v_2(z)=z\) (\(z\ge0\)), \(2z\) (\(z<0\)), what is the certainty equivalent of \(\tfrac12[-1]\oplus\tfrac12[1]\)?
explain: \(EU=\tfrac12(-2)+\tfrac12(1)=-\tfrac12\). Inverting: \(v_2^{-1}(t)=t/2\) for \(t<0\), so \(c=-\tfrac14<0=E[z]=c(\cdot,v_1)\). \(-1/2\) is the EU, not the CE (forgetting to invert).

q: PS2 Q1(c)(i) — step 4/4: Which \(\varphi\) satisfies \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\) for \(v_1(z)=z\), \(v_2(z)=z\) (\(z\ge0\)), \(2z\) (\(z<0\))?
explain: Since \(v_1\) is the identity, \(\varphi=v_2\). Its slope drops from 2 to 1 at 0, so it is concave, which certifies \(v_2\) as more risk-averse. The \(t/2\) version is the inverse direction (convex).

q: PS2 Q1(c)(ii) — step 1/2: \(v_2=\varphi(v_1)\), all twice differentiable. Which expression is correct for \(r_A(z,v_2)=-v_2''/v_2'\)?
explain: Chain rule: \(v_2'=\varphi'(v_1)v_1'\), \(v_2''=\varphi''(v_1)(v_1')^2+\varphi'(v_1)v_1''\). Dividing: \(-v_2''/v_2'=-\varphi''(v_1)v_1'/\varphi'(v_1)-v_1''/v_1'\). The result is a sum, not a product.

q: PS2 Q1(c)(ii) — step 2/2: From \(r_A(z,v_2)=-\frac{\varphi''(v_1)v_1'}{\varphi'(v_1)}+r_A(z,v_1)\), why is \(r_A(z,v_2)\ge r_A(z,v_1)\)?
explain: Concavity gives \(\varphi''\le0\); strict monotonicity gives \(\varphi'>0\); \(v_1'>0\) by assumption. Nothing about the sign of \(v_1''\) is needed: \(v_1\) can be risk-loving.

q: PS2 Q1(c)(iii) — step 1/2: In the chain \(v_2(c(p,v_2))=E_p[\varphi(v_1(z))]\le\varphi(E_p[v_1(z)])=\varphi(v_1(c(p,v_1)))=v_2(c(p,v_1))\), which step uses Jensen's inequality?
explain: The first equality is the definition of the certainty equivalent (and \(v_2=\varphi\circ v_1\)); the third uses \(E_p[v_1]=v_1(c(p,v_1))\); only the inequality uses concavity (Jensen).

q: PS2 Q1(c)(iii) — step 2/2: Having \(v_2(c(p,v_2))\le v_2(c(p,v_1))\), what justifies concluding \(c(p,v_2)\le c(p,v_1)\)?
explain: Undo \(v_2\) on both sides: a strictly increasing function preserves and reflects order. The pattern for certainty-equivalent comparisons: compare the \(v\)-values, then invert.

q: PS2 Q2(a) — step 1/3: To prove '\(\pr\) convex \(\iff\) \(u\) quasiconcave', which pair of definitions do you unfold?
options: Convex: the indifference curves are lines; quasiconcave: \(u''<0\)
Convex: \(a\pr b\Rightarrow\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b\pr b\); quasiconcave: \(u(\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b)\ge\min\{u(a),u(b)\}\)
Convex: \(\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b\succ a\) and \(\succ b\); quasiconcave: \(u(\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b)\ge\alpha u(a)+(1-\alpha)u(b)\)
Convex: \(u\) concave; quasiconcave: \(u\) has convex level sets
explain: These are the Topic 4-1 definitions. \(u(\text{mix})\ge\alpha u(a)+(1-\alpha)u(b)\) is concavity, which is stronger than quasiconcavity. The 'strictly better than both' version is strict convexity-type and not the definition.

q: PS2 Q2(a) — step 2/3: In both directions of 'convex \(\iff\) quasiconcave', which simplifying step makes the definitions line up?
explain: Labelling the bundles so that \(b\) is the worse one turns the min into \(u(b)\) and the hypothesis into \(a\pr b\). Then 'mixture \(\pr b\)' is exactly '\(u(\text{mix})\ge u(b)\)'. Fixing \(\alpha=1/2\) would not prove the statement for all \(\alpha\).

q: PS2 Q2(a) — step 3/3: Since convex preferences are equivalent to quasiconcave utility, a convex preference can only be represented by a concave utility function.
explain: False. Concave \(u\) is sufficient for convex preferences, but not necessary: any increasing transformation of a quasiconcave \(u\) represents the same preference and need not be concave (e.g. \((x_1x_2)^2\)). Confusing concave and quasiconcave is one of the classic mistakes.

q: PS2 Extra 3(b)(i) — step 1/3: Pick-up: 1/10 chance late (cold), independently 1/100 chance the pizza is free; price $10 otherwise. What is the probability of Hot/$0?
explain: Hot (0.9) and free (0.01) are independent: \(0.9\times0.01=0.009\). The full lottery: Hot/$10 0.891, Cold/$10 0.099, Hot/$0 0.009, Cold/$0 0.001. Delivery: Hot/$12 0.98, Cold/$0 0.02.
