q: PS2 Extra 3(b)(iii) — step 2/3: Delivery = Hot/$12 (0.98), Cold/$0 (0.02); pick-up includes Hot/$0 with probability 0.009. Can any ranking consistent with 'hot better, cheaper better' make delivery FOSD pick-up?
options: No: Hot/$0 is the unique best outcome; pick-up gives it with positive probability and delivery never, so just below the top \(F_{\text{pick-up}}=0.991<1=F_{\text{delivery}}\)
Yes, because delivery has the higher probability of hot pizza
explain: Hot/$0 beats every other outcome on both dimensions, so it is the top under any consistent ranking. Delivery cannot match pick-up's mass at the top, so it cannot dominate.

q: PS2 Extra 3(b)(iv) — step 3/3: Ranking Hot/$12 ≺ Cold/$10 ≺ Cold/$0 ≺ Hot/$10 ≺ Hot/$0. Pick-up CDF over this order is \(0,0.099,0.1,0.991,1\). What is the delivery CDF, and what follows?
options: \(0.98,0.98,1,1,1\): pick-up's CDF is everywhere \(\le\), so pick-up FOSD delivery
explain: Delivery puts 0.98 on the worst outcome Hot/$12 and 0.02 on Cold/$0 (third). Cumulating: 0.98, 0.98, 1, 1, 1. Compare: \(0\le0.98\), \(0.099\le0.98\), \(0.1\le1\), \(0.991\le1\), \(1\le1\). Lower CDF = dominates. Always list from worst to best before cumulating.

q: PS2 Extra 3(d)(i): preferences 'farther from the origin is better', \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\). Which property fails, with which witness?
options: None: it is monotone, continuous and convex
explain: \(u(1,0)=u(0,1)=1>\tfrac12=u(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\): the midpoint of two indifferent bundles is worse, so not convex. It is strongly monotone and continuous (continuous utility).

q: PS2 Extra 3(d)(ii): balanced bundles (\(x_1=x_2\)) beat unbalanced ones; among balanced, more is better; among unbalanced, more good 2 is better. Which properties hold?
explain: Not monotone: \((0,0)\succ(1,2)\). Not continuous: \((2,2)\succ(1,1)\) but \((2+\varepsilon,2)\prec(1,1)\). Not convex: \((2,2)\succ(0,4)\) but the midpoint \((1,3)\prec(0,4)\). A utility exists: \(1+x_1\) if balanced, \(x_2/(1+x_2)\) otherwise.

q: PS2 Extra 3(d)(iii): 'first the sum \(x_1+x_2\), then more of good 1'. Which statement is correct?
options: Not monotone, since good 1 is preferred to good 2
Strongly monotone and convex, not continuous, and no utility represents it
Monotone, continuous and convex, represented by \(u=x_1+x_2\)
explain: It is lexicographic: indifference sets are single bundles. Witness for discontinuity: \((2,1)\succ(1,2)\) but \((1,2+\varepsilon)\succ(2,1)\). \(x_1+x_2\) would make \((2,1)\sim(1,2)\), which is wrong.

q: PS2 Extra 3(f)(i): \(u(x_1,x_2)=x_2+g(x_1)\), \(g\) continuous and increasing. How do the indifference sets relate to each other?
options: They all cross at one point
Each is the curve \(x_2=k-g(x_1)\): they are vertical translations of one another
They are radial expansions from the origin
They are horizontal translations of one another
explain: Fixing \(u=k\) gives \(x_2=k-g(x_1)\); changing \(k\) shifts the curve vertically. Equivalently, the MRS depends only on \(x_1\). Indifference curves of a preference relation never cross.

q: PS3 Q1(a) — step 1/3: Demand: all wealth spent and \(p_1x_1/(p_2x_2)=p_2/p_1\). What is \(x_1\)?
explain: Spending \(s_1+s_2=w\), \(s_1/s_2=p_2/p_1\) gives \(s_1=\frac{p_2}{p_1+p_2}w\), so \(x_1=s_1/p_1\). The last option is the spending \(s_1\), not the quantity; \(w/(2p_1)\) is Cobb–Douglas with equal shares.

q: PS3 Q1(a) — step 2/3: To show \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\) rationalizes that demand, why may you use the tangency condition \(MRS=p_1/p_2\)?
options: \(u\) is strictly increasing (budget binds) and \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is strictly concave with infinite slope at 0, so the optimum is interior and unique
Because the demand function is given
Because every utility function has an interior optimum
explain: Tangency is valid only once corners are ruled out: at a corner, moving a little wealth to the good at 0 has infinite marginal utility. Using MRS blindly for substitutes, complements or non-convex utilities is a classic mistake.

q: PS3 Q1(a) — step 3/3: For \(u=\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\), what does \(MRS=p_1/p_2\) give?
explain: \(MRS=\frac{1/(2\sqrt{x_1})}{1/(2\sqrt{x_2})}=\sqrt{x_2/x_1}\). Into the budget: \(p_1x_1+\frac{p_1^2}{p_2}x_1=w\Rightarrow x_1=\frac{p_2w}{p_1(p_1+p_2)}\), matching the given demand.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(i) — step 1/2: \(u=\min\{f,g\}\), \(f=x_1+2x_2\), \(g=2x_1+3x_2-10\), budget \(p_1x_1+2x_2\le w\), \(p_1>0\). Why does an optimal bundle exist?
options: \(u\) is continuous (min of linear functions) and the budget set is compact since all prices are positive
explain: Weierstrass: continuous function on a nonempty compact set. \(u\) is concave but not strictly (it is piecewise linear) and has a kink. That the budget binds is a property of the optimum, not a reason for existence.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(i) — step 2/2: Same \(u=\min\{x_1+2x_2,\,2x_1+3x_2-10\}\). Why must the optimum exhaust the budget?
options: Raising \(x_1\) by \(\delta\) raises \(f\) by \(\delta\) and \(g\) by \(2\delta\), so \(u\) strictly increases; with slack this is affordable
explain: Both pieces rise in each good, so the min rises: \(u\) is strictly increasing, and a bundle with leftover wealth can be improved. Quasiconcavity concerns the shape of upper contour sets, not budget exhaustion.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(ii): \(f=x_1+2x_2\), \(g=2x_1+3x_2-10\). Where are they equal, and which is the minimum at \((2,2)\)?

explain: \(f=x_1+16-p_1x_1\). \(g=2x_1+24-\tfrac32p_1x_1-10=14+(2-\tfrac32p_1)x_1\). The distractors forget the factor 2 or 3 on \(x_2\), or the \(-10\).

q: PS3 Q1(b)(iii) — step 2/3: Along the budget (\(w=16\)), \(f=16+(1-p_1)x_1\), \(g=14+(2-\tfrac32p_1)x_1\). For \(1<p_1<4/3\), where is the optimum?
options: At the crossing \(f=g\): \(f\) is strictly decreasing and \(g\) strictly increasing, so their minimum peaks where they meet
explain: \(1-p_1<0\) and \(2-\tfrac32p_1>0\) (as \(p_1<4/3\)). Left of the crossing the min is the rising \(g\), right of it the falling \(f\). There is no smooth MRS at the kink.
\(x_1+8-\tfrac{p_1}{2}x_1=10\Rightarrow x_1(1-\tfrac{p_1}{2})=2\Rightarrow x_1=\frac{4}{2-p_1}\), and \(x_2=10-x_1\). Forgetting to clear the \(\frac12\) gives \(2/(2-p_1)\).

q: PS3 Q1(b)(iv) — step 1/2: Using \(x_1=4/(2-p_1)\), \(x_2=10-x_1\) (\(w=16\)), what is the optimal bundle at \(p_1=1.3\)?
PS3 Q1(b)(iv) — step 2/2: Raising \(p_1\) from 1.2 to 1.3 (\(w=16\)) moves \(x_1\) from 5 to \(40/7\approx5.71\). What is the economic term?
options: Giffen good: the ordinary law of demand fails
explain: Price up and own demand up is the definition of Giffen behaviour. The problem explicitly asks for the term, so give the word, not just the numbers.
\(p_1x_1+20-2x_1=w\Rightarrow(2-p_1)x_1=20-w\). At \(w=16\) it gives \(4/(2-p_1)\), consistent with (iii). The sign-flipped version would make \(x_1\) negative for \(w<20\).

q: PS3 Q1(b)(v) — step 2/3: For \(x_1=\frac{20-w}{2-p_1}\) and \(x_2=10-x_1\) to be both positive, what is the wealth range?
PS3 Q1(b)(v) — step 3/3: With \(x_1=\frac{20-w}{2-p_1}\) on \(10p_1<w<20\), is good 1 normal or inferior?
explain: More wealth moves the consumer along \(x_1+x_2=10\) toward good 2. Every Giffen good must be inferior; the converse is not true.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(vi) — step 1/2: Start at \(p_1=1.2\), \(w=16\), bundle \((5,5)\). The price rises to \(1.3\) and wealth is adjusted so \((5,5)\) is just affordable (\(p_2=2\)). What is the adjusted wealth?
explain: \(1.3\cdot5+2\cdot5=6.5+10=16.5\). Slutsky compensation: \(w'=p'\cdot x\). 16.1 adds only the price change \(0.1\) instead of \(0.1\times5\).

q: PS3 Q1(b)(vi) — step 2/2: At \(p_1'=1.3\), \(w'=16.5\) (in the range \((13,20)\)), demand is \(x_1=\frac{20-w}{2-p_1}\). What is the new bundle, and does the compensated law of demand hold?
options: \((5,5)\); no, because \(\Delta p\cdot\Delta x=0\) is not negative
explain: \(x_1=3.5/0.7=5\), \(x_2=5\). The compensated law is the weak inequality \((p'-p)\cdot(x'-x)\le0\); equality satisfies it.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(vii) — step 1/2: Uncompensated, \(x_1\) rises \(5\to40/7\); compensated it stays at 5. How is the gap \(5/7\) explained?
options: Wealth effect: uncompensated she has 0.5 less wealth, and good 1 is inferior with \(\partial x_1/\partial w=-1/0.7\), so \(x_1\) rises by \(0.5/0.7=5/7\)
Wealth effect of a normal good
Rounding: the two bundles are essentially equal
Substitution effect: good 1 became relatively cheaper
explain: \(16.5-16=0.5\); \(0.5\times\frac1{0.7}=\frac57=\frac{40}{7}-5\). The substitution effect here is zero (compensated bundle unchanged); the inferior-good wealth effect drives the Giffen behaviour.

q: PS3 Q1(b)(vii) — step 2/2: Why does the Giffen behaviour contradict neither rationality nor WARP?
options: Because WARP implies the ordinary law of demand, which holds here
It does contradict WARP, but not rationality
She maximises a utility function, and WARP only implies the compensated law; directly, \(x'=(40/7,30/7)\) cost \(108/7<16\) at the first budget, while \(x=(5,5)\) costs \(16.5>16\) at the second
Because both bundles cost exactly 16 at both price vectors
explain: \(1.2\cdot\frac{40}{7}+2\cdot\frac{30}{7}=\frac{108}{7}\approx15.43\): \(x\) is revealed preferred to \(x'\); the reverse never happens since \(x\) is unaffordable at \((1.3,16)\). Claiming WARP implies the ordinary law of demand is a classic mistake.

q: PS3 Q2(a)(i) — step 1/3: In a jungle where preferences over houses need not be strict, why can't serial dictatorship be applied directly?
options: Because an equilibrium may not exist with ties
'Take your best remaining house' need not single out one house, so the procedure does not define one allocation
Because the power relation is no longer transitive
Because there may be more houses than individuals
explain: With indifference, the best house may not be unique. Fix: order \(i_1\rhd\cdots\rhd i_n\) and let each take ANY weakly best remaining house, breaking ties arbitrarily. Power is unchanged here; ties are in tastes.

q: PS3 Q2(a)(ii) — step 2/3: Jungle with indifference. Equilibrium: no \(i\rhd j\) with \(a(j)\succ_i a(i)\) (strict). Why is the modified serial-dictatorship allocation an equilibrium?
options: Because every individual gets his favourite house
If \(i_k\rhd i_l\) then \(k<l\), so \(a(i_l)\) was available when \(i_k\) chose a weakly best house; hence \(a(i_l)\succ_{i_k}a(i_k)\) is impossible
Because the allocation is Pareto stable
explain: The stronger one had the weaker one's house in his choice set and picked something at least as good. Not everyone gets his overall favourite; Pareto stability does not imply equilibrium.

q: PS3 Q2(a)(ii) — step 3/3: Which example shows that, with indifference, the jungle equilibrium need not be unique?
options: \(N=\{1,2\}\), \(H=\{A,B\}\), \(1\rhd2\), individual 1 indifferent between A and B: both \((A,B)\) and \((B,A)\) are equilibria
Uniqueness still holds, as in Prop 5-1-2
explain: Only the stronger individual 1 could move, and he is indifferent. If both strictly prefer A, 1 would take A from 2 in \((B,A)\). If only 2 is indifferent and 1 strictly prefers one house, 1 gets it in every equilibrium. Uniqueness needs strict preferences.

q: PS3 Q3(a) — step 1/3: Type A: \(u_A=x_2\), \(e_A=(\alpha,0)\); type B: \(u_B=x_1\), \(e_B=(0,\beta)\). Why must equilibrium prices be strictly positive?
options: If a price is 0, the type that wants that good demands an unbounded amount, so no optimal bundle exists
They need not be: \(p=(1,0)\) is an equilibrium
explain: With \(p_2=0\), type A can buy unlimited good 2 and has no optimum; symmetric for \(p_1=0\) and type B. Letting a price be zero with monotone preferences is a classic CE mistake.

q: PS3 Q3(a) — step 2/3: Type A (\(u_A=x_2\), \(e_A=(\alpha,0)\)), type B (\(u_B=x_1\), \(e_B=(0,\beta)\)), \(p\gg0\). What are the demands?
explain: A's wealth is \(p\cdot e_A=p_1\alpha\), all spent on good 2. B's wealth is \(p_2\beta\), all spent on good 1. Wealth moves with prices: forgetting it gives the last option.

q: PS3 Q3(a) — step 3/3: Same economy with \(n^A=2\), \(n^B=3\), \(\alpha=3\), \(\beta=1\). Clearing good 1 (\(n^Bp_2\beta/p_1=n^A\alpha\)), what are the CE?
options: \(p=(1,2)\) only; each A gets \((0,\tfrac32)\), each B gets \((2,0)\)
\(p_2/p_1=2\) (any \(p=\lambda(1,2)\), \(\lambda>0\)); each A gets \((0,\tfrac32)\), each B gets \((2,0)\)
\(p_2/p_1=\tfrac12\); each A gets \((0,3)\), each B gets \((1,0)\)
explain: \(p_2/p_1=\frac{n^A\alpha}{n^B\beta}=\frac{6}{3}=2\), i.e. \(p=\lambda(n^B\beta,n^A\alpha)=\lambda(3,6)\propto(1,2)\). Each A: \(p_1\alpha/p_2=3/2\); each B: \(p_2\beta/p_1=2\). Check: total good 2 demanded \(2\cdot\tfrac32=3=n^B\beta\). Report the price ray, not one vector.

q: PS3 Q3(b) — step 1/5: \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) (not convex), wealth \(W\), \(p\gg0\). What is demand?
options: All wealth on the more expensive good
All wealth on the cheaper good, a corner \((W/p_1,0)\) or \((0,W/p_2)\); both corners if \(p_1=p_2\)
explain: A convex function on the budget triangle is maximised at a vertex; compare \(W^2/p_1^2\) with \(W^2/p_2^2\). The tangency point is a utility MINIMUM on the budget line here, the classic MRS trap.

q: PS3 Q3(b)(ii) — step 2/5: Two individuals with \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\), positive total supply of both goods. Why must CE prices be equal?
options: If \(p_1<p_2\) everyone buys only good 1, so good 2 has zero demand but positive supply (and symmetrically)
By symmetry of the utility function
explain: Unequal prices send all demand to one good. Symmetry of \(u\) is suggestive but not a proof; the endowments are general here.

q: PS3 Q3(b)(i) — step 3/5: \(u=x_1^2+x_2^2\) for both, \(e(1)=(\alpha,0)\), \(e(2)=(0,\beta)\). Which is a CE?
options: No CE exists because preferences are not convex
\(p=(1,1)\) with each consuming his endowment: 1 takes \((\alpha,0)\), 2 takes \((0,\beta)\)
\(p=(1,1)\) with 1 taking \((0,\alpha)\) and 2 taking \((\beta,0)\), for any \(\alpha,\beta\)
explain: At equal prices both corners are optimal, and the endowment allocation is a corner for each person, hence optimal and feasible. The swapped allocation is feasible only if \(\alpha=\beta\). Non-convexity does not rule out existence.

options: Each has wealth 3 and buys \((3,0)\) or \((0,3)\); total demand is \((6,0)\), \((3,3)\) or \((0,6)\), never the supply \((4,2)\)
Each buys \((2,1)\), but then good 1 is in excess supply
explain: By step 2 prices must be equal. Wealth is \(2+1=3\). Supply \((4,2)\) is not among the possible totals. The deeper reason: demand jumps between corners, so it is not continuous and the IVT existence argument fails.

options: A CE exists: 1 buys \((3,0)\) and 2 buys \((0,4)\)
A CE exists: at \(p=(1,1)\), 1 buys \((0,3)\) and 2 buys \((4,0)\)
explain: \(e_1(2)=3\ne2=e_2(1)\), but \(e_1(1)=1=e_2(2)\). Wealths \(s_1=3\), \(s_2=4\); supply is \((4,3)\). 1 on good 2 and 2 on good 1 gives total \((4,3)\) ✓. The other assignment gives \((3,4)\) ✗. Prices must be equal.

q: PS3 Extra 4(b)(iv): jungle with ties in power (only a strictly stronger individual can displace). Which shows that an equilibrium need not be Pareto stable?
options: 1 and 2 equally powerful; 1 prefers A, 2 prefers B; allocation \((B,A)\) is an equilibrium but \((A,B)\) makes both better off
1 and 2 equally powerful, both prefer A: \((A,B)\) and \((B,A)\)
explain: With equal power nobody can evict anyone, so the bad allocation survives. The same-tastes example shows non-uniqueness, not Pareto failure. With \(1\rhd2\) strictly, 1 would take A. Prop 5-1-3 covers the serial-dictatorship outcome, which is still Pareto stable.

q: PS3 Extra 4(e): demand \(x(p,w)=\frac{w}{p_1^2+p_2^2}p\). With \((p,w)=((1,1),2)\) and \((p',w')=((2,1),3)\), why is WARP violated?
options: \(x\) is not on the budget line
explain: Each bundle was affordable when the other was chosen and they differ: a WARP violation, so no preference (monotone or not) rationalizes it. One-way affordability alone is not a violation.

q: PS3 Extra 4(h): \(p^1=(2,1,2)\), \(w=8\), chosen \(x^1=(1,2,2)\). Which other bundle was affordable at \(p^1\), and is hence revealed worse than \(x^1\)?
explain: \(p^1\cdot x^3=4+2+2=8\le8\); \(p^1\cdot x^2=4+1+4=9>8\). Similarly \(x^2\to x^1\) and \(x^3\to x^2\). Each pair passes WARP, yet \(x^1\to x^3\to x^2\to x^1\) is a cycle: with three goods, pairwise WARP does not guarantee transitivity.

q: Exam playbook: to prove that a relation is transitive, it is enough to verify it on a well-chosen numerical example.
explain: False. An example only disproves a 'for all' statement. Transitivity is proved with arbitrary \(x,y,z\). A single counterexample settles 'not transitive'.

q: Exam playbook: what must a valid counterexample to 'every \(R\) with property P has property Q' show?
options: One \(R\) that has Q but not P
That most relations with P fail Q
One \(R\) that fails both P and Q
One specific \(R\) that satisfies P and fails Q, with both checked
explain: A counterexample must satisfy the hypotheses and break the conclusion. An object failing P says nothing about the implication. Example: the empty relation (symmetric, transitive, not reflexive).

q: Exam playbook: if there are no prizes with \([a]\succ[b]\succ[c]\), the continuity axiom holds vacuously.
explain: True. Continuity is a 'for all strictly ranked triples' statement; with no such triple there is nothing to check. Forgetting vacuous truth is a classic mistake (cf. the empty relation in PS1 a(iii)).

q: Exam playbook: what is the lottery \(0.5\cdot\$100\oplus0.5\cdot\$1\)?
explain: \(\oplus\) mixes probabilities, it does not add prizes. Its expected value is 50.5, but the lottery itself is risky; a risk-averse person strictly prefers $50.50 for sure.

q: Exam playbook: how should you structure a 'Show that … / Is there …?' answer?
options: Start with numerical examples, then generalise
Verdict first, unpack the definitions, chain steps naming each property used, verify examples fully, close with the meaning
Write the conclusion only, since the grader knows the proof
explain: The how-to guide: verdict, then definitions, then a chain of named steps, check every property of an example or counterexample, and finish in words (e.g. 'the axiom that fails is continuity').

q: Exam playbook: you find a CE \((p,a)\) with \(p=(1,2)\). How should you report it?
options: Prices must sum to 1, so \(p=(1/3,2/3)\) is the only CE
As a ray: \((\lambda p,a)\) is a CE for every \(\lambda>0\) (or say 'normalise \(p_1=1\)')
explain: Budgets and demands are homogeneous of degree zero in prices, so scaling all prices changes nothing. Reporting one vector as 'the' CE is a listed mistake.

q: Exam playbook: WARP implies the ordinary (uncompensated) law of demand.
explain: False. WARP is equivalent to the compensated law of demand only (Prop 4-2-2). PS3 1b is a Giffen example consistent with WARP.

q: Errors in the material: Topic 4-3, slide 43 gives the Cobb–Douglas expenditure function \(e(p,u)\) for \(u=x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\). What is the correct constant multiplying \(p_1^\alpha p_2^{1-\alpha}u\)?
explain: \(e=u\,p_1^\alpha p_2^{1-\alpha}/[\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}]=\alpha^{-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{\alpha-1}p_1^\alpha p_2^{1-\alpha}u\). The slide has \(\alpha^{\alpha}\) instead of \(\alpha^{-\alpha}\). Check: \(\alpha=\tfrac12\), \(u=\sqrt{x_1x_2}\), \(p=(1,1)\): \(e=2u\).

q: Errors in the material: Topic 3-3, slide 9 says '\(\pi\) is the probability of each act'. What should it say?
options: \(\pi\) is the probability of each consequence
\(\pi\) is the probability of each state
\(\pi\) is the probability of each lottery
explain: In subjective expected utility, beliefs \(\pi\) are over states; acts map states to consequences and carry no probability themselves.

q: Errors in the material: Topic 5-1 writes society and jungle with \((\succeq_i)\). Why does the correct version use strict preferences \(\succ_i\)?
options: Weak preferences would make the equilibrium fail to exist
Strict preferences are what make the jungle equilibrium unique; with indifference uniqueness fails (PS3 2a)
Because power relations are weak orders
explain: With ties, serial dictatorship with arbitrary tie-breaking still gives an equilibrium, but two allocations can be equilibria. Existence survives; uniqueness does not.

q: Errors in the material: a sketch in the notes draws a risk-loving Bernoulli function as decreasing. What is correct?
explain: More money is still better (increasing); risk-loving means \(EU\ge v(E[p])\), i.e. convex. Increasing and concave is risk-averse.

q: Errors in the material: Topic 4-1, slide 35 says the proof that convex preferences correspond to quasiconcave utility is in Problem Set 3; it is actually PS2 Q2(a).
explain: True (study guide 'Errors' table). The same slide also writes 'for any \(x,y\in\R^2\)' where it should say 'for any \(a,b\)'.
